A 71-year-old female patient with normal pressure hydrocephalus status presented with recurrent and prolonged abdominal discomfort and a history of multiple surgeries. She was admitted due to cellulitis and an abscess around the VP shunt catheter. Her hardware was removed completely, and she underwent an endoscopic third ventriculostomy. Abdominal wound catheter site culture grew Mycobacterium fortuitum. The patient was treated with imipenem and doxycycline, then switched to oral azithromycin and doxycycline, and later doxycycline was changed to oral sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim with azithromycin. At approximately six months, she discontinued antibiotics due to nausea and intolerance and continued to do well without any sign of infection.

Patient no. 2: VP shunt infection with Mycobacterium fortuitum

Patient no. 1: Transitioned to comfort care and passed away

N/A

N/A

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 55-year-old woman from Morocco living in Belgium for almost two decades.
Diagnosis: Tubulo-Interstitial Nephritis with Uveitis (TINU) Syndrome.

Hospital Course:

The patient was referred to the internal medicine consultation for evaluation of bilateral anterior uveitis, which was diagnosed as TINU Syndrome. The patient's initial presentation was with sudden onset painful red eyes and photophobia. She was treated with intravitreal injection of celestone and started on degressive topical corticosteroid therapy in association with a cycloplegic agent.

Laboratory tests were conducted and revealed hemoglobin level, creatinine level, GFR level and serum potassium levels. White blood cells count and serum lysozyme, angiotensin convertase and HLA-B27 haplotype were tested and found to be negative. The patient was tested for infectious serologies for syphilis, toxoplasmosis, HBV, HCV and HIV, and tuberculin skin test but all were found to be negative. No auto-immune markers were detected such as ANCA, antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor.

The patient was diagnosed with renal Fanconi syndrome as a result of laboratory tests. She had glycosuria, proteinuria with mild albuminuria, and elevated urine Beta-2 microglobulin. She underwent renal biopsy revealing nephritis characterized by severe diffuse interstitial inflammatory infiltrates. Foci of acute tubular necrosis and tubulitis were also found.

The patient was started on oral degressive-corticosteroid therapy, which improved renal outcomes. Her leucocyturia persisted, but her creatinine level, GFR level and uric acid normalized after the medication.

Summary:

The patient, a 55-year-old woman from Morocco living in Belgium for almost two decades, was treated for Tubulo-Interstitial Nephritis with Uveitis (TINU) Syndrome. Upon initial presentation with painful, red eyes and photophobia, the patient underwent laboratory tests revealing indications of Fanconi syndrome. Following a renal biopsy, it was found that the patient had nephritis characterized by severe diffuse interstitial inflammatory infiltrates, acute tubular necrosis and tubulitis. Oral degressive-corticosteroid therapy was initiated, resulting in a favorable renal outcome. The patient was discharged with persistent leucocyturia.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 12-year-old Hispanic female

Chief complaint: excess weight gain

Hospital Course:

The patient presented with excess weight gain over the past 12 months. After evaluation, it was identified that the patient had a sedentary lifestyle and frequently ate due to emotional distress or boredom. The patient did not want to consume breakfast which created conflict with her parents. A Time-Restricted Eating (TLE) approach was implemented, consisting of eating between 11 AM-7 PM, 3 days per week, and adhering to an age-appropriate healthy diet for the remaining 4 days. The patient reported satisfaction with the intervention and found it easy to adhere to, resulting in a decrease in zBMI by 0.32 SD over 4 months.

Course in Hospital:

The patient was seen for a 1-month follow-up visit and reported a decrease in zBMI by -0.2 SD. The patient shared that the TLE approach was feasible and easy to adhere to. The patient did not feel deprived and found it more like a lifestyle change than a traditional diet.

Outcome and Plan:

The patient's zBMI decreased, and the family reported the intervention was successful. The patient's parent-teen relationship also improved. The family was advised to continue the TLE approach and adhering to an age-appropriate healthy diet. The patient was advised to maintain a healthy lifestyle and follow-up with primary care as needed.

The patient was stable at the time of discharge, with serum calcium levels of 9.5 mg/dL and ionized calcium levels of 4.9 mg/dL.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A
Date of Admission: N/A
Date of Discharge: N/A

Hospital Course:

A 54-year-old gentleman with a 7-year history of right neck swelling was admitted. The swelling had increased in size without compressive or infiltrative symptoms, causing discomfort exerted by the weight of the mass, accentuated by gravity in the erect position. He denied malignancy in the family or exposure to radiation. Clinical examination was unremarkable except for the 10 × 10 cm swelling in the right anterior triangle of the neck, extending from the submandibular region to the level of the cricoid cartilage, which was smooth in consistency, non-tender, and lobulated.

His biochemical thyroid function was normal, and ultrasonography revealed an ill-defined, homogenous, hyperechoic mass arising from the right submandibular space. MRI showed an atypical lipomatous tumor with a deep extension into the right parapharyngeal space, and FNAC results were inconclusive.

Due to the risk of tumor seeding along the biopsy tract and its encapsulated nature, a decision was made to proceed with surgical excision without further attempts to obtain a preoperative biopsy. A multidisciplinary team discussion was undertaken to determine the possible approaches to excise this lesion.

The patient underwent excision of the lesion with the otorhinolaryngology team on standby for radical surgery if findings suggested malignancy. Intraoperatively, a single, lobulated, lipomatous tumor measuring 10 × 12 cm in size with multiple engorged vessels on the surface was located at the right parapharyngeal fossa. It was well-encapsulated with minimal adhesions to surrounding structures except at the superior part. The right submandibular gland was excised en-bloc as it was most likely the origin of the tumor. No enlarged loco-regional lymph nodes were found to suggest malignancy. A small calibre vacuum drain was placed at the submandibular fossa to prevent sialocoele for a day before removal.

Histopathological examination revealed a benign adipocytic tumor of sialolipoma variant. It measured 9.5 × 12.5 × 8.5 cm with multiple congested blood vessels of varying sizes and nodules composed of benign salivary gland ducts and acini with foci of squamous metaplasia. No fibrin thrombi or atypical stromal cells or lipoblasts were seen. An unremarkable salivary gland tissue was identified.

The patient had an uneventful recovery and was discharged home on day 2 with no complications upon follow up. During follow up at 1 month postoperatively, he was well without any evidence of complications or recurrence.

Diagnosis:

Benign adipocytic tumor of sialolipoma variant.

Procedures Performed:

Excision of the right parapharyngeal fossa tumor with an en-bloc excision of the right submandibular gland at the same time.

Condition at Discharge:

The patient was discharged home on day 2 without any complications and with an unremarkable physical examination. Follow-up was scheduled for 1 month postoperatively to monitor for any recurrence or complications.

Discharge Medications:

N/A

Follow-up:

Follow up at 1 month postoperatively to monitor for any recurrence or complications.

[Hospital Course]
The patient was admitted to the Emergency Department (ED) from a nursing home after presenting with feculent emesis and fecal effluent from his gastrostomy tube. Two months prior to admission, he had a cardiac arrest at another hospital which resulted in anoxic brain injury. He required percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube insertion with tracheostomy prior to discharge to the nursing home. His other medical history included diabetes mellitus, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and right lower extremity deep vein thrombosis.

On physical examination, the patient was nonverbal and ventilator dependent through the tracheostomy tube with feculent material noted on PEG tube aspiration. Laboratory investigations revealed hemoglobin of 9.1 g/dL, leukocyte count of 8.9 K cells/µL with neutrophil predominance, and platelet count of 619 K cells/µL. A computed tomography (CT) scan with oral contrast showed a PEG tube in the transverse colon, and an upper endoscopy revealed feculent material in the stomach with evidence of a fistulous opening suspected to be in communication with the colon. The diameter was determined to be less than 10 mm and was repaired with an over-the-scope clip (OTSC). A colonoscope revealed an internal bumper of the PEG tube located in the transverse colon, which was cut externally at skin level and retrieved with a Roth net. The colocutaneous fistula that could not be repaired with an OTSC was subsequently repaired with through the scope clips using a pediatric colonoscope. The success of the procedures was ascertained by adequate insufflation of the stomach and colon without air leak. Enteral feeding was resumed after 48 hours using a nasogastric tube access.

The patient received treatment with antibiotics for a few days and had an unremarkable hospital course. Ten days after the repair of the fistulas, he had another PEG tube placed before being discharged back to the nursing home.

[Final Diagnosis]
- Colocutaneous fistula
- Gastrostomy Tube in the Transverse Colon

[Condition on Discharge]
The patient's condition improved significantly following treatment and was discharged with stable vital signs and no complications.

[Follow-Up Recommendations]
The patient was advised to follow up with his healthcare provider at the nursing home for further evaluation and management of his medical comorbidities, wound care, and enteral nutrition.

None specified.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient was admitted to our glaucoma clinic at Hospital de Santa Maria with visual field deterioration in his right eye. He was diagnosed with bilateral open-angle glaucoma secondary to pseudoexfoliation and was receiving maximum medical treatment for the same. Due to patient concerns regarding trabeculectomy, we proposed an implant of an ab-internal XEN collagen device under peribulbar anesthesia. The procedure was successful.

However, after three months of follow-up, the patient presented with high IOP and a thickened, non-diffuse bleb. The patient was started on timolol bid, but it did not show any clinical improvement. We proceeded with a surgical revision under topical anesthesia, which assisted with vital dye.

During the procedure, the needle was inserted into the subconjunctival space and advanced slowly until it encounters the space near the XEN distal outflow. A volume of MMC was injected posteriorly near the intended site of revision. The anterior chamber was washed out with a balanced salt solution, and the paracentesis incisions were closed by stromal hydration. The postoperative care included starting the patient on topical prednisolone and antibiotic for 4 weeks.

The patient was monitored during the postoperative period, and the target IOP was achieved under no topical treatment. There were no complications, and the patient was discharged with necessary instructions for follow-up.

Conditions:

Bilateral open-angle glaucoma secondary to pseudoexfoliation.

Procedures:

Implant of an ab-internal XEN collagen device, surgical revision.

Medications:

Topical prednisolone and antibiotic four times daily for 4 weeks.

Follow-up:

The patient was discharged with necessary instructions for follow-up.

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Age: 72 years
Date of admission: [Redacted]
Date of discharge: [Redacted]
Primary diagnosis: Carbon monoxide and methanol toxicity

Hospital Course:
At the time of admission, the patient was found obtunded and cyanotic with agonal breathing, and had a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, renal cell carcinoma, and depression. The patient had a bottle of paint stripper of methylene chloride concentration at the scene, which was found to have caused the toxicity. On admission, intranasal naloxone was administered, but there was no response. The patient was mechanically ventilated and received two grams intravenous calcium gluconate, 10 units regular insulin, 25 grams dextrose, IV sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 200mEq, and nebulized albuterol to address her hyperkalemia. Additional laboratory data revealed a serum methanol concentration of 168 mg/dL. The patient was started on hemodialysis and received 15 mg/kg fomepizole intravenously.

Lab Studies and Findings:
Laboratory values at admission were significant for venous pH of 7.06, anion gap 16, white blood cell count 15,000 cells/mm3, potassium 7.0 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L, and lipase 1,899 units/L. Salicylates and acetaminophen were undetectable. The material safety data sheet (MSDS) of the paint stripper revealed that the product contained 60–100% concentration of methylene chloride and 7–13% concentration of methanol. The initial serum carboxyhemoglobin (CO-Hgb) was 8.2%. 

Treatment and Management:
The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) and started on hemodialysis to address the methanol toxicity. The ventilator settings were adjusted to a FiO2 of 100% to increase dissociation of carboxyhemoglobin. The patient also received nebulized albuterol, and two grams intravenous calcium gluconate, 10 units regular insulin, and 25 grams dextrose to address hyperkalemia. Fomepizole was administered intravenously as an antidote. 

Follow-up Care:
The patient underwent a successful hemodialysis and remained in the ICU for several days until stable, and was then discharged to a rehabilitation facility. The patient's renal function and electrolyte balance were monitored closely following discharge.

Outcome:
The patient responded well to treatment and underwent a successful hemodialysis. The patient was discharged to a rehabilitation facility for further care and monitoring.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 18-year-old Japanese woman

Reason for admission: Abdominal pain and vomiting

Hospital course:
The patient was admitted to our institution due to sudden onset of abdominal pain and vomiting. Upon examination, she had tenderness in the upper umbilical region but showed no signs of peritoneal irritation. Blood test results revealed elevated D-dimer levels, and an abdominal contrast-enhanced CT scan identified emphysema of the small intestine wall with poor contrast enhancement. Despite the suspicion of renal infarction, necrosis of the small intestine was discovered during laparotomy. Surgical intervention was urgently performed to resect the necrotized regions and reconstruct the small intestine. Post-operatively, a thrombotic lesion was suspected and anticoagulant therapy was initiated. However, pathological findings revealed active vasculitis associated with fibrinoid necrosis, as well as destruction, fibrogenesis, and luminal stenosis of the elastic lamina in the muscular arteries. We diagnosed the patient as having PAN-induced necrosis of the small intestine. After discontinuing anticoagulant therapy, we started the patient on 40 mg of prednisolone daily on postoperative day 11. Since she continued to improve, the dose of prednisolone was gradually reduced. It has been a year since the surgery, and she is currently receiving prednisolone at 5 mg a day without recurrence.

Clinical course and treatment:
Anticoagulant therapy with heparin sodium at 20,000 U/day was started immediately after surgery, though it was later discontinued and replaced with a dose of 40 mg of prednisolone daily on postoperative day 11. A postoperative angiograph of the patient's renal arteries demonstrated multiple aneurysms in the renal arterioles, however, the patient showed improvement with the administration of prednisolone. She is currently receiving prednisolone at 5 mg a day without recurrence.

Hospital course:
The patient underwent immediate surgical intervention to resect the necrotized regions and reconstruct the small intestine. Anticoagulant therapy was started immediately after surgery, but was later discontinued and replaced with prednisolone. The patient showed improvement with the administration of prednisolone, and currently receives the medication at 5 mg a day.

Diagnosis:
PAN-induced necrosis of the small intestine associated with active vasculitis, fibrinoid necrosis, destruction, fibrogenesis, and luminal stenosis of the elastic lamina in the muscular arteries.

follow-up conditions:
The patient's blood test was negative for proteinase 3-antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) and hepatitis B surface antigen, but weakly positive for myeloperoxidase (MPO)-ANCA (5.3 U/mL; normal range, 0.0–3.4 U/mL). Postoperative urine analysis was positive for proteinuria. The patient continues to receive prednisolone at 5 mg a day without recurrence.

Key findings:
- Sudden onset of abdominal pain and vomiting
- Elevated D-dimer levels
- Emphysema of the small intestine wall with poor contrast enhancement on CT scan
- Necrosis of the small intestine discovered during laparotomy
- Presence of multiple aneurysms in the renal arterioles on postoperative angiograph
- Negative proteinase 3-antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) and hepatitis B surface antigen blood results
- Weakly positive myeloperoxidase (MPO)-ANCA (5.3 U/mL; normal range, 0.0–3.4 U/mL) blood result
- Positive postoperative urine analysis for proteinuria.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 2-year-old girl, was admitted with a 1-month history of fatigue and irritability. Initial labs revealed pancytopenia and a bone marrow biopsy with hypercellularity and dysplastic cells. Flow cytometry showed no immuno-phenotypic abnormalities and FISH testing revealed T21 and tetrasomy 21. Immunostaining for CD61 revealed immature cells demonstrating histologic megakaryocytic differentiation, resulting in a diagnosis of Acute Megakaryoblastic Leukemia (AMKL). 
The patient was treated with SJCRH AML16 protocol, and by the end of induction, there was no evidence of malignant cells by morphology; however, T21 was still present in 11% of cells. A skin biopsy/fibroblast culture for FISH screening was performed, which confirmed a diagnosis of mosaic T21. The patient's therapy was changed to reduced-intensity chemotherapy for DS-AML according to COG protocol AAML1531. 
The patient tolerated therapy well, with two episodes of grade 3 bacteremia and no other complications. Following 11 months off therapy, the patient is currently doing well without evidence of treatment-related toxicity or relapse. 
Summary:
2-year-old female admitted with AMKL; diagnosed with T21 and mosaic T21. Treated with SJCRH AML16 protocol, with transition to reduced-intensity chemotherapy for DS-AML AAML1531 protocol. Tolerated therapy well, with good prognosis post-treatment.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Gender: Male
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course: 

The patient, a 65-year-old Indian male, presented to the dermatology clinic for palmoplantar keratoderma. The patient had a past medical history of undifferentiated arthritis. Physical examination revealed thick, yellow, callous-like sheets of hyperkeratotic skin on the palms and soles, and pink plaques with silvery scale on the extensor elbows. Based on examination findings, a diagnosis of plaque psoriasis was made. 

The treatment modality was determined to be acitretin 25 mg daily combined with hand-foot narrow band UVB phototherapy. The patient was advised to limit alcohol consumption while taking acitretin. Approximately two months after starting acitretin, sandpaper-like changes were noted at the proximal 1-2 mm of the nail plate of all 20 nails. These changes continued to affect the nails, and acitretin was discontinued five months after starting due to nail discomfort experienced by the patient. The patient resumed alcohol intake at that time.

About seven months after discontinuing acitretin, the patient's nails continued to worsen, with the involvement of the proximal and distal nail plates by coarse fissuring and roughness. Over the subsequent seven months, the nails experienced significant improvement. By 19 months after acitretin was discontinued, significant improvement was observed. At about 21 months after stopping acitretin, the nails were back to baseline. The toenails followed a similar course and improved significantly but incompletely at 21 months after discontinuation.

Summary of Findings: 

The patient was diagnosed with plaque psoriasis and received acitretin 25 mg daily combined with hand-foot narrow band UVB phototherapy. Coarse sandpaper-like changes at the proximal 1-2 mm of the nail plate of all 20 nails were observed about two months after starting acitretin, and this affected the nails. After discontinuing acitretin, the nails worsened for seven months before gradually improving over a period of approximately 14 months to the baseline.

Disposition: 

The patient has been discharged. Follow-up visits and further treatment plans were not discussed. We hope for the patient's continued improvement.

Hemodialysis was required for approximately one week. The patient was weaned off dialysis. The patient was diagnosed with thrombotic microangiopathy like aHUS.

DISCHARGE CONDITION:
The patient was discharged in stable condition.

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient is currently undergoing genetic testing at the University of Iowa laboratory to look for autoantibodies and genetic mutations.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Name]
Medical Record Number: [MRN]
Date of Admission: [Date of Admission]
Date of Discharge: [Date of Discharge]

Hospital Course Summary:

This 20-year-old female patient was admitted to [Hospital Name] due to odynophagia, unmeasured fever, and generalized myalgia. Upon examination, the patient presented with petechiae on her face, upper and lower limbs, purulent tonsils, cyanosis of the extremities, and purpuric plaques. The patient was anuric and required dialysis on admission.

The patient's laboratory tests revealed anemia, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, impaired renal function, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and elevated LDH. Blood cultures were collected, and antibiotic therapy was started due to possible diagnoses of meningococcemia and staphylococci. Despite antibiotics, the patient's clinical condition continued to worsen with hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea, and purpuric lesions becoming bullous. Schistocytes and elevated serum LDH levels indicated a possible diagnosis of TMA. There were no neurological alterations, ruling out thrombotic TTP. Thus, aHUS was suspected, and a thorough investigation of the possible causes of TMA was initiated. All blood cultures and rheumatologic tests were negative.

The patient's serology was negative, except for an IgM positive for dengue collected on the sixth, twelve, and twenty-eighth days of the medical history. The result for arboviruses was negative as well, but it was collected on the sixth day of the onset of the disease, and ideally, the arbovirus survey sample is collected on the first day of symptoms and is acceptable up to the fifth day of the disease.

The patient received supportive treatment, performing daily hemodialysis due to anuria and frequent need for transfusion of red blood cells due to anemia. The patient's illness progressed, and they needed frequent debridement of the necrotic areas in lower limbs, which were performed by the plastic surgery team of the burn treatment center of the service. Plasmapheresis was chosen as an alternative measure since there was an association with TMA, and initially, aHUS was one of the diagnostic hypotheses. Around the 40th day of hospitalization, the patient began to show a significant diuresis, and the necrotic areas in the legs stabilized. Hemodialysis was suspended, and the plastic surgery team started skin grafting with good response. The patient was discharged after 68 days of hospitalization.

Diagnoses:

- Thrombotic Microangiopathy
- Idiopathic Purpura Fulminans
- Acute Kidney Injury

Discharge Instructions:

Upon discharge, the patient was advised to follow-up with their primary care provider for continuity of care and further treatment. They were instructed to maintain a healthy diet, get adequate rest and exercise, and monitor their symptoms carefully. Additionally, the patient was informed about the importance of keeping the follow-up appointments, taking medications as directed, and reporting any abnormalities or concerns promptly. The patient was counseled about the importance of maintaining good hygiene practices, especially in wound care. Finally, the patient was instructed to contact their healthcare provider if any new symptoms or complications arise.

Admitting Diagnosis: Blurred vision
Secondary Diagnosis: Ethambutol toxicity

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 30-year-old female who presented with the complaint of blurred vision that started a month prior to admission. The patient had undergone routine laparoscopic myomectomy eight months earlier and following the procedure, she experienced abdominal pain and subcutaneous edema. An ultrasound and MRI revealed fluid collections along the subcutaneous and muscular plane with adjacent subcutaneous edema. A necrotizing granulomatous inflammation of likely mycobacterial origin of the tissue sample obtained from fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was detected, and the patient was started on an antituberculous regimen.

After being on the antituberculous regimen for five months, the patient started experiencing blurring and haziness in both eyes, hence discontinued ethambutol as a precautionary measure. On examination, the patient’s visual acuity was found to be 6/12(R) and 6/12(L). Her anterior segments and fundi were normal appearing as were her pupillary reactions. Baseline perimetry showed central bitemporal hemianopia that respected the vertical midline, consistent with ethambutol toxicity.

Ethambutol treatment was discontinued, and the patient was advised to undergo a regular follow-up with her primary physician. At the last follow-up visit, the patient was visually asymptomatic and had normal visual acuities bilaterally. The patient declined further field testing.

Discharge Condition:
The patient’s visual acuities were found to be back to normal, and she was discharged in stable condition.

Discharge Medications:
No medications prescribed at discharge.

Disposition and Follow-Up:
The patient was advised to undergo a regular follow-up with her primary physician.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital after experiencing a cardiac arrest due to an overdose of cocaine, benzodiazepines and cannabinoids. He was treated with therapeutic hypothermia and ventilator support. Antibiotics and vasopressors were initiated for septic shock. His condition deteriorated and he continued to experience encephalopathy without seizure activity as observed on electroencephalogram. He had repeated episodes of decerebrate posturing, rhythmic jaw movements, sweating, fever, and tachycardia. He required tracheostomy and gastrostomy tube placement. After initial antibiotic treatment, his sputum cultures grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa which resolved with a course of gentamicin nebulizers. 

Diagnostic Workup:
Infectious disease was consulted for repeated fevers. He had negative blood cultures, sputum cultures, and urine Legionella antigen. His urinalysis was negative for infection. Thyroid function tests did not show hyperthyroidism, and ultrasound of the abdomen was negative for acalculous cholecystitis. Hepatitis B and hepatitis C serologies, interferon-gamma release assay, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) were negative. Tagged white blood cell scan showed uptake in the region of cecum and ascending colon but colonoscopy did not show any evidence of inflammatory bowel disease or colitis.

Diagnosis:
Despite extensive workup, no clear etiology was identified for the patient's repeated episodes of decerebrate posturing, rhythmic jaw movements, sweating, fever, and tachycardia. However, based on his symptoms and clinical presentation, the patient was diagnosed with PSH.

Treatment:
The patient was initially treated with bromocriptine and propranolol for PSH, but his response was poor. Clonidine and diazepam were added to his regimen which eventually helped with his symptoms.

Discharge:
The patient was discharged to an LTC facility after a prolonged hospital course. He has improved slightly and is able to communicate with his family, but remains bed bound.

Clinical Course:
The patient, a 45-year-old woman, was referred to our hospital to evaluate exercise testing results that suggested myocardial ischemia. She underwent a CTCA to rule out coronary artery disease (CAD), which was performed without incident. The examination showed the absence of any artery arising from the right sinus of Valsalva. The left anterior descending artery (LAD) and the left circumflex artery (LCX) presented a regular origin and course with no evidence of CAD (Calcium score = 0). LCX provided a wide obtuse marginal branch, a filiform posterior interventricular artery, and a noticeable posterolateral artery running in the inferior atrioventricular groove reaching the crux cordis up to the right atrioventricular sulcus.  Based on imaging findings, surgical intervention was not required. Therefore, the patient was kept under pharmacological control by anti-platelets and monitored over time without any surgical intervention. Moreover, she was advised to avoid heavy exercise and to observe a proper nutrition and a healthy lifestyle to prevent the onset of coronary atherosclerosis.

The hospital course for this patient was uneventful. No complications or adverse reactions were observed during the CTCA examination, and the patient was closely monitored afterward. The patient responded well to the pharmacological treatment.

The patient was advised to avoid heavy exercise and to observe a proper nutrition and a healthy lifestyle to prevent the onset of coronary atherosclerosis. The patient was discharged and instructed to follow-up regularly to monitor her condition. She was also instructed to seek further medical attention if she experienced any new or worsening symptoms.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course:

The patient was evaluated for a diffuse asymptomatic rash on her anterior neck and chest between her breasts that had been present for four years. Her medical history was significant for polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) diagnosed 10 years earlier. The patient was treated with an oral contraceptive pill.

Physical Examination:

Cutaneous examination revealed reticulated hyperpigmented patches on the patient's chest and anterior neck. Macular hyperpigmentation was also present on her cheeks consistent with melasma. Additionally, velvet-like hyperpigmented plaques were noted on her posterior neck and axilla consistent with acanthosis nigricans.

Diagnosis and Treatment:

Correlation of the presentation and clinical examination of the chest and anterior neck lesions was most consistent with confluent and reticulated papillomatosis (CARP). The patient was treated with azithromycin, 250 mg once a day for two months. The chest and anterior neck dermatosis resolved with plaques flattening and skin hyperpigmentation fading. The velvet-like plaques on the posterior neck and axillae persisted, consistent with acanthosis nigricans.

Outcome:

The patient's dosage of azithromycin was titrated down and eventually stopped during the next month. There was no recurrence of CARP on subsequent follow-up visits. The patient was discharged with instructions to follow up with her primary care physician for ongoing management of her PCOS and acanthosis nigricans.

Hospital Course:

The 72-year-old Caucasian female was admitted with intermittent nausea and vomiting leading to decreased oral intake, intermittent abdominal pain, diarrhea, and unintentional weight loss. She had a past medical history of bilateral lobular breast carcinoma, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and hyperthyroidism.

The patient was diagnosed with lobular carcinoma of the right breast 24 years ago and lobular carcinoma of the left breast approximately 10 years after the initial diagnosis. She was in remission and had undergone lumpectomy and hormone-based chemotherapy with anastrozole. She had a similar admission six months prior to this presentation, where imaging studies had been unremarkable for any acute abnormality and had been managed with proton-pump inhibitors and blood transfusions.

On this admission, the patient had distension with tenderness in the left lower quadrant, and laboratory investigations were noteworthy for anemia along with elevated aspartate and alanine aminotransferases. Imaging studies of the abdomen confirmed the presence of a distal small bowel obstruction. The patient underwent small-bowel resection along with primary anastomosis after the detection of a small bowel tumor.

Histopathology showed the presence of metastatic pleomorphic lobular carcinoma consistent with breast primary. Further workup showed cytoplasmic staining with p120 catenin and positive for GATA-binding protein 3 (GATA-3), focally positive for both estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR), gross cystic disease fluid protein 15 (GCDFP-15) and mammaglobin but negative for human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER-2). Two lymph nodes near the tumor site were identified, out of which one demonstrated the presence of metastatic carcinoma. The patient was subsequently started on fulvestrant and palbociclib and has shown significant improvement in her symptoms.

The patient was discharged in a stable condition and advised to follow up with medical oncology for further management and care.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Small bowel obstruction due to metastatic pleomorphic lobular carcinoma consistent with breast primary.

Discharge Medications:

Fulvestrant and Palbociclib.

Follow-Up:

Patient advised to follow up with medical oncology for further management and care.

The mass also extended rostrally into the right frontal sinus, filling the caudal two-thirds. There was no evidence of abnormal contrast enhancement of the mass or the brain. 

The histologic diagnosis was an osteoma.

Discharge Summary:

Patient name: [Redacted]
Date of admission: December 3, 2017
Date of discharge: January 6, 2018

Admission diagnosis: Severe acute pancreatitis (SAP) and multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (heart, liver, kidney)
Treatment: Positive expansion, gastrointestinal decompression, and nutritional support; continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) treatment; intraperitoneal puncture and drainage; and jejunal nutrition

Hospital course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital on December 3, 2017, with severe abdominal distention and pain. She was previously admitted for acute pancreatitis (AP) due to high cholesterol on May 9, 2017. However, she discontinued the lipid-lowering drugs prescribed by her doctor and resumed a high-fat diet during the 3 months before her current admission. She was diagnosed with SAP and multiple organ dysfunction syndrome, including heart, liver, and kidney dysfunction.
Following admission, the patient was treated with positive expansion, gastrointestinal decompression, nutritional support, and CRRT treatment. She underwent intraperitoneal puncture and drainage four times. On the 16th day of admission, jejunal nutrition was initiated. The patient's renal function restored by day 18, and her intraperitoneal pressure decreased. She showed improvement in her APACHE II and SOFA scores. However, on day 19, she experienced high fever and chills even after blood culture. A deep vein puncture tube was administered, and remaining six abdominal drainage tubes were removed. Blood and gene detection tests revealed that the patient had a fungal blood infection. Treatment was adjusted accordingly, and her body temperature returned to normal after 10 days of caspofungin treatment. Her WBC count gradually returned to normal on the 32nd day of treatment.

Condition at discharge:
The patient's condition improved significantly, and she was discharged on January 6, 2018. She continued to maintain a low-fat diet. She was followed up every 10 days for 30 days after discharge, and her temperature remained normal.

Treatment plan at discharge:
The patient was advised to continue her low-fat diet and was prescribed follow-up appointments as necessary.

Follow-up plan:
The patient was advised to follow up with her primary care physician and gastroenterologist as necessary.

Hospital Course: 

The 61-year-old man with a history of upper GI bleeding presented to the ED with black stools for 24 hours, preceded by abdominal cramps, dyspnea, fatigue, and light-headedness. On initial examination, he appeared lethargic with conjunctival pallor. Cardiovascular examination revealed a systolic ejection murmur with late systolic peaking and soft second heart sounds. Laboratory tests showed anemia and a deficient in high molecular weight multimers of von Willebrand factor (vWF). CT and upper GI endoscopy yielded negative results. Two-dimensional transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a severely sclerotic aortic valve with the area of 0.65 cm2. The patient was diagnosed with Heyde syndrome.

Treatment:

The patient was treated with intravenous administration of a proton pump inhibitor and received two units of packed red blood cells. He subsequently underwent a minimally invasive aortic valve replacement, with the insertion of a 27-mm tissue valve.

Follow-up:

At present, three years after the procedure, the patient remained asymptomatic with no further episodes of bleeding.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 52-year-old male

Medical History: Chronic kidney disease, secondary hypertension, chronic hepatitis C virus infection, and arrhythmia

Clinical Presentation: Sudden vision loss in the left eye

Diagnosis: Occlusion of the superotemporal branch of the left retinal artery

Treatment: A single dose of 500 cc intravenous dextran-40 and 200 mg intravenous pentoxifylline

Etiologic Studies: Doppler ultrasonography revealed an atherosclerotic stenosis in the right and left main carotid arteries and a calcified plaque causing luminal narrowing in the left internal carotid artery. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed second- to third-degree aortic valve regurgitation and first-degree tricuspid valve regurgitation.

Follow-up: Peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer thickness was within normal limits, but thinning was observed in the superior, inferior, and temporal areas. Decreased vascular density in the superficial and deep capillary plexus consistent with ischemia in the regions supplied by the superotemporal branch of the retinal artery was observed. Capillary density was reduced in the superotemporal region, and collateral vessels were present in the area. 

The patient was discharged after treatment. At follow-up, there was no improvement in visual acuity or visual field despite receiving a single dose of intravenous medication. Further diagnostic studies revealed stenosis in the main carotid arteries and aortic valve regurgitation. Follow-up imaging revealed thinning of the peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer and decreased vascular density in areas supplied by the left retinal artery. Further measures may be needed to address these underlying conditions.

Discharge Date: [date]

Hospital Course:
This 60-year-old male patient was admitted to our emergency room with complaints of headache, severe dizziness, and nausea at night. The patient had a history of untreated hypertension and a smoking habit. On arrival, the patient's symptoms improved but his blood pressure was noted to be high. Neurological examination detected slight nystagmus. Laboratory data, ECG, and cardiac/carotid echography were found to be normal. However, the patient's MRI/A study revealed an acute infarction in the right cerebellar area, and fenestration was noted on the union of the right vertebral artery and basilar artery without intramural hematoma. 

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with acute cerebral infarction caused by right vertebral artery dissection.

Treatment:
The patient received antiplatelet therapy and blood pressure control to help with the acute cerebral infarction.

Follow-Up:
On the following MRI/A, the right vertebral artery was observed, but an intimal flap was still detected in the right fenestrated area. The patient will need further monitoring and follow-up with a specialist to evaluate his condition and continue any necessary treatment. 

Summary:
This patient presented with a history of high blood pressure and smoking and developed symptoms of headache, dizziness, and nausea. The patient was diagnosed with acute cerebral infarction caused by right vertebral artery dissection. Antiplatelet therapy and blood pressure control were initiated, and the patient will need further monitoring and follow-up with a specialist to evaluate his condition and continue any necessary treatment.

The patient was advised to continue anticoagulant therapy according to the prescription, as no symptom onset was observed during follow-up. Additionally, the patient was advised to undergo periodic blood pressure checks due to the presence of hypertension.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to our emergency department with vomiting, loose motions, confusion, fever, slurred speech, and blurring of vision. The patient had been treated with IV fluids for hyperemesis gravidarum in another hospital with no improvement. On examination, there were signs of confusion, ophthalmoparesis, and restricted extraocular movement. The patient's muscle stretch reflexes were normal in all four limbs, but power was 4/5 in both upper limbs and 0/5 in lower. Laboratory investigations were significant for leukocyturia and nitrite-positive urine. MRI showed hyper-intense areas in peri-tectal and bilateral medial thalami, indicating Wernicke's Encephalopathy.

Management:
The patient was treated with thiamine and other vitamin B supplements. The patient's condition improved significantly over the next few days and was discharged on parenteral nutrition.

Follow-up:
The patient is advised to continue taking thiamine and other vitamin B supplements as prescribed. The patient should also continue with the parenteral nutrition regimen until further notice. A follow-up appointment with an obstetrician is recommended to monitor the pregnancy.

The discharge medications of the patient will not be mentioned here as these have not been explicitly defined in the provided case report.

Hospital Course:

A 72-year-old Hispanic male was admitted with shortness of breath due to fluid overload secondary to peritoneal dialysis catheter malfunction. The patient had missed dialysis for two weeks. Vitals at presentation were abnormal with temperature 96 °F, heart rate 53 bpm, respiratory rate 24 per minute, blood pressure 88/60 mm of Hg, and pulse oximetry 93% on 6L nasal canula. The patient was hyperkalemic and bradycardic, and hemodialysis was arranged with CVC. Labs revealed severe azotemia with high creatinine and potassium levels. Chest X-ray showed pulmonary venous congestion. Mannitol and 3% hypertonic saline were administered during dialysis. The patient developed confusion and twitching all over the body 90 minutes into hemodialysis. The patient's hemodialysis session was terminated, and the patient received mannitol. Postdialysis labs showed improvement in BUN and creatinine levels, however, the patient had to be dialyzed again for hyperkalemia and fluid overload state the following day. The patient showed gradual neurological improvement with full recovery in four days.

Patient: Male patient in his late 60s with a history of malignancy, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus who was admitted to the Neurology Department of Padova City Hospital with acute onset of confusion.

Diagnosis: West Nile Virus (WNV) infection

Hospital Course:
- The patient was admitted to the hospital after experiencing a mild headache that progressed to severe confusion and apraxia.
- Initial tests, including brain CT scan and MRI, did not reveal any vascular causes for the patient's symptoms.
- Lumbar puncture revealed a slight increase in protein level and monocyte cell count.
- Empirical antiviral therapy with acyclovir was initiated for suspected viral encephalitis.
- FilmyArray testing ruled out common pathogens causing central nervous system infections.
- The patient was screened for autoimmune causes of encephalitis.
- Due to the surveillance plan for WNV and USUV infections, the patient was tested for both viruses, and USUV RNA was detected in blood samples.
- The patient showed gradual improvement, and aphasia and apraxia completely resolved.
- The patient was discharged at day 10 with a full recovery.
- Virological testing during follow-up revealed the persistence of USUV RNA in blood up to 40 days after symptom onset.

Treatment and Medications:
- Empirical antiviral therapy with acyclovir for 10 days.

Follow-Up:
- A second brain MRI and electroencephalography performed at day 4 post-discharge were normal.
- The patient will require follow-up for USUV infection.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a six-year-old boy with a history of early childhood autism, mental retardation, and ADHD. At the age of 6 years and 1 month, the patient was initiated on a classic ketogenic diet (KD) with a 2:1 ratio of fats to proteins+carbohydrates. One month later, the diet was switched to a modified Atkins diet (MAD) for five months and eventually to the low glycemic index treatment (LGIT). Metabolic outcome was monitored at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months after diet initiation without clinically meaningful changes in blood laboratory parameters. Improvements in clinical outcomes were observed as early as 1 month after the classic KD initiation, including behavior normalization with less hyperactivity and aggressive behaviors. The patient adhered to the diet according to the dietician’s recommendation, with no side effects or need for psychopharmacological treatment. Another psychological evaluation was performed when the patient was on the LGIT at the age of 7 years and 5 months, resulting in improved scores on the Childhood Autism Rating Scale and Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children-Revised. The patient's communication abilities also improved, and there was no evidence of clinically meaningful abnormalities based on urinalysis.

Pathologic compression fractures of L4 and L5, with epidural tumor invasion and neural foraminal encroachment.

The patient underwent right femoral IMN fixation and prophylactic left femoral IMN fixation.

The patient was discharged under stable condition.

The patient was advised to follow-up with their primary care physician for further evaluation and management.

Patient Information: 
Name: [Redacted]
Gender: Male
Age: 42 years old
Admission Date: March 14, 2020
Discharge Date: [Redacted]

Hospital Course: 
The patient was admitted to the hospital with acute dyspnea and fever. He had suffered from fever and fatigue for the past 7 days and received amoxicillin treatment at home. Upon admission, his physical examination was unremarkable except for a body temperature of 375 °C, respiratory rate of 20/min, and heart rate of 105 beats/min. His peripheral blood saturation level was 92%, and his blood pressure was 130/95 mmHg. Blood gas analysis conducted under oxygen therapy 4 L/min showed pH 7,41, pCO2 426 mmHg, pO2 955 mmHg, sO2 97%.

Laboratory blood tests showed moderately high WBC count of 5,6 × 103/μL and elevated CRP level of 139 mg/dL. A chest film indicated bilateral pulmonary opacities and a ground-glass opacity in the right hilum. Nasopharyngeal swab confirmed the presence of Covid-19. The patient was treated with a combination therapy that included hydroxychloroquine, lopinavir, ritonavir, azytromicin, and low-molecular-weight heparin. Due to progressive respiratory distress and severe hypoxemia, high-flow oxygen therapy with CPAP (PEEP 7,5 cm H2O, FiO2 60%) was initiated. Fever and respiratory symptoms improved following the treatment, with oxygen requirement decreasing to 2 L/min over the course of 2 weeks.

However, during the course of the hospital stay, the patient experienced nausea and upper abdominal pain. Physical examination showed diffuse abdominal tenderness and rebound pain. Laboratory tests showed WBC 1679 × 103/μL, CRP 0,3 mg/dL, amylase 140 u/L, and d-dimer 0.3 u/L. On upper abdominal ultrasound, the gallbladder appeared distended with minimal pericholecystic fluid and a positive Murphy sign. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) confirmed the absence of contrast enhancement of the gallbladder and a micro-perforation of the fundus. The patient underwent emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

Final Diagnosis and Disposition:
The patient was diagnosed with acute calculous cholecystitis with micro-perforation and underwent emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy with no complications. The treatment was successful, and the patient was discharged on [Redacted] with instructions to continue his medications and to follow-up as scheduled.

Follow-up Plan: 
The patient is instructed to follow-up with their primary care physician as scheduled. They were advised to maintain a healthy diet and exercise regimen and to avoid smoking and alcohol. The patient is to continue monitoring their symptoms and to seek prompt medical attention if symptoms worsen or new ones arise.

Hospital Course:

A 75-year-old male patient was admitted with a complaint of abdominal pain and melena. The patient was diagnosed with stage IVa (pT3N2M1) gastric cancer which had metastasized to the liver and lungs. The primary tumor was identified as a well to mixed differentiated gastric adenocarcinoma which had invaded the subserosa layer. The patient underwent palliative gastrectomy to prevent bleeding and perforation, and chemotherapy treatment was initiated as first-line therapy.

The patient's liver metastatic lesions were shrunk with the mFOLFOX6 regimen, and cryoablation was performed for hepatic metastases. Post-operation chemotherapy was continued for 3 cycles with the efficacy evaluated as stable disease. The patient received a second-line chemotherapy treatment of Paclitaxel plus S-1 which resulted in progressive disease after 3 cycles. Further treatment followed with FOLFIRI regimen chemotherapy for 9 cycles, and the efficacy was evaluated again as progressive disease.

During the treatment period, HER-2 gene amplification was identified using peripheral blood sample. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of Anlotinib was initiated as second-line therapy for the patient and after 6 cycles, the efficacy was evaluated as stable disease. However, after the 8th cycle, treatment-related proteinuria occurred, and the efficacy was evaluated as progressive disease. The patient ultimately withdrew from the clinical trial.

The patient's CA19-9 and CEA were essentially maintained at normal levels throughout the treatment periods. Unfortunately, new metastases were identified, and the patient's overall survival was 39 months. The patient passed away on July 24, 2017.

Diagnosis:

- Stage IVa gastric cancer with metastasis to the liver and lungs
- HER-2 gene amplification

Treatment:

- Palliative gastrectomy
- Chemotherapy: mFOLFOX6 protocol, Paclitaxel plus S-1, FOLFIRI regimen, and Anlotinib

Course:

- Liver metastatic lesions were shrunk with mFOLFOX6 protocol
- Cryoablation was performed for hepatic metastases
- Post-operation chemotherapy was continued with efficacy evaluated as stable disease

- FOLFIRI regimen chemotherapy followed with efficacy evaluated as progressive disease

- Treatment-related proteinuria occurred during the second cycle of Anlotinib
- Efficacy of Anlotinib evaluated as progressive disease after the 8th cycle

A 63-year-old male with a history of diabetes mellitus and esophageal cancer presented to the emergency department with left shoulder pain and chest tightness. Upon admission, the patient exhibited a temperature of 37.6 °C, a blood pressure of 123/87 mmHg, a pulse of 103 bpm, a respiratory rate of 20 per minute, and an oxygen saturation of 97%. A massive pyopneumopericardium, bilateral pleural effusion, and collapse of the lower lobe of the left lung were observed via chest computed tomography. The patient underwent ultrasound-guided pericardiocentesis and 300 ml of pus was drained. Analysis of specimens of the pericardial pus indicated a WBC of 20 × 109/L (100% neut), LDH > 17,000 IU/L, and glucose of 0.05 mmol/L. Parenteral treatment with ceftriaxone 2000 mg IV every 24 h was given at admission, but no clinical improvement was achieved.

On the day after admission, the patient’s condition worsened. The pericardial fluid culture identified E. corrodens and Streptococcus anginosus and the patient exhibited a WBC of 28 × 109/L and elevated levels of alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, LDH, amylase, and hypoalbuminemia. Serum myocardial markers levels also increased dramatically. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed apparent acidosis and type I respiratory failure. The antibiotic therapy was changed to imipenem 500 mg IV every 8 h and mechanical ventilation was provided. Despite these interventions, the patient’s condition continued to deteriorate and he passed away 3 days after admission.

The patient was presented to the orthopedic emergency department due to a sudden sharp pain in his right upper extremity after attempting a parachute jump. On examination, significant ecchymosis and edema were observed in the forearm with a muscle defect palpable, indicating the presence of a Popeye's deformity. Simple radiographs did not reveal any bony pathology, but magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a proximal rupture of the biceps brachii at the musculotendinous junction.

Given the patient's age and occupation, the decision was taken to undergo surgical intervention to restore strength and diminish the deformity. The surgery was uneventful, and postoperatively, a posterior splint with the elbow at 90° was used for four weeks. Active ROM exercises were started after the splint was removed, and physiotherapy was initiated after eight weeks, emphasizing on strengthening exercises. The patient was able to fully return to former activities in six months, with great functional and cosmetic results, as confirmed by a follow-up examination at the one-year mark and subsequent annual checkups.

Discharge Diagnosis: Rupture of the biceps brachii at the musculotendinous junction

Discharge Condition: Good

1. Continue physical therapy and strengthening exercises as advised by the physiotherapist.
2. Avoid any strenuous activity for two weeks post-discharge.
3. Do not hesitate to contact your healthcare provider in case of redness, swelling, or fever.

Follow-up Appointments: Annual checkups recommended.

Hospital Course:
The 84-year-old female patient was admitted to our hospital after developing severe and painful ulcers on her bilateral index fingers. She had a 5-year history of Raynaud’s phenomenon and had been treated for interstitial pneumonia and Raynaud’s disease by a rheumatologist. Two months prior to admission, she experienced peripheral cyanosis on her fingers, which eventually led to the development of ulcers. Angiography findings revealed poor arterial perfusion in her fingers. Blood test results showed slightly increased inflammatory indexes, including an erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. Skin biopsy did not show any specific findings.

The patient was given conservative therapy with a calcium-channel blocker and anti-platelet drugs, which included oral administration of nifedipine, cilostazol, and Beraprost. However, her condition worsened, and she was indicated for hyperbaric oxygen therapy to improve digital ischemia.

Outcome:
During her hospitalization, the patient underwent 10 sessions of hyperbaric oxygen therapy with 100% oxygen at 2.0 atm of absolute pressure for 60 minutes each. The patient experienced no side effects associated with the hyperbaric oxygen therapy. Following the treatment, the cyanosis around the ulcers disappeared, and the pain due to the ulcers was remarkably reduced. The ulcer size gradually decreased, and complete healing was accomplished 6 weeks after discharge. The patient experienced no recurrence in the 12-month follow-up period.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was discharged from the hospital with no painkillers required. The patient was advised to follow up with her rheumatologist for her Raynaud’s disease and interstitial pneumonia treatment. Additionally, she was recommended to maintain proper hand hygiene and keep her fingers warm to prevent future ulcers.

None prescribed 

Follow-up:
Follow up with rheumatologist recommended for continued treatment of Raynaud's disease and interstitial pneumonia.

Patient Information:
Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 42
Gender: Female
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Chronic Hepatitis B Virus (HBV)

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital with a history of chronic HBV. During evaluation for antiviral treatment, ultrasonography of the liver revealed an incidental liver mass. A confirmatory magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a huge mass with several metastases surrounding the right liver with right portal vein invasion that measured 9.6 × 9.1 cm.

Due to the presence of tumor thrombus and limited liver function reserve, the patient was not a candidate for liver transplant. Therefore, plans were made to use robotic-assisted laparoscopic partial hepatectomy (RALPP) without portal vein ligation (RALP).

The first stage of RALPP was performed successfully, which involved the induction of rapid hypertrophy of the future remnant liver (FLR) in order to increase liver function reserve. On postoperative day (POD) 3, postoperative MRI confirmed coagulative necrosis of the hepatic parenchyma created by radiofrequency ablation to cease blood flow from the FLR to the diseased hemiliver.

After 2 weeks, the patient underwent the second stage of RALPP, which involved the resection of the tumor and the successful right hepatectomy. The FLR was secured to the anterior abdominal wall at the falciform ligament, a surgical drain was left at the resection margin, and the abdominal wall was closed in the standard manner. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 11.

Follow-Up:

The patient underwent follow-up for 7 months after the operation. After being in remission for 3 months, HCC relapsed near the edge of resection, and the patient died 7 months postoperatively.

Final Diagnosis on Discharge:
Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)

Discharge Summary:

Patient 1:
This is a 32-year-old previously healthy female who presented with intermittent pain and swelling in the left jaw. Investigations revealed a solitary expansile left mandibular low density lesion with associated cortical thinning. Blood tests showed elevated parathyroid hormone and normal corrected calcium and phosphate levels. Imaging confirmed the presence of a brown tumour in the left mandible, which was caused by a parathyroid adenoma. The diagnosis was confirmed through ultrasound and 99mTc-sestamibi SPECT/CT scan. Further diagnostic and treatment plan were provided.

Patient 2:
This is a 31-year-old female patient who presented with bilateral jaw pain. Investigations revealed bilateral mandibular brown tumours from underlying hyperparathyroidism. The diagnosis of the brown tumour was confirmed through the same imaging pathway as for Patient 1.

Patient 3:
This is a 40-year-old female patient who had rickets as a child and presented with worsening of chronic bilateral hip pain. Investigations revealed an incidental brown tumour in the left sacral ala in light of clinical and imaging findings.

Patient 4:
This is a 57-year-old male patient who presented with a displaced fracture of the left femoral shaft with associated lytic lesions at the fracture site. Further investigations showed multiple expansile mixed lytic/sclerotic bone lesions. Blood test showed markedly elevated PTH, which suggested primary hyperparathyroidism as the most likely cause. The diagnosis of the brown tumour was confirmed through ultrasound and 99mTc-sestamibi SPECT.

Patient 5:
This is a 54-year-old male patient who presented with chronic left knee pain. Investigations revealed a multiloculated lytic lesion in the proximal tibial metaphysis in the context of hyperparathyroidism. A targeted biopsy of the lesion was performed and histologically confirmed a grade 1 chondrosarcoma.

Patient 6:
These are two patients with chronic renal failure and receiving long-term haemodialysis. CT imaging of these patients demonstrated asymptomatic bilateral mixed lytic/sclerotic expansile rib lesions, a lytic lesion in the left humeral head and centrally lucent vertebral bodies and sclerotic endplates producing the characteristic rugger-jersey spine. The bone lesions could also affect the orofacial area and result in facial or oral cavity swelling. Both CT and/or MRI would be helpful for diagnosis and management.

Overall, the different cases presented highlight the importance of considering brown tumours among other differential diagnoses in patients with hyperparathyroidism.

Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Reason for Admission:
The patient was admitted to the Emergency Department with a two-month history of low back pain that had recently worsened and localised to the right hip. After having been prescribed various painkillers without relief, the patient was unable to bear weight on his right lower extremity for the previous two weeks. Admission radiographs demonstrated a lytic bone lesion within the right femur's intertrochlear region, which led to the patient's admission.

Hospital Course:
MRI findings showed the presence of either a solitary intraosseous cyst or aneurysmal bone cyst, as has a characteristic "soap-bubble" appearance. Open biopsy showed the lesion to be aneurysmal bone cyst, with no endothelial lining but benign giant cells, fibroblasts, and thin strands of woven bone. The patient was treated with open biopsy, curettage with bone grafting, and cephalomedullary nailing after consulting the hospital's radiology diagnosis, which ruled out the need for a biopsy prior to definitive fracture fixation for diagnosis confirmation.

Summary of Therapy:
The patient was thromboprophylaxed throughout their treatment, ambulated immediately with crutches post-operation for two weeks, followed by unassisted walking, and returned to work after three weeks, with improved symptoms. At six and nine months, follow-up shows the patient is asymptomatic, with no recurrence of lesion.

Final Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with aneurysmal bone cyst based on the imaging findings and biopsy.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient was discharged with a stable condition, ambulating normally, asymptomatic, with no signs of lesion recurrence.

Follow-up Care:
The patient is scheduled for periodic follow-up visits with their oncologist to monitor their condition and ensure there is no recurrence of the lesion.

Hospital Course:

The 29-year-old G3P2002 woman at 39-week and 1-day gestation was referred from a health center for management of fetal demise. On admission, she had stable vital parameters and an emergency ultrasound confirmed fetal demise. 

Treatment:

Cervical ripening was started with 50µg of misoprostol vaginally every 6 hours, but failed to induce cervical changes. A decision for operative delivery was made, and the intraoperative findings were a third-degree macerated female fetus floating freely in the peritoneal cavity, weighing 2650g with a tight cord round neck. Postoperatively, she was placed on antibiotics and received methotrexate to reduce the risk of disseminated intravascular coagulation. 

Follow-up:

The patient's recovery was uneventful, and she was discharged on day 8 postoperation to continue follow-up as an outpatient. Regular βHCG and ultrasound checks were recommended for the monitoring of her condition. Placenta resorption occurred 6 months later.

Diagnosis:

Fetal demise at 39 weeks, 1 day gestation with third-degree macerated female fetus and tight cord round neck. Placenta implanted on the ascending colon and mesocolon.

Procedures:

Operative delivery with removal of the third-degree macerated female fetus floating freely in the peritoneal cavity and leaving the placenta in place. 

Medications:

Ampicillin, gentamycin, and metronidazole parenterally for 5 days. Methotrexate every other day (04 doses) with 5mg of folinic acid each day proceeding the methotrexate.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with acute onset fever and driveline site discharge and was found to have Parvimonas micra bacteremia and a Corynebacterium spp. infection. Ischemic cardiomyopathy with LVAD placement, type 2 diabetes, tobacco dependence, and chronic MSSA LVAD infection.

Treatment:
The patient was treated with PO metronidazole for six weeks and plans were made to transition to amoxicillin-clavulanate or doxycycline for chronic suppression of previous infections.

Follow-up:
Upon discharge, the patient is advised to continue to follow up with his cardiologist and to maintain good oral hygiene by regularly visiting a dentist to help avoid future infections.

Summary:
The patient presented with fever, bacteremia and a Corynebacterium spp. infection that were likely due to poor oral hygiene. After treatment with metronidazole, he was sent home with plans for chronic suppression of his previous infections. He was later readmitted with LVAD thrombosis. He is advised to continue to follow up with his cardiologist and maintain good oral hygiene.

Hospital Course Summary:

This 55-year-old Chinese male was admitted with a week-long history of fever, upper abdominal pain, and yellowing of his eyes. On admission, he was found to be lethargic with jaundice and tenderness in the right hypochondrium. Diagnostic imaging revealed a diffusely thickened and oedematous gallbladder, thrombosis in the right portal vein, and in the splenic vein with splenic infarcts seen. A diagnosis of severe sepsis from acute acalculous cholecystitis was made, and a laparoscopic cholecystectomy was carried out. Intraoperatively, the gallbladder was found to be distended, inflamed, and containing turbid bile. Postoperatively, the patient developed septic shock and multiorgan failure requiring mechanical ventilation and inotropic support in the ICU. Burkholderia pseudomallei, a bacterial infection, was identified in peripheral blood and intraoperative bile fluid cultures. The patient had undiagnosed diabetes mellitus and suffered additional complications of dry gangrene of his hands and feet from the severe sepsis and high inotropic requirements. The patient was continued on intravenous meropenem for a month before converting to enteral trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole for another three months. The patient stayed in the ICU for almost a month before being discharged.

By postoperative day 4, the patient became afebrile, her tachycardia resolved, and her blood glucose remained within normal limits. She was transitioned to oral antibiotics and discharged home in good condition on postoperative day 10.

The patient is advised to continue oral antibiotics at home. She should avoid heavy lifting or any strenuous activities for at least one week. [Patient Name], a 31-year-old female, was admitted to the department of oral and maxillofacial surgery at Apollo main hospital in Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India, with chief complaints of painless swelling over the right side of her face for the past four years.

The patient's postoperative recovery and wound healing was uneventful without any complications. She was discharged in good condition after one day of hospitalization. The patient is under periodic review, and there is no evidence of recurrence after one year of follow-up.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
A 50-year old female with PD-L1+ metastatic lung adenocarcinoma was admitted to our hospital with petechiae three cycles after pembrolizumab treatment.

Hospital Course:
During the admission, a thorough evaluation was performed, and CBC was notable for normal hemoglobin with grade 2 thrombocytopenia. Renal function was normal, and there was no evidence of platelet consumption or hemolysis on a peripheral blood smear. Hemolysis labs including serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), haptoglobin, indirect bilirubin, and CBC were normal. HIV, hepatitis B/C virus and H. pylori were negative.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with ICI-mediated immune thrombocytopenia.

Treatment:
The ICI treatment was withheld for 2 weeks, and a repeat CBC did not show improvement in platelet count until prednisone 1 mg/kg/dose was started. Re-evaluation at 2 weeks revealed improvement to grade 1 thrombocytopenia. Prednisone was tapered over 4 weeks, and the patient was able to be recommenced on pembrolizumab.

Follow-up:
The patient was discharged with clear instructions to continue the medication as directed by the physicians. The patient is also being monitored closely by a hematology service for any possible complications or severe toxicities.

Recommendations:
Most patients with low-grade thrombocytopenia improve with ICI withholding and initiation of oral corticosteroids. For higher-grade toxicities, a hematology service should be consulted for consideration of additional therapies for severe toxicity, such as IVIG, rituximab, cyclosporine A, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide, or thrombopoietin receptor agonists. If indicated, IVIG initial dosing is recommended at 1 g/kg as a one-time dose which can be repeated if necessary.

Prognosis:
The prognosis of the patient remains guarded, but the patient has been advised to follow up with her oncologist regularly for further management and treatment.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 57-year-old male with no past medical history, was admitted to the hospital with a 20-day history of black color stool, upper abdominal pain, abdominal distension, and dizziness. An occult blood test was positive and an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed a 1.5 × 1.5-cm ulcer of the descending part of duodenum with irregular border. Total abdomen Computed Tomography revealed a large mass in the right mid-upper abdomen, which was considered to originate from the duodenum.

Diagnosis:

A biopsy of the duodenal ulcer showed diffuse proliferation and infiltration of small blue cells. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for CD20(+++), CD10(+), and Ki-67 >40%. All other tests were negative, leading to the diagnosis of primary intestinal diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PI-DLBCL).

Treatment:

The patient was treated with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vindesine, and prednisolone. The chemotherapy process went smoothly with no adverse reactions reported. The patient showed great improvement in symptoms and after 6 courses of chemotherapy treatment, the duodenal ulcer was completely healed.

Hospital Stay:

The patient had a hospital stay of [number of days] with a treatment plan consisting of chemotherapy and symptom management. Constant monitoring was performed to ensure the patient's safety and health.

Condition at Discharge:

The patient's symptoms had improved significantly and he was discharged in stable condition with instructions to continue follow-up care.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient was instructed to continue follow-up care with the oncologist. Immediate medical attention was recommended if any symptoms or adverse effects occurred. The patient was advised to adhere to a healthy lifestyle with routine check-ups and follow-up imaging. All medications were to be taken as prescribed and any new medications or supplements were to be discussed with the healthcare provider prior to use.

Follow-up:

The patient will continue follow-up care with the oncologist to monitor for any recurrence or further developments of PI-DLBCL.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Gender: Female
Age: 68 years

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the haematology clinic with left-sided above-knee deep vein thrombosis (DVT), which was unprovoked. Her medical history included osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, and sciatica. She had undergone a subtotal colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis for large bowel obstruction due to colonic diverticular disease 16 years ago. Additionally, she had a history of consuming alcohol in large amounts until 4 years ago when her daily intake increased additionally. She also had asymptomatic mild thrombocytopenia since 2006 and mild liver function derangement. A portovenous phase CT scan showed bulky enlargement of the left thyroid lobe with multiple nodules. There was an incidental finding of an extrahepatic portosystemic connection, with an enlarged vein arising from the portal vein, and ultimately draining into the left renal vein.

Assessment and Treatment:
During her hospital stay, a full assessment including physical examination was conducted to rule out any clinical signs of chronic hepatic disease or cardiac abnormalities. There was no evidence of hyperdynamic circulation or audible murmurs on auscultation. The liver was not palpable, and there was no free fluid in the abdomen. There was, however, a mildly enlarged spleen, about 2 cm below the left costal margin; this was also confirmed on the CT images. To further investigate the cause of her extrahepatic portosystemic connection, a non-invasive liver screen with immunoglobulins, autoimmune and viral hepatitis markers were done, along with a fibroscan and endoscopy to look for portal hypertension and varices. The fibroscan showed a median liver stiffness measurement value, which was within the normal range to exclude liver fibrosis. The platelet count on the most recent pathology test was also normal.

Outcome and Follow-up:
Given the findings, chronic liver disease and portal hypertension were ruled out, and a long-standing congenital anomaly was suspected to be the cause of her shunt. The patient was discharged back to the care of her general practitioner without any further follow-up planned, as she was asymptomatic with Type II Abernethy malformation. She was advised to avoid alcohol and monitor the enlargement of the left thyroid lobe with multiple nodules. Further investigations were not indicated. 

Diagnosis:
Type II Abernethy malformation with an extrahepatic portosystemic communication. Left-sided above-knee deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

Plan:
Avoid alcohol intake. Monitor the thyroid lobe enlargement with multiple nodules.

Hospital Course:

Discharge Summary

Medical History:
The patient is a 60-year-old male who underwent ABO-incompatible kidney transplantation with a donor blood type A to a recipient blood type O. The patient's wife voluntarily donated the kidney. The patient had been undergoing hemodialysis since the age of 59. The preoperative HLA-DNA typing revealed 6 mismatches in antigens. Initial FCXM testing was negative and Flow PRA screening tests were also negative.

Hospital Course:
The patient underwent desensitization therapy for 3 months with MMF 750mg/day and Rituximab 200 mg before the planned transplant. After 3 months, he underwent two sessions of DFPP and anti-A blood type antibody titer decreased but rebounded to high levels. Desensitization therapy was resumed (MMF 750mg/day) for 4 months, but the anti-A blood-type antibody level rebounded again. The patient developed herpes zoster infection and underwent antiviral treatment while the MMF dose was reduced. The transplantation was postponed and rescheduled to occur 210 days from the initiation of MMF. Rituximab was administered, followed by 4 sessions of selective PE to remove anti-blood type antibodies. TacER was also administered and the graft was transplanted into the right iliac fossa. A biopsy showed no evidence of hyperacute rejection and post-op induction immunosuppression protocol consisted of TacER, MMF 2000mg/day, basiliximab 20mg and systemic steroids.

Postoperative Course:
The s-Cr level immediately decreased, and the anti-A blood-type antibody titer levels remained at 16-fold and 4-fold dilutions of IgG and IgM antibodies, respectively. However, a CMV antigenemia was diagnosed on POD 12, and the dose of MMF was decreased to 1000mg/day. A biopsy was performed on POD 50, which revealed acute T cell-mediated rejection IB and no evidence of acute antibody-mediated rejection. Steroid pulse therapy was administered. The patient has maintained stable levels of sCr, eGFR, and anti-A blood-type antibodies for 18 months after ABO-iLKT, as well as normal serum IgG levels.

Plan:
The patient was discharged on a triple immunosuppression consisting of TacER, MMF 1000 mg/day, and steroid 5 mg/day. The patient is advised to follow up with a nephrologist and undergo regular monitoring of blood pressure, sCr, eGFR, urine albumin, urine red blood cells, and urine white blood cells. Repeat biopsy may be considered in the future to check for signs of chronic rejection.

At the age of 31, he suffered from epileptic seizures which increased in frequency. Thereafter, the involuntary movements spread to the upper limbs and orofacial automatisms appeared.

The patient was prescribed haloperidol (2 mg three times a day) and baclofen (10 mg three times a day) for 2 years for the choreic and dystonic problems, but he responded poorly to drug treatments. During the hospitalization, neurological examination revealed poor muscle tone and absent deep tendon reflexes in all limbs. Additionally, right positive babinski sign was elicited. The patient's MMSE score was 27 indicating mild cognitive impairment, but he did not present with any psychiatric problems. The patient's father had no neurological abnormality and died from pneumonia at age 65. Tyr2941*) in VPS13A gene was identified, which was not detected in 100 healthy controls. The patient was discharged with stable vital signs and satisfactory healing of the fractures. He was advised to follow up with his primary care physician for further management.

Not Applicable
