Discharge Summary:

Patient: 13-year-old male
Diagnosis: Telangiectatic osteosarcoma

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with a one-month history of chronic cough in addition to dyspnea. CT scan showed a huge mass with compression effects on the heart. An incisional biopsy was performed and reported as aneurysmal bone cyst. On echocardiography, there was observable compression of the mass on right atrium and inferior vena cava. Peripheral ECMO was installed through cannulation of left femoral artery and vein under general anesthesia. After ECMO installation, a wide posterolateral thoracotomy was done. Diaphragmatic and pulmonary adhesion with pulmonary collapse were seen. A large hemorrhagic tumor was excised completely with adjacent seventh and eighth ribs as the origin of the tumor. The patient was stable after the surgery with 100% O2 saturation without the need for using ECMO in the postoperative period. According to hemorrhagic nature of the tumor, bleeding was modest at the time of operation but after complete resection of the tumor, there was no major bleeding but due to low hemoglobin level (Hg=6 mg/dL) packed cell transfused. He was extubated in the operating room after ECMO removal and finally was discharged on the sixth postoperative day.

Follow-up Care:
The patient's final pathologic diagnosis was compatible with telangiectatic osteosarcoma and adjuvant chemotherapy has been administered. Follow-up care will be provided by the treating oncologist.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admitted: 67-year-old male with respiratory insufficiency, requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation due to progressive dyspnea over 2 days. The patient had a history of high-dose steroid therapy for spinal bleeding and paraplegia. On admission, the patient had a fever, elevation of inflammatory markers, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates without evidence of pulmonary embolism. The patient was started on anti-infective therapy and underwent prone positioning which improved oxygenation. Bronchoalveolar lavage revealed a positive PCR for Pneumocystis jiroveci, Legionella species, and cytomegalovirus infection. Anti-infective therapy was switched and the patient was started on extracorporeal veno-venous oxygenation due to septic shock. The patient's condition continued to deteriorate despite treatment, resulting in the patient's death.

Discharge Summary:

The patient was admitted to the ICU due to respiratory insufficiency and was intubated and put on mechanical ventilation. The patient had a history of high-dose steroid therapy and was found to have a fever, elevation of inflammatory markers, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. A diagnosis was established after bronchoalveolar lavage was performed, revealing a positive PCR for Pneumocystis jiroveci, Legionella species, and cytomegalovirus infection. Anti-infective therapy was started and the patient underwent extracorporeal veno-venous oxygenation due to septic shock. Despite treatment, the patient continued to deteriorate and died due to disseminated intravascular coagulation, cerebral edema, and intracerebral hemorrhage. Cognitive imaging revealed the presence of intracerebral hemorrhage, intramedullary malignant melanoma, lung parenchymatous hemorrhage, and multiple infarctions with fungal growth in various organs and tissues.

The patient's course was characterized by a persistent and escalating infection leading to sepsis and multiorgan failure. Despite aggressive treatment and management, the patient's condition did not respond to therapy and the patient ultimately succumbed to their illness. The exact cause of death was due to disseminated intravascular coagulation, cerebral edema, and intracerebral hemorrhage. The patient was treated with anti-infective agents, anticoagulation therapy, and extracorporeal veno-venous oxygenation, but these interventions were ultimately futile in saving the patient's life.

Discharge Summary:
Admission Date: [DATE]
Discharge Date: [DATE]

Medical History:
The patient was admitted to the emergency room with left buttock pain. The patient had a history of being a hepatitis B virus carrier. There was no remarkable medical history except for two weeks of left buttock pain.

Hospital Course:
The patient had a generalized fever up to 37.8°C, and tenderness and swelling on the left buttock and proximal area of the posterior thigh. Plain radiography showed no evidence of fracture around her hip joint. The emergency medicine physician had a clinical impression of early stage cellulitis or contusion of the hip. The patient was discharged with empirical antibiotics and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications.

One week later, the patient visited the orthopedic outpatient department with aggravated pain and weakness on her left lower extremity. A patchy erythematous rash with sharp pain existed on the left buttock and posterior thigh without any sign of vesicle formation. The blood laboratory test showed mildly elevated CRP and normal procalcitonin levels. Lumbosacral MRI was urgently performed. The MRI revealed mild bulging disc with bilateral facet arthritis at L4-5 level which was not thought to be the direct cause of the symptoms. The result of EMG-NCV tests showed severe left sciatic neuropathy that no motor nerve responses from the left peroneal nerve and reduced compound muscle action potential on the tibial nerve were found. Pelvis MRI with contrast enhancement revealed asymmetrical diffuse swelling of the left sciatic and femoral nerve, which suggested neuritis. Herpes zoster infection of the left buttock three years ago was discovered in thorough systematic review. The putative diagnosis of herpes zoster was confirmed by detecting VZV DNA in her blood sample using the polymerase chain reaction test. 

Treatment:
The patient was treated with famciclovir 500 mg every eight hours and 20 mg/day of prednisolone for two weeks and changed to oral pregabalin 75 mg every 12 hours thereafter. After 12 weeks of an inpatient rehabilitation admission, the patient had a partial neurological recovery and could walk with a foot drop splint. The manual muscle test showed that muscular strength of her left ankle dorsi-flexor, plantar-flexor, and great toe extensor improved to grades II, III, and III, respectively. The hypoesthesia of S1 dermatome was completely recovered, while L4, L5 dermatomes showed 50% improvement. The skin rash and pain around it were completely alleviated.

Follow-up:
Follow-up pelvis MRI taken at 10 weeks after the treatment showed markedly diminished swelling of the left sciatic and femoral nerve. 

Summary:
The patient had a history of being a hepatitis B virus carrier, which was not related to the current symptoms. She had left buttock pain for two weeks until she slipped down on her way to the bathroom. The patient was diagnosed with early stage cellulitis or contusion of the hip, and a week after she was diagnosed with severe left sciatic neuropathy. After a thorough investigation, S1 dermatome had completely recovered, while L4 and L5 dermatomes improved by 50%. The patient was treated with famciclovir 500 mg, prednisolone 20mg, and oral pregabalin 75mg. She had a partial neurological recovery after 12 weeks of inpatient rehabilitation. Follow-up pelvis MRI showed markedly diminished swelling of the left sciatic and femoral nerve.

Admitting Diagnosis: Bullous retinal detachment in the right eye with focal retinal pigment epithelial detachment in the inferior retina of the left eye.

Hospital Course:

The patient presented with blurred vision and photopsia in both eyes for 3 months. Her BCVA was 20/63 OU. Upon examination, her right eye revealed bullous retinal detachment in the posterior pole, while the left eye had focal retinal pigment epithelial detachment in the inferior retina. The patient had been receiving oral prednisone treatment for nephritic syndrome for over 6 years. FFA of the right eye revealed hyperfluorescent leakage in areas corresponding to exudative retinal detachment, while OCT of the right eye disclosed neuro-retinal detachment.

The patient received a 50% dose of verteporfin PDT with a spot size of 5000 μm to cover the abnormal vascular area in indocyanine green angiography. One month later, the SRF was partly reduced, while 3 months later, there was retinal reattachment. At the 6-month examination after photodynamic therapy, the BCVA improved to 20/50 in the right eye, and a mottled appearance was observed in the fundus. FFA showed a mottled shape upon fluorescence transmission, and no fluorescein leakage was observed. ICGA showed hypofluorescence in the lesion area.

The patient responded well to treatment and was discharged in stable condition. Follow-up appointments were scheduled as needed.

Discharge Diagnosis: Bullous retinal detachment in the right eye with focal retinal pigment epithelial detachment in the inferior retina of the left eye.

Treatment: Verteporfin PDT with a spot size of 5000 μm to cover the abnormal vascular area in indocyanine green angiography.

Discharge Summary

Patient: 17-year-old female

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our hospital for a humeral shaft fracture nonunion. She had undergone osteosynthesis with intramedullary nailing at another hospital; however, bony union was not achieved. Upon admission to our hospital, a radiograph and bone scintigraphy were performed, revealing little callus formation and intense uptake at the nonunion site, respectively. The primary causative factor of nonunion was surmised to be lack of mechanical stability, especially rotational stability due to the small number of interlocking screws.

Treatment:
An anterior approach with two incisions was used to perform minimally invasive plate osteosynthesis without autogenous bone grafting. One distal approach reached the bone through the lateral side of the biceps, while another proximal approach passed between the deltoid and the biceps. A narrow locking compression plate with 10 holes was slid onto the surface of the humerus from distal to proximal without exposure of the nonunion site. One year after surgery, bony union and good functional recovery was achieved; the implant was subsequently removed. At the final follow-up of 4 years after the surgery, she had obtained full range of motion with no restrictions in activities of daily life.

Condition on Discharge:
The patient was discharged in good condition with full range of motion and no restrictions in activities of daily life, 4 years after surgery.

Follow-up:
The patient is advised to follow-up regularly with her primary care provider for any concerns and to inform them of any future surgeries or injuries.

Hospital Course:

Patient B, a 32-year-old female, was admitted to the hospital with presenting symptoms of frontal headache, blurred vision, and slurred speech, followed by several tonic-clonic seizures in close succession which ultimately led to a coma. She had suffered from three similar presentations in the past at the ages of 10, 12, and 18. The patient's family reported preceding upper respiratory tract infection symptoms.

Diagnostic Findings:

MRI neuroimaging showed diffuse, confluent cerebral and cerebellar white matter high signal changes, edema, and mass effect. CSF sampling showed an inflammatory picture with no bacterial or viral pathogens detected by routine culture or PCR. C3 was borderline low, and acute phase proteins remained normal. The patient was treated with empirical antibiotics and antivirals with no improvement. However, after pulsed methylprednisolone treatment, a slow recovery ensued with no residual neurological deficit, although the patient had a very mild cognitive deficit. Genetic testing revealed two heterozygous variants on CFI, c.191C>T; p.P64L and c.262C>A; p.Q88K.

Diagnosis:

Based on the genetic testing results, the patient was diagnosed with complement factor I (CFI) deficiency, which was responsible for the presenting symptoms.

Treatment:

The patient was treated with pulsed methylprednisolone, following which a slow recovery ensued with no residual neurological deficit. 

Follow-up:

The patient was discharged in good condition and will follow up with their primary care physician for continued monitoring.

Patient Name: [Name]
Gender: Male
Age: 77

Hospital Admission Dates: [Date]

Admission Diagnosis: Pulmonary Nodule, Lung Cancer, Aortic Stenosis

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our department for the evaluation of a pulmonary nodule detected by chest computed tomography (CT), which showed an increased size. The patient was diagnosed with Stage IA-3 lung cancer based on radiologic examinations, and it was suspected that the pulmonary nodule may be the cause.

Additionally, the patient was diagnosed with severe aortic stenosis (AS) having a maximum pressure gradient (mPG) of 44mmHg and aortic valve area (AVA) of 0.73 cm2. Due to the possibility of sudden cardiac death, treatment for AS was deemed mandatory before pulmonary resection. Given that the patient had a history of coronary artery disease and thoracic aortic aneurysm, conventional AVR was considered to be risky. Trans-apical TAVI with left-sided intercostal thoracotomy was performed successfully without postoperative complications.

The patient underwent surgery for lung cancer 70 days after TAVI. Right middle and lower lobectomy with mediastinal lymph node dissection was performed. The pathologic diagnosis was squamous carcinoma, pT1cN0M0 stage IA3. Postoperative heparin bridging was performed for low-dose aspirin therapy. Severe adhesion was present, so thoracotomy was performed instead of video-assisted thoracic surgery (VATS). The postoperative course was uneventful.

Discharge Diagnosis: Pulmonary Nodule, Lung Cancer, Aortic Stenosis

Discharge Plan:

The patient was discharged fourteen months after the surgery and is doing well without relapse or cardiac symptoms. Close follow-up and care is advised to monitor for potential relapse or recurrence of the pulmonary nodule, lung cancer, and aortic stenosis.

The patient was admitted to the medical service for acute cholecystitis. An urgent robotic-assisted cholecystectomy was performed after consultation with the cardiology and surgical departments.

The patient presented with an acute onset of nonradiating and sharp RUQ pain, primed by food intake and associated with nausea and fever. She had a past medical history of hypertension, allergic sinusitis, and multiple abdominal surgeries. Labs were unremarkable, and imaging showed a dilated GB with a large stone without signs of cholecystitis. The patient was treated with IV antibiotics and pain management.

Operative Summary:
Under general anesthesia and robotic assistance, the GB was successfully removed after the identification of numerous omental and intestinal adhesions. The torsion of the GB hilum was identified, accompanied with a distended and gangrenous GB. After dissection of the cystic artery and duct and transection in between Hem-o-loks, the small attachment between the fundus and the liver bed was then taken down with the cautery hook. The patient's postoperative course was uneventful.

The patient was discharged on postoperative day 2, with anticoagulation treatment for atrial fibrillation, ambulating, and with resolved pain. The pathology report informed gangrenous cholecystitis. Postoperative appointments were scheduled with the surgical and cardiology departments.

The patient was advised to follow up with the prescribed anticoagulation treatment for atrial fibrillation, maintain a healthy diet, and avoid strenuous activity for 6 weeks after surgery. Hospital Course Summary:

Patient presented with symptoms of influenza-like syndrome and pain in the right subcostal region. The patient was diagnosed with an undifferentiated hepatitis with cholestasis and underwent further testing. Upon admission to the Tropical and Parasitic Disease Department of Poznań University of Medical Sciences, suspicion of Echinococus infection was done and ELISA serology test was found to be positive.

The patient was diagnosed with liver alveococcosis with P2M0N0 stage. Albendazol therapy was initiated along with ursodeoxycholic acid in order to protect from apoptosis healthy liver tissue. The patient underwent a right hepatectomy and anatomic resection of the fifth, sixth, seventh and eighth liver segments was performed.

Postoperative course was complicated by lymphorrhea, which was treated conservatively. The patient was discharged after normal levels of bilirubin, alanine transaminase and aspartate transaminase were achieved. Follow-up performed 10 months after the operation revealed thrombocytopenia, leucopenia and sideropenic anemia. The examination also revealed splenomegaly as a result of portal hypertension, first-degree varices oesophagi, gastritis and duodenitis.

A recent control MRI revealed no active outbreaks of alveococosis in the liver parenchyma, compared to previous studies, the image is stable. Collateral vessels are visible in the liver cavity and the spleen remains enlarged. The patient is clinically asymptomatic and requires regular, every six months follow-up in the Tropical and Parasitic Clinic.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Age: 54

Gender: Female

Admission Date: [REDACTED]

Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Admitting Diagnosis: Bilateral breast pain, axillary node metastases, advanced bilateral breast cancer

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 54-year-old female, was admitted to our hospital on [REDACTED] for evaluation of bilateral breast pain that had persisted for the past six months. Upon examination, our clinical team palpated pathological nodes bilaterally in the axillae and observed left-sided nipple inversion with a palpable mass in the upper outer quadrant. A physical examination of the right breast revealed skin tethering of the nipple and palpable masses, with the largest mass measuring 5 cm in diameter.

Further diagnostic tests revealed advanced bilateral breast cancer with axillary node metastases. Ultrasound and mammography revealed multiple lesions involving both breasts. The right breast had a large lesion at 12 o’clock measuring 44.3 mm, and 7 smaller satellite lesions were distributed throughout the right breast, with the largest pathological node in the right axilla measuring 42 x 30 mm. The left breast had a lesion at the 2 o’clock position measuring 31.2 mm, with the largest node in the left axilla measuring 13.1 x 10.2 mm. The hormone receptor status of the right breast lesion was ER negative, while the left breast lesion was ER positive. HER2 immunohistochemistry score was 3+. Core biopsies revealed that both breast lesions were invasive carcinoma, no special type.

The patient was presented at a multidisciplinary oncology team meeting. Additional staging scans, including a CT of head, neck, abdomen, and pelvis, a nuclear medicine bone scan, and a PET scan, were arranged. No evidence of metastatic disease was found on CT scan, but bilateral breast malignancies with bilateral pathological axillary lymph nodes were observed (with the right being most pronounced). A mild FDG avid, ill-defined ground glass pulmonary opacity was detected in the left lower lobe of the lung, which was thought to represent an inflammatory or infective process given its absence on the CT scan. A follow-up CT scan was recommended.

The patient was referred to medical oncology to commence neo adjuvant chemotherapy and hormone therapy. Based on the response to therapy, the patient will be considered for bilateral mastectomy and axillary clearance.

Discharge Diagnosis: Advanced bilateral breast cancer with axillary node metastases

Medical Management: Neo adjuvant chemotherapy and hormone therapy

Disposition: The patient was referred to medical oncology to continue management and treatment.

Follow-up: The patient will be monitored closely by her medical oncology team for signs of adverse effects related to neo adjuvant chemotherapy and hormone therapy. A follow-up CT scan of the chest will be performed to ensure resolution of the ground glass pulmonary opacity.

The 2D echocardiogram, which was performed after three weeks of recovery, was normal.

Intravenous cefotaxime

The patient had complete recovery and was discharged with normal full blood count, renal and liver function tests.

The patient is advised to follow up with the healthcare provider if there are any signs of recurrence or further symptoms.

Gender: Female
Age: 35 years
Medical Record Number (MRN): [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the emergency room with abdominal distension mainly on the right side, abdominal tenderness, and sluggish bowel sounds. The patient had a history of three cesarean sections and known gastroesophageal reflux disease taking proton pump inhibitors. The initial treatment in the outpatient clinic with prescription laxatives was unsuccessful. Hematological tests revealed anemia and elevated platelet count, and radiological tests showed cecal volvulus with complete large bowel obstruction. An urgent exploratory laparotomy was performed, leading to a diagnosis of cecal volvulus with an axial rotation with serosal tears, which were repaired by right hemicolectomy and side-to-side anastomosis.

Hospital Outcome:

The patient was transferred to the surgical intensive care unit after the surgery and was extubated eight hours later. She was admitted to the intermediate care unit for two days for pain management and cardiorespiratory monitoring. The patient tolerated feeding on postoperative day two and bowel motion on postoperative day three. She was followed up at the outpatient department one week later and showed no symptoms and signs of nausea, vomiting, or constipation. The laparotomy scar was clean, and the abdomen was soft and lax with no incisional hernia.

Pathological Report:

The pathological examination revealed ischemic necrosis of the cecum consistent with a diagnosis of volvulus.

Summary:

The patient was admitted to the emergency room with abdominal distension, tenderness, and sluggish bowel sounds due to cecal volvulus with complete large bowel obstruction. The condition was diagnosed through radiological tests and an urgent exploratory laparotomy, leading to right hemicolectomy and side-to-side anastomosis. The patient was transferred to ICU for postoperative care and was then shifted to the intermediate care unit. The follow-up at the outpatient department one week later showed no symptoms or signs, and the laparotomy scar was clean with no incisional hernia. The pathological report confirmed the diagnosis of volvulus with ischemic necrosis of the cecum.

Diagnosis: Mucus Retention Cyst (MRC) of the Penis


Hospital Course:

The patient presented to our clinic with a complaint of a soft, painless swelling at the tip of the penis since childhood. Upon physical examination, a solitary, soft, translucent cystic lesion of about 2-cm diameter at the ventral aspect of the glans penis was observed. The results of the patient's urinalysis and hemogram were normal. Ultrasonography (USG) of the cyst was advised, which demonstrated an isoechoic cystic lesion at the tip of the penis, while the urethra was separated from the cyst. On the basis of clinical and USG findings, MRC of the penis was diagnosed.

The cyst was excised with the patient under local anesthesia. The whole specimen was sent for histopathological examination, which showed that the cyst wall was lined partly by ciliated, pseudostratified columnar epithelium and partly by columnar epithelium with apical mucin. The lamina propria showed mild chronic inflammatory infiltrates. No features of dysplasia or malignancy were noted.

The excised site healed without any residual effect, and there were no issues related to urination or sexual activities. Recurrence was not observed during the 2-year follow-up period.

The patient should continue to follow up with his primary care physician as recommended and report any new or concerning symptoms, as necessary.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

DOB: [REDACTED]

Sex: Male

Admission Date: August 2004

Discharge Date: N/A

Diagnosis Code: LHON (Leber hereditary optic neuropathy)

Clinical Summary:

The patient was a 35-year-old man diagnosed with bilateral JOAG (juvenile-onset open-angle glaucoma) and was first attended the clinic in August 2004. He did not have any previous systemic disease but had a family history of LHON (Leber hereditary optic neuropathy). Pachymetric measurements showed average corneal thickness and gonioscopy revealed a normal iridocorneal angle. Fundoscopic examination revealed paled optic disc with enlarged disc cupping of the optic nerves and sectorial excavation in both eyes. OCTA disclosed diffuse RNFL thinning, while ERG was revealed to be subnormal showing decreased N95 amplitudes in both eyes. The genetic test revealed an ND4 m11778G > A mtDNA mutation, which is pathognomonic for LHON.

Course of Hospitalization:

The patient received ongoing therapy with timolol 0.5%, and the IOP remained relatively stable throughout the hospitalization. The patient was also regularly monitored to assess the progression of the disease. The BCVA gradually decreased over time, with the patient's visual acuity reducing to 20/200 in both eyes in 2006 and counting fingers at 25-30 cm in both eyes in 2016. The VF (30–2 SITA standard) was characterized by progressive central scotoma in both eyes.

Medical Management:

The patient's treatment involved ongoing therapy with timolol 0.5% to control intraocular pressure. The medical team monitored the progression of the disease through regular OCTA and ERG tests. The patient was advised to seek treatment immediately if he experienced any further loss of visual acuity or central scotoma.

Future Treatment Plan:

The patient is recommended to continue medical management for LHON, which in this case, involved ongoing therapy with timolol 0.5%. The medical team recommends that the patient receives regular monitoring to assess the progression of the disease.

Summary:

The 35-year-old male had been diagnosed with biletral JOAG, with a family history of LHON. Multiple diagnostic tests were conducted to analyze the progression of his condition. The genetic test confirmed an ND4 m11778G > A mtDNA mutation, which is pathognomonic for LHON. The patient's BCVA gradually decreased, with the VF (30–2 SITA standard) characterized by progressive central scotoma in both eyes. Ongoing therapy with timolol 0.5% was the recommended treatment to control intraocular pressure. The medical team recommends regular monitoring of the patient to assess the disease's progression.

Patient was admitted for cough, fever, altered mental status, bibasilar infiltrates, and profuse polymorphonuclear leukocytes. Blood cultures and viral PCR were negative. The predominant bacteria identified from the sputum culture was Corynebacteria identified as C. propinquum by MALDI-TOF. Patient was treated with vancomycin and discharged to complete a 10-day course of linezolid.

Hospital Stay:
Patient responded well to treatment with no reported adverse reactions. The patient was discharged to continue with scheduled hemodialysis treatments.

Follow-up Care:
The patient was scheduled a follow-up appointment with his primary care physician in 2 weeks for monitoring. The patient was instructed to continue prescription medications as directed, monitor for any new symptoms, and follow-up with his healthcare providers if any concerns arise.

Summary:
Patient admitted for pneumonia attributed to C. propinquum identified by sputum culture. Treated with vancomycin and discharged to complete 10-day course of linezolid. Responded well to treatment with no reported adverse reactions. Discharged with follow-up appointment scheduled with primary care physician.

Hospital Course:
The patient, an 85-year-old woman with a right femur fracture, was admitted to the hospital for treatment. The fracture occurred after minor trauma and the patient had a history of right total hip arthroplasty and revision arthroplasty. The patient had also been taking alendronate for more than five years.

Assessment and Plan:
Radiographs showed localized thickening of the lateral femoral cortical bone and complete transverse fracture with internal spikes. The patient was diagnosed with Vancouver type B1 periprosthetic fracture. Open reduction and internal fixation were performed using a locking plate with cable grip. Bisphosphonate use was discontinued and the patient was prescribed weekly subcutaneous injections of 56.5 μg teriparatide and LIPUS. The patient was allowed non-weight-bearing exercise.

Progress and Follow-up:
At the three-month follow-up after surgery, the patient was using a wheelchair without pain and a radiograph revealed no displacement or loosening of the implants. The patient was discharged from the hospital in stable condition.

Discharge Summary

Patient: 10-month-old male infant
Hospital: Children's Hospital Zagreb


Admission Date: 2016
Discharge Date: N/A

Reason for admission: Delay in psycho-motoric development and megalencephaly

Chief Complaint:

The patient was referred to the Department of Pediatrics at Children's Hospital Zagreb due to a delay in the psycho-motoric development and megalencephaly. Extensive tests were conducted to diagnose the reason for the delay in development.

Hospital Course:

The clinical phenotype of the child was described as familial benign megalencephaly with both motor and sensory developmental delay, coupled with speech and language delay, stereotypical movements, unresponsiveness to name calling at the age of one, lack of sentence formation with a limited number of used words for age, short attention span, bad tolerance to frustration, and the onset of walking at 22 months. At the age of 1 year and 2 months, macrohematuria and proteinuria were recorded for the first time, with proteine/creatinine ratio of 284 mg/mmol. At the age of 2 years, he had proteinuiria 189 mg/mmol and severe microhematuria.

Diagnostic Tests:

Genetic, metabolic, cytogenetic, and neurologic workup were done to diagnose the reason for the developmental delay. A kidney biopsy was performed, which showed one out of 69 globally sclerosed glomeruli and 30% of immature/partly immature glomeruli. There was one small focus of interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy (IFTA) that affected 1% of the cortical parenchyma. Routine immunofluorescent analysis was unremarkable. Electron microscopy (EM) of the GBM showed areas of thinning and thickening. The thickened areas of GBM exhibited lamellation and basket-wave appearance. There was focal podocyte foot process effacement in the areas above the thickened and lamellated basement membranes. Kidney biopsy report concluded that the findings corresponded to AS and suggested genetic counseling and testing.

Treatment:

Ramipril treatment (6 mg/m2) reduced proteinuria to 73 mg/mmol creatinine; however, severe microhematuria persisted.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient is advised to follow up with the appropriate professionals for further evaluation and counseling.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Identification:
24-year-old female with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) presenting with multiple neck masses, fever, anemia, and profound thrombocytopenia.

Hospital Course:
The patient was initially diagnosed with CML based on bone marrow (BM) smear image, cytogenetic karyotype, and the BCR/ABL fusion transcript. She was treated with hydroxyurea and then imatinib with some success. However, she was readmitted to the hospital with multiple lymphadenopathies and progressive swelling, indicating blast crisis involving T cells. The BM showed marked hyperplasia with more than 20% blasts. The patient was treated with dasatinib and showed a significant decrease in the WBC. However, she stopped taking the medication and died two months after blast crisis treatment.

Diagnosis:
Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) with blast crisis involving T cells.

Treatment:
The patient was treated with hydroxyurea, then imatinib (400mg/day), and finally, dasatinib. The dasatinib treatment showed a significant decrease in the WBC. However, the patient stopped taking the medication and died two months after blast crisis treatment.

Follow-up:
The patient died two months after blast crisis treatment.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: _____
Age: 52
Gender: Female

Clinical Course:
The patient was admitted to our hospital for further investigation of a right breast mass that was noticed during routine breast examination. The patient had a medical history of early gastric cancer and early esophageal cancer, and a family history of breast cancer and gastric cancer. Mammography showed a 1.5-cm coarse heterogeneously high-density calcified lesion at the upper outer portion of the right breast. Ultrasonography revealed a hypoechoic mass containing multiple calcifications with relatively smooth borders.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the tumor showed small clusters of either normal or benign epithelial cells without any marked atypia. Since no malignancy was noted, a core needle biopsy was not performed. However, the patient was followed up regularly.

About 8 months later, mammography revealed a slight enlargement of the coarse calcification, but US showed the same size tumor. About 13 months after the first medical examination, the mass had grown to 2.3 cm in size, and after another 3 months, it had grown to 4.5 cm, and new coarse calcifications that were irregular in shape and different in density from the initial one appeared around the enlarged original coarse calcified tumor on mammography.

MRI showed a 4.5-cm mass at the upper outer portion of the right breast. A core needle biopsy showed a nodule with bone formation that was not malignant. The pathology report showed extraskeletal osteosarcoma of the breast.

Treatment and Management:
The patient received doxorubicin and ifosfamide (AI, three cycles) as adjuvant chemotherapy, and then underwent additional resection with latissimus dorsi flap reconstruction. She resumed AI (two cycles), but at 16 months from the first extirpation procedure, multiple lung metastases appeared, and her treatment was changed to doxorubicin and cisplatin (AP, two cycles). The lung metastatic lesions grew, and the treatment was changed again to trabectedin (seven cycles), but it had no effect. She is currently receiving eribulin and radiotherapy for multiple lung metastases.

Follow-up:
The patient is advised to continue regular follow-up care and further management with the oncology team. The patient and her family have been counseled on the diagnosis, prognosis, and future treatment plan. The patient understands the importance of regular follow-up care and has been advised to report any new symptoms or changes in her condition.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 54-year-old female, was admitted to the hospital with symptoms of intestinal obstruction. She underwent exploratory laparotomy and sigmoid colectomy, and the histopathology report revealed moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma with tumor metastasis. The patient underwent extensive evaluation by gynecology and urology departments to identify the source of malignancy, which was negative. The patient recovered well from the surgery and was discharged for follow-up.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was admitted with symptoms of intestinal obstruction and underwent exploratory laparotomy and sigmoid colectomy, due to an exophytic sigmoid colon tumor proliferating extraluminally with small bowel adhesions. Histopathology report revealed moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma with tumor metastasis, for which the patient underwent extensive evaluations by gynecology and urology departments to identify the source of malignancy which were negative. The patient recovered well from the surgery with parental nutrition support and was ambulatory with oral feeds on 7th postoperative day. A subsequent CT Scan of the abdomen suggested a small fluid collection at the site of surgical anastomosis with few air pockets suggesting abscess formation/leakage and concomitant ascites and pleural effusion. Wound infection was treated with regular dressings initially and later vacuum dressing was applied. After improvements in health, enteral nutrition and wound, the patient was discharged for follow-up to the surgical team.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: Female in her fifties
Reason for Admission: Jaundice and stenosis of the inferior bile duct
Diagnosis: Pancreatic head cancer; Celiac Trunk Stenosis due to Median Arcuate Ligament Syndrome (MALS)

Hospital Course: The patient underwent a successful surgery, SSPPD, for pancreatic head cancer. Pre-operative CT angiography showed stenosis of the celiac trunk which was due to MALS. During the operation, the median arcuate ligament was released to confirm improvement of the hepatic blood flow. Post-operative CT angiography showed improvement of the celiac trunk stenosis. No post-operative complications were reported. The patient was discharged 15 days post-operation.

Follow-Up: Follow-up appointments should be scheduled as recommended by the treating physician.

Instructions: The patient should continue to rest and avoid strenuous activities. It is important to continue with all medications as prescribed by the treating physician. Any new symptoms or concerns should be immediately reported to the physician.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Age: 14 years
Sex: Female

History of present illness:
The patient presented to the department of endodontics with a complaint of painful swelling in the right maxillary region for two months. Clinical examination revealed a sinus tract associated with tooth #8, while the clinical crown of tooth #7 was unusual with a pronounced lingual cusp and deep lingual pit.

Past medical history:
The patient's past medical history was noncontributory.

Hospital course:
An ISO #40.02 gutta-percha was inserted through the sinus opening, confirming tooth #7 as the lesioned tooth. A radiographic examination of tooth #7 revealed a lateral radiolucency and confirmed the presence of a dens invaginatus (DI). Tooth #7 was diagnosed as DI with pulp necrosis and chronic apical periodontitis. Endodontic treatment and microscopic removal of DI was planned, and the possibility of the endodontic surgical intervention was also explained to the patient’s parents.
Endodontic access was started with a round diamond bur, followed by troughing of the DI with an ET20 ultrasonic tip. The DI was then engaged with an H-file and gently removed. The root canal was irrigated with 5% sodium hypochlorite and calcium hydroxide paste was placed into the canal for two weeks. After two weeks, the patient was asymptomatic and the sinus tract was resolved. Final obturation of the root canals was performed with Schilder’s warm vertical compaction technique. The final coronal restoration was accomplished using composite resin. At the 2-year follow-up, the tooth was asymptomatic and the periapical radiograph showed complete healing of periapical radiolucency of tooth #7.

Summary:
The patient, a 14-year-old female, presented with a complaint of painful swelling in the right maxillary region for two months. Clinical examination revealed a sinus tract associated with tooth #8, while the clinical crown of tooth #7 was unusual with a pronounced lingual cusp and deep lingual pit. Tooth #7 was diagnosed with dens invaginatus (DI) with pulp necrosis and chronic apical periodontitis. Endodontic treatment and microscopic removal of DI were performed followed by calcium hydroxide paste placement and final obturation with Schilder’s warm vertical compaction technique. At the 2-year follow-up, the tooth was asymptomatic, and the periapical radiograph showed complete healing of periapical radiolucency of tooth #7.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Provided Patient Name]
Gender: Male
Age: 54 years
Admission Date: [Provided Date]
Discharge Date: [Provided Date]

Diagnosis:
1. Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) with overlapping hypotensive phase and oliguric phase
2. Hormonal deficiency resulting from secondary hypoadrenalism and hypogonadism

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with symptoms of fever, headache, and backache along with ocular pain, dizziness, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Upon physical examination, the patient had low blood pressure and conjunctival suffusion. Laboratory test results showed increased liver enzymes, abnormal renal function, positive RT-PCR Hantaan virus test result, and positive Hantaan virus antibody IgM result. The patient was diagnosed with overlapping hypotensive phase and oliguric phase of HFRS. After receiving supportive treatment, the patient progressed into the diuretic phase within a week. The regular blood cell test result was normal, but the patient developed symptoms of hormonal deficiency, which were confirmed by abnormal pituitary function test results and brain MRI. The patient's symptoms improved with hormone replacement therapy (hydrocortisone, L-thyroxine, and testosterone) and the only discomfort – fatigue – disappeared 1 month later.  

Condition at Discharge:
The patient was discharged with normal pituitary function and urine output. The patient was advised to follow-up on hormone replacement therapy and maintain a healthy lifestyle.

Follow-up:
The patient should schedule regular follow-up appointments with an endocrinologist to monitor the hormonal deficiency resulting from secondary hypoadrenalism and hypogonadism. Additionally, the patient should receive routine medical check-ups to prevent any reoccurrences of HFRS. 

Disposition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with instructions for follow-up and self-care.

Discharge Summary

Patient: Nine-year-old Hispanic female with a history of autism and developmental delay

Hospital Course:

The patient presented to the emergency department with complaints of extremity pain that had been ongoing for the past year. The pain initially started in the right leg and was managed with supramalleolar/ankle foot orthosis. However, she developed episodic pain in her bilateral upper extremities a month later. Laboratory evaluations revealed elevated alkaline phosphatase and low serum calcium levels, leading to the diagnosis of severe hypocalcemic rickets due to vitamin D deficiency.

During her hospitalization, the patient was treated with calcium carbonate and calcitriol therapy followed by gradual supplementation of vitamin D3, which led to significant improvement of pain and gait issues. She was followed by endocrinology and taken off calcitriol with normalization of calcium and serum levels. She had improved dietary calcium intake with supplemental nutritional shakes and remained on 2,000 IU of vitamin D3 daily.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Severe hypocalcemic rickets due to vitamin D deficiency

Discharge Medications:
None listed

Discharge Follow-up:
The patient will need to follow up with her primary care doctor and endocrinologist for continued monitoring of her condition and dietary needs.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient and her family should continue to ensure adequate dietary calcium intake and supplement with vitamin D3 as prescribed. It is important for the patient to follow up regularly with her physicians to ensure continued improvement and monitoring of her condition.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 57-year-old female, presented to the hospital with vision loss in the left eye after endoscopic DCR surgery. During preoperative evaluation, the patient's medical history was notable for thrombocytopenia and MHA. The patient's BCVA was 20/20 in the right eye and light perception in the left eye at the time of admission. The patient's eye exam revealed mild periorbital bruising and swelling in the left eye and mild maxillary sinusitis. The use of fluorescent angiography did not reveal any leakage or a filling defect at the disc. Multiple tests were performed for underlying diseases. The patient's platelet count was low, and she was transfused with six units of platelets preoperatively.

Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with left optic neuropathy, which was confirmed by a pattern visual evoked potential that revealed delayed P100 latency. Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbit showed a focal hyperintensity within the intra-orbital segment of the left optic nerve on the T2-weighted image and flair image. The MRI showed an enhancement on the T1 post-contrast imaging.

Treatment:

The patient was given 1 g/day of intravenous methylprednisolone for 3 days, followed by 1 mg/kg/day of oral prednisone with subsequent dose tapering. The patient's vision improved to 20/30, but she was left with a visual field defect in the left eye.

Follow-up:

The patient was discharged in stable condition and instructed to follow up with an ophthalmologist for continued care. The patient was also advised to continue taking prednisone as prescribed.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the emergency department with complaints of bilateral lower extremity swelling and abdominal discomfort of two weeks duration. Further evaluation revealed a large soft-tissue mass with internal vascularity in the liver, small hypodense lesions throughout the liver parenchyma, bilateral suprarenal soft-tissue masses, and sclerotic lesions in the pelvis and lower thoracic spine. The patient was diagnosed with high-grade diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with C-MYC positivity and ki-67 reactivity greater than 90%. The patient received ART for HIV and was started on chemotherapy consisting of etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and rituximab. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, the patient developed neutropenia and neuropathic pain of the hands and feet. The patient was treated with G-CSF until the neutropenia resolved. The patient was readmitted after an echocardiogram showed decreased left ventricular ejection fraction. The patient was started on Carvedilol and Lisinopril and completed cycles 2-4 of chemotherapy. Repeat echocardiogram showed improvement in left ventricular ejection fraction to 45-49%. Outpatient PET-CT showed complete radiologic response and the patient was advised to follow-up with medical oncology in 3 months.

Course of Treatment:
The patient received antiretroviral therapy for HIV and chemotherapy consisting of etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, rituximab, and a double dose of doxorubicin until cardiomyopathy developed. The doses of cyclophosphamide and etoposide were increased by 20% without complications. G-CSF was used to treat neutropenia and Carvedilol and Lisinopril were used to treat doxorubicin-induced cardiomyopathy.

Follow-up Care:
The patient was advised to follow-up with medical oncology in 3 months.

Summary:
The patient presented to the emergency department with symptoms of high-grade diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, which was treated with antiretroviral therapy and chemotherapy consisting of etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, rituximab, and doxorubicin until cardiomyopathy developed. The patient received follow-up care and was advised to follow-up with medical oncology in 3 months.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: N/A
Sex: Male
Date of Admission: N/A
Date of Discharge: N/A
Admitting Physician: N/A

Hospital Course:
The patient was a 26-year-old male who presented to the emergency department at Hamad Medical Corporation complaining of severe colicky epigastric and right upper quadrant abdominal pain, radiating to the back, associated with two episodes of vomiting and constipation. He had a past surgical history of open appendectomy during adolescence and was currently on oral medications for sciatica (prednisolone 5 mg BID for one-week, Naproxen 225 mg BID and Gabapentin 300 mg daily). Otherwise, he had no comorbidities, and the other systemic review was unremarkable. No recent travel or interaction with sick contacts was mentioned at the initial encounter at the emergency department.

Initial vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed severe epigastric and right upper abdomen tenderness. Initial labs including CBC, complete metabolic panel were within normal range. Imaging including abdomen and chest x-rays, and CT angiogram abdomen were normal. However, US abdomen showed gallbladder sludge but with no signs of cholecystitis. The patient was admitted by the surgical team with an initial diagnosis of possible persistent biliary colic.

During the night of admission day, the patient was still having severe colicky pain that required high doses of opioids, paracetamol and NSAIDs. A repeat set of all labs were undertaken and due to the colicky nature and persistent severe pain, a CT with oral contrast was done to exclude proximal bowel obstruction that might not have shown on the previous CT with IV contrast. The CT was normal, and the labs showed slightly rising transaminases (AST 94 IU, ALT 95 IU). The patient was kept nil per oral, on pain medications with IV hydration, and a repeat set of labs were ordered to be done in 8 hours. During that time, the patient started to develop, for the first time, a few vesicles on the chest wall, his liver enzymes were rising (AST 375 IU, ALT 263 IU), and other labs were normal.

The diagnosis of VZV hepatitis was immediately considered and the medical team was involved. Full hepatitis work up was undertaken and viral panel came out to be positive for VZV PCR, but other (metabolic, toxicology, viral) workups for hepatitis were negative. Thus, acyclovir was started by the infectious disease team. On day 2, the patient was shifted to the ICU as he was developing confusion, high INR, DIC, and multiorgan failure that progressed rapidly despite all supportive measures. The patient died on day 3.

Summary:
The patient presented with severe colicky epigastric and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. He was admitted with an initial diagnosis of possible persistent biliary colic. During the admission, he developed a few vesicles on the chest wall, and his liver enzymes were rising, and he was diagnosed with VZV hepatitis. The patient was started on acyclovir by the infectious disease team. Unfortunately, he developed multi-organ failure and died on day 3 of admission despite all supportive measures.

Hospital Course:

This 48-year-old-male presented to the emergency room with recurrent angina that was described as pressure-like, substernal, and radiating to both arms. The patient had a history of inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) status post percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stent (DES) to the distal right coronary artery (RCA) eight months prior. His angina occurred at rest and was alleviated with sublingual nitroglycerin. His family history did not have any history of premature coronary artery disease or of sudden cardiac death. He never smoked and rarely consumed alcohol. His initial serum troponin was elevated, and the patient was diagnosed with non-STEMI.

Treatment and Management:

The patient was started on heparin infusion per acute coronary syndrome (ACS) protocol and underwent left heart catheterization, which revealed severe focal stenosis just proximal to the previously placed stent. A decision to perform PCI was made. After guidewire passage into the RCA, acute spasm developed, resulting in diffuse, severe stenosis, extending over previously normal segments to the proximal RCA. This completely resolved with intracoronary nicardipine and nitroglycerin. The patient was diagnosed with vasospastic angina (VSA) and was continued on guideline-directed medical therapy with dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT), statin, and beta-blocker (BB) with the addition of the non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (CCB), verapamil.

The patient then had intermittent angina despite the treatment, and various second CCBs were added, including a dihydropyridine CCB, but intermittent angina continued. At this point, the patient was diagnosed with refractory VSA. Clonidine (alpha-2-agonist) was also tried, with no benefit. Eventually, a nitroglycerin patch was added with reduced headaches and a modest decrease in the frequency of angina episodes.

Follow-up:

The patient was instructed to follow up with his cardiologist to monitor signs and symptoms of angina and to adjust his treatment accordingly. The patient should continue to take his prescribed medications and maintain healthy lifestyle habits, including smoking cessation and limited alcohol consumption. The patient was discharged with a good understanding of vasospastic angina (VSA) and the importance of medical compliance and follow-up care.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Medical Record Number: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with Takayasu arteritis, a rare form of vasculitis. The patient was initially treated with methotrexate and prednisolone, but she relapsed after two months of treatment, resulting in the addition of tocilizumab (TCZ)-SC and an increase in prednisolone from 15 mg to 100 mg. While tapering prednisolone in the following 4 months, the patient suffered from two minor and one major relapse. Prednisolone was increased from 15 mg to 100 mg, and TCZ-SC was switched to TCZ-IV. Since the switch, no further relapse occurred during a follow-up of 20 months, and prednisolone could be tapered to 4 mg.

Diagnosis:

The patient is diagnosed with Takayasu arteritis.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted for Takayasu arteritis and received treatment with methotrexate and prednisolone. However, the patient relapsed twice during corticosteroid tapering. TCZ-SC was added to treatment, and prednisolone was increased to 100 mg. The patient suffered few relapses during this period, requiring corticosteroid pulses. Due to a lack of improvement with TCZ-SC, she was switched to TCZ-IV. No further relapse occurred during the 20-month follow-up, and prednisolone could be tapered to 4 mg.

Discharge Medications:

Not applicable.

Discharge Condition:

The patient was discharged in stable condition.

Discharge Instructions:

Follow-up appointments with the treating rheumatologist are recommended. Close attention should also be paid to any relapse in symptoms, and urgent medical attention should be sought in any such events.

Hospital Course Summary:

This is an 18-year-old female patient who was admitted to the hospital at 34 weeks of gestation due to fever, malaise, and otalgia. She presented with hepatitis which worsened over time, resulting in coagulopathy and seizures. The patient was started on empiric antibiotics but her condition continued to worsen despite treatment. She delivered an infant by C-section five days following admission, but unfortunately, the mother passed away due to liver necrosis four days after delivery. Her autopsy revealed the presence of HSV in cultures from her liver, rectum, and throat, the type of which was not specified. Her HSV antibody levels were negative upon admission but became positive on hospital day eight. Unfortunately, the infant also had an unfavorable outcome, developing hyaline membrane disease of prematurity and intraventricular hemorrhage, ultimately passing away two days after delivery. The infant tested negative for HSV.

During her hospitalization, the patient's medical team provided supportive treatment, with appropriate measures taken, while also managing her seizures. Despite this, her condition did not improve and she ultimately passed away. The infant was also provided with appropriate medical care for his medical issues but also had an unfortunate outcome. The family was provided with counseling and support services during this difficult time.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information: The patient is a 53-year-old African-American female with a history of uterine fibroids.

Hospital Course: The patient presented with a two-month history of nausea, vomiting, nervousness, weight gain, and left lower quadrant abdominal pain. Physical examination revealed a soft, non-distended abdomen with pain upon deep palpation localized to the left lower quadrant. She was found to have a bilaterally enlarged thyroid gland consistent with a goiter and was diagnosed with hyperthyroidism. The patient was started on antithyroid medications. Additionally, an abdominal CT scan showed an enlarged uterus along with fibroids, a hemorrhagic cyst of the right ovary, and a teratoma of the left ovary. Beta-hCG intact levels were measured twice, showing a value greater than 450,000mIU/mL. The patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. Tissue diagnosis confirmed the ovarian teratoma with sections of the myometrial wall containing massive hydropic chorionic villi. It was consistent with the presentation of a complete hydatidiform mole. The patient underwent chemotherapy and monitored for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. Post-surgical management included thyroid hormone level monitoring and continued low-dose methimazole. The patient reported no symptoms and had a normal thyroid hormone level one month following surgery. The patient has sought treatment at the Mayo Clinic and the results are negative. The methimazole was then discontinued.

Diagnoses: Hyperthyroidism, Uterine fibroids, Hemorrhagic cyst of the right ovary, Teratoma of the left ovary, Complete hydatidiform mole

Discharge Medications: Methimazole (discontinued)

Follow Up: The patient was advised to follow up with her primary care physician for routine monitoring of her thyroid hormone level and for any issues related to her previous diagnoses.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 53
Sex: Male

Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Reason for Admission:
Patient presented with an incidental finding of a mass on an MRI scan of the neck.

Hospital Course:
The patient underwent an excision procedure to remove the mass found on the MRI scan. The procedure was successful, and the patient recovered without any complications. An irregular, moderately firm, encapsulated fatty mass was removed. Microscopically, the mass was identified as a hibernoma containing numerous areas of brown fat with small foci of admixed skeletal muscle.

Clinical Findings:
The patient was asymptomatic and did not show any signs of discomfort or pain. On physical examination, there were no palpable masses.

Impression/ Diagnosis:
The MRI scan revealed a 2.5 × 3.8 × 4.2 cm lobulated mass within the right semispinalis capitis muscle. The excision procedure identified the mass as a hibernoma.

Plan:
The patient has successfully undergone an excision procedure to remove the identified hibernoma mass. No further treatment or follow-up was necessary.

Summary:
The 53-year-old male was admitted following an incidental finding of a mass on an MRI scan of the neck. Following an excision procedure, a lobulated mass within the right semispinalis capitis muscle was identified as a hibernoma. The patient recovered without any complications and was discharged without any further treatment or follow-up necessary.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 66-year-old male who was admitted to our hospital for a workup of an abnormal tumor in the upper lobe of the left lung and a right adrenal hemorrhage. The enhanced CT scan showed a massive shadow in the left lung S1 + 2 progressing to S6 beyond the lung lobe, with a maximum diameter of about 42 mm, and a right adrenal hematoma with no active bleeding. The patient’s laboratory data revealed mild anemia, a slight elevation of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), and neuron-specific enolase (NSE). A bronchoscopic trans-bronchial lung biopsy showed no evidence of malignancy. A CT-guided percutaneous needle biopsy was performed, and the pathological examination revealed a non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that was suspected to be a pleomorphic carcinoma. The adrenal lesion was diagnosed as a nonfunctional tumor based on endocrine examinations and adrenal medulla scintigraphy (123I-MIBG). 18-Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) showed the accumulation of FDG not only in the left lung nodule but also in the right adrenal one. Based on the results, the clinical stage was classified as cT2bN0M1b, stage IV.

Treatment:

To reduce the risk of rebleeding from adrenal metastasis, the patient underwent a right adrenalectomy. As the adrenal metastasis was an oligometastasis, a complete resection of the primary lung cancer was considered possible. A pathological analysis of the lung tumor demonstrated areas of atypical cells with eosinophilic cytoplasms as well as a sarcomatous component with extensive necrosis. Immunohistochemistry revealed that the tumor cells were positive for cytokeratin AE1/3, CAM5.2, CK7, and p63 (partial) but negative for 34βE12, CK20, TTF-1, calretinin, and D2-40. The adrenal tumor was similar in pathologic and immunohistochemical analyses. The final diagnosis was pleomorphic carcinoma of the lung with an adrenal metastasis, pT2bN0M1b, stage IV.

Discharge Summary:

The patient was discharged in a stable condition. He received chemotherapy as stage IV NSCLC but decided to quit intravenous chemotherapy after two courses due to adverse events including general malaise and anorexia. He refused to take TS-1 due to his fear of adverse events and chose to take UFT (600 mg/day) for 2 years instead. He has survived without any recurrences for 6 years since the surgery.

Diagnosis: 

Pleomorphic carcinoma of the lung with an adrenal metastasis, pT2bN0M1b, stage IV.

Discharge Medications:

None.

Follow-Up Care:

The patient will be scheduled for regular follow-up appointments to assess his condition and monitor any potential recurrences.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

Admission Diagnosis: Occupancy lesion in the left lower lobe

Summary of Hospital Course:

The patient, a 53-year-old male, was admitted to the hospital with a persistent cough and blood in the phlegm. Plain CT imaging revealed an occupancy lesion in the left lower lobe, which indicated a potential lung neoplasm. Subsequently, the patient underwent a dual-source CT scan that showed the lesion to be an anomalous systemic arterial supply (ASA) originating from the descending aorta with a saccular aneurysm in the basal segments of the left lower lobe. Further investigation using the intelligent/interactive qualitative and quantitative analysis (IQQA) 3D reconstruction system and its web-based workstation helped to fully understand the morphology and spatial position of the structures.

The patient experienced significant improvement in symptoms with medical treatment and was discharged with instructions to continue with prescribed medications. The risk of conservative measures was explained to the patient, and they were advised to follow up with their primary care physician for further monitoring.

Discharge Diagnosis: Anomalous systemic arterial supply to normal basal segments of the left lower lobe

Follow-up Recommendations: The patient has been advised to attend regular follow-up appointments with their primary care physician for ongoing monitoring and management of their condition.

HOSPITAL COURSE SUMMARY

Patient PS was admitted to the hospital after presenting with oppressive and burning chest pain, with irradiation to the left upper limb and chin, associated with nausea and insidious diaphoresis, which he had been experiencing for six months after high-intensity exercise. He had sought emergency care several times during this time, and resting electrocardiograms (ECGs) had shown altered ventricular repolarization (ARV) in the lower wall with small Q waves and T wave inversion. Echocardiography revealed slight segmental disturbance in the left ventricular wall contractility at rest. During hospital admission, the patient presented regular general conditions and high systolic blood pressure. Serial ECGs demonstrated the same changes as those described in a previous resting ECG during typical chest pain crises, and after risk stratification, the patient underwent coronary angiography that showed thrombosis in a large, large, non-lesioned anterior descending artery (ADA) with major extensions and thick caliber, a non-dominant, non-injured circumflex artery (ACX) with a short extension and large caliber leading to a moderately important atrioventricular branch, and large SCAD with a large caliber apparently ectasized occluded with multiple thrombus images and collateral circulation present with other uninjured arteries. Primary coronary transluminal angioplasty (TCA) was performed with the removal of a large number of thrombi and a lesion with 100% occlusion began demonstrating some irregularities and a final TIMI 2 flow, characterizing the condition as non-ST-segment acute myocardial infarction (STEMI).

The patient was discharged one week after the event with no further symptoms. Simvastatin 40 mg, 50 mg atenolol, clopidogrel 75 mg, and enalapril 10 mg were prescribed once per day, and the patient remained using medication for two and a half years before discontinuing use on his own. The patient remained asymptomatic and practicing moderate-intensity exercise for another two and a half years. After five years since the primary event, there was a recurrence of chest pain and associated symptoms a few hours after intense and strenuous physical activity, and he was diagnosed with a new STEMI and measures for ACS with consequent stratification to perform a new coronary angiography that, once again, showed thrombosis in SCAD, without collateral circulation for SCAD from the left coronary. He underwent TCA, with dilation and aspiration of intraluminal thrombi. The patient was discharged 10 days after hospitalization and prescribed daily warfarin 5 mg, clopidogrel 75 mg, and Ramipril 5 mg. Other causes of coronary obstruction were disregarded in an in-hospital investigation, and the patient remains on medication and performs high-intensity physical activities to this day without symptoms.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 68-year-old Japanese male who had a subtotal esophagectomy with three-field lymph node dissection and the removal of the remnant stomach with the abdominal lymph nodes due to intrathoracic esophageal cancer (T3, N2, M0, stage III) history. The alimentary continuity was reconstructed with a pedicled jejunal limb through the antethoracic route. The surgery was successful, and the patient was discharged four weeks postoperatively.

The patient was readmitted to the hospital six months post-surgery because of abdominal discomfort and vomiting. The patient was diagnosed with Intrathoracic Pedunculated Herniation (IPDH) after an enteral contrast study showed a bird’s beak deformity. A Computed Tomography scan of the thoracoabdominal region confirmed that the reconstructed jejunum was in the pericardium anterior to the heart. An emergency laparotomy was performed, and it was found that the reconstructed jejunum had herniated into the pericardium through an approximately 4-cm-diameter diaphragmatic defect without a hernia sac. The herniation was easily reduced, and the congestion of the incarcerated jejunum resolved. Primary closure of the diaphragmatic defect was accomplished using vertical mattress sutures with 1–0 silk. The diaphragm adhered to the pericardium around the diaphragmatic defect; thus, these were closed together. To reinforce the closure of the diaphragmatic defect, an 8 x 6 cm graft from the rectus abdominis posterior sheath was used, and interrupted sutures with 3–0 nylon were placed to fix the graft to the diaphragmatic defect.

The postoperative upper gastrointestinal study confirmed free flow of contrast medium from the cervical esophagus into the intra-abdominal jejunum through the pedicled jejunum. The patient had an uneventful recovery, and he was discharged on the seventh postoperative day.

Diagnosis:

Intrathoracic Pedunculated Herniation (IPDH)

Procedures:

- Subtotal esophagectomy with three-field lymph node dissection
- Removal of remnant stomach with abdominal lymph nodes
- Hernia reduction
- Primary closure of diaphragmatic defect using vertical mattress suture with 1-0 silk
- Use of an 8 x 6 cm graft from the rectus abdominis posterior sheath
- Interrupted sutures with 3-0 nylon to fix the graft to the diaphragmatic defect

Condition at Discharge:

The patient was in stable condition with no complaints of abdominal discomfort or vomiting. The patient's vital signs were unremarkable. The patient was given postoperative instructions and advised on further follow-up appointments with his primary care physician.

Follow-up:

The patient was advised to schedule a follow-up appointment with his primary care physician to monitor his progress.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted as an emergency to the hospital due to sudden loss of consciousness. The MSCT scan of the brain showed the presence of an intracerebral hematoma in the temporobasal region with the penetration of blood into the ventricular system. The patient had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 8 on admission with right-side hemiplegia and sensorimotor aphasia.

Diagnosis and Treatment:

An urgent angiography revealed that the patient had a duplicated left Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA), which merged in the area of the M2 segment, and immediately divided into the dorsal and ventral branches. The dorsal branch of the MCA duplication was found to have a 6x4mm aneurysm. In addition, a 4x3mm aneurysm was detected in the area between the dorsal branch of the DMCA and the origin of the left Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA). Another aneurysm was detected on the distal part of the left ACA. The patient underwent emergency surgical intervention using the pterional approach. Intraoperative findings showed that a clear MCA duplication was present, with both branches of the MCA and the initial segment of the ACA being of almost identical diameters. The branches of the DMCA merged at the level of the insular segment of the MCA, and normal branching of the MCA in the dorsal-frontal and ventral-temporal branches was found. The 6x4mm ruptured aneurysm was located in the central part of the dorsal branch of the DMCA, and had a perforating branch arising from the neck. Two smaller aneurysmal changes were observed – one in the ICA bifurcation area between the initial segment of the ACA and the dorsal branch of the DMCA, and another one on the distal part of the ACA. All three aneurysms were clipped. At the very origin of the ICA bifurcation, in the area between the MCA duplications, a caruncule was observed with the perforating branches arising from it. This lesion was wrapped and the intracerebral hematoma was removed. 

Follow-Up:

A second angiogram was performed 7 days after surgery, which showed that the aneurysms were occluded but there was evidence of vasospasm. After stabilization, the patient was transferred to a rehabilitation center where she remained for 6 months. An examination performed after 6 months showed hemiparesis and aphasia. 

Conclusion:

The patient had a duplicated left MCA with aneurysms located in multiple areas, which led to a sudden loss of consciousness and hemiplegia. Emergency surgery yielded successful outcomes by removing the intracerebral hematoma and clipping all aneurysms. However, the patient continued to exhibit neurological deficits after 6 months.

Discharge Summary:

This is a case report of a 41-year-old male who presented with a nonfunctioning thyroid nodule and subsequently underwent hemithyroidectomy with left recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy as a postoperative complication. Histopathological examination reported the presence of a follicular adenoma without any evidence of malignancy. However, in November 2018, the patient experienced disabling acute symptoms that required high doses of analgesic drugs. An 18F-FDG PET/CT scan revealed several bone lesions with evidence of DTC metastases on histological examination. He was diagnosed with RAI-refractory disease and treated with TKI Levantinib.

After three cycles of treatment, a new 18F-FDG PET/CT scan showed a reduction in the size of lesions, mainly in the soft tissue component, and serum thyroglobulin levels also decreased. Based on this response, conventional treatment was considered suitable, and the patient underwent resection of the thyroid gland remnant with no postoperative complications and no evidence of malignancy on the histopathological exam. Subsequently, RAI treatment was performed, which detected disease only in the tumor bed as well as isolated vertebral metastasis. Later, multiple foci of metastasis in the axial and peripheral skeleton were observed. 

Regarding adverse events, the patient experienced hypertension, diarrhea, transient low-grade stomatitis, neutropenia grade II, and moderate to severe palmar-plantar erythrodysaesthesia. Treatment was adjusted accordingly. 

The patient is now being discharged in stable condition with continued follow-up appointments and a plan for ongoing management of his condition.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 40-year-old woman with a past medical history of hypertension and severe endometriosis, was admitted to the hospital due to a serum creatinine of 17 mg/dL and BUN of 86 mg/dL. A renal sonogram was performed which showed moderate hydronephrosis with hydroureter compressed by a large myomatous uterus. The patient underwent a hysterectomy which resulted in an improvement in renal function, but did not fully normalize. However, the patient continued to experience multiple bouts of AKI and progressive CKD for the next several years.

Significant Findings:
During the course of the hospitalization, a colonoscopy was performed due to an episode of lower gastrointestinal bleeding, which revealed a mass at the rectosigmoid junction. This was later confirmed to be colonic endometriosis. Leuprolide was initiated for the patient. These findings were significant in determining the patient's diagnosis and treatment plan.

Diagnosis:
Based on the findings, the patient was diagnosed with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) and was placed on maintenance hemodialysis. The patient's ongoing history of severe endometriosis was also a contributing factor in the development of her renal illness.

Treatment:
The patient underwent a hysterectomy to relieve compression on her urinary tract caused by myomatous uterus. She was also initiated on leuprolide for treatment of colonic endometriosis. As a result of her ESRD, the patient was placed on maintenance hemodialysis.

Consultations:
Multiple consultations were obtained during the course of the hospitalization including a gynecologist for the hysterectomy, a gastroenterologist for the colonoscopy, and a nephrologist for the management of the patient's ESRD and AKI.

Follow-up:
The patient was transported to an outpatient hemodialysis center for ongoing hemodialysis treatments. She was scheduled for follow-up with her nephrologist for continued management of her ESRD and AKI.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Suspected Acute Coronary Syndrome

Hospital course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with a complaint of left-sided chest pain with associated nausea and vomiting. On physical examination, she complained of pressure in her jaw and experienced lightheadedness. She was brought to the emergency department by emergency medical services (EMS) after being administered an injection of polidocanol. On arrival to the hospital, her electrocardiogram showed T-wave inversions, and her troponin I level was elevated to 0.62 ng/mL. Her cardiac enzymes were monitored, and six hours after admission, her troponin I level had increased to 2.26 ng/mL. She was started on continuous unfractionated intravenous heparin and remained asymptomatic. Echocardiogram and nuclear stress testing confirmed an ejection fraction of 50% with the presence of apical hypokinesis and Grade II diastolic dysfunction. The stress test further revealed an akinetic cardiac apex and a severe-intensity, fixed defect. The patient was later diagnosed with Takotsubo syndrome, and her cardiac catheterization was performed to rule out any underlying cardiac event.

Clinical course:
The patient's chest pain returned during the stress test, accompanied by shortness of breath, and her ECG showed deeper T-wave inversions compared to the initial presentation. CT angiogram ruled out any underlying pulmonary embolism or aortic dissection as a potential source of her pain. The patient underwent cardiac catheterization, and the procedure established that all vessels were patent, ruling out acute ischemic event and atherosclerotic disease as the source of her symptoms.

Discharge instructions:
The patient was discharged home on aspirin 81 mg and simvastatin 20 mg for preventative purposes, with instructions to follow up for a repeat echocardiogram as an outpatient. The patient and her family were educated on healthy lifestyle measures aimed at reducing the risk of heart disease, including a healthy diet, regular physical activity, and smoking cessation. She was instructed to immediately report any new or worsening symptoms to her primary care physician or specialist. A referral to cardiology was made, with the intention of long-term management and monitoring of her cardiac condition.

Summary:
This was a 66-year-old female admitted with suspected acute coronary syndrome. The initial workup revealed T-wave inversions in ECG and elevated cardiac enzymes. She was later diagnosed with Takotsubo syndrome, and her cardiac catheterization was negative for any underlying cardiac event. The patient was discharged home on preventative medication, instructed on healthy lifestyle measures, with a referral for long-term cardiac follow-up. The patient was conscious, alert, and ambulatory on discharge.
