Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to [Hospital Name] with a chief complaint of a painless left scrotal mass. The patient had no significant past medical history and reported discovering the mass one month prior to admission. Physical examination revealed a 2 cm well-defined mass in the upper pole of the left testis with a firm consistency. Palpation of the right testis and lower pole of the left testis were normal. Routine blood tests were unremarkable. A bioassay of testicular tumor markers was ordered which revealed normal levels of Alpha-fetoprotein, human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). An extratesticular mass was observed on scrotal ultrasound, attached to the upper pole of the patient's testis. The mass was isoechoic to the testis parenchyma and poorly vascularized on Doppler. The patient underwent a radical inguinal orchiectomy. Histological examination of the operative specimen confirmed the presence of regular splenic tissue in the suspect mass without any signs of malignancy. The splenic proliferation had a preserved capsule, demarcating from the testis. Testicular pulp, the albuginea, and the tunica vaginalis had a preserved microscopic architecture. The patient was discharged on the second postoperative day.

Discharge Diagnosis: Painless scrotal mass

Summary:
A 38-year-old North African man presented with a painless left scrotal mass. A scrotal ultrasound showed an extratesticular mass, attached to the upper pole of his testis. The patient underwent a radical inguinal orchiectomy which confirmed the presence of splenic tissue in the suspect mass without any signs of malignancy. The patient was discharged on the second postoperative day and was examined again after 3 weeks and 2 months in our out-patient unit, where his spleen was found to be of habitual location with standard measurements and a regular aspect.

Hospital Course Summary:

This is the course summary for a 75-year-old woman with a history of gastrointestinal stromal tumor resected eight years ago and presented with adenocarcinoma in the head of the pancreas which was encasing the superior mesenteric artery and presented with invasion of the duodenum and biliary obstruction. The patient was offered consolidative concurrent chemoradiation and was treated with nine cycles of fluorouracil, leucovorin, irinotecan, and oxaliplatin (FOLFIRINOX) over eight months. After seven months of chemotherapy, there was an excellent response.

The patient underwent a simulation for radiation therapy, a helical exhale breath-hold CT with intravenous and oral contrast, and a 4DCT. The internal target volume (ITV) was isotropically expanded by 5 mm to create the planning target volume (PTV) in the first volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) plan. Daily image-guidance based on cone-beam CT (CBCT) with a bone match showed shifts in stent position by up to 30 mm which was accounted for by using a surgical clip from eight years prior as a surrogate for the SMA node on CBCT. A second VMAT plan was initiated because of these observed changes. An MRI on fraction 14 confirmed that intra-fractional motion was less than inter-fractional motion. A third 'robust' four-field box (FFB) technique was used to cover the inter-fraction motion seen on previous fractions.

The patient developed grade 2 thrombocytopenia and neutropenia, and gemcitabine was held for the second half of treatment. She also developed grade 2 fatigue, anorexia, and diarrhea which resolved before the completion of treatment. She remained clinically well with no progression on follow-up CT six months after treatment.

Hospital Course Summary:

Patient, 51-year-old male, admitted to surgical unit with chronic pancreatitis was treated and discharged. He had been experiencing abdominal pain for a year that radiated from the right upper abdomen to the back and was associated with nausea. The pain was partially relieved by injectable analgesics and worsened by food ingestion. The patient had lost weight. Additionally, he had been experiencing occasional episodes of malabsorption and developed insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus. The patient had been to different hospitals for recurrent pain attacks, but no other medical or surgical condition had been treated. There was no family history of the same condition, and there was no abdominal trauma history.

Laboratory examination showed an increased level of blood sugar, normal levels of serum amylase, renal function tests and liver function test (LFT). Radiology results revealed opacities in the middle and right upper quadrant of the abdomen. A CT scan showed impacted stones at the ampulla within the distal bile duct and pancreatic duct. MRCP indicated stones within the main pancreatic duct (MPD) in the head of the pancreas, and dilated common bile duct suggested a stone in the distal part of it.

Based on the results, the surgical procedure was performed. The impacted stones were removed from the ampulla within the distal bile duct and pancreatic duct, and no further surgical interventions were needed. The patient’s recovery was appropriate, and the abdominal pain was resolved. The patient was discharged in stable condition, with instructions to follow up with their primary care physician, to continue pancreatic enzyme supplementation and insulin therapy. The patient was also advised to maintain a low-fat diet and avoid alcohol to prevent recurrent attacks. The patient was given a cardiology referral for further evaluation of mild hypertension, and a referral to a nutritionist was also ordered to manage the patient's malnourished state.

In summary, the patient with chronic pancreatitis was treated and discharged after undergoing a successful surgical procedure to remove impacted stones at the ampulla within the distal bile duct and pancreatic duct. The patient was advised to continue pancreatic enzyme supplementation and insulin therapy, maintain a low-fat diet and avoid alcohol to prevent recurrent attacks. Additionally, the patient was referred to a cardiology and nutritionist specialist to manage mild hypertension and malnourishment.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Age: 71 years
Sex: Male
Clinical Diagnosis: New-onset Epilepsy Due to Sequelae Following Right Frontotemporal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage and Subsequent Aneurysm Clipping Affecting the Right Frontal Eye Field (FEF), with Contralateral Ictal Gaze Deviation and Isolated Postictal Gaze Palsy with Ipsilateral Eye Deviation as an Unusual Todd’s Phenomenon

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the Emergency Department of our institution after suffering a first unprovoked witnessed focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure with forced ictal gaze deviation to the left. The patient presented the following abnormalities in the neurological examination: slowed psychomotor response, disorientation in space, time, and situation. Native cranial CT-imaging was carried out shortly after admission and showed right mesiotemporal and frontotemporal substance defects including the right frontal eye field (FEF) following the right frontotemporal subarachnoid hemorrhage and subsequent aneurysm-clipping.

Initial bloodwork showed slight leucocytosis (12.6/nL) paired with CRP increase (126 mg/L), elevated glucose levels (214 mg/dL), and gamma-GT (99 U/L) as well as elevated TSH (10.16 mU/L). Follow-up bloodwork showed normalized leucocyte levels and progressively declining CRP levels. The patient showed no clinical signs of infection. A follow-up cranial CT with arterial angiography revealed no new results. Three days after admission, routine-EEG revealed intermittent dysfunction that was particularly severe in the right frontotemporal region.

After initial therapy with levetiracetam, the patient suffered a focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure with the following postictal features: involuntary eye deviation (without involuntary head deviation) to the right as a sign of left-sided gaze palsy and disorientation in time with preserved responsiveness. Hemiparesis, nystagmus, sensory deficits, and visual deficits were absent. The patient was oriented in time, space, and situation within the following 48 h.

Four days after admission, a cranial MRI showed no signs of ischemia, intracerebral hemorrhage, or cerebral tumor. The isolated gaze palsy was present for three days, and was initially apparent through manifest involuntary contralateral gaze deviation. During those approximately 72 h, the intensity of the involuntary contralateral gaze deviation progressively declined as the patient’s eye movements returned to normal, until the gaze palsy to the left was only evident during the neurological examination.

The patient received appropriate care and treatment during their hospital course, which contributed to their stable clinical condition at the time of discharge.

Discharge Assessment:

The patient was discharged in a stable clinical condition.

Discharge Instructions:

1. The patient should follow up with their primary healthcare provider as scheduled.
2. The patient should adhere to their prescribed medication regimen.
3. The patient should maintain a healthy lifestyle and avoid stressors that may trigger seizures.
4. The patient should seek medical attention immediately if they experience any seizure-related symptoms or changes in their overall condition.
5. The patient should inform their healthcare provider of any new symptoms or changes in their condition.

Hospital Course:
A 63 year-old male with known hypertension was evaluated for diffuse bony aches, polyuria, polydipsia, constipation, fatigue, loss of appetite, and weight loss of 25 pounds over two months. Biochemical testing revealed an elevated serum calcium level and elevated parathyroid hormone levels, among others. Imaging showed metastatic disease in lungs and multiple renal cysts. The patient underwent a total thyroidectomy with central and left neck node dissection which revealed infiltrative intrathyroidal neuroendocrine tumor with metastasis to nearby lymph nodes and lungs. Subsequent investigations led to the diagnosis of parathyroid neoplasm that was found positive for multiple biomarkers of malignancy. Genetic testing did not reveal any pathogenic variants. The patient was started on targeted therapy to control metastatic disease.

Summary:
A 63 year-old male with known hypertension was diagnosed with metastatic disease in the lungs and multiple renal cysts. After undergoing thyroidectomy with central and left neck node dissection, the patient's symptoms improved, and biochemical abnormalities returned to near normal levels. Subsequent investigations led to the diagnosis of parathyroid neoplasm that was found positive for multiple biomarkers of malignancy. The patient was started on targeted therapy to control metastatic disease.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient, a 78-year-old male, was admitted to our department with complaints of cough and trouble breathing. He had a history of hypertension and gemfibrozil was the medication he had been taking for this condition. Glycated hemoglobin test revealed impaired glucose metabolism. The patient was found to have pneumonia and had undergone chest computed tomography (CT) scan, echocardiogram, and serum creatinine tests during his previous outpatient visits.

Upon admission, the patient was conscious, but shortness of breath symptoms worsened, resulting in his transfer to the ICU and requiring intubation. The diagnosis was ANCA-associated vasculitis, and treatment with plasmapheresis and intravenous methylprednisolone was started. The patient was transferred to the nephrology department and continued on hemodialysis and antibiotic therapy. Steroid regimen was gradually tapered to oral prednisone. 

However, the patient’s pneumonia worsened, and Candida albicans and multi-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae infections were suspected. Tigecycline was used on day 20, but it was later discovered to have caused severe and sustained hypoglycemia, which was unresponsive to treatments such as oral glucose and repeated doses of intravenous 50% glucose solution. 

On day 28, the patient's treatment plan was changed to polymyxin B and imipenem for pneumonia, but his condition deteriorated, and despite medical efforts, he passed away.

- Found to have ANCA-associated vasculitis
- Plasmapheresis and intravenous methylprednisolone was started
- Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) started
- Hemodialysis, antibiotic therapy, and steroid regimen were continued
- Tigecycline was used, but sustained hypoglycemia occurred, which was unresponsive to treatments
- Died due to deteriorating medical condition

The patient, a 59-year-old postmenopausal woman, presented to the gynecologist with abnormal vaginal bleeding. Pelvic ultrasonography and abdominopelvic computed tomography revealed a polycystic and solid mass adjacent to the normal-appearing uterus measuring 135 × 92 × 100 mm, which was connected to the right ovarian vein. Serum CA125 was slightly high, and contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging suggested ovarian mucinous carcinoma. The cancer cells showed high-grade nuclear atypia and various histological patterns including solid, pseudo-endometrioid, and transitional cell-like patterns. The cancer cells had spread into the left ovary and para-aortic lymph nodes, resulting in pathological FIGO staging of IIIA (pT1bN1aM0). Immunohistochemical analyses showed diffuse positive staining for p53 and block positive for p16. The TP53 mutation analysis showed a c.730G>A mutation, which alters glycine to serine in codon 244 of exon 7 in TP53.

Treatment:
The patient received total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy, intra-pelvic, and para-aortic lymphadenectomy.

Outcome:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with a diagnosis of high-grade serous ovarian cancer with SET feature and mucinous differentiation. Referral to an oncologist for follow-up and further management was advised.

The 8-year-old Hispanic male was referred to Brenner FIT for ongoing weight gain, excessive appetite, and elevated triglycerides and liver enzymes. The patient has been gaining weight since the age of 4, despite the efforts of his primary care pediatrician and a pediatric dietitian.

The patient's mother reported difficulty in implementing changes to the patient's diet due to his picky-eating habits and outbursts over food. After six months of treatment, the patient's weight status showed remarkable improvement, with a decrease in BMI from 24.4 to 22.5 and a decrease in BMI z-score from 2.43 to 2.09. The mother reported a decrease in the patient's outbursts over food, limited complaints of hunger, and the incidence of begging for food reduced significantly.

Recommendations/Instructions:

The patient's mother was advised to continue the nonrestrictive feeding approach and to include meals with a wide variety of foods at home. The pediatric dietitian recommended providing fruits and vegetables at every meal and snack, and encouraging physical activities to maintain the patient's improved weight status.

Follow-up:

The patient is scheduled for follow-up with the pediatric dietitian in three months to monitor his progress. The primary care pediatrician will continue to monitor the patient's weight status during regular visits.

Hospital Course Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]
Age: 13
Sex: Female
Admitting Diagnosis: Displaced medial epicondyle fracture and avulsed fragment of the lateral epicondyle due to elbow injury.

History of Present Illness: The patient presented to the clinic with swelling and severe pain of the right elbow following a fall. Active and passive movement of the elbow was hindered due to pain. No neurovascular deficits were observed in the left arm. The diagnostic imaging revealed a displaced medial epicondyle fracture and an avulsed fragment of the lateral epicondyle.

Past Medical History:
- Dwarfism
- Developmental dysplasia of the left hip
- Habitual patellar dislocation of the right knee
- Underwent reconstructive surgery of the medial patellofemoral ligament at age 12
- History of joint laxity diagnosed with a Beighton score of 6 points

Hospital Course: 
The patient underwent a surgery under general anesthesia the next day after the injury. Ultrasonography and stress X-rays of the elbow were evaluated before the surgery. The diagnostic imaging showed proximal avulsion of the lateral collateral ligament from the epicondyle. Valgus and varus stress tests were performed bilaterally with the patient's elbows at a 20-degree flexed position. The side-to-side differences of the joint space widening were significantly worse in the right elbow. Conventional open reduction and internal fixation was performed using tension band wiring technique for the medial epicondyle fracture. Complete avulsion of the lateral collateral ligament complex was observed during the procedure. Three suture anchors were inserted into the footprint, and the lateral collateral ligament complex was sutured by double-row fixation technique. A plastic cast immobilized the patient’s elbow for 3 weeks after the surgery. After the immobilization period, the patient was allowed active and passive motion with a soft brace. The wires were removed 4 months after the primary surgery. The follow-up completed after 7 months of the primary surgery revealed no pain, no limitation of range of motion, and no functional deficits due to the elbow injury. 

Discharge Diagnosis: Displaced medial epicondyle fracture and avulsed fragment of the lateral epicondyle due to elbow injury.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is recommended to follow up with the assigned healthcare provider at the earliest convenience.

Significant Events:
- Diagnostic imaging revealed a displaced medial epicondyle fracture and an avulsed fragment of the lateral epicondyle.
- Valgus and varus stress tests were performed, and the diagnostic imaging showed proximal avulsion of the lateral collateral ligament from the epicondyle.
- Conventional open reduction and internal fixation was performed on the medial epicondyle fracture.
- Complete avulsion of the lateral collateral ligament complex was observed during the surgical procedure.
- The lateral collateral ligament complex was sutured by double-row fixation technique.
- A plastic cast immobilized the patient’s elbow for 3 weeks.
- Wires were removed 4 months after the primary surgery.
- No pain, no limitation in the range of motion, and no functional deficits were observed after 7 months of the primary surgery.

Reason for Admission:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of generalized weakness, pain with urination, urinary frequency, and incontinence.

The patient, a 65-year-old male, had a history of cirrhosis of liver due to alcohol addiction, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, hyperlipidemia, and a history of deep venous thrombosis. He presented to the hospital with symptoms of urinary tract infection, and his physical examination was significant only for mild epigastric tenderness. The patient was treated for alcohol withdrawal and was empirically started on antibiotic treatment with ceftriaxone for urinary tract infection. Blood and urine cultures were sent, and the patient's urine culture showed the growth of Staphylococcus warneri which was sensitive to fluoroquinolone antibiotics and Bactrim.

Outcome:
The patient was treated with levofloxacin, and his symptoms, including dysuria and urinary frequency, resolved. Hematuria in the patient also resolved after urology evaluation, and there was no recurrence of rectal bleeding during the hospital course. The patient required benzodiazepines for alcohol withdrawal, and he was given resources and counseling for alcohol cessation. The patient was discharged home on oral levofloxacin with scheduled outpatient follow-up.

Follow-up:
The patient was encouraged to quit drinking alcohol and was advised to follow the medication regimen as prescribed. He was also advised to follow up with his primary care physician, avoiding alcohol intake and to improve self-care since he had a history of deep venous thrombosis.

Patient Information:
The patient is a 60-year-old Chinese male with a history of acute granulo-monocytic leukemia.

Reason for Hospitalization:
The patient was admitted with a 20-day history of fever and swelling of the calves.

Hospitalization Course:
The patient was diagnosed with Candida tropicalis infection following fine-needle aspiration biopsy of calf lesions. The cerebrospinal fluid was negative for Candida and viral infections.

Treatment:
The patient was treated with amphotericin B and flucytosine for 1 month. Caspofungin was later administered for 1 month due to the side effects of amphotericin B.

Follow-Up:
Repeat CT scans of the abdomen and lower limbs after 1 month of treatment revealed stable hepatosplenic and muscle lesions. One month after treatment was completed, the patient exhibited normal alkaline phosphatase and reduced swelling of his limbs.

Conclusion:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with no further need for hospitalization.

Discharge Summary for Patient with Severe Aortic Stenosis and Reduced Ejection Fraction

Mr. X is a 75-year-old male who was followed up by the Cardiology team for severe narrowing of the aortic valve and a weakened heart muscle. He was found to have an ejection fraction of 30% and was classified as being in New York Heart Association functional class III.

During his hospital stay, Mr. X received appropriate medical management for his condition. He was monitored for fluid and electrolyte imbalances, and his blood pressure was controlled with medication. The patient received oxygen supplementation as needed to maintain appropriate oxygen levels. He underwent routine laboratory testing and imaging studies to assess his response to treatment.

Upon review, the patient's medical team deemed Mr. X stable and fit for discharge. They provided him with detailed instructions regarding his prescribed medications, dietary restrictions, and recommended follow-up appointments with his primary care provider and cardiologist. The patient and his family were counseled on the importance of adhering to medical recommendations and monitoring for any changes or worsening of symptoms.

In summary, Mr. X was successfully treated for his aortic stenosis and related complications during his hospitalization. He was discharged in a stable condition with appropriate follow-up and care instructions.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 65-year-old man with AS
Admission Date: [DATE]
Discharge Date: [DATE]
Diagnosis: Displaced transverse three-column fracture of C6/7 in the setting of severe kyphosis and evidence of multilevel ankylosis consistent with AS.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with neck pain after a fall from a roof. Complete precautions were followed, and he was placed in a rigid collar. The patient was neurologically normal after falling. A non-contrasted computed tomography (CT) revealed a displaced transverse three-column fracture of C6/7 in the setting of severe kyphosis and evidence of multilevel ankylosis consistent with AS. The original surgical plan was to perform a staged circumferential cervical fusion with anterior cervical fusion first to make prone positioning for the planned posterior fusion safer. The patient underwent standard anterior cervical fusion from C5 to C7 filling the gap created by the fracture with bone allograft. A postoperative CT showed improvement in the alignment of the fractured posterior elements. Due to concern of increased peak airway pressures and awkward positioning due to kyphosis, the planned prone positioning for the posterior approach was abandoned. We performed the posterior long segment fusion in the seated position spanning C4 to T3 segmentally with "free hand" placement of cervical lateral mass screws and thoracic pedicle screws. Corticocancellous bone allograft and demineralized bone matrix were used for posterior lateral fusion.

Discharge Condition:
The patient was kept in a rigid collar. His neurological examination was normal. His hospital course was smooth and uncomplicated.

Discharge Medications:
None.

Follow-up:
The patient followed up in clinic on regular basis with cervical spine x-rays. During his two-year follow-up visit, he denied any neck pain and was pursuing his job normally.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 41-year-old male with a past medical history significant for PTSD, ADHD, bipolar disorder, and multiple physical injuries, was admitted to the hospital with reported multiple seizures and left-sided post-ictal paralysis. He had a history of multiple admissions to the hospital due to seizures.

On examination, the patient presented with paralysis of the left arm and leg, accompanied by hemi-sensory loss on the left side of the body. The patient's psychiatric examination was significant for anxiety and auditory hallucinations.

During the hospital stay, the patient underwent various medical tests, including a brain MRI and routine EEG, which were all within normal range. Given the lack of evidence of epilepsy and psychogenic weakness, the patient was successfully weaned off all anti-seizure medications.

The patient was discharged from the hospital after six days, fully functional and showing no signs of weakness. The patient was glad to know that he did not have epilepsy, and was very thankful for the care and diagnosis received.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Seizure disorder, without any definitive evidence of epilepsy.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient was admitted to the hospital with seizures and left-sided post-ictal paralysis, a long-standing issue attributed to post-traumatic epilepsy. The medical staff conducted various tests to exclude an epileptic etiology, including a brain MRI and a five-day video-EEG recording, which were both unremarkable. As a result, it was determined that the patient's symptoms were not associated with epilepsy, and he was successfully weaned off all anti-seizure medications. The patient was discharged six days later, fully functional and showing no signs of weakness.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 2.5-year-old male child
Medical Record Number: ######
Diagnosis: Waardenburg Syndrome Type 4C (WS-4C)

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the pediatric developmental wellness clinic at The Children’s Hospital, Lahore, Pakistan, with the complaints of complete hearing loss since birth and aphasia. The patient was found to have a body mass index (BMI) of 17.7 and was underweight. The patient had blue homochromatic irises, coarse hair texture, pallor of nails, and a slightly broad high nasal root. Segmental depigmentation was seen affecting the forehead and left forearm.

The patient's mother reported the presence of a white hair patch in the frontal hair distribution since birth, diminished upon cutting the hair, and developmental delays in achieving multiple milestones. Past medical history included episodes of bilious vomiting, failure to thrive, and multiple bouts of severe constipation at the age of six months. On imaging, a diagnosis of Hirschsprung's disease was made and confirmed with a rectal biopsy. The patient had a positive family history of WS present in the father and paternal aunt.

An auditory brainstem response was done to evaluate the hearing deficit and showed a bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. The patient also demonstrated complete mutism and lack of response to commands. A DNA sample from the patient was used for PCR analysis to amplify exon 2 of gene SOX10. The resulting product was sequenced and found to have a novel truncating mutation of the SOX10 gene on 22q13. The diagnosis of WS-4C was made.

The patient was managed by a multidisciplinary team, including the pediatrician, developmental pediatrician, clinical geneticist, audiologist, speech therapist, occupational therapist, and physiotherapist. The patient also received counseling regarding the condition, and the possibility of genetic inheritance was explained to the family. Appropriate referrals were made for follow-up care and genetic counseling.

The patient was discharged and advised to continue follow-up with the pediatrician, developmental pediatrician, clinical geneticist, audiologist, speech therapist, occupational therapist, and physiotherapist.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient's condition was stable at discharge.

Follow-Up Care:
The patient was advised to continue multidisciplinary follow-up care and to follow any additional recommendations made by the clinicians. Genetic counseling was also recommended to the family.

Discharge Summary

Hospital Course:
This 64-year-old man presented with a 6-month history of worsening dyspnea, intermittent fevers, chills, cough, and wheezing. He had a significant smoking history, as well as a history of ablation for atrial fibrillation and surgery and radiation for prostate cancer. The patient was initially treated for presumed community-acquired pneumonia with no response. He was ultimately hospitalized, and a CT scan of the chest showed a LLL consolidation with evidence of narrowing of the LLL bronchus. A bronchoscopy showed a "rounded, nonulcerating, pink mass-like growth." He was referred to our center for further evaluation.

Diagnosis and Treatment:
The patient subsequently underwent another bronchoscopy, which revealed a narrow LLL bronchus with a fleshy endobronchial mass lesion. Multiple biopsies revealed an aspirated almond. The foreign body was removed using a Zero Tip Airway Retrieval Basket and biopsy forceps. A bronchoalveolar lavage was performed, and specimens were sent for culture. The patient was given a 10-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate due to evidence of aspiration pneumonia. On follow-up examination, he reported drastically increased exercise tolerance, and his cough and wheezing had disappeared. Repeat pulmonary function tests showed an increase in FEV1, and a follow-up CT scan revealed complete resolution of parenchymal infiltrates.

Follow-up:
The patient successfully quit smoking and his exercise tolerance had returned to baseline at the 6-month follow-up.

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged in good condition with instructions to continue follow-up with his primary care physician.

During his hospitalization, he developed intermittent fever and leukocytosis, with positive blood cultures for Staphylococcal species. The 72-year-old male was admitted due to anemia and fecal occult blood with a diagnosis of obstructive esophageal cancer. During his hospital stay, he developed a fever and leukocytosis, and further evaluation revealed Staphylococcal species in his blood cultures. A transthoracic echocardiogram described mild aortic regurgitation, while an intracardiac echo revealed the presence of perivalvular aortic root abscess with moderate aortic regurgitation, indicating complicated infective endocarditis. An urgent surgical intervention was performed, leading to the successful drainage of the abscess and replacement of the infected bioprosthetic valve.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course Summary:
The 51-year-old male patient with symptoms of recurrent abscess formation in the right maxillary buccal vestibule near the right upper first molar was admitted to the endodontic department of a private dental clinic. The patient underwent a surgical endodontic retreatment for a lesion presumed to be a symptomatic apical periodontitis; root-end resection, root-end preparation, and root-end filling with calcium-enriched mixture cement were performed. However, there was no amelioration in symptoms and signs in the two-month follow-up. A cone-beam computed tomography scan was taken but no evidence of vertical root fracture was found. Subsequently, endodontic therapy for maxillary second molar was selected, and it was observed that the mesial root canal had no bleeding/vital pulp. Cleaning and shaping using full-strength sodium hypochlorite was performed, root canals were obturated with gutta-percha using Roth 808 endodontic sealer, and coronal restoration with amalgam was carried out. The patient was notified and gave consent at every step of the diagnosis and treatment. Symptoms and clinical signs were fully resolved after one week, and complete healing of the periapical lesion was achieved at the 18-month follow-up.

Medical History:
The patient is a previously healthy 19-year-old nonsmoker Caucasian male who presented with acute epigastric pain, recurrent vomiting, and watery diarrhea. He has no significant family history of gastrointestinal disease or cancer.

Hospital Course:
An abdominal CT scan identified a significant and irregular thickening of the ascending colon wall, indicating intussusception. During laparoscopy, a tumor was found in the ascending colon with peritoneal seeding. The patient underwent a right hemicolectomy and anastomosis procedure, with a suspicious liver lesion identified and resected for biopsy. Pathology reports indicated a poorly differentiated signet ring cell adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon, at stage IV. Immunohistochemistry and gene mutation analyses were negative for microsatellite instability and mutations in KRAS, NRAS, and BRAF genes.

Treatment:
The patient was initiated on 11 cycles of bevacizumab and oxaliplatin with capecitabine tablets for 10 days each cycle. The patient completed and complied with the protocol. Follow-up MRI and CT scans after completing chemotherapy showed resolution of peritoneal nodularities and minimal omental thickening.

Discharge Summary:
The patient presented with acute abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea and was found to have a stage IV poorly differentiated signet ring cell adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon with metastasis to the omentum and pericolonic fat. After undergoing right hemicolectomy, anastomosis, and liver biopsy, the patient completed 11 cycles of chemotherapy with resolution of peritoneal nodularities and minimal omental thickening. The patient should follow-up as directed by his care team for ongoing monitoring and preventive care.

HOSPITAL COURSE SUMMARY:

Patient was admitted to our institution with bilateral lower extremity edema and concern for CLL transformation. Baseline dementia was noted.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:

Patient was found to be normothermic with mildly elevated potassium level and stable hyperleukocytosis. Unremarkable physical exam with the exception of symmetric 1+ lower extremity edema without signs of cellulitis.

DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT:

Despite elevated potassium levels, there was no evidence of hyperkalemia or ECG changes. Normal saline and furosemide were given intravenously, but potassium level continued to escalate. Point-of-care potassium level was drawn and determined to be consistent with the outside hospital level, and no further interventions were performed in the emergency department. Hyperkalemia cocktail was given on at least one occasion during hospital stay.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:

Patient was discharged with no specific complaints and will continue to follow up with his primary care physician.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 27-year-old female who was brought to the trauma bay after being involved in a motor vehicle accident. She was found to have a low Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of 3 and agonal breathing, and was intubated. Imaging studies were performed and revealed bilateral vertebral artery injuries at the C2 level, significant craniocaudal separation of the C2-3 spine, and a prevertebral hematoma. The patient underwent C1-C4 posterior instrumentation and posterolateral arthrodesis, C1-2 sublaminar wiring with posterior fusion, as well as C3-C4 laminectomy. Following the surgery, she underwent a C2-3 anterior cervical discectomy and fusion. The patient had a prolonged hospital stay due to difficulty with her swallow evaluation and continued to have a percutaneous gastrostomy (PEG) tube. She eventually demonstrated full strength in her upper and lower extremities with intact sensation.

Hospital Course Summary:
- 27-year-old female involved in a motor vehicle accident with low GCS of 3 and agonal breathing
- Bilateral vertebral artery injuries at C2 level, craniocaudal separation of C2-3, and prevertebral hematoma found on imaging
- C1-C4 posterior instrumentation and posterolateral arthrodesis, C1-2 sublaminar wiring with posterior fusion, and C3-C4 laminectomy performed
- C2-3 anterior cervical discectomy and fusion performed
- Difficulty with swallow evaluation led to percutaneous gastrostomy (PEG) tube placement
- Eventually demonstrated full strength in upper and lower extremities with intact sensation

Discharge Summary

Patient Information:
Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 44 years old
Gender: Female
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Admission Diagnosis:
Distal joint pain

Hospital Course:
The patient was initiated on HCQ 200 mg daily for her distal joint pain and subsequently developed pruritic erythematous patches with pustules on the upper chest and upper limbs five days after initiation. Despite the use of topical steroids, her condition deteriorated and she presented to the rheumatology clinic ten days after the onset of her symptoms. HCQ was immediately withdrawn, and the patient was started on 30 mg prednisolone daily. A dermatologist was also consulted, and supportive treatment including antihistamines, topical steroids, and intravenous hydration were provided. A skin biopsy was performed, which demonstrated nonfollicular superficial pustules in the epidermis filled with neutrophils and a mixed eosinophilic and neutrophilic perivascular infiltration consistent with AGEP. The patient was discharged with a tapering dose of oral prednisolone after a moderately controlled improvement of her pustules and erythema.

Follow-Up:
The patient visited the clinic 37 days after her discharge with mild pruritic eruption and desquamation on upper limbs and trunk and distal lower extremities. She was instructed to taper prednisolone 5 mg weekly. The patient returned for a follow-up 3 months later, and the eruption had completely resolved with no recurrence. She was also referred to a psychologist due to intermittent joint pain complaints.

Hospital Course:
A 40-year-old male presented with complaints of ill-defined right periorbital pain associated with intermittent photosensitivity. His symptoms progressed to involve discomfort in the right upper neck. MRI of the brain was normal. MRI of the cervical spine revealed age-appropriate mild degenerative changes and diminutive venous caliber in the neck. A computed tomography venogram (CTV) demonstrated enlarged paravertebral and suboccipital plexus, right worse than left, and dynamic compression of the ipsilateral extracranial internal jugular vein (IJV) by a hypertrophic hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage, worsened with leftward head turn in the presence of contralateral IJV compression in the upper neck. The focus of IJV compression, as well as hypertrophy of the paravertebral venous plexus is well illustrated on 3D reconstructions.

Treatment:
After extensive counseling and exclusion of alternative possible explanations of his disabling symptoms, it was decided to proceed with decompression of the right IJV via an anterior approach. After induction of anesthesia, a transverse right-sided incision was made following a natural skin crease to expose the posterior half of the greater horn of the hyoid, which was then bisected, and the posterior free portion was disconnected from the thyrohyoid ligament and excised. The superior horn of the thyroid cartilage was also resected to adequately decompress the IJV.

Outcome:
There were no immediate postoperative complications and the patient was discharged home the same day. At a three-month follow-up visit, he reported improvement in his symptoms and return to work full-time. A repeat CTV confirmed the patency of the IJV, both in neutral position and with head turning.

Hospital Course:

He underwent trans-sphenoid endoscopic surgery but experienced a sudden drop in blood pressure, increase in heart rate, and a drop in oxygen saturation during lumbar puncture injection. Supportive management was provided, and the surgery was postponed. Discharge Diagnosis:

CSF leakage

He experienced a sudden drop in blood pressure, increased heart rate, and a drop in oxygen saturation during the injection. After the administration of supportive management, the surgery was postponed, and the patient was transferred to the ICU. The patient was eventually weaned from mechanical ventilation and discharged two days after transfer with good general condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient's Name: [Redacted]
Sex: Male
Age: 53 years old

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to address a recurring tumor in the left kidney, which was successfully treated with radiofrequency ablation and partial nephrectomy. As part of his medical history, he had a Whipple's pancreatectomy for pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors and had known Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome.

During the patient's subsequent follow-up appointments, he was found to have abnormal testicles and underwent a diagnostic right radical orchiectomy, followed by a left radical orchiectomy three months later. Pathological examination of the testes confirmed bilateral metastatic low-grade clear cell renal cell carcinoma or RCC.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the patient's abdomen were conducted and they indicated multiple tumors in both kidneys consistent with RCC, with the largest tumor measuring 2.6 cm.These were also successfully treated using radiofrequency ablation. The smaller tumors have been monitored via radiographic imaging and have remained stable. Postorchiectomy surveillance for 24 months did not reveal any additional metastatic disease.

The patient was discharged in stable condition, with prescribed follow-up appointments for regular medical monitoring. 

Discharge Diagnosis:

1. Possible failure of previous surgery and recurrent tumor
2. Known Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome
3. Bilateral metastatic low-grade clear cell RCC

Discharge Instruction:

1. Attend scheduled follow-up appointments as directed
2. Report any worrisome symptoms or changes to primary care physician or oncologist
3. Follow any prescribed medication regimen as directed by physician
4. Attend follow-up radiographic and imaging appointments as required
5. Follow regular self-care routine, including a healthy diet, exercise plan, and stress management techniques.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: [Name]

Medical Record Number: [MRN]

Sex: Female

Age: 34 years

Date of Admission: [Date]

Date of Discharge: [Date]

Admission Diagnosis:

The patient was admitted with unfocused mild back pain and chronic headache for 2 months, which had increased in severity in the past 2 days. The patient had no history of recent trauma or receiving anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy. Physical examination revealed mild tenderness of the cervical and thoracolumbar spine. Hematological analyses revealed no abnormalities. 

Hospital Course:

Initial unenhanced CT scan of the brain revealed a small subdural hemorrhage. Further imaging revealed the presence of a wide-neck saccular aneurysm originating from the left posterior communicating artery and a subdural hemorrhage in the lumbar spine, likely a continuum of the subdural hemorrhage of the brain.

Emergency clipping of the aneurysm and evacuation of the underlying cerebral hematoma were performed without any complications. The patient completely recovered after the procedure. Follow-up CT and CTA of the brain revealed no evidence of a recanalized aneurysm sac or recurrence. No neurological complications or persistent symptoms were observed for 2 weeks post surgery, and subsequently, the patient was discharged.

Follow-up:

The patient was kept under clinical observation to monitor for any neurological complications that could have resulted from the subdural hematoma in the spine. The patient was administered corticosteroid treatment to inhibit inflammation that could also play a key role in the hematoma formation.

Outcome and Discharge Condition:

The patient showed complete recovery after the emergency clipping and evacuation of the aneurysm. The patient was discharged in a stable condition and advised to follow-up with their neurosurgery clinic. 

Follow-up Plan:

A detailed and prolonged follow-up (every month for the first 6 months and every 3 months thereafter) in the neurosurgery clinic for 2 years was recommended.

Hospital Course Summary:

Identification:
Patient is a 71-year-old female non-smoker with hemiparesis who presented with an MRI indicating a right frontal lesion having characteristics of a cystic primary glioma versus metastasis.

Medical History:
There is no primary systemic cancer that has been identified despite serial pan-imaging, multiple negative biopsies, and laryngo-colonoscopies. The patient has a history of TTF-1 positive metastatic high-grade neuroendocrine neoplasm with high cellularity, necrosis, minimal brain infiltration, and small cell phenotype. The patient has received stereotactic radiosurgery postoperatively, fractionated radiotherapy plus cisplatin/etoposide for 6-month recurrence, and surgery plus whole-brain radiotherapy for 12-month further progression.

Methylation Analysis:
The course of disease progression being unusual, the case was flagged for methylation analysis which resulted in a diagnosis of an IDH wildtype glioblastoma (calibrated score of 0.94) with a characteristic gain of chromosome 7, and loss of chromosome 10 on the CNV plot.

Treatment:
The patient received temozolomide but progress continued. The TTF-1 positivity remains positive in the recurrent tumor and TTF-1 positivity has been reported rarely in glioblastomas. The patient is now deceased, 20 months from the initial surgery.

Discharge Condition:
The patient did not receive a discharge as the patient has passed away.

Hospital Course:
The patient was a 38-year-old female admitted to our department due to severe malaise, systemic edema, and liver malfunction. She had a long-standing history of AN-BP and had been hospitalized multiple times for infusion therapy to improve dehydration and electrolyte imbalance. The patient developed laxative abuse over the last year and consumed 100 or more tablets daily. Physical examination revealed systemic edema, and blood tests showed high levels of ALP and γ-GTP. An abdominal ultrasonogram confirmed ascites and a chronic hepatitis pattern. Endoscopic examination revealed esophageal varices, while liver biopsy revealed slight pericellular fibrosis. The patient was treated with diuretic drugs to control systemic edema and ascites and discharged with decreased edema and ascites after 2 weeks of hospitalization. Follow-up care revealed neither the recurrence of edema and ascites nor the improvement in hepatic enzyme levels.
 
Diagnosis:
Chronic hepatitis pattern with esophageal varices and pericellular fibrosis.

Medical Management:
The patient was treated with diuretic drugs, including spironolactone and tolvaptan, to control systemic edema and ascites.

Summary:
The 38-year-old female patient with a history of AN-BP for 15 years was hospitalized with severe malaise, systemic edema, and liver malfunction. The patient had laxative abuse over the last year and consumed 100 or more tablets daily. Medical examinations revealed ascites and a chronic hepatitis pattern with pericellular fibrosis. After 2 weeks of hospitalization and treatment with diuretic drugs, the patient's edema and ascites decreased. Follow-up care showed no recurrence of edema and ascites but no improvement in hepatic enzyme levels. The patient was diagnosed with chronic hepatitis pattern with esophageal varices and pericellular fibrosis and was treated with spironolactone and tolvaptan.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Identification:
Name: [patient's name]
Medical Record Number: [patient's MRN]
DOB: [patient's date of birth]
Gender: Female

Admission and Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital due to central hypothyroidism and short stature. Assessment of pituitary functioning confirmed cortisol and growth hormone deficiency. Subsequent MRI scan showed a solid/cystic suprasellar lesion measuring 3 × 1.9 × 2.3 cm. The patient underwent a transsphenoidal near total resection of the mass.

Treatment and Progress:
The patient recovered well after the surgery and was started on levothyroxine and hydrocortisone therapy. The patient had no neurological deficits following resection and post-operative visual field testing was comparable to presentation. Growth hormone replacement was planned to commence once clinical and radiological stability were confirmed. The patient developed transient diabetes insipidus which resolved within days. Post-operative MRI scans showed residual enhancing cyst wall but no measurable solid component. The patient remains clinically and radiologically stable with no evidence of disease progression 11 months following surgery.

Diagnosis and Histopathology:
The histopathological analysis of the lesion demonstrated stratified squamous epithelium accompanied by superficial goblet cells and ciliated cells. Underlying tissue stroma comprised loose connective tissue and blood vessels. The morphological appearances were consistent with a diagnosis of papillary craniopharyngioma. Next-generation sequencing analysis of the lesion confirmed a BRAF V600E mutation, thereby validating the histopathological diagnosis. 

Follow-up:
The patient will require regular follow-up monitoring to assess for any possible recurrence or progression of the disease. 

Disposition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with appropriate follow-up arranged.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Reason for Admission: Sudden onset of diplopia, dysarthria, facial drooping, and vomiting

History of Present Illness: The patient presented to our Emergency Department with symptoms of diplopia, dysarthria, facial drooping, and vomiting. These symptoms were preceded by a week of general malaise with progressively worsening headache and nausea.

Past Medical History: The patient had a previous history of recurrent oral and genital ulcers for which he had been prescribed oral antibiotics two years earlier.

Hospital Course: On examination, the patient was noted to have fever, nuchal rigidity, mild right upper and lower limb weakness, right upper facial nerve palsy, and right abducens nerve paresis. Initial investigations showed mildly raised inflammatory markers with a C-reactive protein and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate. A T2-weighted brain MRI scan revealed a large lesion involving the pons and the medulla, with mild mass effect and ring enhancement. Blood cultures grew Streptococcus parasanguis and Streptococcus mitis in one out of two bottles, and the cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed a raised cell count with lymphocytosis and raised protein level.

Empiric treatment with intravenous antibiotics and antivirals was initiated, but the patient's condition continued to deteriorate. He developed dysarthria, dysphagia, poor pharyngeal sensation, and ataxic gait, in keeping with progressive bulbar dysfunction. Due to declining consciousness and poor respiratory effort, the patient required intensive care unit admission for tracheostomy and invasive ventilation.

A presumptive differential diagnosis of Neuro-Behçet’s Disease was made, and the patient was transferred to a tertiary center Neuro intensive care unit for specialist management. Prompt initiation of aggressive intravenous immunosuppression resulted in dramatic clinical improvement, allowing respiratory weaning after 72 hours.

Outcome: Six months after the initial presentation, the patient remains asymptomatic with no neurological deficit, having completed a six-month regimen of oral medications. There was a parallel resolution of radiological abnormalities.

Follow-up Plan: The patient will have close follow-up with a neurologist and rheumatologist to monitor for potential relapse and adjust treatment as necessary.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 49 year old female, presented with progressive lymphedema at the right leg refractory to conservative measures. Medical history revealed a laparoscopic hysterectomy and adnexectomy as well as a radical pelvic lymphadenectomy on the right side due to a uterine cervical carcinoma four years prior. Despite previous treatments, the lymphedema exacerbated resulting in functional impairment and poor quality of life. After inconspicuous follow up care and lymphoscintigraphy scan, a microsurgically transplanted omentum majus flap containing lymph nodes and lymph vessels was planned. The flap was successfully anastomosed to the right femoral artery and vein, with well-perfused vessel arcades via the right gastroepiploic artery being defined, and mal-perfused parts of the omentum majus revealed through ICG angiography. After discarding mal-perfused tissue parts, the omentum majus was placed and spread out in the subcutaneous tissue to enable lymph vessels to grow, establishing a new lymph collector for the right lower extremity.

Bone marrow biopsy showed subtle infiltrates by low-grade B-NHL, associated with groups of clonal plasma cells which stained with IgG heavy chain. Lymphatic infiltrate was surrounded by a rim of CD138+ plasma cells.

The patient is currently monitored on a 3-monthly basis.

She is advised to follow up regularly with her primary care physician.

Age: 69
Gender: Female
Medical Record Number: [MEDICAL RECORD NUMBER]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted for possible lung volume reduction due to progressive dyspnoea over 6 years from a history of COPD. Her medical history included past smoking, thyroidectomy, uncomplicated systemic hypertension, and type 2 diabetes. At the time of referral, her treatment included inhaled tiotropium and salmeterol/fluticasone, levothyroxine, valsartan, hydrochlorothiazide and metformin.

During the course of her hospitalization, she had a physical examination showing severely diminished breath sounds on the lower part of the right hemithorax. Pulmonary function tests showed severe airway obstruction with GOLD stage 3 and significant lung hyperinflation. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no significant pulmonary hypertension.

After exclusion of collateral ventilation through the use of the Chartis Diagnostic System, two one-way EBV were placed in the patient's right lower lobe, under general anaesthesia. She experienced fever 48 hours after valves placement. A chest X-ray showed ground glass opacities in the inferior part of the right lung while the right hemidiaphragm was shifted upwards. She rapidly improved and was discharged home on the 7th day without any change in inhaled therapy.

Patient was included in a pulmonary rehabilitation program for 3 months following the EBV placement. After 1 month, the patient reported marked improvement, with no limitation in daily-life activities by dyspnoea. Her CAT score markedly improved, as did the 6MWT. Chest auscultation still revealed diminished breath sounds on the posterior right side but asymmetry was reduced. HRCT showed a marked reduction in the right lower lobe volume with accompanying right upper lobe re-expansion and the disappearance of mediastinal shift.

The improvement in PFT was even more remarkable. Indeed, the patient no longer met the GOLD initiative spirometric criteria for COPD. These improvements were confirmed at 4 months and were maintained at the latest control, nearly 3 years after the procedure.

At the latest control, the patient was experiencing 5 exacerbations requiring ambulatory antibiotic treatment in the 3-year follow-up. The SpO2 measured at rest were stable in the follow-up and the minimal SpO2 during the walk tests remained above 90%.

Discharge Diagnosis:
COPD with dyspnoea

Discharge Medications:
None specified

Discharge Instructions:
None specified.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted for acute onset of high fevers, chills, and myalgia. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis, lactic acidosis, new onset thrombocytopenia, and increased levels of plasma d-dimers. Clinical examination revealed cold and pale palms and feet with a petechial rash. The patient was diagnosed with septic shock secondary to community-acquired pneumonia caused by gram-positive cocci (Streptococcus pneumoniae).

Treatment:

The patient was treated with vancomycin and cefepime. He required mechanical ventilation, vasopressors, IV fluids, and hemodialysis. Attempts were made to salvage his limbs, however due to the rapidly spreading infection, the patient underwent a right distal forearm amputation, excision, and skin grafting to the left hand, and bilateral below knee amputation.

Outcome:

One year later, the patient is able to walk with a prosthesis. He has some complaints of phantom limb. 

Follow-up:

The patient will require ongoing follow-up for prosthetic management and wound care. It is recommended that he receives post-splenectomy vaccinations.

Hospital Course: 

The patient, a 55-year-old female, was admitted to our hospital with increased bleeding tendency and respiratory infection. The initial peripheral blood count showed pancytopenia with absolute neutropenia and myeloid blasts. Cytomorphology and flow cytometry confirmed bone marrow infiltration by AML blasts. Subsequent genetic testing diagnosed a FLT3-TKD low mutation. The patient progressed to receive a HAM regimen in combination with midostaurin. Following the treatment, complete remission was confirmed by bone marrow aspirate, and the patient underwent allo-HSCT. The patient developed mild acute skin and gastrointestinal GvHD after the procedure, which were treated topically and with prednisolone. The patient underwent routine follow-up, and relapse of AML was diagnosed post allo-HSCT. An APA regimen was administered, resulting in complete remission in cytomorphology and flow cytometry. After discontinuation, the patient relapsed with AML. A salvage combination of azacytidine and venetoclax was administered, but unfortunately failed to induce remission.  

Discharge Diagnosis:

1. Acute Myeloid Leukemia (FAB M1)
2. Disease Relapse

Discharge Condition:

Due to the patient's refractory disease, the treatment options were exhausted, and the patient was discharged with palliative care. The patient's family was appropriately counseled regarding the grave prognosis and provided hospice care options. 

Disposition:

Discharged with palliative care and referred to hospice care options.

Reason for Admission: Left Hemifacial Spasm 

Hospital Course: 

The patient presented with a two-year history of left-sided typical Hemifacial Spasm (HFS). The irregular clonic contraction of the facial muscles gradually spread to other muscles innervated by the facial nerve on the left side of the face. The paroxysm was induced or aggravated by emotional tension, stress, and voluntary and reflexive movements of the face. The patient has had two prior treatments with botulinum toxin injections with no significant improvements in his condition. He had also gone through medical treatment with carbamazepine and baclofen, which were ineffective. Surgical treatment was recommended, and under the impression of HFS caused by neurovascular compression of the distal facial nerve, standard microsurgical procedure was performed. Intraoperative monitoring was performed throughout the operation. Upon exposure of the REZ of the facial nerve, the distal, cisternal segment of the facial nerve was found to be bent by a meatal loop of the AICA. A small piece of Teflon felt was interposed between the facial nerve and the meatal loop of the AICA. 

Outcome: 

HFS resolved completely following the surgery. The postoperative course was uneventful, with no signs of facial weakness or hearing impairment by pure-tone audiometry. The patient has had no recurrence of HFS or neurologic sequelae evident at the 12-month follow-up. 

Recommendations: 

The patient is advised to follow up with their primary care physician or a neurologist as needed for any further concerns regarding their hemifacial spasm.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 68-year-old male with a history of left upper pneumonectomy for lung cancer and subsequent recurrence in the transverse colon.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with dyspnea and positive fecal occult blood test. Colonoscopy revealed a hemorrhagic ulcerated lesion in the transverse colon, and biopsy confirmed the presence of cancer cells that were positive for cytokeratin 7 and negative for cytokeratin 20, CDX2, and thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1). The preoperative diagnosis was lung cancer metastatic to the colon.

Laboratory evaluation showed anemia, extremely low albumin and choline esterase, and high inflammatory markers. Electrocardiogram showed incomplete right bundle branch block, and echocardiogram showed asynergy with dyskinesis around the apex of the heart, akinesis and thinning of the anterior wall. Chest and abdominal CT scans were performed, which showed left pleural effusion and irregular thickening of the left pleura, multiple dilated lymph nodes in the left lung hilum and mediastinum, and thickened left side transverse colon with several nearby dilated lymph nodes, suggesting metastatic lung cancer.

After antibiotic treatment and control of left pleural effusion, laparoscopic resection was successfully performed. Histopathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung cancer metastatic to the colon.

Postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on the thirteenth postoperative day. No gastrointestinal bleeding or progression of anemia was observed after restarting antithrombotics.

Follow-up:
The patient died from systemic deterioration on the 40-second postoperative day. No further follow-up was possible.

Discharge Summary

Patient: 19-year-old woman

Admitted: 1-month history of high fever and polyarthralgia

Diagnosis: PTU-associated ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV)

Hospital course:

- Patient was found to have pain and swelling in her right forearm upon admission.
- Blood tests showed elevated levels of C-reactive protein, MPO-ANCA, antinuclear antibody, anti-double-stranded DNA antibody, anticardiolipin antibody, and lupus anticoagulants with a biological false-positive reaction.
- Results of urinalyses and renal function analyses were normal.
- PTU was discontinued and the patient was given methylprednisolone pulse therapy followed by prednisolone.
- Patient developed a diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, and was given additional courses of methylprednisolone pulse therapy, rituximab, and plasmapheresis.
- Patient's symptoms showed improvement after intensive immunosuppressive treatments.
- NET regulation in the neutrophils of a patient with PTU-AAV was examined, and results showed NET formation with hyper-citrullinated histone in PTU-AAV neutrophils during the active phase.
- ANCA panel kit testing was used to examine the presence of autoantibodies to NET components, and revealed a perinuclear-ANCA staining pattern.
- Further testing showed PTU-AAV IgG and idiopathic MPA IgG had a high NETs-inducibility compared to HC-IgGs.

Recommendations:

- Patient should continue to follow-up with her healthcare provider for ongoing monitoring of her condition.
- Patient should be advised to avoid medications that are associated with a risk of PTU-associated AAV.
- Patient should be advised to watch for any symptoms that may indicate a flare-up of her condition and to seek medical attention promptly if these symptoms occur.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Hospital Course:
A 2-year-old Labrador dog and a 14-year-old mixed breed dog were referred to the Department of Surgery at the University of Agricultural Sciences and Veterinary Medicine Cluj-Napoca, Romania for evaluation and treatment. The Labrador dog presented with a well-defined subdermal mobile swelling on the craniolateral aspect of the tibia, while the mixed breed dog presented with an extensive skin defect on the lateral aspect of the distal tibia and tarsus. The Labrador dog underwent surgical excision of the tumor, while the mixed breed dog received flap surgery. Hospital Course Summary:
Two dogs were referred to the Department of Surgery for evaluation and treatment. One dog underwent surgical excision of a tumor, while the other underwent flap surgery, both under general anesthesia. Postoperatively, both dogs received medications and were evaluated at various intervals.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Date of Admission: [REDACTED]

Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Reason for Admission:
The patient was admitted with acute painless urethral bleeding associated with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS), mainly voiding obstruction.

Hospital Course:
Physical examination confirmed several haemangiomas in the glandular urethra, located at submeatal level. Those were only visible by gently spreading the external urethral meatus. In addition, there were scrotal haemangiomas and prominent varicose veins in both legs. Digital rectal examination revealed a nonsuspicious medium-sized adenomatous prostate and uroflowmetry showed no value due to a low voiding volume. A short proximal bulbar urethral stricture was diagnosed through a retrograde urethrogram and voiding cystourethrogram. An internal urethrotomy under direct vision was performed as the preferred treatment. During this procedure, glans haemangiomas and small haemangiomas in prostatic urethra were identified. The latter were only visible after opening the strictured segment, but since they did not cause any further bleeding, conservative management was applied. The urethrotomy did not present any haemorrhagic incident, and the catheter was removed on the fifth day after the procedure without any subsequent complications. Follow-up flowmetry evidenced Qmax=12.9 mL/sec, Qmed=5.3 mL/sec with 180 mL of voided volume.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with haemangiomas in the glandular urethra and scrotal area. A short proximal bulbar urethral stricture was diagnosed through a retrograde urethrogram and voiding cystourethrogram.

Treatment:
The patient was treated with an internal urethrotomy under direct vision.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient is asymptomatic, with no further episodes of urethral bleeding. In addition, regarding the urethral stricture, our patient is voiding properly presenting adequate uroflowmetry values, with no need for further procedures or dilatations and with a good quality of life.

Follow-up:
The patient is advised to visit for follow-up.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission Diagnosis: Crohn's disease

Hospital Course: The patient was initially treated with oral mesalamine and prednisolone but in 2010 was changed to azathioprine. The disease continued to relapse despite azathioprine therapy. In 2014, adalimumab was initiated after screening for infectious diseases. The patient was found positive for the presence of mycobacterium tuberculosis (TB) by the QuantiFERON®-TB Gold test (QFT-G). INH preventive therapy was started and 14 weeks later the patient developed erythematous plaques on the neck and back with clear zones of demarcation resembling sunburn erythema on the dorsum of his hands, and hyperkeratotic plaques on the elbows. The patient reported frequent diarrheal stools, loss of appetite, and episodes of delirium and behavioral changes. Pellagra was suspected due to the low serum niacin level. Pharmacovigilance survey confirmed INH-induced pellagra. The management plan included INH withdrawal, nutritional review, and vitamin supplementation. The patient was treated with niacin orally (200mg/d). Three weeks later, the rash disappeared and diarrhea stopped. The patient was subsequently started on adalimumab.

Discharge Diagnosis: INH-induced Pellagra in a patient with Crohn's disease

Condition on Discharge: The patient’s clinical symptoms improved after treatment with niacin and adalimumab. No rash or diarrhea was reported.

Discharge Medications: None

Follow-Up: Follow-up with the gastroenterology team is recommended to ensure the patient's Crohn's disease is managed appropriately. No follow-up for the management of INH-induced pellagra is necessary.

Instructions: The patient is advised to maintain a healthy diet and avoid foods that may cause vitamin B3 deficiency. No further precautions are required.

Hospital Course Summary:

58-year-old male with poorly controlled diabetes and high cholesterol on pravastatin and ezetimibe presented with a six-fold increase in ALT and AST levels. Hepatitis serologies were negative and a liver sonogram was unremarkable. A diagnosis of drug-induced liver injury was made and all medications were discontinued. ALT and AST returned to baseline levels after discontinuation of sitagliptin, pravastatin, and ezetimibe. Rechallenge with sitagliptin resulted in a five-fold increase in the levels of serum ALT and AST.

44-year-old female with type 2 diabetes treated with sitagliptin, pioglitazone, and rosuvastatin, experienced a ten-fold elevation in ALT and AST levels. Hepatitis B surface antigen was negative and a liver sonogram was normal. Discontinuation of sitagliptin, pioglitazone, and rosuvastatin normalized the patient's ALT and AST levels. The patient refused rechallenge with sitagliptin.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 59-year-old female

Diagnosis: Schizophrenia and catatonia

Admission and Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital after experiencing delusions, hallucinations, grossly disorganized and catatonic behavior, and negative symptoms lasting more than 6 months. She was diagnosed with schizophrenia and remained under treatment for two years. She developed catatonia, and no EEG and CSF analysis had been performed. Therefore autoimmune NMDA-R-encephalitis and potentially associated viral infections had not been sufficiently ruled out.

Treatment:

The patient received electrical convulsion therapy (ECT) for 14 sessions (three times per week) in accordance with the revised edition of the Electrical Convulsion Therapy Recommendation of the Department of Neuropsychiatry of Japan. Thiopental or ketamine was used as an anesthetic. Her gut microbiota differed before and after ECT.

Outcomes:

The patient's symptoms improved significantly after the 14 ECT sessions, and the BPRS score decreased from 83 to 65, and her BFCRS score decreased from 51 to 28. She had no symptoms indicating organ disease, and her diagnosis for schizophrenia and catatonia remained the same.

Follow-Up and Recommendations:

The patient is recommended to continue her prescribed medication for severe symptoms, including risperidone and magnesium oxide as well as her laxative as prescribed by her treating physician for constipation. She should receive a follow-up evaluation with her treating physician to assess her symptoms and response to her prescribed medication.

None specified.

The patient is advised to schedule follow-up appointments with their primary care provider or surgeon as necessary.

History and Physical Exam:
The patient (II-1) was diagnosed with non-syndromic hearing loss after comprehensive medical history, family history, and detailed physical examination. His hearing threshold was evaluated by pure tone audiometry (PTA) and brainstem evoked response audiometry (BERA). No other related audiological symptoms were identified. Computerized tomography (CT) scan was performed to evaluate the temporal bone, and vestibular function analysis was done by caloric stimulation. Tympanogram was performed to exclude middle-ear associated causes of (HL). No abnormality was found in the vestibular organs.

Hospital Course:
The patient (II-1) was admitted and treated accordingly. The patient denied having any previous potential causes of acquired hearing loss. The speech perception ability was not impaired. Computed tomography scan revealed no abnormality in the medial and inner ear with normal temporal bone.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with the recommendation to follow up with a physician and continue the audiological treatment if needed. Written informed consent has been obtained from the patient in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

Hospital Course: 

The patient, a 15-year-old boy, presented with multiple asymptomatic cutaneous white patches. His clinical features of bushy arched eyebrows, thick everted lips, broad nasal bridge, facial nevi, and developmental delay prompted metabolic and genetic testing. A diagnosis of Coffin-Siris syndrome (CSS) was established via whole-exome sequencing revealing a premature stop codon mutation leading to a truncated protein in the ARID1B gene. The patient exhibited various characteristics of CSS including distinctive coarse facial features, fifth finger hypoplasia, first metatarsal hypermobility, hypertrichosis, depigmented macules and patches, and several melanocytic nevi.

The hospital stay for the patient was uneventful. The patient was managed conservatively under the care of the hospital staff. Nursing care was provided, and the patient was closely monitored for any changes in his condition. The patient was discharged with appropriate medications and follow-up instructions. The patient and his family were given counseling on proper care and management of the patient's condition. 

Disposition: 

The patient was discharged in stable condition with recommendations for regular follow-up visits to his primary care physician and specialist. The patient and his family were instructed on appropriate care and management of his condition. They were also advised to notify their physicians in case of any changes in his condition.

Patient Name: [Name]
Medical Record Number: [Number]
Admission Date: [Date]
Discharge Date: [Date]

Hospital course:

The patient was a four-year-old Iranian boy who was admitted to the hospital due to fever and symptoms of coryza and otitis media. During admission, the patient's vital signs were measured, which revealed he had a high temperature, and he was subsequently diagnosed with ANEC affecting the cerebellum, thalamus, and basal ganglia. The patient's liver enzymes were reported to be elevated, while all serological, parasitological, and urinary analyses were normal.

The patient's level of consciousness deteriorated, and he was unable to respond to environmental stimuli. The patient also had blurred vision, decreased muscle tone and force, increased DTRs, and bilateral Babinski sign. Multiple generalized tonic-clonic seizures occurred the following day. The CSF examination findings suggested encephalitis and infectious disease were ruled out. Gastrointestinal consultation also ruled out hepatic encephalopathy. The neurological consultation led to a brain MRI, which indicated the involvement of cerebellum, thalamus, and basal ganglia, which led to the diagnosis of ANEC.

Methylprednisolone was prescribed for seven days but was discontinued because of oral thrush, following which oral prednisolone was administered. After twelve days, the patient's level of consciousness improved, but his eyesight remained poor. Bridging the strabismus issue, involvement of the sixth nerve was considered. On the twentieth day after admission, the patient's general condition improved, and he was able to speak.

Summary:
The patient's ANEC diagnosis led to methylprednisolone treatment that was discontinued due to oral thrush symptoms. Oral prednisolone was then administered for about 20 days, leading to the improvement of the patient's general condition. After being carefully monitored, the patient was discharged.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
- Name: Not provided
- Age: 49
- Gender: Transgender male
- Diagnosis: Chest pain, high cardiac troponin

Hospital Course:
- Patient presented with central chest pain.
- High-sensitivity cardiac troponin was elevated.
- There is debate concerning the use of sex-specific reference ranges for high-sensitivity cardiac troponin.
- Despite being on established testosterone therapy for 10 years, there is currently insufficient data to suggest that cardiac remodeling or a change in cardiac size occurs with high testosterone concentrations.
- To minimize the risk of missing an acute coronary event, the sex presumed at birth (female) reference range was used to interpret high-sensitivity cardiac troponin levels.
- Patient was informed of this rationale and monitored with serial troponins to ensure no rise.
- Patient's subsequent high-sensitivity cardiac troponin was elevated above the male reference range and ECG revealed anterior ST-segment depression consistent with acute coronary syndrome.

Summary:
- Patient presented with chest pain and elevated high-sensitivity cardiac troponin.
- Despite being on testosterone therapy for 10 years, there is currently insufficient data to suggest that cardiac remodeling occurs.
- To minimize the risk of missing an acute coronary event, the sex presumed at birth (female) reference range was used to interpret high-sensitivity cardiac troponin levels.
- Patient was informed of this rationale and monitored with serial troponins to ensure no rise.
- Elevated subsequent troponin levels and ECG findings were consistent with acute coronary syndrome.
