Admitting Diagnosis: Aortitis

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 60-year-old female with a past medical history of breast cancer and depression, was admitted due to high fevers, myalgia, fatigue, productive cough, and chills. She had recent gastrointestinal illness after eating at a new restaurant which spontaneously resolved. She reported headaches, sinus congestion, and sore throat that resolved with antibiotics prescribed for sinusitis. CT of the chest with contrast showed diffuse, abnormal soft tissue around the ascending aorta and aortic arch with fat stranding, which was consistent with aortitis. She was transferred to this hospital for rheumatological management of aortitis. The differential diagnoses included infectious and noninfectious inflammatory conditions, such as tuberculosis, human immunodeficiency virus, giant cell arteritis, Takayasu’s arteritis, anti-neutrophilic cytoplasmic autoantibody vasculitis, systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, immunoglobulin G4-related disease, and Erdheim-Chester disease. Serologic and fecal testing for infectious etiologies were negative, and imaging did not suggest involvement in other organs. Subsequently, the patient was diagnosed with isolated aortitis given her presenting constitutional symptoms, significantly elevated inflammatory markers, and CT chest finding of diffuse fat stranding surrounding the ascending aorta and aortic arch. The patient was initiated on prednisone therapy and tocilizumab 162 mg subcutaneous injections within one month of diagnosis due to steroid intolerance. Her elevated inflammatory markers and symptoms resolved quickly and remained in remission at 10 months of follow-up. Follow-up CT chest demonstrated the attenuation of inflammation around the aorta. Even though pseudoaneurysms were noted, these were felt to be likely sequelae of the initial episode. They were stable on further repeat imaging.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was admitted for rheumatological management of aortitis following high fevers, myalgia, fatigue, productive cough, and chills. The patient's diagnosis was isolated aortitis, and standard imaging confirmed fat stranding surrounding the ascending aorta and aortic arch. The patient responded well to treatment with prednisone followed by tocilizumab, and was discharged after having remained in remission at 10 months of follow-up.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course: The patient was evaluated by the oral medicine clinic for a slowly growing mass on the hard palate. An intraoral examination revealed a large, compressible, oval-shaped mass of the right hard palate extending to the soft palate. A 5 mm incisional punch biopsy was performed, revealing a benign salivary gland tumor consisting of pools of plasmacytoid cells and numerous double-layered ducts with significant areas of adipose tissue. The final diagnosis was pleomorphic adenoma with significant adipose tissue component. The patient was referred to oral surgery for complete surgical excision, and a CBCT was performed to confirm the benign behavior of the lesion. Surgical excision was completed, and the pathology findings were consistent with the incisional biopsy results. The patient has had no recurrences and is doing well upon 2-year follow-up.

Hospital Course Summary: The patient presented to the oral medicine clinic with a slowly growing mass on the hard palate, and a diagnosis of pleomorphic adenoma with significant adipose tissue component was made after an incisional punch biopsy. The patient was referred to oral surgery for excision, and pathology findings were consistent with the incisional biopsy results. A 2-year follow-up revealed no recurrences, and the patient is doing well.

Hospital Course: The patient was admitted for the management of ascites and worsening pedal edema. Blood investigations revealed hypoalbuminemia and raised serum globulins without evidence of hyperbilirubinemia or coagulation failure. A repeat liver biopsy revealed dense sinusoidal and terminal hepatic perivenular fibrosis with parenchymal extension and nodule formation suggestive of chronic SOS-associated cirrhosis.

History: The patient suffered from bilateral lower limb swelling for six months, three years ago, and was found to have hypoproteinemia on blood investigation. On upper gastrointestinal endoscopic evaluation and thereafter, on push enteroscopy, he was found to have extensive duodeno-jejunal lymphangiectasia, which was confirmed on small bowel biopsy. In view of waxing and waning of lower limb symptoms, he ingested a polyherbal Ayurvedic medicine twice daily for 10 days from a traditional Ayurveda practitioner. Two weeks after consuming the complementary and alternative medicine, he developed anasarca and mild jaundice with elevated serum bilirubin, aspartate aminotransferase, and alanine aminotransferase levels. Contrast imaging of the abdomen revealed hepatomegaly with patchy liver enhancement and ascites without hepatic vein or inferior vena-cava obstruction.

Assessment and Plan: Evaluation for acute hepatotropic and non-hepatotropic viruses including Herpes virus infection and chronic viral hepatitis, Wilson’s disease and autoimmune hepatitis was non-contributory. Family history of liver disease was absent and mutational studies for hemochromatosis, alpha-1 anti-trypsin deficiency and adiponutrin were non-contributory. R ratio for identification of type of liver injury was more than five, suggestive of hepatocellular pattern. The Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM) in drug-induced liver injury (DILI) score was eight, suggestive of probable adverse drug reaction. Liver biopsy showed extensive sinusoidal dilatation with mild perivenular, sinusoidal and perisinusoidal fibrosis. Clinical improvement was observed over 12 weeks but the patient was lost to follow up.

Follow-up: The patient was discharged with instructions to follow up with their primary care physician and gastroenterologist for ongoing management of chronic SOS-associated cirrhosis.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 51
Sex: Male

Final Diagnosis: Stage IIIB intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC) with metastasis in the liver and lymph nodes.

Hospital Course:

The patient presented with a ten-year history of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection and underwent surgical resection of the lesion in the left hepatic lobe. Subsequently, he was diagnosed with Stage IIIB ICC.

11 months after the surgery, a recurrence was noted in the right lobe with hepatic hilar and retroperitoneal lymph node metastasis. Further evaluation revealed a Tumor Mutational Burden (TMB) of 0.98 muts/Mb with high microsatellite stability (MSS) and proficient mismatch repair (pMMR). Programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression was found to be less than 1%. The patient was treated with Cyberknife therapy for the left hepatic lobe lesion and the left retroperitoneal lymph node, and subsequently underwent immunotherapy with pembrolizumab for 16 cycles and chemotherapy with Furflucil for six cycles. Recombinant human endostatin was also administered for four cycles.

One month after the initiation of the combined therapy, MRI revealed shrinkage in both irradiated and non-irradiated intra-hepatic and lymph node lesions, which continued to decline for four months. Subsequent monitoring revealed that the patient achieved complete response (CR) 12 months after initiation of the combined therapy, and maintained CR for 11 more months till January, 2019. No toxicity was observed as a result of the therapy involving SBRT with PD-1 blockade.

Discharge Instructions:

The patient is being discharged in a stable condition with the recommendation to follow up with regular check-ups to monitor any relapse or progression of the disease. He should be encouraged to follow a healthy lifestyle, including a balanced diet and exercise regimen. The patient is required to take his medications regularly and report any side effects or complications to his healthcare provider immediately.

Follow-up:

The patient will be scheduled to follow up with the treating oncologist and undergo further monitoring and imaging to detect any signs of relapse or progression.

Hospital Course:

This is a case report of a 59-year-old Chinese man who presented to the hematology unit with headache, lethargy, and exertional dyspnea for the past 1 month. He had undergone an uneventful cadaveric renal transplant 20 years ago for chronic glomerulonephritis-induced end-stage renal disease and had been on long-term immunosuppressants since then.

On examination, he was found to have normochromic normocytic anemia, leukocytosis, and a palpable liver and spleen of 3 cm. A bone marrow smear showed a markedly hypercellular marrow with diffuse infiltrates of abnormal lymphoid cells consistent with T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL), an aggressive form of a lymphoproliferative disorder.

The patient was treated with one cycle of chemotherapy but failed to respond. He was subsequently started on venetoclax and developed severe auto tumor lysis syndrome on day 15, which required mechanical ventilation and continuous veno-venous hemodialysis. Unfortunately, he died 2 days later at the intensive care unit.

Diagnosis:

T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL)

Summary:

This is a case report of a 59-year-old Chinese man who presented with symptoms of headache, lethargy, and exertional dyspnea. He was diagnosed with T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL) and treated with chemotherapy and subsequently with venetoclax. He developed severe auto tumor lysis syndrome which required mechanical ventilation and continuous veno-venous hemodialysis. Unfortunately, he died 2 days later at the intensive care unit.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our facility for surgical resection of a recurrent right neck mass. She underwent right radical neck dissection and wide local excision of the neck mass, but residual tumor plaque on the carotid and trachea were unable to be fully resected. Pathology revealed components of both classic papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and solid/trabecular variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma (SMECE). The tumor involved all margins, indicating that the tumor likely arose from a thyroid remnant. The patient received adjuvant treatment with 131I and underwent subsequent follow-up scans.

Presenting Complaint:
Swallowing difficulty.

History of Presenting Illness:
Eleven months postoperatively, the patient reported difficulty swallowing and had repeat imaging done. The imaging revealed a mass in the region of the thyroid bed posterior to the trachea. These findings were confirmed on a PET scan.

Past Medical History:
The patient had a history of PTC treated with total thyroidectomy, and subsequently had recurrence of the disease.

Diagnostic Studies:
CT of the neck revealed a heterogeneously enhancing and partially necrotic mass within the right thyroidectomy bed extending posteriorly to the esophagus and involving the right recurrent laryngeal nerve. The mass measured 2.2 × 3.0 × 2.8 cm in its respective anterior-posterior, transverse, and craniocaudal dimensions. Pathology revealed components of both classic PTC and SMECE. There was also a background of lymphocytic thyroiditis. Upon immunohistochemistry, both PTC and SMECE stained positive for CK AE1/AE3 and negative for calcitonin. The PTC component stained positive for thyroglobulin, whereas SMECE was negative. The SMECE-involved areas of the specimen were scattered to diffusely positive for CK5/6 and p63. BRAF V600E mutation was identified by PCR in both the PTC and SMECE tumors.

Hospital Course and Treatment:
The patient underwent a right and left radical neck dissection with laryngectomy, though again the tumor was not able to be fully resected, because it was densely adherent to the carotid and innominate arteries. Surgical pathology showed anaplastic and poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma, which again tested positive for BRAF V600E mutation. The patient was being considered for radiation therapy and BRAF inhibitor treatment, but insurance did not cover the latter.

Clinical Condition at Discharge:
The patient was lost to follow-up.

Admission Summary:
The patient is a 25-year-old female with a history of obesity who had undergone RYGB 2 years prior to admission. She presented with frequent episodes of hypoglycemia causing tachycardia, sweating, and neuroglycopenic symptoms, including confusion, dizziness, and blurred vision. These symptoms occurred during the day and night and impacted her work and quality of life negatively. 

Hospital Course:
The patient underwent Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM) with Dexcom G4 PLATINUM for seven days, which revealed ample blood glucose excursions throughout the day with glucose peaks above 200 mg/dL after meals, followed by a rapid fall below 55 mg/dL. CGM also showed low glucose levels during the night, as demonstrated by significant time spent below 55 mg/dL. Based on the continuous glucose profile, the diagnosis of PBH was posed. Glucose variability indexes with coefficient of variation (CV), standard deviation (SD), and mean amplitude of glycemic excursions (MAGE) increased. 
The patient was prescribed a normocaloric high-fiber, low-carbohydrate index diet with multivitamin and mineral supplements to address deficiencies of vitamin D and iron. After nutritional therapy, the symptoms improved, but the patient continued to report early morning asthenia and tiredness, associated with glucose levels below 70 mg/dL. A starting dose of uncooked cornstarch, gradually increased from 30 g to 85 g over time, administered before going to bed, resulted in a remarkable reduction in glucose variability indexes and postprandial glycemic peaks. 

Discharge Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with Post-Bariatric Hypoglycemia (PBH) related to Roux-en-Y Gastric Bypass (RYGB). 

Discharge Medications:
No medication reportable at this time.

Follow-up Instructions:
The patient should continue the prescribed normocaloric high-fiber, low-carbohydrate index diet with multivitamin and mineral supplements, along with the uncooked cornstarch supplementation before bedtime, which was incrementally increased to 85 g for PBH management. Further follow-up for RYGB and PBH management is recommended with endocrinology consultation due to ongoing symptoms of hypoglycemia. 

Disposition and Condition on Discharge:
The patient was discharged in stable condition.

Chief Complaint:
The patient presented to the department of nephrology with complaints of right flank pain and swelling with a high-grade fever.

Hospital Course:
The patient was diagnosed with type II diabetes with a Hba1c level of 8% and was found to have a low hemoglobin level of 9 gm/dL, polymorphonuclear leucocytosis of 16500/mm3, high serum creatinine level of 4.3 mg/dL, and 100 mg/dL proteinuria with burning sensation during micturition.

Diagnostic Tests and Imaging:
Non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a large-size intrarenal abscess which was treated with an ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage. The aspirate culture was positive for C. tropicalis which was identified by the Vitek 2 Compact automated system, showing sensitivity to caspofungin, micafungin, and amphotericin, but resistance to fluconazole.

Treatment:
The patient was administered with amphotericin B deoxycholate for 3 weeks. Improvement was observed within a week of initiating antifungal therapy in terms of settling of fever and serum creatinine, which showed a downward trend.

Clinical Course:
The patient was discharged in good health and advised to attend the outpatient clinic for follow-up on a weekly basis for 2 weeks, followed by bi-weekly referral for 4 weeks and another referral 3 months after hospital discharge. The patient was asymptomatic and had no evidence regarding the recurrence of fungal infection with a serum creatinine of 1.8 mg/dl at the end of 3 months.

Follow-up:
The patient was advised to continue diabetic management and maintain a healthy lifestyle to prevent further complications.

Final Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with type II diabetes and intrarenal abscess caused by C. tropicalis, treated using amphotericin B deoxycholate.

Discharge Summary - Elastofibroma in Bilateral Infrascapular and Gluteal Regions

Patient Information:
- Name: John Doe
- Age: 63 years
- Gender: Male
- Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]
- Admission Date: [REDACTED]
- Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
Mr. John Doe is a 63-year-old male who presented with a 6-month history of a gradually increasing swelling on the right upper back. Physical examination revealed the presence of a palpable, non-tender, firm mass with limited mobility located beneath the scapular tip of each shoulder. The patient underwent contrast-enhanced CT, which showed well-defined, bilateral, solid masses located deep to the serratus anterior muscles in the infrascapular region. It also showed two soft tissue masses bilaterally present between the gluteus maximus and gluteus minimus muscles. A presumptive diagnosis of elastofibroma was made, and biopsy was recommended during a multidisciplinary oncology meeting.

Histopathological analysis revealed the presence of fibrous collagenous tissue, occasional fibroblasts, and a large number of eosinophilic fibers intermixed with islets of mature adipose tissues. The diagnosis of elastofibroma was established through core-needle biopsy of the right infrascapular mass. The patient underwent surgical resection of the infrascapular masses. Both infrascapular masses were completely excised, and the gluteal masses were asymptomatic and did not warrant surgical management. The resected lesions had clear surgical margins, and at the follow-up visit, the patient was asymptomatic and showed no functional limitation in the movement of the shoulder joint.

Final Diagnosis: Elastofibroma

Condition on Discharge:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with the diagnosis of bilateral infrascapular and gluteal elastofibroma. The patient's surgical interventions were successful, and the patient is expected to make a full recovery.

Treatment:
The patient underwent surgical resection of both infrascapular masses. The gluteal masses were asymptomatic and did not warrant surgical management.

Follow-up:
The patient was referred for follow-up care with a primary care physician and was instructed to return if there were any changes in the size or pain of the remaining gluteal masses.

Summary:
Mr. John Doe, a 63-year-old male, was admitted for a 6-month history of bilateral, palpable, solid masses located deep to the serratus anterior muscles in the infrascapular region, with occasional discomfort and unintentional weight loss. The diagnosis of elastofibroma was established through core-needle biopsy. The patient underwent surgical resection of both infrascapular masses and was discharged in stable condition. The gluteal masses were asymptomatic and did not warrant surgical management. The patient was referred for follow-up care.

Implantation of capsular tension ring with PCIOL was possible in the bag at the conclusion of surgery. Prophylactic LPI was done in the fellow eye.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted for evaluation of noncompliance with medications.

History and Physical:
A 63-year-old right-handed man with a history of frontotemporal brain injury and a large craniotomy defect was evaluated. The patient had spent 23 years in prison after hearing voices that instructed him to commit suicide, resulting in an attempted murder. After being shot several times by the police, including the head, the patient experienced a major personality change characterized by persistent feelings of mirth and “happiness.” His medical history includes seizures treated with divalproex and lacosamide, as well as right eye blindness.

Examination:
The patient was observed to be unconcerned and generally not taking his situation seriously. He would occasionally Valsalva to self-inflate his craniotomy defect to amuse others. His mood appeared excessively good for the context but not overtly euphoric. The patient underwent a Montreal Cognitive Assessment and scored 16/30, missing the memory and orientation questions, serial 7's, an abstraction, and verbal fluency.

Diagnostic Studies:
Computerized tomography and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head showed extensive volume loss and gliosis of the right frontal lobe, the right anterior temporal lobe, and the left orbitofrontal region. Fluorodeoxyglucose- (FDG-) positron emission tomography imaging showed corresponding hypometabolism in the same areas of the brain without extension to other areas.

Neuropsychological Testing:
The patient underwent neuropsychological testing which indicated a profound impairment in memory and variable executive functions. His estimated premorbid full-scale IQ was 115. He was amnestic in both verbal and nonverbal modalities. He had deficits on some executive function tests, and the most salient executive deficits were in inhibitory control.

Behavioral Tasks:
The patient underwent examinations with a specific set of behavioral tasks, including the Joke and Story Completion Test, recognition of the six Ekman and Friesen facial emotions, the Sally and Anne Task, the Hinting Task for screening of Theory of Mind, and the Subjective Happiness Scale. On all the tests, the patient appeared to have intact abilities for humor appreciation and recognition of facial emotions. The patient's score on the Subjective Happiness Scale was perfect.

Impressions and Plan:
Given the patient's injury and extensive volume loss and gliosis in the brain, his mirthful behavior and poor cognitive performance on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment were considered typical and consistent with his injury. The patient will be monitored for compliance with medications and referred for psychiatric follow-up.

Hospital Course:

The native Brazilian female patient came to our hospital at 8 weeks of pregnancy with symptoms of a maculo-papular rash, arthralgia, and asthenia. She had tested positive for ZIKV IgG in Brazil, however, her specific IgM was negative. At 15 weeks of pregnancy, a urine sample was positive for ZIKV RNA, while her plasma and saliva were negative. The mother showed positive ZIKV and DENV IgG and negative ZIKV and DENV IgM. Virus-neutralizing antibodies were positive at a higher titer for DENV 1 with respect to ZIKV NS1. Neurosonography performed at 20 weeks of pregnancy did not show any fetal brain abnormalities. ZIKV RNA was not detected in amniotic fluid, and additional maternal plasma and urine collected for testing were negative as well. At 28 weeks of gestation, fetal cMRI was performed in Brazil, showing an absence of cerebral malformations.  

Discharge Summary: 

The patient, a 26-year-old Brazilian woman, presented at our hospital at the recommendation of her husband, who is from Lombardy, Italy. She reported symptoms of a maculo-papular rash, arthralgia, and asthenia, which had started seven weeks before pregnancy in Brazil. In loco ZIKV serologic testing showed positive ZIKV IgG with specific IgM negative. At 15 weeks of pregnancy, she tested positive for ZIKV RNA in her urine sample. The mother demonstrated positive ZIKV and DENV IgG and negative ZIKV and DENV IgM. Unfortunately, the ELISpot assay for DENV and ZIKV had not yet been developed at that time. Neurosonography and fetal cMRI were performed at different stages of the pregnancy, and no fetal brain abnormalities or cerebral malformations were observed. 

At the time of discharge, the mother had given birth to a healthy baby who did not show any signs of ZIKV congenital infection. This concludes the patient's hospital course, and she was advised to follow up with her physician for continued monitoring.

Discharge Summary:

Patient was admitted to the hospital due to fever and 5% weight loss in one month. Upon admission, laboratory tests revealed marked thrombocytosis, normocytic anemia, and slight leukocytosis with elevated ferritin and C-reactive protein levels. Subsequent imaging tests revealed a left adrenal tumor, which was diagnosed as pheochromocytoma. In addition, the patient presented with episodes of palpitations, sweating, headache, and limb paresthesia related to efforts. Elevated plasma and urinary normetanephrine levels confirmed the diagnosis.

Patient was started on preoperative alpha-blockade treatment with phenoxybenzamine and beta-blockade treatment with propranolol. After 23 days, successful left adrenalectomy was performed without complications. Histological examination of the tumor revealed that it was well delimited with a potential for malignant biological behavior.

After surgery, the patient's alpha- and beta-blockade was stopped, and hydrocortisone was prescribed to treat the suppressed ACTH and autonomous cortisol production. At reevaluation two months after surgery, imaging tests showed no evidence of persistent disease.

No germline mutations were detected in the following genes: RET, VHL, SDHAF2, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, MAX, and TMEM127. The patient's plasma and urinary normetanephrine levels were within reference range, and IL-6 was undetectable. The patient was discharged in good condition and advised to follow up with her endocrinologist for further evaluation.

Summary:
- Admitted to hospital due to fever and weight loss
- Diagnosed with pheochromocytoma
- Preoperative alpha-blockade and beta-blockade treatment started
- Left adrenalectomy successfully performed after 23 days 
- Hydrocortisone prescribed post-surgery
- No evidence of persistent disease two months after surgery 
- No germline mutations found 
- Discharged in good condition

Brief Hospital Course:
The patient, a 54-year-old Caucasian male with a history of profound intellectual disability, schizophrenia, posttraumatic stress disorder, Parkinson's disease, gastroesophageal reflux disease and seizure disorder, was admitted to the hospital with fever, tachycardia, nausea and vomiting of three days duration. On admission, he was diagnosed with sepsis of unknown origin. The patient was treated with antibiotics and fluid resuscitation. On hospital day 2, the patient developed muscle rigidity, tremors, hypoxemia, increasing temperature, tachypnea, and worsening tachycardia. The patient had been receiving haloperidol injections at his assisted living facility and had been refusing many of his scheduled medications. The patient was diagnosed with Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome (NMS) and treated with dantrolene, intravenous vecuronium, and supportive care measures. The patient's total creatine kinase level trended downward, BUN and creatinine levels trended down, and he was eventually transferred to the general medicine unit.

Hospital Course Summary:
The hospital course was marked with several challenges. The patient was initially admitted with sepsis of unknown origin and was treated with antibiotics and fluid resuscitation. However, on hospital day 2, the patient developed several symptoms consistent with NMS. Close review of the medical records from his assisted living facility indicated that the patient had received several doses of haloperidol injections before being admitted. The patient was diagnosed with NMS and was treated with dantrolene, intravenous vecuronium, and supportive care measures. The patient was eventually transferred to the general medicine unit where he was closely monitored.

Discharge Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with NMS. Following treatment, the patient was diagnosed with psychosis and delusional paranoia. Carbamazepine and lorazepam were recommended for management of agitation, and trazodone 100mg at bedtime was started for sleep. Psychotic symptoms and agitation persisted and low dose quetiapine was started. The patient was monitored closely.

Discharge Condition:
The patient's condition improved significantly with treatment. The patient was discharged back to his assisted living facility.

Discharge Medications:
Carbamazepine, lorazepam, and trazodone were prescribed to manage the patient's agitation and sleep. Low dose quetiapine was prescribed for the patient's psychosis and delusional paranoia.

Follow-up:
The patient was advised to follow-up with his primary care physician and psychiatrist. The patient will need ongoing medical management to monitor his condition and adjust his medication regimen as needed.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Date of Admission: June 2018
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

Hospital Course
The patient is a 2-year 11-month-old male with a history of chronic hemodialysis secondary to polycystic kidney disease (PCKD) who underwent bilateral nephrectomy. Following his second nephrectomy, the patient began intermittent hemodialysis five days a week, which was later decreased to four days a week after six months. He was being treated for hypertension and was started on 2.5 mg midodrine during hemodialysis for systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg. Prior to discharge, the patient was diagnosed with bilateral AION and was given a five-day course of intravenous pulse methylprednisolone. Optic nerve size and signal intensity were normal. He was discharged after treatment with midodrine and fluids were titrated for a blood pressure goal above 70/40 mmHg.

Hospitalization Summary
The patient was admitted to the hospital with an unsteady gait and difficulty focusing and following objects, starting approximately two hours after completion of hemodialysis that day. Parents noted a pupil size change from small to large bilaterally, documented at 8 mm. On his initial neurological examination, his pupils were dilated but responsive, and he had poor visual acuity and an unsteady gait. He was otherwise alert, oriented, and comfortable. Vitally, his blood pressure was 59/33 mmHg, heart rate was 92 bpm, and he was afebrile. Laboratory findings on admission demonstrated a normocytic, mild anemia with a hemoglobin level of 101 g/L and an MCV of 92.7 fL. His sodium was found to be low at 127 mmol/L, with a potassium level of 4.4 mmol/L, and a chloride level of 98 mmol/L. Repeat blood work displayed a sodium level of 134 mmol/L, and thus, no hypertonic saline was administered. Creatinine was elevated at 166 μmol/L. Tox screen was negative, and AST, ALT, and INR were all normal. Head CT displayed nonspecific findings of bifrontal subcortical white matter hypodensities. MRI displayed multiple foci of increased fluid-attenuated inversion recovery signal, mainly on bilateral subcortical white matter of the frontal lobes and corona radiata. Ophthalmology noted decreased visual acuity to hand motion and optic disk pallor, and diagnosed optic nerve atrophy.

Discharge Condition
The patient was discharged with a diagnosis of bilateral AION. Ophthalmology follow-up two months after his acute presentation revealed his vision to be 20/800 in the left eye and 20/30 in the right eye. He continued midodrine until his related living donor kidney transplant. He is currently stable and normotensive six months posttransplant. His vision at 10 months following his initial presentation is 20/40 in the right eye and no light perception in the left.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Gender: Male
Age: 45
Clinical Diagnosis: ACL reconstruction with post-surgical complications.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient presented with persistent pain and effusion at the lateral aspect of his right knee, ten years after an uneventful ACL reconstruction. The suspected diagnosis was postsurgical seroma, and treatment included percutaneous drainage, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and RICE (rest, ice, compression, and elevation). Initial evolution was satisfactory, with complete symptom release for 6 months. After this period, recurrent swelling at the lateral aspect of the knee reappeared and remained despite percutaneous drainage. The patient underwent surgical treatment in collaboration with plastic surgery. The bone tunnel was filled with autologous marrow bone graft, and the cortical bone defect was covered with local fascial flap. Three years after the femoral tunnel revision surgery, the patient remained with full functional recovery and without any clinical symptoms, effusion, or pain recurrence.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Gender: Male
Age: 74
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Presumed fungal keratitis

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our clinic with acute-onset eyelid swelling, redness, pain, and vision loss in his right eye. The initial diagnosis of presumed fungal keratitis was made by the referring ophthalmologist and he was treated with topical fortified antibiotic and antifungal therapy. However, there was no improvement in his clinical signs. Upon examination at our clinic, the patient had severe periocular skin hyperemia and swelling. Visual acuity was hand movements in the right eye and 20/20 in the left. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy revealed conjunctival chemosis, corneal epithelial defect, diffuse corneal haze, multiple foci of keratitis, fibrinous anterior chamber reaction, and hypopyon in the right eye. The patient was further evaluated with in vivo corneal confocal microscopy and numerous hyperreflective, linear needle-shaped structures resembling fungal hyphae were seen.

After reevaluating the patient's medical history, it was learned that the patient had tried to remove a small tent-like nest from a pine tree in his garden before his complaints started. Upon high-magnification slit-lamp examination, numerous caterpillar hairs embedded in the cornea were seen. Corneal debridement was performed under a surgical operating microscope and the patient was treated with topical prednisolone acetate 1.0% solution hourly, cycloplegic eye drops 3 times a day, and moxifloxacin 0.5% eye drops 4 times a day as prophylaxis against secondary infection.

On the third day of treatment, the patient's visual acuity improved to 20/200, eyelid edema and conjunctival chemosis decreased, hypopyon disappeared, +1 anterior chamber reaction was seen, and the corneal edema began to resolve. Steroid therapy was tapered slowly over a month and all clinical signs resolved at the end of the month.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Caterpillar hair keratitis

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to follow up with his primary care provider or ophthalmologist as needed for further evaluation and care. He is advised to take preventive measures when working in the garden or surrounding areas that may have harmful insects. Any visual changes or discomfort should be reported to the healthcare provider immediately. No further antibiotics or medications are required at this time.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: II-1
Age: 28
Gender: Female
Date of Admission: [Not specified]
Date of Discharge: [Not specified]

Hospital Course Summary:
II-1, a 28-year-old woman, was admitted to our hospital for profound HL without any syndromic phenotype. She had bilateral hearing loss at all frequencies, and predominantly at middle to high frequencies. Other associated symptoms were not observed in II-1, including vestibular disorders, optic problems, mal-development, and intellectual disability. She had a congenital HL, but did not find obvious progression these years. II-1's parents had consanguineous marriage. No deafness history was found in the last three generations of their family.

MT-RNR1: m.827A > G was identified by Sanger sequencing of four common HL-associated genes. However, it was insufficient to result in hearing impairment. Whole exome sequencing (WES) analysis was performed for II-1 and her parents. A missense variant, LOXHD1: c.5948C > T; p.S1983F, was identified within LOXHD1 and was co-segregated and validated in this family by Sanger sequencing. This variant was not found in all public databases (dbSNP, 1000 Genomes, ExAC and gnomAD), and predicted as damaging by multiple bioinformatics tools (SIFT, Polyphen2, and Mutation Taster, etc.). Evolution analysis also indicated that this variant was located at the well-conserved region. Although homogeneous MT-RNR1: m.827A > G was identified in II-1, her asymptomatic brother and mother also carrier this variant, implying that MT-RNR1: m.827A > G contributed little to the pathogenesis of II-1.

Upon comprehensive evaluation, II-1 was discharged with the diagnosis of profound HL without any syndromic phenotype. She was advised to have regular follow-up visits with her primary physician.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 69-year-old Hispanic female with a medical history of high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes mellitus type 2 and peripheral vascular disease.

Admission Diagnoses:
-Partial occlusive deep vein thrombosis of the axillary and brachial veins with a superficial thrombus involving the right basilic and cephalic veins, multiple patchy airspace opacities suspicious for multilobar pneumonia. 
-Posterior wall myocardial infarction (STEMI) with a tubular 100% thrombotic occlusion at the ostium of the left circumflex artery.
-Acute hypoxic respiratory failure requiring intubation for airway protection. 
-New ischemic cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction of 25%-30%, with akinesis of the entire inferolateral and inferior wall.

Hospital Course:
-Urgent cardiac catheterization and placement of a drug-eluting stent for STEMI. 
-Treatment with intravenous antibiotics for pneumonia, dual-antiplatelet therapy for myocardial infarction, and anticoagulation for deep vein thrombosis. 
-Development of acute painless blackish discoloration of the left middle finger, requiring amputation due to a presumptive diagnosis of CAPS. Treatment with steroids and five cycles of plasmapheresis.

She underwent urgent cardiac catheterization for STEMI and received treatment with intravenous antibiotics, dual-antiplatelet therapy, and anticoagulation. As a consequence of multiple thromboses, the patient suffered from acutely ischemic cardiomyopathy and underwent amputation of the left middle finger due to presumed embolic phenomenon in the setting of multiple thromboses due to an underlying hypercoagulable state. The patient was further diagnosed with CAPS and treated with steroids and plasmapheresis. She was discharged with instructions for close follow-up with hematology/oncology.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient name: [Redacted]
Patient ID: [Redacted]
Medical record number: [Redacted]

Hospital admission date: [Redacted]
Hospital discharge date: [Redacted]

Hospital course:
The patient was a 40-year-old male admitted with episodic high-grade intermittent fever, nonproductive cough, and shortness of breath for a duration of three days. He had a history of severe pneumonia two years ago which did not respond favorably to antibiotics. On examination, the patient was febrile and dyspneic with bilateral lower zone crepitations in the lungs. The patient was diagnosed with severe pneumonia with poor response to antibiotics. On day 5 of admission, he was transferred to an intensive care unit and started on noninvasive ventilation to maintain oxygenation. The patient was diagnosed with probable myocarditis complicating severe pneumonia. Over the course of the next three weeks, the patient was given intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics for seven days followed by intravenous Piperacillin-tazobactam. Then, on the 20th day of illness, the patient was started on indomethacin 50 mg three times a day assuming the possibility of Still's disease. The patient had a rapid response to initiation of indomethacin and became afebrile within next 24 hours and had significantly improved vital parameters. After 48 hours, the patient was taken off from BiPAP ventilation. Piperacillin-tazobactam was continued along with indomethacin for further 12 days. The patient remained afebrile and clinically improved and regained appetite and weight. A complete diagnosis of pulmonary onset AOSD was made, and treatment was continued. On the 35th day of illness, the patient developed re-emergence of moderate-grade intermittent fever while on indomethacin. He was given intravenous methyl prednisolone 1 g/daily for three days and later converted to oral prednisolone. All antibiotics were discontinued. Soon after starting steroid treatment, the patient demonstrated signs of complete improvement. The patient was discharged on the 42nd day of illness.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with severe pneumonia with poor response to antibiotics, probable myocarditis complicating severe pneumonia, and pulmonary onset AOSD.

Treatment:
The patient was initially treated with intravenous amoxicillin and clavulanic acid with oral clarithromycin. Later, the treatment was changed to intravenous meropenam and vancomycin. The patient was then started on indomethacin 50 mg three times a day. Upon re-emergence of moderate-grade intermittent fever, the patient was given intravenous methyl prednisolone 1 g/daily for three days and later converted to oral prednisolone.

Condition at discharge:
The patient was afebrile and clinically improved. The patient was discharged with oral prednisolone treatment.

Follow-up plan:
The patient was advised for a follow-up after the first and six months. The patient's oral prednisolone treatment was continued and gradually tailed off over the next 6 months.

Summary:
The patient was a 40-year-old male admitted with severe pneumonia with poor response to antibiotics, probable myocarditis complicating severe pneumonia, and pulmonary onset AOSD. The patient was initially treated with intravenous antibiotics which were later changed to indomethacin. Upon re-emergence of moderate-grade intermittent fever, the patient was given intravenous methyl prednisolone. The patient demonstrated signs of complete improvement and was discharged with oral prednisolone treatment. The patient's follow-up plan includes a follow-up after the first and six months.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient is a 76-year-old female who presented with intermittent left-sided jaw and lower face pain. The initial differential diagnosis included acute myocardial infarction, temporal arteritis, trigeminal neuralgia, and various causes of acute jaw pain in an elderly female patient. The patient underwent a CT angiogram, electrocardiogram, chest radiograph, and laboratory analysis.  Neurology was consulted, and methylprednisolone 250 milligrams IV was administered along with ketorolac and fentanyl, with no significant pain reduction. The patient underwent a CTA scan of the head and neck that revealed a CAD of the left internal carotid artery. The neurosurgeons recommended continuing anticoagulation with close follow-up. During hospitalization, the patient did not exhibit any neurologic deficits and was discharged within 24 hours on oral apixaban and steroids. The patient is advised to follow up with her dentist prior to outpatient neurology follow-up to rule out dental causes.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient Name: Unknown

Admission Date: Unknown

Discharge Date: Unknown

Reason for Admission:

The patient was admitted to the ED with a two-day history of intermittent substernal chest pressure increasing in frequency and intensity.

Medical History:

The patient has a significant family history of premature coronary artery disease (CAD) and a history of hypertension. Chronic smoking was also noted.

Hospital Course:

Cardiac catheterization was performed for unstable angina. The results revealed an anomalous origin of left main coronary artery from the right sinus of Valsalva. The presence of LMCA compression due to an intramuscular course in its proximal segment was the cause of myocardial ischemia.

The patient was taken to the operating room, and the LMCA was successfully re-implanted on the anterior surface of the aorta. Postoperatively, the patient had an unremarkable hospital course.

One week later, the patient was re-admitted for a pericardial effusion requiring drainage and pericardial window.

Follow-up:

On follow-up, the patient has continued to do well.

Summary:

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 62-year-old Caucasian man, was admitted to the hospital for treatment of non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, community-acquired pneumonia, and Staphylococcus hominis mitral valve endocarditis. The patient was scheduled to complete a six-week course of intravenous vancomycin, but on Day 32 of treatment developed whole body pruritus and an erythematous macular rash that spread centrifugally to the extremities. The rash continued to evolve, and the patient developed desquamation, intense skin pain, and intermittent fevers.

Differential Diagnosis:

The patient was initially suspected to have vancomycin-induced red man syndrome but was ruled out due to the rash appearing over 80% of the total body surface area, and that there was no mucosal involvement or pulmonary symptoms. Stevens-Johnson Syndrome/Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis was also considered, but was excluded due to the lack of classic dermal, mucosal, or hematologic findings. DRESS syndrome was suspected due to the characteristic features identified, leading to a probable diagnosis.

Treatment:

All antibiotics were discontinued upon suspicion of drug-induced rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms. Topical and systemic steroids were administered to treat the skin condition. The patient was discharged from the hospital without antibiotics but continued to use topical steroids and symptomatic treatment at home.

Outcome and Follow-up:

The patient saw marked improvement in the erythema on his trunk and normalized white blood cell count over two weeks. The rash completely resolved except for mild erythema on his hands and feet at his 3-month follow-up. He noted improvement in ageusia, and his blood pressure medications were resumed without any sequelae at his 5-month follow-up.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 71-year old woman with bilateral FECD

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to our eye clinic with bilateral FECD. She had a medical history of previous cataract surgery and was being treated for polymyalgia rheumatica and psoriasis arthritis with oral prednisolone 5 mg (Prednisolon ratio 5 mg, Ratiopharm GmbH, Germany) once a day combined with oral pantoprazole 40 mg (Pantozol 40 mg, Takeda GmbH, Germany) and subcutaneous adalimumab 40 mg (Humira 40 mg, Cc-Pharma GmbH, Germany) biweekly. Due to a previous stroke without any residual deficits, she was also treated with aspirin 100 mg daily (ASS Hexal 100 mg, Hexal AG, Germany).

The patient underwent DMEK surgery on her right eye using a liquid bubble dissection technique for lenticular preparation. The surgery was successful with no complications or abnormalities noted. However, during the following days, she experienced progressive stromal edema, Descemet’s membrane folds, and subtotal Descemet detachment. A second air-gas mixture bubble was injected into the anterior chamber on the sixth day after the initial surgery. Although she showed stable, well-centered graft with an air-gas bubble, she presented with blurred vision and was found to have stromal corneal edema, Descemet’s folds, and Detachment infero-temporally.

The patient agreed to undergo a second re-bubbling procedure to correct the detachment and the distorted orientation of the graft, which was found to be upside-down. The surgeon inverted and reoriented the graft before injecting the air-gas mixture inside the anterior chamber. Follow-up examinations showed a graft with a clearer center compared to before the reorientation process.

The patient presented three weeks later with a 20/40 vision in her right eye and only slight Descemet’s membrane folds, clear corneal center, and without graft detachment. Further on, she achieved 20/32, 20/20, 20/20, and 20/32 BCDVA 3, 6, 9, and 15 months after the reorientation of the upside-down graft, respectively.

Conclusion:
The patient underwent successful DMEK surgery and subsequent re-bubbling procedures due to stromal edema, Descemet’s folds, and detachment. She responded well to the second re-bubbling procedure after the graft was found to be upside-down and was discharged without any complications.

Hospital Course:
A 62-year-old man presents with acute severe abdominal pain, tachycardia, hypotension, and marked abdominal guarding and rigidity. He has a past history of squamous cell carcinoma of the lower thoracic oesophagus and underwent transhiatal oesophagectomy with orthotopic gastric tube conduit five years ago. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed gross ascites with multiple septations, and erect X-ray abdomen confirmed the diagnosis of perforation peritonitis. 

Treatment:
The patient was resuscitated with intravenous fluids and antibiotics. Emergency dialysis was performed in view of refractory hyperkalemia and severe metabolic acidosis. Bilateral flank drains were inserted with a view to draining out the infected fluid in order to attain partial source control. He responded favorably to initial resuscitation and was taken up for emergency surgery.

Procedure:
At laparotomy, there was gross intraperitoneal contamination with biliopurulent fluid. There were dense inter-bowel and parietal adhesions. After extensive adhesiolysis, a large perforation was found on the anterior aspect of the distal part of the gastric tube conduit, approximately 2 cm proximal to the pylorus. The perforation site was immediately below the right crus, which was partially covering the perforation site. The edges were edematous and friable. After thorough peritoneal toileting, the perforation was closed primarily after freshening the margins. Witzel-type feeding jejunostomy was placed to ensure enteral nutrition in the postoperative period.

Outcome:
Postoperatively, the patient remained intubated and on inotropic support in view of severe sepsis and shock. Dialysis was repeated on postoperative day one. However, he failed to respond to supportive management and succumbed to his illness on postoperative day two. Histopathologic examination of biopsy from perforation edge revealed non-specific inflammation. 

Follow-up:
The patient was discharged to the morgue for further management.

Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
Sex: Male

Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Length of Stay: 3 months

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with dyspnea and flank pain. After further investigation, multiple lesions were observed in his liver, lungs, chest wall, bone and left adrenal gland. A biopsy revealed a metastatic high-grade malignant tumor with a neuroendocrine profile and unknown primary location. He was started on chemotherapy (carboplatin and etoposide) and was administered fentanyl, ondansetron, and sodium phosphate laxatives to manage his symptoms. He also received cortisone gradually and was administered furosemide intravenously when needed.

After the first round of chemotherapy, he developed partly therapy-resistant back pain. Following an external radiation directed at his pelvis and lower back for palliative purposes, he developed a left-sided pathological hip fracture. The excised femoral head and neck were sent for histopathological examination, revealing infiltration by a nest-forming tumor with large atypical nuclei displaying multiple nucleoli and partly loose chromatin. The diagnosis was consistent with a metastatic epithelioid malignant melanoma with neuroendocrine differentiation. He subsequently developed bilateral pleural effusions, which were managed with intermittent pleurocentesis, and also developed respiratory failure. This was aggravated by the occurrence of lobar pneumonia. Given his status, no clinical investigations regarding the occurrence of an undiagnosed primary cutaneous or mucosal malignant melanoma were initiated. The patient ultimately developed septicemia and passed away three months after initial presentation.

Diagnosis: 
Metastatic high-grade malignant tumor with a neuroendocrine profile and unknown primary location, consistent with a neuroendocrine carcinoma

Treatment:
Chemotherapy (carboplatin and etoposide)
Radiation therapy directed at his pelvis and lower back for palliative purposes

Disposition:
Patient passed away after three months of hospitalization.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Patient name redacted]
Gender: Male
Age: 41 years
Admission Date: [Admission date redacted]
Discharge Date: [Discharge date redacted]

Chief Complaint:
Traumatic injuries due to a high-velocity car accident resulting in multiple injuries.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the emergency department with a severe bleeding head wound, symmetric breathing, and normal abdominal findings. Blood pressure and saturation were normal. On arrival to the hospital, the patient had worsening bradypnea and bilateral rhonchi. A chest X-ray revealed multiple left-sided rib fractures without pneumothorax and blurry consolidations in both lungs, probably lung contusions. After stabilization, the patient underwent a computed tomography (CT) of the head, followed by a total body CT from the circle of Willis up to the pelvis with a split bolus intravenous contrast injection. The study showed multiple intracranial subdural and subarachnoid bleeds, with secondary edema of the left hemisphere and a skull base fracture. 

Furthermore, multiple rib fractures on the left side with underlying lung laceration, contusion, RCA dissection, resulted in an acute myocardial infarction. Urgent angiography was performed, which showed a complete occlusion of the right coronary artery, probably due to a traumatic dissection. Multiple stents were placed to approve reflow of the myocardium, but there was no reflow to the myocardial tissue established, and the patient passed away.

Diagnosis:
Traumatic injuries resulting in multiple rib fractures, lung laceration, contusion, skull base fracture, and intracranial subdural and subarachnoid bleeds. The acute myocardial infarction was diagnosed as a result of the RCA dissection.

Summary:
A 41-year-old male was admitted to the emergency department after a high-velocity car accident. The patient suffered from multiple injuries, including skull base fracture, multiple rib fractures, lung laceration, contusion, and intracranial subdural and subarachnoid bleeds. The patient had also experienced an acute myocardial infarction, which was diagnosed as a result of the RCA dissection. Despite the efforts to approve reflow with multiple stents, the patient did not survive.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Name]

Date of Admission: [Date]

Date of Discharge: [Date]

Admitting Diagnosis: Encephalitis

Discharge Diagnosis: EBV Meningoencephalitis

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 77-year-old male with no significant personal or family history, was admitted with fever, headache, mental disorder, and unconsciousness. Physical examination showed neck stiffness and unconsciousness with a GCS score of 6 points. Laboratory investigations were unremarkable except for a lymphocyte ratio of 14.8%. Lumbar puncture showed increased pressure, pleocytosis, and elevated protein levels while cytology examination of CSF showed increased lymphocytes and activated monocytes. MRI scans revealed cerebellum and cerebral cortex swelling with cytotoxic edema and micro-bleeding. A 24-hour EEG showed diffuse 2 to 3 Hz waves, and EBV–DNA was detected by NGS detection of CSF, indicating EBV meningoencephalitis.

The patient was treated with ganciclovir, corticosteroids, and IV immunoglobulins. Twenty days after admission, his lumbar puncture pressure was reduced, but his clinical symptoms did not improve, he was still in a coma. The patient was hospitalized for 32 days. His family refused further medical treatment and discharged from the hospital. 

Follow-Up:

Two months after discharge, the patient was still in a coma. Four months later, the patient died of pulmonary infection complications.

Discharge Plan:

The patient was discharged to home with no medications or treatment plans. Outpatient follow-up was not recommended due to the patient's poor prognosis.

Hospital Course:
The patient was a 24-year-old male who presented with pain and swelling in the right elbow, which was attributed to a fall on the outstretched hand three weeks prior. The patient received previous osteopathic treatment in the form of crepe bandaging with no relief of symptoms. Examination showed a generalized swelling of the right elbow, with tenderness over the lateral condyle of the humerus. An X-ray showed a coronal fracture of the lateral column of the distal humerus.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with a coronal fracture of the lateral column of the distal humerus, with associated posterolateral comminution (Dubberley type 3b).

Treatment:
The patient consented to an open reduction and internal fixation of the fracture using the anterolateral approach to the elbow. Initial fixation of the anterior, large fragment was done with a single Herbert screw. After the anterior fragment was fixed, a varus stress was given, along with traction, to open the joint so that the posterior fragments could be pushed back into place. One large, lateral fragment was fixed with a lateral-to-medial cannulated cancellous screw. The wound was closed in layers over a negative-suction drain. A posterior above-elbow plaster slab was given for a week, after which active, assisted elbow movements were started.

Outcome:
At the six-month follow-up, the patient had no pain. The patient had a range of motion of 10-120 degrees in the flexion-extension arc, with full pronation and supination. Although the patient felt a slight loss of elbow strength, they were able to do most of their daily activities without difficulty. The Mayo Elbow Performance Index (MEPI) score was 92, indicating an excellent result.

Admitting Diagnosis: Large, 5 x 3 cm dural-based left temporal tumor causing locoregional mass effect with occasional convulsions and hypermetabolic lung lesion causing diagnostic difficulties.
Final Diagnosis: Small cell carcinoma of the lung

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with progressively worsening headaches and occasional convulsions. Neuroimaging showed a large, 5 x 3 cm dural-based left temporal tumor causing locoregional mass effect. The chest, abdomen, and pelvis CT scan and PET scan showed a small, hypermetabolic lung lesion. 

A catheter cerebral angiogram for preoperative embolization of the tumor showed an incidental, 2.0 x 1.6 mm unruptured left ACA proximal A1 segment aneurysm. The patient elected to undergo both tumor resection and aneurysm clipping concurrently, which was successfully performed under general anesthesia. 

The patient developed transient mild right-sided hemiparesis that resolved by postoperative day 3. Postoperative cerebral angiography showed complete aneurysm occlusion, and brain magnetic resonance imaging showed gross total resection of the tumor with a punctate infarct in the left anterior thalamus.

The final histopathological analysis of the tumor revealed a diagnosis of small cell carcinoma of the lung. The patient was discharged to a rehabilitation facility and underwent chemotherapy for lung cancer diagnosis.

The patient has been advised to continue her chemotherapy treatment for lung cancer and follow up with her oncologist regularly. She has been given instructions for physical therapy, including exercises to improve mobility and strength, as well as precautions for any surgical incisions. She should also follow up with her primary care provider and report any new or worsening symptoms.

Please refer to the medication list provided by the patient's oncologist.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 74-year-old female with a history of hypertension and high cholesterol, presented with intermittent postprandial epigastric pain lasting for several hours with nausea and emesis. Laboratory results revealed scleral icterus and elevated total bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, aspartate aminotransferase, and alanine aminotransferase levels, indicative of liver impairment. To address biliary obstruction, initial treatment with ampicillin-sulbactam was followed by a computed tomography (CT) scan that identified radiopaque foreign bodies and marked biliary dilation. Subsequent tests including magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) confirmed the presence of a surgically implanted clip and stone causing the obstruction. The clip and stone were successfully removed through balloon sweep, leading to the resolution of symptoms and normalization of liver function.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was admitted with postprandial epigastric pain, nausea, and emesis. Diagnostic imaging revealed biliary obstruction due to a migrated surgical clip with an attached stone, successfully treated through balloon sweep. The patient was discharged in stable condition. Follow-up care with a gastroenterologist and regular liver function testing was recommended.

Hospital Course:

This is a comprehensive summary of the hospital course of a 71-year-old male patient who presented with slowly enlarging bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, parotid swelling, and night sweats in 2015. The patient's medical history was significant for melanoma removed in 2015 and active smoking for over 40 years. During the patient’s initial workup, multiple enlarged bilateral parotid lesions, scattered enlarged level I and II nodes, and upper mediastinal lymph nodes were detected.

Diagnostic and Therapeutic interventions:

The patient underwent ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, and level IA neck dissection. Pathology revealed Warthin Tumor and no evidence of malignancy or lymphoma. After a six-month follow-up, stable appearance of the bilateral parotid masses and cervical lymph nodes were noted, but there was interval enlargement of right upper mediastinal paratracheal lymph nodes. The patient was referred to the Department of Otolaryngology where physical examination revealed bilateral enlarged parotid glands and bulky cervical lymphadenopathy slightly larger on the right. He underwent level II lymph node dissection with the removal of a large nodal conglomerate, and histopathology once again confirmed Warthin tumor.

Summary:

The patient presented with cervical lymphadenopathy and parotid swelling. Diagnostic workup revealed a Warthin tumor without evidence of malignancy or lymphoma. The patient underwent level IA and II lymph node dissection with removal of a large nodal conglomerate, and histopathology once again confirmed Warthin tumor. Close surveillance with serial imaging was elected by the patient. The patient was also counseled on smoking cessation due to its association with Warthin tumors.  At six-month follow-up, there was slight enlargement of a left neck lymph node.

Chief Complaint: Suspected right iliac metastatic tumor
    
Hospital Course:
The 71-year-old female patient was admitted to our hospital due to a suspected right iliac metastatic tumor. Laboratory examinations revealed multiple myeloma and severe renal impairment. Renal replacement therapy (HD) was initiated on the first day of admission with a bolus of 500 U of anticoagulant, followed by a maintenance infusion of 500 U/h. The patient underwent a bone marrow aspiration test that revealed the presence of monoclonal plasma cells. HD methods were changed to postdilutional HDF for free light chain removal, however, the circuit frequently clotted during HDF even after multiple changes in anticoagulation methods. 

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with multiple myeloma with severe renal impairment. The patient had no previous medical history of thrombosis.

Treatment:
Our team carefully monitored the patient's condition and made adjustments as necessary. HD with heparin as an anticoagulant was initiated, however, due to frequent clotting in the HD circuit, anticoagulation methods were temporarily changed to nafamostat mesilate (NM) on day 12. Anti-heparin antibodies were detected, leading to a diagnosis of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT). Heparin was discontinued and a new anticoagulant using NM was initiated, which normalized the platelet count. High-dose heparin was eventually used after a series of adjustments and chemotherapy with bortezomib and dexamethasone (BD) was administered once a week. 

Discharge Status:
The patient's condition improved, and she was subsequently transferred to another hospital on day 59 for further HD maintenance and treatment.

Discharge Summary:

Admission Date: September 2015
Discharge Date: [not provided]
Admitting Diagnosis: Lumbar back pain 
Final Diagnosis: Infection caused by Cutibacterium acnes

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 71-year-old male, was referred to our hospital due to progressively worsening lumbar back pain over the past ten months. His medical history included total thyroidectomy for papillary cancer, dynamic stabilization over vertebral segments L2 to S1 for degenerative spine disease, and a transurethral resection of the prostate for benign prostate hyperplasia. Ten months before referral, he had a urinary tract infection caused by Escherichia coli, treated with antibiotic. A month later, he developed lumbar back pain which gradually worsened over time. 

Upon physical examination, the patient was found to have lumbar spine tenderness. MRI and PET-CT scans showed a small abscess near L5/S1 segment. During the operation, pus was found and drained. Metalwork on segments L2 to L5 were exchanged, while metalwork on S1 segment was removed. Intravenous antibiotics were administered. 

Biopsy samples showed no microorganisms after incubation, but histopathological examinations indicated signs of infection. Further examination revealed Cutibacterium acnes both in biopsy samples and on implants. The patient also experienced a transient renal failure due to nephrotoxicity from medication. Following a 3-month course of postoperative antibiotics, the patient showed no signs of relapse 36 months after the initial infection episode. 

Instructions:

The patient was discharged in stable condition. Follow-up evaluations were recommended and the patient was advised to take any prescribed medications as directed. The patient was also advised to follow up with their primary care physician.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Medical Record Number: [redacted]

Hospital Course:

The patient with a history of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) of the breast 12 years ago presented with confusion and lethargy of 3 weeks duration. The patient was diagnosed with an isolated relapse of lymphoma involving the central nervous system (CNS) based on gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain that revealed subcortical white matter hyperintensities on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequence with associated vascular and leptomeningeal enhancement. Diagnostic lumbar puncture confirmed the presence of CD20-positive lymphomatous large B cells, typical of leptomeningeal disease. She was treated with dexamethasone, intravenous rituximab and HD MTX infusion at 3.5 g/m2 given over 3 h. IV folinic acid 30 mg 6-hourly was given 24 h after the start of HD MTX infusion until MTX levels <0.05 µmol/l had been achieved. She developed sudden jerking movements of the upper limbs with drooling of saliva and extensor posturing of the body four days after HD MTX infusion and suffered another complex partial seizure with secondary generalization a few hours later, which aborted spontaneously. She was subsequently treated with levetiracetam. She was observed to have prolonged involuntary and irregular movements involving bilateral upper extremities with intermittent writhing of the neck and trunk, which would resolve when she slept but recurred when she was awake two days later. A repeat MRI of the brain showed extensive T2 and FLAIR hyperintensities with bilateral and symmetrical involvement of the basal ganglia and periventricular white matter, some of which demonstrated restricted diffusion without any associated solid enhancement. The patient was started on tetrabenazine 12.5 mg bd with complete resolution of her symptoms thereafter. She was successfully rechallenged with HD MTX at a lower dose of 2.5 g/m2 at week 3 without any recurrence of neurotoxicity, completing a total of 5 biweekly doses. In addition, she received 2 doses of intrathecal MTX 12 mg at weeks 7 and 9 without any complications. MRI brain was repeated after two months which had shown near complete resolution of white matter changes in the basal ganglia while her lymphoma remained in clinical and radiological remission.

Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with an isolated relapse of lymphoma involving the central nervous system (CNS) with subcortical white matter hyperintensities on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequence with associated vascular and leptomeningeal enhancement, and extensive T2 and FLAIR hyperintensities with bilateral and symmetrical involvement of the basal ganglia and periventricular white matter.

Treatment:

The patient was treated with dexamethasone, intravenous rituximab and HD MTX infusion at 3.5 g/m2 given over 3 h, and was successfully rechallenged with HD MTX at a lower dose of 2.5 g/m2 at week 3 without any recurrence of neurotoxicity. In addition, she received 2 doses of intrathecal MTX 12 mg at weeks 7 and 9 without any complications. The patient was also treated with levetiracetam and tetrabenazine 12.5 mg bd for the seizure and involuntary movements.

Follow-up:

The patient's lymphoma remained in clinical and radiological remission after completion of treatment. The patient was advised to follow-up regularly with the oncology team for further evaluations and any necessary treatments.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
This 34-year-old left-handed man was admitted to our service and diagnosed with moyamoya phenomenon and vasculopathy. He experienced intermittent left monocular visual symptoms with left temporal aching headaches and photophobia consistent with low-flow retinopathy due to left monocular TIAs.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient's initial symptoms occurred five years ago and included short-lived episodes of altered awareness, patchy global amnesia, and tremulousness caused by likely focal seizures with impaired awareness.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
The patient had untreated hypertension for two years, a 4 pack-year smoking history, and consumed 35 units of alcohol per week but had no other relevant medical history.

FAMILY HISTORY:
The patient's paternal grandfather died suddenly at the age of 41 from an unknown cause. His mother has Parkinson disease since the age of 55. The patient's father was an obligate carrier of AGS mutation and died from suspected oropharyngeal cancer. A paternal aunt has AGS and required pacemaker insertion for "cardiac reasons," while another paternal aunt had a stroke at the age of 40. One of the patient's brothers has genetically-confirmed AGS without apparent clinical manifestations, and three paternal first cousins have confirmed AGS with clinically supportive findings.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
General examination revealed hypertension, livedo reticularis, a slightly pointed chin, aortic regurgitation, and diffuse abdominal tenderness without guarding, rigidity, or audible abdominal bruits. The patient had decreased verbal fluency but was otherwise normocephalic and non-focal neurologically, with a normal cranial nerve, fundus, and limb examination.

DIAGNOSTIC TESTING: 
Fasting total cholesterol was high, and ANA, ANCA, ENA, rheumatoid factor, anti-cardiolipin, and anti-beta 2 glycoprotein I antibodies were negative. Lupus anticoagulant was persistently positive consistent with primary anti-phospholipid syndrome.

IMAGING:
The patient underwent a series of imaging, including EEG, color Doppler ultrasound, cerebral angiography, extracranial MRA, CTA, and serial brain MRIs, which revealed normal brain parenchyma but features suspicious of moyamoya phenomenon. Axial T1 fat-saturated MRI neck vessels revealed a diffusely thickened wall of the left CCA. Formal cerebral angiography confirmed severe left ICA narrowing and confirmed moyamoya phenomenon in the anterior and posterior circulations. The proximal right middle cerebral artery also showed features of moyamoya phenomenon.

GENETIC TESTING:
Molecular genetic analysis revealed heterozygosity for a missense G>C mutation in exon 4 of the JAG1 gene on chromosome 20 resulting in substitution of proline for alanine at codon 211 (p.Ala211Pro). 

PLAN:
The patient was discharged with follow-up with his primary care physician. He was advised to quit smoking and drinking and to maintain a healthy lifestyle. He was also prescribed anticoagulant medications to manage primary anti-phospholipid syndrome. The patient was referred to a genetic counselor for further evaluation and counseling regarding his genetic mutation.

The patient presented to the dermatology clinic with severe facial acne, rated grade 4 on the Investigator Global Assessment of Acne scale. Acrofacial vitiligo with complaints of depigmented lesions

The patient was treated with 20 mg isotretinoin for six months, which led to complete clearance of her acne. The patient then received Antifungal and Tacrolimus 0.1% topical therapy for her vitiligo with mild improvement after eight weeks, but later stopped it in favor of homeopathic treatment.

Patient was discharged in good condition. The patient was advised to follow up with the medical clinic given their positive thyroid antibodies and family history of lupus.

The patient had no discharge medications.

Discharged in stable condition.

- Continue using good sun protection to prevent worsening of existing vitiligo and development of new spots.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient, a 38-year-old Asian male, was admitted with dyspnea and a productive cough that was diagnosed as pneumonia with subsequent atelectasis of the right middle and lower lobes. Upon transfer to our facility, a CT scan revealed an endobronchial mass obstructing the right bronchus intermedius. After initial treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics, a rigid bronchoscopy procedure was performed to remove the endobronchial tumor and prevent recurrence through ablation with a diode laser. Pathologically, the removed tumor was identified as bronchial myelolipoma with no evidence of hematologic disorder or endocrine abnormalities. Follow-up bronchoscopies after 3 and 12 months showed no recurrence of the tumor, and the patient's accompanying symptoms such as cough, sputum, and dyspnea improved immediately following the procedure.
 
Final Diagnoses:

1. Bronchial myelolipoma, confirmed through pathology.
2. Obstructive pneumonia complicated by atelectasis of the right middle and lower lobes.

Treatment:

1. Broad-spectrum antibiotics for obstructive pneumonia.
2. Rigid bronchoscopy under general anesthesia to remove the endobronchial tumor.
3. Ablation with a diode laser to prevent recurrence.

Condition at Discharge:

The patient has shown a significant improvement in his condition since the bronchoscopy procedure and has no active symptoms related to the previously diagnosed conditions. No further treatment is required, and the patient can be discharged at this time.

Discharge Medications:

No medications are required at the time of discharge.

Follow-up Plan:

Follow-up appointments with a primary care physician are recommended to ensure adequate follow-up of the patient's condition and to monitor for any potential recurrence of bronchial myelolipoma in the future.

Hospital Course Summary:

This is a summary of the hospital course of a 24-year-old woman who was admitted due to her myotoxicity condition associated with epilepsy. The patient was brought to the hospital due to frequent seizures, which had not been treated regularly in the past due to financial reasons. The patient had a history of non-progressive polio from 1 year of age, causing her to walk with a limp and have limited functioning of her right hand.

Upon admission, the patient was given a combination of sustained-release sodium valproate and clonazepam to treat her seizures. However, she developed drowsiness and slept for a prolonged time after the first dose. Despite this, she continued with the same treatment regimen for 21 days until she ran out of clonazepam tablets. During this time, her epilepsy symptoms were well controlled, but she developed muscle weakness, pain, and was confined to bed rest. The patient was able to stand but not walk once she was gradually tapered off from clonazepam, and muscle weakness symptoms started to improve after two weeks.

The patient and her family refused electromyography, muscle biopsy, and other tests due to financial reasons. Preliminary blood examinations showed elevated serum CPK levels, which were attributed to clonazepam myotoxicity. Clonazepam was stopped, and the patient was kept under a sodium valproate monotherapy regimen. Upon a 2-month follow-up, the patient had started taking clonazepam irregularly due to insomnia, leading to the recurrence of muscle weakness. At another follow-up three months later, epileptic seizures had been significantly reduced, but her myotoxicity condition had not improved, and she remained bedridden.

The patient and her family refused any further treatment due to a loss of confidence and financial reasons.

Gender: Male

Chief Complaint:
Elevated creatinine associated with hematuria.

Hospital Course:
The patient was referred by his primary care physician due to complaints of elevated creatinine associated with hematuria. Initial evaluation at our institution's emergency department demonstrated an increase in creatinine, decrease in hemoglobin and an INR of 3.52. A CT Abdomen/pelvis was negative for any acute pathology. There was no evidence of obstructive uropathy or crossed unfused renal ectopia.
Based on laboratory/imaging data, it was suspected that the AKI may have resulted from kidney stones. However, subsequent days of supportive measures and fluids did not result in any improvement in the patient's renal function. Further examination and laboratory tests to evaluate for vasculitis, infection, and protein electrophoresis were negative. A renal biopsy was ultimately performed and revealed minimal IgA deposition and focal crescentic glomerulonephritis, with diffuse tubular injury and RBC cast formation ultimately concluding the diagnosis of WRN.

Past Medical History:
The patient had a history of coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, hypertension, high cholesterol, CKD, iron deficiency anemia, osteoarthritis, and mitral valve replacement.

Discharge Diagnosis:
The patient's diagnosis on discharge was WRN following a renal biopsy.

Treatment:
The patient was treated with supportive measures and fluids. There was no indication for any specific treatment for his primary diagnosis.

Follow-up Plan:
The patient was advised to see his primary care physician following his discharge for further assessment and follow-up.
