Clinical History:

A 37-year-old Japanese woman (gravida 2, para 1) was admitted to [(hospital name)] at 36 weeks of gestation due to an abnormality detected during a routine ultrasound examination. The presence of an abnormal number of umbilical cord vessels was discovered during prenatal screening. No other clinical problems were reported during the early period of her pregnancy. 

Hospital Course:

A fetal ultrasound examination was performed which revealed the presence of both a four-vessel part and a three-vessel part within the free loop of the umbilical cord. Further ultrasound screening confirmed that the fetal insertion site of the umbilical cord comprised four vessels, whereas the placental insertion site consisted of three vessels. The blood flow was demonstrated in both veins. A healthy female neonate was delivered at 38 weeks of gestation through spontaneous vaginal delivery. The baby's Apgar scores were 9 and 10 at 1 minute and 5 minutes, respectively. 

Follow-Up:

The baby underwent ultrasonographic examination at the age of 54 days which revealed normal anatomy and no congenital anomalies. The umbilical cord measured 40 cm in length, and a four-vessel part continued up to a distance of 18 cm from the surface of the baby's body. The remaining umbilical cord comprised three vessels. On histological examination, the fetal side of the umbilical cord consisted of two arteries and two veins, whereas the placental side contained two arteries and one vein. The placenta was both macroscopically and microscopically unremarkable. 

Clinical Outcome:

The patient was discharged in good health on [(discharge date)]. No further follow-up was needed. The patient was advised to seek medical attention in the event of the development of any future complications.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 28-year-old male, presented with a two-day history of headache and confusion. He had no fever or abnormal findings upon examination. CT scan of the head was normal and lumbar puncture was not performed. After 12 days, the patient returned with dull headache, neck stiffness, and fatigue, and was seen in the infectious disease clinic. MRI of the brain was unremarkable, and LP performed two and a half weeks after symptom onset was normal. The patient was noted to have positive JCV IgM ELISA and a positive Saint Louis encephalitis virus (SLEV) IgM on arbovirus testing. However, the positive SLEV IgM test was considered false-positive after subsequent confirmatory testing at the CDC. At six-month follow-up, the patient continued to have intermittent dull headaches.

Summary:
The patient presented with a headache and confusion. A CT scan of the head was normal and lumbar puncture was not performed. The patient presented again with dull headache, neck stiffness, and fatigue, and was evaluated in the infectious disease clinic. LP was normal, and MRI was unremarkable. The patient was positive for JCV IgM ELISA and SLEV IgM on arbovirus testing, but the latter was considered a false-positive after confirmatory testing at the CDC. The patient continues to report intermittent dull headaches at the six-month follow-up.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Age: 82

Sex: Female

Admission Date: October 2013

Discharge Date: Still in treatment

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient was admitted to the Oncology Unit in October 2013 due to the development of costal pain and cough. A chest CT-scan showed a complete atelectasis of the left lung inferior lobe, a solitary nodule in apex segment of the upper right lung lobe, the presence of multiple small nodules in basal posterior segments of the right lung lobe as well as in the middle and upper left lung lobes, and a left pleural effusion. The patient had a history of surgical excisions of two nodular BCCs of the trunk in 2003. She is an active smoker with a history of 40 packs per year.

The patient's whole-body 18FDG-PET/CT and bronchoscopy with a biopsy of the left lung lesion confirmed the diagnosis of lung squamous cell carcinoma. The patient was staged as a stage IV NSCLC (according to TNM staging 7th edition).

The patient underwent six cycles of chemotherapy with gemcitabine plus cisplatin. A whole-body CT scan in May 2014 showed a partial response following the six cycles of chemotherapy with 90% reduction of the hilar lesion and disappearance of the pleural effusion. The patient then received a consolidative radiotherapy treatment on the residual disease, obtaining a stable disease for an additional 8 months. 

However, in April 2015, a whole-body CT scan showed a progression of disease with an increased diameter of the left hilar lesion and the appearance of several hilar lymph nodes. The patient then received a second-line chemotherapy with 6 cycles of docetaxel, obtaining a stable disease. 

In January 2016, a whole-body CT scan showed a progression of disease with an increase of the pulmonary hilar lesion associated with atelectasis of the inferior left lobar bronchus and several pathological mediastinal lymph nodes. The patient underwent a re-biopsy of the left lung lesion, which confirmed the diagnosis of lung squamous cell carcinoma. No targetable oncogenic alterations were detected. PD-L1 expression on tumor cells was scored as > 1% on tumor proportional score.

Based on these results, the patient started a third-line treatment with the anti-PD-1 mAb nivolumab. In May 2016, a CT scan showed a stable disease, which was confirmed in successive restaging of the disease. After 18 cycles of nivolumab treatment in January 2017, the patient developed an ulcerated lesion localized at the right ala of nose. She underwent an excisional skin biopsy which showed an ulcerated nodular BCC. The patient is still being treated with nivolumab and has received 46 cycles of nivolumab. Sustained stable disease control is still ongoing for metastatic NSCLC. She is in good health conditions. No additional BCC relapses have been detected so far.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 69-year-old right-handed man who presented with mild speech difficulties, without language comprehension impairment, was assessed and treated. Over a period of five years, the patient's condition progressed and he developed lexical retrieval problems, speech apraxia, agrammatism in spontaneous speech, and memory impairment worsened. He had difficulty learning, exhibited executive dysfunction with low verbal and design fluency, and exhibited altered motor bimanual and three-stage sequences. During the fourth year, the patient presented with dopa-unresponsive right-sided rigidity, hypokinetic dysarthria, and supranuclear oculomotor palsy with slowed voluntary saccades. Oral and written language production and comprehension were impaired, and he eventually became almost mute, using only nonverbal communication.

At that time, the patient also began to express executive and behavioral symptoms, including perseveration, emotional blurring, alternating apathy and disinhibition, and episodic compulsive laughter. A neurological examination found a mild resting tremor and right arm bradykinesia. Unfortunately, during the fifth year, the patient lost comprehension skills and eventually passed away.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Patient Name: Unidentified

Admission Date: Unidentified

Discharge Date: Unidentified

Hospital Course: 

The patient presented with 3 months history of intermittent abdominopelvic pain, nausea, and vomiting. The CT scan showed a mass in the head and uncinate process of the pancreas, making the lesion unresectable. The SMA was encased by the tumor. Palliative antiperistaltic gastrojejunostomy and Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy bypass were performed successfully in the right paracolic position due to the abnormal colonic location. Histopathology results revealed moderately differentiated PDA with perineural tumor involvement at the uncinate process margin. Postoperatively, the patient underwent gemcitabine-based chemotherapy and radiation. The tumor was downstaged through successful resection 12 months later through a classic pancreaticoduodenectomy. Postoperative histopathology showed three out of 13 lymph nodes were positive for metastatic disease. The patient was discharged on postoperative day eight. Recurrent malignant disease led to death ten months following resection.

Summary:

The patient presented with symptoms of abdominopelvic pain, nausea, and vomiting. CT scan revealed an unresectable pancreatic mass due to tumor encasement of the SMA. Surgical procedures, palliative antiperistaltic gastrojejunostomy and Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy bypass, were performed successfully. Histopathological analysis revealed moderately differentiated pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma with perineural tumor involvement. The patient underwent chemotherapy and radiation which successfully downstaged the tumor. One year later, successful resection of the lesion was performed via classic pancreaticoduodenectomy. Histopathology of the resected specimen revealed lymph node involvement with metastatic disease. The patient was discharged and died ten months later due to recurrent malignant disease.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
 
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
 
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
 
Admission Diagnosis: Recurrent Ovarian Cancer
 
Hospital Course:

The patient, a 44-year-old married woman (gravida 2), was admitted to our hospital with a diagnosis of recurrent ovarian cancer which was confirmed by a series of tests and evaluations. The patient had a history of undergoing concurrent right adnexectomy for the ovarian mass, subtotal hysterectomy, and left adnexectomy five years prior which resulted in a diagnosis of ovarian serous papillary carcinoma (stage IV). The uterine wall and cervix were affected by cancer tissue and the left fallopian tube and ovary were invaded as well. The patient received a series of 12 courses of taxinol plus carboplatin chemotherapy post-surgery. Two years before admission, a new pelvic mass was found by ultrasound which was cystic and solid mixed and had a size of about 6 cm × 4.6 cm. Considering the diagnosis of ovarian cancer recurred after chemotherapy, the patient did not continue to receive treatment. After six months, CT images showed that multiple nodules and masses in the abdominal cavity and pelvis had increased; therefore, the patient received two courses of chemotherapy (paclitaxel liposome plus carboplatin) again.

Upon admission, the patient’s Karnofsky Performance Scale score was 90 and an abdominal examination revealed a hard pelvic mass with unclear boundaries. The patient’s white blood cell count and hemoglobin level decreased, and degree I chemotherapy-induced myelosuppression was considered.

Several diagnostic tests were performed during the hospital course, including carbohydrate antigen 19–9, carcinoembryonic antigen, human epididymal protein 4, carbohydrate antigen 153, and carbohydrate antigen 125 which showed an increase. The patient’s premenopausal risk ovarian malignancy algorithm (ROMA) index was 99.72%, and postmenopausal ROMA index was 99.46%. CT scan showed multiple nodules and masses in the abdominal and pelvic cavity, and some lesions were accompanied by calcification. The larger mass in the pelvic cavity was 10.2 cm × 5.8 cm in the maximum section image and had an irregular shape and unclear boundaries with the surrounding bowel. Multiple lymph nodes were found on the right axilla, mediastinum, right chest wall, and retroperitoneal space. The right renal pelvis and ureter dilatation (not shown in the figures) was caused by the oppression of swollen lymph nodes.

Upon multidisciplinary team consultation, it was determined that the multiple metastatic lesions and lymph nodes could not be completely removed by reoperation. After communicating with the patient and her family, the decision was made to continue chemotherapy.

Instructions Upon Discharge:

The patient has been discharged and will be followed up in the clinic regularly for further disease management. Detailed instructions on medication, diet, and activity were provided to the patient and their family before discharge. Any further concerns or questions should be directed to the patient’s healthcare provider.

He was found to have a maternally inherited PLS3 pathogenic variant which explained his bone fragility. 

Past Medical History:

The patient had a history of delayed speech and was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder at 3 years of age. He also had a family history of osteoporosis in his maternal grandfather.

Clinical Examination:

The patient was not dysmorphic. There was hypermobility in the small joints of the fingers, but little evidence of hypermobility elsewhere.

Diagnostic Testing:

DXA scans showed reduced bone mineral density with Z-scores of −2.7 at the lumbar vertebrae and − 2.6 total body measurement adjusted for age and gender. A bone biopsy at 12 years of age demonstrated severe low turnover cortical and trabecular osteopenia.

Treatment:

The patient received 3-monthly infusions of pamidronate.

Summary:

Patient 5 is a 13-year-old male with a history of delayed speech and autism spectrum disorder. He was diagnosed with idiopathic osteoporosis and received regular infusions of pamidronate. The patient was found to have a maternally inherited PLS3 pathogenic variant. DXA scans showed reduced bone mineral density and a bone biopsy demonstrated severe low turnover cortical and trabecular osteopenia. The patient was found to have hypermobility in the small joints of the fingers, but no other evidence of hypermobility.

Discharge Summary

Patient: 46-year-old White male

Medical History: Malignant melanoma (2010)

Hospital Course:

In October 2014, the patient presented to the clinic with a rapidly growing axillary swelling that was painful. He had a history of melanoma and occasional sun exposure during holidays. Examination revealed a 10 cm firm swelling under the left axilla with no palpable lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound and fine needle aspiration confirmed metastatic melanoma with a BRAF V600E mutation. Brain MRI was normal, and PET-CT showed a large FDG avid axillary mass likely to represent a lymph node with no metabolically active primary lesion.

Due to the size and location of the mass, surgical resection was not safe. Therefore, systemic treatment with the BRAF inhibitor, Dabrafenib, was commenced. Four months later, there was a significant reduction in the size of the lesion, and the patient underwent axillary node clearance. The procedure was uncomplicated, and histopathology reported no malignancy, indicating a complete response to Dabrafenib. The patient continued with the treatment for a full year without any toxic side effects.

The patient was regularly followed up in the Oncology and Plastic surgery clinics and had yearly PET-CT scans that showed no metastatic disease. After two years of remission, the patient re-presented with a small palpable infraclavicular lymph node that was amenable for surgical excision, followed by a course of radiotherapy. The patient is currently completing systemic therapy with Pembrolizumab and continues to be in remission with negative follow-up scans.

Summary:

The patient had a history of malignant melanoma that later metastasized to the axilla. Due to its size and location, surgical resection was not safe, and the patient was treated with Dabrafenib for a full year that resulted in complete response to the treatment. Following two years of remission, the patient had a small infraclavicular lymph node that was surgically excised, and radiotherapy was completed. The patient is currently completing systemic therapy with Pembrolizumab.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [redacted]	Date of Discharge: [redacted]

Hospital Course 
The 14-year-old Caucasian female was admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) after being transferred from a community hospital emergency department due to an anaphylactic reaction to a hypoallergenic nutritional supplement. The patient, who had a history of suspected food allergies, intermittent asthma, complex regional pain syndrome, and delayed gastric emptying, had lost 18 kg (40 lbs) in the year prior to admission due to food restriction and exercise. Her body mass index (BMI) was at the 63rd percentile, down from the 94th. 

During her stay, the patient presented with several episodes concerning for idiopathic anaphylaxis requiring transfer to the ED, four of which resulted in PICU admissions. Additionally, the patient also complained of perioral swelling and difficulty breathing, but providers had difficulty confirming visible swelling. The patient had low blood pressure at baseline and experienced hypotension during three of her ED visits. She never had an urticarial rash or protracted vomiting. The patient was treated with intramuscular epinephrine, antihistamines, and steroids. 

To confirm anaphylaxis, the patient had five serum tryptase levels drawn during acute episodes, but all had negative results. Mast cell activation syndrome was ruled out based on no significant increase in serum tryptase or other mast cell mediators when symptomatic. A bone marrow biopsy to assess for a mast cell disorder was equivocal due to poor sample. 

Diagnosis 
The patient was diagnosed with other specified eating disorder (OSFED) anorexia nervosa type (meeting anorexia nervosa criteria except the low weight criterion), major depressive disorder (MDD), social anxiety disorder, obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD), and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) secondary to bullying. Additionally, the patient's final diagnoses included: possible but unconfirmed idiopathic angioedema, possible vocal cord dysfunction (VCD), and factitious disorder. 

Treatment 
The patient was prescribed fexofenadine 180 mg daily, ranitidine 150 mg twice daily, cromolyn 200 mg, and a prolonged prednisone course, weaned down slowly from 30 mg. Rescue medications included cetirizine 10-20 mg and lorazepam 1-2 mg given the concern that episodes were at least in part due to anxiety. Diphenhydramine was avoided due to prolonged QTc during one PICU admission. The patient was started on aripiprazole and up-titrated to 10 mg, which stopped hallucinations and improved depression. The patient's fluoxetine was gradually decreased and eventually stopped. 

Outcome 
The patient was discharged after 15 weeks in the hospital. At the time of this writing, the patient had one ED visit for angioedema 2 months after discharge, but had not been admitted to a PICU in 22 months.

Discharge Summary
Patient Name: N/A
Medical Record Number: N/A
Date of Admission: N/A
Date of Discharge: N/A

Hospital Course:
A 62-year-old man visited our hospital due to a persistent fever of up to 38°C for one week. Chest radiography showed infiltrates in the upper lung fields bilaterally, and in the right middle to lower lung fields. The infiltrates were confirmed on the thoracic CT, which showed multiple large nodules up to 7 cm in diameter, which were in turn composed of numerous discrete small nodules like fireworks, the so-called "cluster" signs. Some of the large nodules had a hyper-dense portion centrally as a result of the coalescence of smaller nodules surrounded by partially discrete small nodules, not as densely assembled, suggestive of the "galaxy" sign. Based on a suspicion of TB or sarcoidosis, multiple tests were conducted including sputum or gastric contents samples, bronchial brushings, and CT scans. On Day 1, right thoracentesis was performed, which showed elevated lactate dehydrogenase levels, consistent with an exudative pleural effusion. The pleural fluid showed an increased total cell count with a lymphocytic predominance, and marked elevation of adenosine deaminase levels in the pleural fluid was noted. Serum laboratory test for TB, T-SPOT, was positive. At Day 8, anti-TB medication was commenced.

At Day 4, the second bronchoscopy was performed and the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid obtained demonstrated an elevated total cell count with lymphocytic predominance and the CD4-to-CD8 ratio of the lymphocytes in the BAL fluid was elevated. Additionally, acid-fast culture of the BAL fluid was negative. Furthermore, on haematoxylin and eosin staining, the transbronchial biopsy specimens showed non-caseating granulomas. Taken together, these results favour the diagnosis of pulmonary sarcoidosis, rather than TB. However, at Day 21, acid-fast culture from the pleural effusion sample proved to be positive for M. tuberculosis. At Day 42, acid-fast culture of sputum taken soon after the first bronchoscopy was positive for M. tuberculosis, but was negative in all materials derived from both bronchoscopic procedures.

Based on the results, the patient is diagnosed with bilateral pulmonary TB pleuritis on the right side. During the hospital course, anti-TB medication was administered to treat the condition.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Bilateral pulmonary TB pleuritis on the right side.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient is advised to continue taking the prescribed medication and follow the recommended dosages and timings. It is important to complete the entire course of medication for effective treatment. It is advised to maintain good hygiene practices and infection control measures to prevent the spread of TB bacteria. The patient is also asked to follow up with their primary care physician regularly for ongoing monitoring and check-ups. In case of any new or worsening symptoms, it is advised to seek medical attention immediately.

Follow-Up:
The patient is advised to follow up with their primary care physician regularly for ongoing monitoring and check-ups.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with unspecific complaints of weakness and weight loss, along with a rapidly progressive renal failure. Initial laboratory studies showed normocytic and normochromic anemia, mild thrombocytopenia and elevated inflammation markers, with normal anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Urine sediment had no alterations, but the urinary protein/creatinine ratio was elevated.

Diagnostic Procedures:

Renal ultrasound and chest X-ray were unremarkable, but based on the presentation, a rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis was suspected. Complementary studies revealed hypertriglyceridemia and hypercholesterolemia, and viral serologies were negative. Peripheral blood cultures were sterile.

Treatment:

The patient was given empiric therapy with pulse methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisolone. Statin and antiagregation therapy with acetylsalicylic acid were prescribed.

Follow-up:

Ten days after discharge, the patient presented with sudden unilateral vision loss. Ophthalmological examination revealed emboli in the retina, and clopidogrel was added to the therapeutic schema. 

Three months after the initial episode, the patient was asymptomatic, had a further improvement of renal function, and vision loss was also partially recovered.

Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with atheroembolic renal disease and diabetic nephropathy (stage IIb).

Recommendations:

The patient was advised to follow up with his primary care physician and nephrologist to monitor his renal function and manage his underlying conditions, including type 2 diabetes, arterial hypertension, and dyslipidemia. Additionally, the patient was advised to maintain a healthy lifestyle with diet and exercise to further prevent complications related to his medical history.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Medical Record Number: [Redacted]

Hospital Course
The patient is a 63-year-old female, who was hospitalized with Guillain-Barré Syndrome, following an episode of viral enteritis. On Day 18 of hospitalization, the patient developed respiratory distress, and her vital capacity declined to 0.625 L. The Rapid Assessment Team (RAT) was activated, and an emergent intubation was performed. Soon after receiving medications, the patient's sinus rhythm deteriorated into a pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Advanced cardiac life support protocol was initiated, followed by cardioversion and administration of calcium chloride and sodium bicarbonate for suspected hyperkalemia. The patient underwent defibrillation and was stabilized within 13 minutes post the initial rhythm change, with the return of normal sinus rhythm, spontaneous circulation, and neurologic function.

Hospitalization
During her 118-day hospitalization, the patient was cared for by a team of clinicians who provided prompt and appropriate care at all times. The patient received proper medication and treatments and was shown compassion by her caregivers. The patient underwent several tests and procedures, which helped to inform her care plan.

Consultations
Anesthesiology consultants were involved in the patient's care during the period of intubation. The team provided prompt assistance and ensured the smooth functioning of the procedure.

Follow-Up Care
The patient was discharged home with a tracheostomy button for continued respiratory care. Follow-up care will be provided to assist with the patient's recovery.

Discharge Medications
The patient was discharged home with medications prescribed by the physician to manage the symptoms of Guillain-Barré Syndrome, as well as continue her recovery.

Discharge Instructions
The patient was advised to continue with therapy and home respiratory care, including the administration of prescribed medication. The patient was also advised to follow-up with the healthcare provider in the future to review follow-up care.

Discharge Condition
At the time of discharge, the patient's condition had improved, and she was discharged home with a tracheostomy button.

Follow-Up
The patient will continue to follow-up with her healthcare providers for continued care and management.

Hospital Course:
The patient, an 8-year-old female with a medical history of eczema, presented with bilateral facial petechiae and thrombocytopenia. Initial workup was suggestive of ITP; however, after a period of observation, the patient presented again with petechiae and thrombocytopenia. A bone marrow biopsy was performed, which revealed increased numbers of morphologically normal megakaryocytes. Three years after the initial presentation, the patient presented with retrosternal and epigastric pain and underwent a chest X-ray, which showed a right pleural effusion and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. A CT scan revealed a right anterior mediastinal mass, thoracic, and abdominal lymphadenopathy, and bilateral renal infiltrates. A core biopsy of an enlarged lymph node showed medium-sized overtly malignant lymphoid cells. The patient was diagnosed with T-lymphoblastic lymphoma (stage III) and was treated per COG AALL1231, Arm A, which has been successful thus far. 

Discharge Summary:
The 8-year-old female patient presented with thrombocytopenia and bilateral facial petechiae, which was later diagnosed as T-lymphoblastic lymphoma (stage III). The patient underwent treatment per COG AALL1231, Arm A, which has been successful in achieving complete remission. The patient presented with encephalopathy during treatment, which was mitigated with the use of dextromethorphan rescue. The patient has continued to receive treatment per the aforementioned protocol and is currently in remission. The patient's platelet count has returned to normal limits. The patient is expected to continue surveillance as per the COG AALL1231 protocol.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
- Name: [redacted]
- Age: 38 years old
- Gender: Male
- Medical Record Number: [redacted]
- Admitting Physician: [redacted]
- Discharge Date: [redacted]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital due to blurred vision in his right eye for 1 year. He was diagnosed with central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC) in the left eye 10 years prior, which was treated with argon laser photocoagulation. Ophthalmoscopy of the right eye revealed retinal detachment accompanied with yellowish, fibrinoid exudative lesions in the temporal macula. An ophthalmic B scan confirmed bullous retinal detachment in the right eye, while fluorescein fundus angiography (FFA) disclosed multiple intense sub-retinal leakage in areas corresponding to exudative lesion and in the superior retina. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed large amounts of sub-retinal fluid (SRF) in the macular and temporal retinal areas.

Treatment:
The patient received a 50% dose of verteporfin photodynamic therapy (PDT) with three spots in the right eye under the guidance of indocyanine green angiography (ICGA). Ophthalmic B scan disclosed reduction in bullous retinal detachment 1 month after PDT, and the patient's BCVA improved to 20/25. Although the OCT image revealed a reduction in sub-retinal fibrin, the SRF remained and resolved slowly until the second month after PDT. Therefore, the patient received a second 50% dose of verteporfin PDT in the right eye with a spot size of 5000 μm under the guidance of ICGA. One month after the second PDT, ophthalmoscopy of the right eye revealed the disappearance of the yellowish, fibrinoid exudative lesions. Additionally, the reattached retina was observed on B-scan, and SRF in the temporal area markedly decreased in the OCT image.

Results:
OCT revealed nearly resolved SRF 2 months after the second PDT, and the SRF was completely resolved 3 months after the second PDT. The patient's BCVA of the right eye improved to 20/20 in the third month after the second PDT and remained stable until the sixth month after the second PDT. No recurrence occurred during the follow-up of more than 6 months after the second PDT.

Diagnosis:
- Blurred vision in the right eye
- Retinal detachment with yellowish, fibrinoid exudative lesions in the temporal macula
- Central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC) in the left eye

Condition at Discharge:
The patient's condition has significantly improved, as evidenced by the disappearance of the yellowish, fibrinoid exudative lesions and the nearly resolved sub-retinal fluid. The patient's BCVA in the right eye improved to 20/20 and remained stable until the sixth month after the second PDT. The patient is discharged in stable condition without any complications.

Follow-up:
The patient is recommended to follow up with his ophthalmologist for regular check-ups and to report any changes in his vision. The patient is advised to avoid smoking and alcohol consumption, as these may worsen his ocular condition. The patient is also advised to maintain a healthy lifestyle and to adhere to his prescribed medications.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 25-year-old G2 P0010 Caucasian female with a past medical history of obesity, depression, and multiple sclerosis.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital at 18 weeks gestation with bilateral lower extremity weakness and right-sided flank pain. Upon examination, there was evidence of a new extensive demyelinating lesion in the craniocervical cord. An MRI was performed, and a urinary tract infection, caused by pan-sensitive Escherichia coli, was also detected. Following 6 days of intravenous methylprednisolone, the patient showed moderate improvement, and she was discharged to an acute inpatient rehabilitation center.

However, she re-presented to the hospital three weeks later with right-sided flank pain, generalized weakness, and a tingling sensation in her extremities. Treatment by antibiotics and IV methylprednisolone 250 mg were initiated but showed only minimal motor improvement. TPE was performed, and five treatments were given every other day, alternating with IV methylprednisolone. The patient's neurologic symptoms improved significantly, and she was consequently discharged to the acute rehabilitation service.

At 36 weeks' gestation, the patient presented to the hospital with contractions, vaginal spotting, hypertension, headache, and lower extremity edema. She went through cesarean delivery due to pre-eclampsia and preterm labor, delivering a male infant weighing 2495 g with a good APGAR score.

After delivery, fingolimod was reinitiated in the outpatient setting.

Diagnosis and Treatments:

The patient was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis at age 17 and had tried multiple modifying agents. The patient developed an acute MS flare in the setting of pyelonephritis and received treatment by antibiotics and intravenous methylprednisolone. TPE was initiated later, and five treatments were given every other day, alternating with IV methylprednisolone. The patient responded well and had a near complete resolution of her tetraparesis with mild residual sensory loss in her left arm.

After delivery, fingolimod was reinitiated in the outpatient setting. The patient was treated with methylprednisolone 1000 mg as a single infusion every three weeks for the remainder of her pregnancy and was discharged without any neurologic deficits.

Follow-up:

The patient will need routine follow-up with her obstetrician and neurological care team to monitor her symptoms, medications, and any potential relapses of multiple sclerosis.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 22
Sex: Male

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with a 2-year history of right shoulder pain that worsened over time. Imaging and clinical examination findings suggested impingement syndrome and he was advised for physiotherapy with no improvement. The patient received 3 intra-articular corticosteroid injections which did not relieve the pain, and he had arthroscopic sub acromial decompression surgery which also failed to result in pain improvement. Afterward, the patient developed increased pain at rest.
MRI of the cervical spine and brachial plexus along with a nerve conduction study were all reported to be normal. A non-contrast MRI of the affected shoulder showed a suspicious lesion at the base of the coracoid, which was confirmed by a contrast-enhanced MRI and CT scans. The presence of a benign osteoid osteoma (OO) of the coracoid process was identified. A senior consultant of orthopedic surgery operated on the patient with image intensifier-guided drilling of the OO lesion under general anesthesia, followed by arthroscopic shaving and debridement of the lesion.
After surgery, the patient had complete resolution of pain and was discharged home on the same day with a cuff and collar brace and oral analgesics. Subsequent follow-ups confirmed complete resolution of symptoms, and the patient was advised to mobilize the arm and engage in normal daily activities.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with a benign osteoid osteoma (OO) of the coracoid process.

Treatment:
The patient received arthroscopic sub acromial decompression surgery which did not improve symptoms. Next, a senior consultant of orthopedic surgery operated on the patient who had image intensifier-guided drilling of the osteoid osteoma lesion followed by arthroscopic shaving and debridement of the lesion, which fully resolved the patient's symptoms.

Disposition:
The patient was discharged home on the same day in a stable condition with a cuff and collar brace and oral analgesics.

Follow-up:
The subsequent follow-ups confirmed complete resolution of symptoms, and the patient was advised to mobilize the arm and engage in normal daily activities. Further follow-up visits were not scheduled as the patient's issue had been fully resolved.

Hospital Course: 

The patient, a 9-month-old baby girl from Cameroon, was admitted to our hospital with a snake-like rash on her abdomen. She had no fever, cough, or other systemic symptoms. On physical examination, multiple erythematous, raised, and thin serpiginous lesions of varying lengths were found over her trunk and arms.

Diagnosis: 

The patient was diagnosed with cutaneous larva migrans (CLM).

Treatment: 

The patient was treated with albendazole syrup for 3 consecutive days and chlorpheniramine syrup for 3 days. Topical ivermectin cream was prescribed and the patient experienced complete resolution of the lesions at follow-up, 1 week later.

Follow-Up: 

At the follow-up visit 3 days after treatment initiation, the patient's irritability had resolved, although a few serpiginous lesions persisted.

Instructions: 

No further instructions were provided.

Summary: 

A 9-month-old baby girl from Cameroon was diagnosed with cutaneous larva migrans (CLM) after presenting with a reddish, snake-like rash on her abdomen. She was treated with albendazole syrup, chlorpheniramine syrup, and topical ivermectin cream, resulting in complete resolution of the lesions. At the follow-up visit 3 days after treatment initiation, the patient exhibited no further irritability, although a few serpiginous lesions still persisted. No further instructions were provided.

Hospital Course:
A 38-year-old Japanese man presented with dull pain and swelling in the right masseteric region and paresthesia of his lower lip and mental region following the removal of his lower third molar in the right side. He was previously treated with mecobalamin and adenosine triphosphate disodium hydrate with no improvement, then referred to our department for further examination. Clinical examination at the initial visit showed mild swelling at the right masseteric region, mild paresthesia of his lower lip and mental region in the right side, and trismus (25 mm). Further diagnostic tests, including panoramic radiograph, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, and bone scintigraphy, confirmed a diagnosis of osteomyelitis of the mandible caused by late fracture following third molar extraction. 
Treatment:
The patient underwent sequestrectomy and curettage via a mandibular vestibular approach under general anesthesia, followed by administration of ampicillin/sulbactam for 5 days. After the surgical procedure, the trismus and paresthesia of his lower lip and mental region in the right side disappeared completely. The patient had no relapse during the 6-month follow-up. 
Follow-Up:
The patient's condition improved, and he was discharged in good condition with plans for continued outpatient management by his primary care physician. Educational materials were provided to the patient regarding good oral hygiene practices, signs and symptoms of osteomyelitis, and ways to minimize the risk of complication following tooth extraction. A referral to a dentist was also made for routine follow-up and dental care.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with a seven-day history of hematemesis along with other symptoms such as weight loss, recurrent epigastric pain, and post-prandial vomiting for the past year. He had a prior medical history of laparoscopic cholecystectomy, ischemic brain stroke, and lumbar herniated disc. Physical examination revealed cachexia, weakness, hypotension, and tachycardia. Laboratory reports showed abnormal findings. Following supportive care, esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) revealed a clean base ulcer in the lower third of the esophagus (Mallory Weiss syndrome) caused by repetitive vomiting. Additionally, a submucosal lesion was observed in the bulb area of the duodenum, which was confirmed by endoscopic ultrasonography adjacent to the right kidney that measured 45x55mm.

Further imaging studies with contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed multiple cortical cysts in both the kidneys. One of the cysts measured 45x55mm and exerted pressure on the duodenum. The patient refused surgical treatment, and considering his adverse condition, conservative treatment was suggested. The treatment included para-enteric infusion of amino acids and intralipids, infusion of crystalloid fluids, and intravenous metoclopramide. The patient was advised to consume small-sized meals 5-6 times a day and high-calorie liquids. The patient's general condition improved over two weeks, and he tolerated the mentioned diet well.

Discharge Diagnosis: Mallory Weiss Syndrome, Submucosal Lesion in the Duodenum, and Multiple Renal Cysts

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was advised to follow a low-fat and high-protein diet. Scheduling a follow-up appointment with a gastroenterologist for further evaluation of submucosal lesion was recommended. The patient was also advised to follow up with a urologist for the evaluation of renal cysts. Medications and further treatment options were not prescribed. 

Follow-up appointments were scheduled with the patient's Primary Care Physician within 2 weeks of discharge. Furthermore, the patient was advised to seek immediate medical attention in case of any symptoms including hematemesis, epigastric pain, or vomiting. 

The patient and his family were advised of his condition and treatment plan, and they expressed their understanding and agreement with the discharge instructions.

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 13-year-old boy who presented to our hospital with complaints of abdominal distension, upper gastrointestinal bleed (UGIB), worsening abdominal distension, exertional dyspnea, and black, tarry stools. Upon physical examination, the patient was found to have splenomegaly and gross ascites. Diagnostic and therapeutic tap was performed, and endoscopic variceal band ligation was done. Further evaluation by transthoracic echocardiogram showed mild pericardial effusion with an ejection fraction of 55%. Bubble contrast echocardiogram was performed which showed intra-pulmonary shunts (but no intra-cardiac shunts). A diagnosis of hepatopulmonary syndrome was made on the basis of the above-mentioned findings. Continuous oxygen therapy was provided and the patient's condition improved gradually in a few days. The patient and his family were made aware of his condition and were referred to the national liver transplant center for live donor liver transplantation (LDLT).

Course of Treatment:

- Intravenous resuscitation with fluids, antibiotics, dextrose, terlipressin and oxygen therapy
- Packed red blood cells transfused
- Endoscopic variceal band ligation performed
- Diagnostic and therapeutic tap performed
- Continuous oxygen therapy provided

Diagnosis:

- Decompensated liver disease with ascites complicated by variceal bleeding and hepatopulmonary syndrome

Plan:

The patient and his family were referred to the national liver transplant center for live donor liver transplantation (LDLT).

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: XXXXXX
Date of Admission: XX/XX/XXXX
Date of Discharge: XX/XX/XXXX

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 54-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension was admitted to the hospital with a high fever and right hypochondriac pain. Upon investigation, a diagnosis of liver abscess was made, which was managed by immediately performing a percutaneous puncture with drainage. Further laboratory evaluation found poor liver function and very high levels of Alpha-Fetoprotein (AFP), Protein Induced by Vitamin K Absence or Antagonist-II (PIVKA-II), and AFP-L3. A diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with triple-positive tumor marker status was made, indicating highly malignant disease. The patient also had a portal vein tumor thrombosis (PVTT) in the right posterior branch of the portal vein. 

The patient was treated with chemoembolization using a Hepatic Arterial Infusion of Cisplatin and 5-FU, followed by a combination of cisplatin and mitomycin C. After the first round of chemoembolization, the patient showed incomplete lipiodol accumulation within the tumor, and the PVTT progressed to the right main portal vein. Subsequently, surgical PVL was done to avoid involvement of the left portal vein. Three disseminated peritoneally nodules were also removed, and three additional rounds of transient chemoembolization were performed after the initial surgical procedure.

The patient showed marked improvement upon the fourth chemoembolization, with the tumors responding to the treatment and showing a significant reduction in size without enhancement. The patient also did not have any new tumors in the liver, and the tumor markers returned to their normal levels. A suspicious lesion that recurred 15 months after the initial treatment was treated with percutaneous radiofrequency ablation, which led to complete remission.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with HCC with macroscopic PVTT, triple-positive tumor marker status, and peritoneal dissemination.

Condition at the Time of Discharge:
The patient is currently in complete remission and has shown marked improvement in liver function. The patient has been advised to continue with regular follow-up appointments for long-term monitoring.

Recommendations:
The patient is advised to follow a healthy lifestyle and dietary habits to ensure better liver function and overall health. The patient should also adhere to the prescribed medication regimen and attend all follow-up appointments as per the instructions of their medical care provider.

Patient: 

The patient is a 47-year-old male who was brought to the emergency department after being involved in a motorcycle accident.

Hospital Course: 

Upon presentation, the patient had sustained gross head trauma and multiple fractures in his upper and lower extremities. As a result, the patient was intubated and fluid resuscitation was initiated. Subsequent imaging revealed severe global hypokinesis of both ventricles, and the patient's condition rapidly deteriorated. The patient suffered from severe decompensated heart failure, which ultimately led to multi-organ failure and his passing away 10 days following admission.

Summary:
 
The patient was admitted to our hospital following a motorcycle accident and was found to have suffered gross head trauma and multiple bilateral upper and lower extremity fractures. Due to the severity of his injuries, the patient required intubation and fluid resuscitation upon presentation. Imaging revealed severe global hypokinesis of both ventricles, and the patient's condition quickly deteriorated. Despite successful angioplasty following the diagnosis of a dissection of the mid-rca, the patient's severe decompensated heart failure progressed to multi-organ failure, and he ultimately passed away 10 days following admission.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Background:
A female patient was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit as a premature baby born via caesarean section at 32 weeks gestation. After two months of observation, she was diagnosed with maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 6 (UPD6).

Hospital Course:
During her stay, paternity testing was performed and revealed genetic inconsistencies at loci F13A01 and D5S818. Further tests, including PowerPlex© ESX, PowerPlex© Fusion, and PowerPlex© LC5 test batteries, were conducted to confirm paternity, and HLA testing was performed. The patient was homozygous for maternal alleles on all loci located on chromosome 6, and the results led to suspicion of maternal UPD. Chromosomal microarray (CMA) testing supported the diagnosis of maternal UPD6.

At ten months of age, the patient was presented to a medical geneticist. The patient's mother reported that the patient appeared to be developing well and reaching milestones as expected. Upon physical examination, her weight was less than the 3rd percentile (even when corrected for prematurity) and length was less than the 3rd percentile (10th percentile when corrected for prematurity). Head circumference was at the 25th percentile. The family history was notable for a maternal half-brother with attention-deficit/ hyperactivity disorder and grandparents with hypertension.

The patient was seen again at 14 months of age to discuss the CMA results. It was noted that the patient had continued to develop appropriately and had no new symptoms or concerning physical exam findings. The family was counseled on the possibility of the patient developing an autosomal recessive condition due to unmasking caused by UPD.

Diagnosis:
Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 6 (UPD6)

Discharge Condition:
The patient's prognosis is good based on the reassuring first two visits. The patient will require routine follow-up care with a medical geneticist and a pediatrician.

Recommendations:
The family was advised of the possibility of the patient developing an autosomal recessive condition due to UPD. It is recommended that the patient continue to receive appropriate medical follow-up care, including regular check-ups with a pediatrician. The family should also continue to provide detailed family medical history to healthcare providers during follow-up visits to help with the management of the patient's health.

Hospital Course:

The 66-year-old male patient underwent a left total knee arthroplasty due to left knee osteoarthritis and varus deformity. The surgery was performed using conventional surgical procedures, and the patient was draping using standard aseptic procedure. During the surgical incision sterilization, there was a skin avulsion, which was approximately 6.5 × 30 cm in the posterior part of the patient's left crus. Petrolatum gauze was used for dressing the areas of epidermal avulsion. Routine postsurgical dressing was done, including gauze, cotton pad, and bandage. The patient was advised to raise the affected leg, keep the wound dry, and sulfadiazine cream was applied to the area of epidermal avulsion. On postoperative day 3, oral cefixime therapy of 100 mg BID was initiated for anti-infection treatment. The wound healing process was observed daily, and dressing changes were performed accordingly.

Hospital course summary:

The patient had an elective left total knee arthroplasty for left knee osteoarthritis and varus deformity. During surgery, the patient suffered a skin avulsion, which was approximately 6.5 × 30 cm in the posterior part of the patient's left crus. The wound was appropriately treated by initially using petrolatum gauze for dressing. Daily dressing changes were performed, and sulfadiazine cream was applied to the area of epidermal avulsion. Oral cefixime therapy was initiated on postoperative day 3 for anti-infection treatment, and the patient was observed daily. After 6 weeks of treatment, the avulsed wound showed no signs of infection and had undergone re-epithelialization. The patient was discharged from the hospital after 2 weeks and was advised to change the dressing every 3 days until the avulsion area was dry. There were no significant abnormalities or complications observed during the hospital course.

Diagnosis: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma

Hospitalization Dates: [insert dates here]

Hospital Course:

The patient presented with difficulty swallowing. An endoscopic study revealed an ulcerative tumor in the esophagus, and biopsy results confirmed squamous cell carcinoma.

The medical team administered two courses of neoadjuvant chemotherapy before performing funnel chest surgery via the Nuss method to widen the mediastinum. Radical esophagectomy followed by gastric conduit reconstruction was then performed.

The surgery was completed without complications, and the patient was observed for postoperative complications without any events. The metal bars were removed from the chest one year after surgery, following which the patient was reevaluated and monitored. He was noted to be in a good condition at his two-year follow-up examination.

The medical team treated the patient with neoadjuvant chemotherapy, followed by funnel chest surgery to widen the mediastinum before performing radical esophagectomy and gastric conduit reconstruction. The patient was observed and no complications were noted. The metal bars were removed from the chest, and he was monitored, after which he was noted to be in good condition.

Primary Diagnosis: Stage IIIc high-grade serous papillary adenocarcinoma

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of an increased CA125 serum concentration and the detection of a metastatic para-aortic lymph node by CT scan. She was diagnosed with Stage IIIc high-grade serous papillary adenocarcinoma after undergoing cytoreductive surgery, total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, omentectomy, appendectomy, bilateral pelvic and para-aortic lymph node dissection, and the removal of metastases from the uterus-rectum-fossa. The patient was treated with 6 cycles of paclitaxel and carboplatin, which led to complete clinical remission.

Approximately 65 months later, the patient presented with an increased CA125 serum concentration and the identification of a metastatic para-aortic lymph node with a diameter of 4 cm at the renal hilum level by CT scan. The patient refused invasive treatment due to her religious beliefs and took olaparib on her own. The patient experienced mild fatigue, appetite loss, and a decrease in hemoglobin levels as part of treatment-emergent adverse events. Later, the patient stopped taking olaparib for 21 days due to fever caused by erysipelas but later resumed the treatment.

The second CT scan showed a decrease in the metastatic para-aortic lymph node to 2.2 cm in diameter. In the following months, the patient took olaparib at a dose of 150 mg twice per day as the serum CA125 increased. The third CT scan revealed an increase in the diameter of the metastatic lymph node to 2.77 cm but remained at a similar size otherwise.

The patient was asymptomatic at the time of discharge and is advised to continue follow-up visits. The patient should be monitored for any signs of recurrent cancer and any side effects related to medications. The patient was educated on the importance of routine visits and advised to contact the hospital in case of any urgent or emergency issues.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital for an elective gynecologic procedure that was without complication. During a surgical consultation, a mass on the dorsum of the right foot was incidentally found. A thorough dermatologic examination did not reveal any other concerning lesions. The patient underwent a punch biopsy, which was consistent with basal cell carcinoma (BCC). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a large soft tissue irregularity surrounding the second to fifth extensor tendons.

The patient underwent a wide local excision of the BCC with full-thickness skin graft for coverage. The lesion was excised in its entirety with a 5-mm circumferential margin beyond the extent of visible tumor. The pathology report showed an 8.2 x 6.4 x 1.4 cm lesion consistent with nodular subtype BCC with clear margins. A full-thickness skin graft measuring 7 x 10 cm was obtained from the right lower abdomen and was tacked onto the wound bed using 5-0 chromic sutures. 

The patient was maintained on bed rest with extremity elevation until postoperative day 3, at which point she was allowed to ambulate with toe-touch weight bearing precautions on her right lower extremity. Dressings were removed on postoperative day 4, revealing a healthy and viable graft. She had palpable pedal pulses and intact motor and sensory function. She was discharged on postoperative day 4 with instructions to continue toe-touch weight bearing precaution on her right foot with continued outpatient follow-up.

Follow-up:
At 1-year follow-up, the patient's wound had fully recovered without complication. At 2-year surveillance, she remained without any recurrence of disease. 

Diagnoses at Discharge:
- Basal cell carcinoma

Procedures:
- Wide local excision of basal cell carcinoma with full-thickness skin graft for coverage

Condition at Discharge:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with a healed wound and no signs of disease recurrence.

None were prescribed at this time.

Follow-up instructions:
The patient was instructed to continue weight-bearing precautions on her right foot and to follow-up with her primary care physician and dermatologist as scheduled.

Discharge Summary:

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 33-year-old female, presented with progressive backache and lower limb aching, 7 months after undergoing laparoscopic right ovarian cystectomy. Pathology reports revealed that the cyst was a mature teratoma. Further imaging studies showed the presence of a mass in the right iliac region and a malignant metastatic lesion in the hip bone. Pathological examination of the first surgical section revealed the possibility of an immature teratoma. 

Treatment and Management:
The patient underwent 11 courses of cisplatin-based chemotherapy, along with two courses of radiotherapy. Despite undergoing these treatments, the disease continued to progress, with multiple metastases being identified in the iliac fossa, iliac bone, sacrum, and liver. A biopsy of the liver lesion was taken, which confirmed the presence of metastatic pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (PNET) originating from the ovaries. Palliative radiotherapy was attempted, but it failed to provide relief from her symptoms. Ultimately, palliative surgery was performed, which included partial hepatectomy of the left lobe of the liver and resection of metastatic lesions in the omentum. 

Outcome:
The final pathological examination revealed that the patient had metastatic PNET originating from the ovaries. Despite further treatment being available, the patient declined to undergo any additional therapy. She passed away 2 years after being diagnosed with bone metastasis, due to the progression of the disease. 

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient was referred to palliative care, and her pain was managed in an attempt to enhance her quality of life. During her final days, the patient was provided with emotional support and counseling to help her cope with the nature of her illness. 

Consults:
The patient was referred to an oncologist, radiologist, and a palliative care specialist to manage her symptoms and provide further treatment recommendations.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 61-year-old male, was admitted for evaluation of a palpable mass in his right inguinal area. He had a history of advanced gastric cancer for which he underwent subtotal gastrectomy with Billroth I anastomosis and chemotherapy treatment (XELOX) five years prior. Computed tomography (CT) revealed a bilobed mass with 2 components - a 2.5 cm round portion at the caudal aspect of the right inguinal canal, and an additional 6.6 cm irregular elongated portion straddling the right inguinal canal and right pelvic cavity along the right external iliac vessels. The right scrotal sac was empty without the normal right testis. CT showed another 4 cm mass in the aortocaval space at the third lumbar spine level, presumed to be metastatic lymphadenopathy. A presumed right undescended testis was affected by the right inguinal canal mass rather than primary testicular cancer, as evidenced by its preserved size and contour. Differential diagnoses for the right inguinal and aortocaval masses included metastatic lesion, testis cancer, lymphoma, or sarcoma originating in the inguinal canal. Right orchiectomy was planned initially, but an US-guided biopsy from the right inguinal mass revealed metastatic adenocarcinoma with necrosis. The primary sites were considered to be the pancreatobiliary tract and stomach. The patient received multiple cycles of chemotherapy (FOLFOX), and all metastatic masses decreased in size at the 5-month outpatient follow-up. 

Discharge Summary:

This 61-year-old male presented with a palpable mass in his right inguinal area, and imaging studies revealed a bilobed mass with 2 components affecting the right undescended testis and aortocaval space. A biopsy from the right inguinal mass showed metastatic adenocarcinoma with necrosis from the pancreatobiliary tract and stomach. The patient received multiple cycles of chemotherapy and all the metastatic masses decreased in size at the 5-month outpatient follow-up.

Medical History:
The patient presented with sudden vision loss in the right eye for one month. She had experienced binocular diplopia in the past three months worsening while looking to the right. Her history includes repeated headaches over the past three years. A non-contrast CT scan showed non-specific inflammation in the sphenoid sinus and she received treatment with steroids. On examination, she had a relative afferent pupillary defect and a right sixth nerve palsy.

Clinical Findings:
Anterior segment examination showed an abduction restriction consistent with a right sixth nerve palsy. Fundus examination showed a resolving disc edema in her right eye. Other cranial nerves were normal. The systemic workup showed an elevated ESR of 87 mm/h.

Imaging Findings:
MRI showed mucosal thickening in both compartments of the sphenoid sinus, which suggested fungal sphenoid sinusitis with osteomyelitis involving the right cavernous sinus, adjacent dura, right optic nerve pathway, and pituitary gland. Post contrast T1 image showed an asymmetry of the right cavernous sinus due to enhancing soft tissue within it.

Biopsy:
The biopsy of the sphenoidal lesion was negative for fungal or bacterial infections.

Treatment:
The patient was started on amphotericin B empirically, and on follow-up after 1 month, her BCVA had improved to 3/60, her abduction defect had resolved, and the disc was pale, suggesting of a resolved disc edema.

Follow-up Plan:
The patient should continue to follow-up for improvement of vision in the right eye and other symptoms, and a further treatment plan will be discussed based on biopsy results.

Discharge Summary

Patient Information
Name: [redacted]
Gender: Female
Age: 23 years

Hospital Course Summary
The patient was admitted with a 4-month history of fluctuating weakness of the right upper and lower extremities associated with a band-like sensation of the trunk along with bowel and bladder disturbances. There was also a month-long history of neck movement-related electric-like sensation on the nape. Weakness progressed to the left lower extremity causing difficulty in ambulation and eventually became quadriparetic. The patient's condition deteriorated and she developed dysphagia, dysphonia, difficulty breathing, and projectile vomiting.

Initial Assessment
The patient was hemodynamically stable upon admission with no spinal deformities noted. She had lax sphincter tone and hypesthesia was described. The patient was hyper-reflexic on both the upper and lower extremities along with bilateral extensor toe sign.

Diagnostic Tests
Initial work-up included a cranio-spinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealing a long expansile contrast-enhancing mass involving the entire spinal cord, from the level of the cervical region to the conus medullaris with extension to the lower medulla oblongata. 

Medical Management
The patient was started on dexamethasone, which provided minimal relief of symptoms. She was referred to the neurosurgery service and was advised for surgery.

Outcome
Unfortunately, on the 20th hospital day, the patient's symptoms progressed to quadriplegia and respiratory failure. She subsequently developed healthcare-associated pneumonia succumbing to septicemia.

Autopsy
On autopsy, all lobes of the lungs were consolidated secondary to pneumonia. There was swelling of the entire spinal cord with white to yellow mucoid material coming out from the central canal. Cut sections showed that the entire spinal cord and caudal medullary region were replaced by mucoid material. Histopathologic examination of the spinal cord revealed a cellular tumor arranged around the central canal of the cord. The cells are generally small, with round to slightly ovoid nuclei. Fibrillary processes were noted in the cytoplasm.

Diagnosis
The patient was diagnosed with holocord oligodendroglioma.

Recommendation
Further genetic characterization of the tumor such as IDH, 1p/19q codeletion, MGMT, EGFR and TP53 mutations were not done because of its unavailability in the institution but its histologic and immunochemical features are consistent with holocord oligodendroglioma.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Gender: Male
Age: 66 years
Admitted: [REDACTED]
Discharged: [REDACTED]

History and Findings:
The patient is a 66-year-old Caucasian man who was admitted with an enlarged prostate and urinary retention. Pelvic ultrasonography confirmed a prostate volume of 158 cc. The patient underwent Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP). During the procedure, a damaged lens in the nephroscope resulted in an extremely poor cystoscopic image. A 3.5-MHz convex abdominal transducer was used under B-mode ultrasound to view the bladder and guide morcellation. The enucleated adenoma was seen in the dependent portion of the distended bladder with both the nephroscope and Piranha morcellator just entering the bladder neck. Transurethral morcellation was initiated with the Wolf Piranha Scope and the Piranha morcellator at the manufacturer's recommended settings.

Treatment and Outcome:
With guidance from the ultrasound probe, the operator successfully aimed the morcellator tip in the direction of the enucleated adenoma and safely removed it from the walls of the bladder. A final inspection with both ultrasound and a functional cystoscope lens confirmed no remaining adenoma pieces within the prostatic fossa and bladder. The patient was discharged from the hospital the next day and experienced an uneventful postoperative recovery. Pathology analysis demonstrated a specimen weight of 69 g of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH).

Impression and Recommendations:
The discharge summary is provided as documentation of the patient's HoLEP procedure. The patient was discharged after an uneventful recovery from the procedure. Close monitoring is recommended to ensure the successful resolution of the patient's enlarged prostate and urinary retention.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Age: 11 months
Gender: Female
Breed: Brown
Diagnosis: Bovine viral diarrhea virus persistent infection (BVDV-PI)

Hospital Course:
The patient, an 11-month-old female PI calf, was admitted to the Veterinary Hospital of the Department of Veterinary Medicine of the University of Bari, Italy on 12 April 2021 for diagnostic confirmation of BVDV PI. The calf had been identified in a herd of Apulia region, Italy, that consisted of 99 Alpine Brown cattle, all under the age of 1 year. The patient had undergone virological and bacteriological investigations before arrival, which revealed the presence of BVDV and bovine coronavirus (BCoV). Upon arrival, the patient was hospitalized in the Infectious Diseases Unit and clinically examined two times a day during the entire period of hospitalization. The patient was kept in a separate room with straw bedding, was fed a commercial concentrate twice daily, and had access to haylage and water ad libitum. The facility was closed for other animals and had restricted admission for people. Two days after arrival, the patient showed hyperthermia (39.8 °C), and additional samples were collected to monitor its health status and to assess the presence of concomitant virological/bacteriological infections.

Diagnostic Findings:
The presence of BVDV and BCoV was confirmed in nasal swabs, fecal swabs, and EDTA-treated blood collected from the patient, and BVDV antibodies were detected in serum samples.

Treatment:
The patient did not receive any specific treatment for BVDV-PI during hospitalization.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was observed for 60 days, during which stool samples, nasal swabs, serum samples, and EDTA-treated blood were collected weekly until BCoV tests were negative. The patient is currently in the hospital and has not been discharged. Further treatment will be provided, as needed.

Age: 2
Sex: Male
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Diagnosis: Kartagener syndrome with cryptorchidism

Hospital Course:
The two-year-old male patient was admitted to the hospital for bilateral cryptorchidism and was diagnosed with Kartagener syndrome. The patient required mechanical ventilation for 20 days after birth due to severe respiratory distress. Even after withdrawal of mechanical ventilation, oxygen administration was required up to 9 months of age. Preoperative computed tomography examination indicated deviation of the trachea. Hospital Course Summary:
The two-year-old male patient was admitted to the hospital for bilateral cryptorchidism and was diagnosed with Kartagener syndrome. The patient had a history of respiratory distress and required mechanical ventilation after birth. The preoperative computed tomography examination indicated deviation of the trachea. The patient underwent a successful orchiopexy under general anesthesia using LMA (size 2.0). The patient was closely monitored throughout the procedure and showed no signs of adverse respiratory events. The patient was transferred to the general ward and was discharged from the hospital the next day with an uneventful recovery.

ADMISSION DIAGNOSIS: Pancreatic tail carcinoma with retroperitoneal and bilateral inguinal adenopathy.

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient presented with bilateral flank pain and unintentional weight loss. A CT scan revealed a 3-cm mass in the pancreatic tail suspicious for malignancy associated with retroperitoneal and bilateral inguinal adenopathy. EUS-guided FNA confirmed malignant tumor with prominent multinucleate-cell component and readily identifiable mitotic activity. The patient underwent distal pancreatectomy, splenectomy, and left partial adrenalectomy. Histopathological examination revealed UC-OGC. The carcinoma was associated with bone formation and extended into peri-pancreatic soft tissue. Adjuvant chemotherapy with gemcitabine and capecitabine was started but was discontinued due to significant colitis. The patient is currently receiving gemcitabine as adjuvant chemotherapy.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS: Pancreatic tail carcinoma with retroperitoneal and bilateral inguinal adenopathy.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient is advised to continue taking medications as prescribed by her primary care physician. She should monitor her weight and eat a healthy, well-balanced diet to prevent further weight loss. It is recommended that the patient attend follow-up appointments with her oncologist for routine evaluation and monitoring of her condition. The patient is encouraged to report any new symptoms to her care team.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient, a 28-year-old gravida 4, para 0-0-3-0, was admitted to the hospital at 15 4/7 weeks of pregnancy with complaints of facial and lower extremity edema along with a single episode of substernal chest pain. Her medical history was significant for insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, high cholesterol, nephrotic syndrome, diabetic neuropathy, and tobacco use. She had a significant obstetrical history with three prior spontaneous abortions in the setting of poorly controlled diabetes. Upon admission, the patient's blood pressure was elevated at 134/95 mmHg, and her pulse was 111 bpm. She was diagnosed with non-ST elevation myocardial infarction based on conclusive EKG and elevated cardiac biomarkers.

TREATMENT:
The interdisciplinary team recommended cardiac catheterization which revealed atherosclerotic 90% stenosis of the mid-left anterior descending artery, which was treated with a single drug-eluting stent. The patient was managed with various medications, including aspirin, clopidogrel, enoxaparin, metoprolol, and pravastatin.

DISPOSITION:
The patient's hospital course was complicated by acute kidney injury, hyperkalemia, pediculosis capitis, and cystitis. Due to her complex medical condition, the patient was presented with options counseling for termination of the pregnancy, which she declined. She later developed superimposed preeclampsia and severe fetal growth restriction, ultimately delivering a neonate at 25 1/7 weeks who unfortunately passed away due to complications of extreme prematurity and intrauterine growth restriction. The patient did not experience a postpartum hemorrhage.

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient's medical team recommended that she follow up with her cardiologist and obstetrician to discuss the potential risks for future pregnancies and the management of her chronic medical conditions, including diabetes, hypertension, and high cholesterol.

Discharge Summary:

Patient demographics: 63-year-old male.

Chief complaint: Total laryngectomy due to recurrent laryngeal cancer.

Hospital course:

The patient was admitted to undergo total laryngectomy after a semi-laryngectomy eight months prior. He had a medical history of hypertension for 17 years and mild impairment of left ventricular diastolic function as defined by an echocardiogram. Upon examination, erythema and swelling were found under his right mandible with an erupted ulcer caused by the invasion of the tumor. The airway was evaluated and determined to be Malampatti grade III with normal mouth opening.

The patient's blood pressure was elevated at 180/95 mmHg, which was subsequently reduced to 130/80 mmHg following urapidil (25 mg). After the administration of 2% lidocaine (4 ml) to the tracheal and oropharyngeal areas, intravenous injection of midazolam (1 mg) and fentanyl (50 μg) was followed by fibroscope-guided nasal intubation. However, the larynx's structural deformation was noted, with impaired vocal cord mobility, leaving only a "fissure" of space, hindering the fibroscope's passage, even with a 2.8 mm diameter.

The patient then underwent tracheostomy under bilateral superficial cervical plexus block with assisted mask ventilation by 100% oxygen, followed by placement of a 7.0 mm coiled tracheal tube. General anesthesia was maintained by intravenous propofol and inhalational sevoflurane. Excision of the larynx revealed the distorted structure of the glottis with an S-shaped stenosis.

Summary of hospital stay:

The patient was successfully treated for total laryngectomy with tracheostomy under general anesthesia and recovered well after the surgery. The patient's vitals were monitored throughout the hospital stay, and no complications were reported. He was discharged with appropriate care instructions, including wound care and follow-up appointments with the treatment team. A follow-up plan was explained to the patient and scheduled after his discharge.

The patient was admitted with left loin pain and intermittent gross hematuria. An abdominal contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed a heterogeneous lobulated mass in the left renal parenchyma, with calcification foci and cystic spaces. A lung nodule and a metastatic lesion were also found. A clinical diagnosis of left renal cell carcinoma with invasion into renal vein and metastasis to the left lung and 7th thoracic vertebra was made. The patient underwent robot-assisted left radical nephrectomy with renal vein thrombectomy and lymph node dissection after renal arterial embolization. The gross specimen showed a huge growth extending to renal pelvis and bulging into the perirenal fat, and microscopically, a diagnosis of primary renal MC was made according to IHC staining results. The tumor was resected with negative surgical margins, and the tumor thrombus was confirmed to be malignant. The patient was admitted for investigation of left loin pain and intermittent gross hematuria. Imaging identified a heterogeneous lobulated renal mass with calcification foci and cystic spaces, as well as a lung nodule and thoracic vertebral lesion, suggestive of metastatic disease. The patient underwent left radical nephrectomy with renal vein thrombectomy and lymph node dissection as well as renal arterial embolization, with wide negative surgical margins. The resected specimen demonstrated a primary renal MC. Skull metastasis was noted on postoperative follow-up. The patient was managed supportively with pain management until death from widespread metastases at postoperative 1 month. Adjuvant chemotherapy or radiotherapy was not adopted.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our surgical oncology clinic with a chief complaint of a growing lump in the anterior compartment of the neck that has been present for a year. The patient was diagnosed with a suspected benign right nontoxic goiter. Further evaluation with thyroid gland ultrasonography and CT scan with contrast revealed a complex cystic mass in the right parasagittal area of the neck, attached to the right infrahyoid muscle, with differential diagnosis of the thyroglossal duct cyst or epidermoid cyst. On the 6-month follow-up, there was no locoregional complication nor clinically palpable lymph node enlargement; however, a lymph node enhancement was discovered by cervical contrast CT scan, and the patient was planned for a lymph node biopsy.

Diagnosis:
- Suspected benign right nontoxic goiter
- Thyroglossal duct cyst with a classic and follicular variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma

Treatment:
- Sistrunk procedure

Follow-up:
The patient reported no clinical complaints on the 6-month follow-up after the surgery; however, a lymph node enhancement was discovered by cervical contrast CT scan, and the patient was planned for a lymph node biopsy. If the biopsy result showed to be malignant, selective neck dissection and total thyroidectomy would be the treatment of choice.

Condition on Discharge:
The patient's condition was stable and improved upon discharge.

Instructions at Discharge:
The patient was instructed to follow up with the medical oncologist for further management and treatment. The patient was also advised to continue taking prescribed medications for hypertension and dyslipidemia and maintain a healthy lifestyle.

Hospital Course Summary:

Patient Information:
- Name: [redacted]
- Age: 15
- Gender: Male
- Chief Complaint: Excessive sleepiness, muscular weakness, hallucinations

History of Present Illness:
The 15-year-old male patient presented with a history of excessive sleepiness, sudden muscular weakness, visual and auditory hallucinations while falling asleep, and sleep paralysis since the age of 12. He had an Epworth Sleepiness Scale score of 15 and could not attend school regularly as a result of his symptoms. The patient had no previous treatments before presenting to our hospital.

Physical Examination & Laboratory Findings:
The patient's physical examination was mostly normal, and routine laboratory tests did not indicate any abnormalities. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings also appeared normal.

Diagnostic Tests:
The patient underwent a polysomnographic examination that showed a sleep efficiency of 95.5%. The patient's sleep was composed of 11.5% Non-rapid eye movement 1 (NREM1), 34.9% NREM2, 27.8% NREM3, and 25.9% Rapid Eye Movement (REM). The apnea hypopnea index (AHI) was 1.3/h, the periodic limb movement disorder index (PLMDI) was 2.1/h, and REM sleep without atonia (RSWA) was observed. A multiple sleep latency test (MSLT) showed a mean sleep latency of 3.5 min, <8 min, and the presence of 5 REM sleep-onset periods.

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with narcolepsy type 1.

Treatment:
The patient was administered venlafaxine (75 mg/day) once a day in the morning, which led to significant improvement in the patient's clinical symptoms after only one month of treatment. However, when the patient discontinued the medication six months later, his cataplexy symptoms reappeared, and so he resumed taking venlafaxine again.

Discharge Recommendations:
The patient was asymptomatic at the time of discharge with an Epworth sleepiness scale score of 9. It was recommended that the patient continue to take venlafaxine (75 mg/day) to alleviate his symptoms.
