Discharge Summary:

This is a discharge summary for a 9-year-old boy who was admitted to the hospital due to rhabdomyolysis. The patient reported having dark-colored urine and muscle tenderness after practicing throwing a rubber ball filled with sand for 45 minutes. Additionally, the patient had missed supper and fasted for at least 12 hours prior to developing symptoms. The urine analysis revealed mild proteinuria without red blood cells, and urine dipstick showed positive results for myoglobin and hemoglobin. CK levels were elevated, and the patient was diagnosed with rhabdomyolysis. 

The patient had a history of rhabdomyolysis when he was 19 months old and had eaten several river prawns before developing lethargy, weakness, and oliguria. The patient's urine had turned dark-colored at that time, and he had been treated in the intensive care unit for 15 days. After the current episode, the patient had mild CK elevation and had received supportive therapies, including adequate rest, nutrition support, and fluid therapy. 

The patient's parents refused the muscle biopsy and electromyogram but agreed to whole exome sequencing, which revealed that the patient carried the heterozygous compound variants c.1162C > T (p.Arg388*) and c.2428C > T (p.Arg810Cys) from his mother and father, respectively. The p.Arg388* variant is a known nonsense variant that creates a stop Codon at residue 388 and results in truncated proteins lacking catalytic activity. The p.Arg810Cys variant is a novel missense variant that involves Arg-to-Cys substitution at position 810 and was classified as "likely pathogenic."

The patient was discharged in stable condition, and the CK levels, as well as the ALT, AST, and LDH levels, had gradually improved. The patient's urine had turned clear, and repeated urine myoglobin and hemoglobin testing were negative. The patient has neither any other chronic diseases nor long-term medication taken but had a history of similar episodes triggered by exercise and fever. The patient's motor and cognitive development were normal. 

In summary, the patient was diagnosed with rhabdomyolysis, most likely triggered by prolonged exercise and fasting. The whole exome sequencing revealed that the patient carried heterozygous compound variants p.Arg388* and p.Arg810Cys. The patient was discharged after receiving supportive therapies and demonstrated improvement in CK, ALT, AST, and LDH levels with normal urine testing.

Hospital Course Summary:

Patient was admitted with flu-like symptoms including fever, chills, fatigue, cough, clear-sputum production, myalgia, arthralgia, rhinitis, adynamia, and weakness. Upon admission, the patient was placed on strict isolation and underwent various laboratory tests and screenings. Initial laboratory findings included mild leukopenia, absolute lymphopenia, low monocytes count, mild erythrocytosis, moderate thrombocytopenia, and increased C-reactive protein.

Various tests were performed to determine the cause of the symptoms including ELISA for Dengue. Although negative ELISA results, community-acquired pneumonia was suspected based on chest radiographs which showed peripheral ground-glass opacities in the mid-and lower-third of the thorax. Treatment with ampicillin/sulbactam and clarithromycin was initiated.

On the third day of admission, patient tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 infection through rRT-PCR of the nasopharyngeal swab specimen. Chloroquine phosphate was added to the treatment regimen on the fourth day and oseltamivir was continued.

The patient's platelet counts gradually improved over the course of the stay. On the sixth day, dyspnea was experienced and the patient received a chest computed tomography which showed peripheral ground-glass opacities with partial occupation improving and the reversed halo sign was observed.

On the ninth day, the leukocyte counts became normal with no other significant clinical findings. A control sample for SARS-CoV-2 was taken which returned negative. The patient was discharged and is to remain isolated at home for 14 days under medical follow up.

Overall, the hospital course of this patient was eventful with COVID-19 infection detected and treated. The patient was deemed to be in good condition and was successfully discharged.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [patient's name]
Age: 14 years
Gender: Male
Admission Date: [date of admission]
Discharge Date: [date of discharge]
Admitting Diagnosis: Nontransmural myocardial infarction
Principal Diagnosis: Anomalous origin of left coronary artery

History of Present Illness:
The patient presented with severe chest pain during jogging, which lasted for 2 hours. This was followed by generalized weakness, dyspnea, and confusional state. The initial electrocardiogram showed ST segment depression in all precordial leads and serum Troponin I levels were found to be > 30 ng/mL within 24 hours of symptom onset. The patient developed pulmonary edema and was admitted to the intensive care unit.

Hospital Course:
After stabilization, the patient was referred to our tertiary care hospital. The electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with ST segment depression and repolarization abnormalities in precordial leads V1 to V3. A transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a hypokinetic anteroseptal wall with normal systolic and diastolic function. Polymerase chain reaction tests for various viruses on peripheral blood samples were negative. A rest perfusion magnetic resonance imaging detected an anterior, anteroseptal and lateral nontransmural myocardial infarction with systolic left ventricular dysfunction (ejection fraction of 45%) alongside an anomalous origin of the left coronary artery arising at the right sinus of Valsalva with an interarterial stenotic tract. A CT angiography demonstrated a left coronary artery arising at the right sinus of Valsalva with an acute take-off angle and proximal oval-like narrowing with an extension of 11 mm running throughout the interarterial segment. Coronary translocation was discarded because the proximal interarterial segment was very stenotic and hypoplastic.

Treatment and Management:
The patient was pharmacologically managed with aspirin, atenolol, and ivabradine. Through median sternotomy, cardiovascular surgeons performed revascularization of the anterior descending coronary artery with an internal mammary artery graft. Seven days after surgery, the patient was discharged. The patient underwent treadmill stress testing and accomplished 9 sessions achieving a work level of 10.2 METS with adequate tolerance. The cardiology team decided to restrict any strenuous physical activity.

Follow-up:
The patient has been followed up in the cardiology outpatient clinic. Up to 18 months after surgery, he is reported asymptomatic with normal electrocardiograms and echocardiographic evidence of normal systo-diastolic function. 

Discharge Diagnosis:
Anomalous origin of left coronary artery 

Condition at Discharge:
Stable 

Discharge Instructions:
The patient should continue taking aspirin, atenolol and ivabradine as prescribed. The cardiology team has advised the patient to refrain from strenuous physical activity. The patient should continue follow-up in the cardiology outpatient clinic. 

Discharge Medications:
Aspirin 
Atenolol 
Ivabradine

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Medical Record Number: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 23-year-old woman who presented to the Emergency Department due to severe headaches accompanied by focal motor seizures. She has a history of quadriplegia and autonomic dysreflexia due to a cervical spinal cord injury. Further assessments revealed subarachnoid hemorrhage and multifocal narrowing of the anterior cerebral artery, bilateral middle cerebral arteries (MCA), right posterior cerebral artery, and pericallosal artery. The patient experienced recurrent headaches whenever she tried to flush her urinary catheter, which she had been experiencing from the previous days. During the hospital stay, her headaches recurred, which were associated with episodes of flushing, sweating, and elevated blood pressure. Midodrine was discontinued, and her headaches improved significantly at the time of discharge.

Diagnosis:
The patient's condition appears to have been related to the blockage of her urinary catheter, which resulted in recurrent headaches and subsequent flushing, sweating, and elevated blood pressure. No significant abnormality or underlying medical condition was found during routine blood tests, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), comprehensive drug screening, antinuclear antibodies, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) panel, and angiotensin-converting enzyme.

Treatment:
The patient was treated by discontinuing midodrine and closely monitoring her condition. A diagnostic cerebral angiogram revealed stenosis of the right middle cerebral artery, bilateral posterior cerebral arteries, callosal, and pericallosal branches of the right anterior cerebral artery.

Follow-up:
The patient was discharged from the hospital, and no recurrence of symptoms was reported during the subsequent follow-up visit. Three months after her discharge, she underwent repeat diagnostic cerebral angiogram, which showed no significant abnormalities.

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition.

Instructions:
The patient should continue to monitor her condition and report any recurrent symptoms. She should also avoid catheter blockage by following the guidelines provided by her care team. The patient should follow up with her care team as directed.

Discharge Diagnosis: Benign epithelial odontogenic tumour

Hospital Course:
A 74-year-old female was admitted to the Otolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery Department on [Redacted] with complaints of obstruction on the right nasal cavity. The patient had frequent mild nosebleeds and a mild feeling of pressure in the right side of her face for the past year. The medical history of the patient included hypertension and Behcet's syndrome under treatment. No known allergies and no smoking or alcohol drinking habits were reported.

Endoscopy revealed a mass lesion adhered to the middle meatus causing complete obstruction of the right nasal cavity. Computed tomography of the paranasal sinuses revealed a soft tissue density lesion occupying the maxillary sinus and nasal cavity of the right side. This measured 2.6 cm x 3.1 cm x 3 cm and extended to the right middle and inferior meatus of the right nasal cavity. Disintegration of the outside and inside wall on the maxillary sinus was also obvious. Magnetic resonance imaging added no further relevant information.

Biopsy of the lesion indicated benign epithelial odontogenic tumour. Treatment with surgical removal of the lesion was decided. Endoscopic sinus operation was performed under general anaesthesia. The patient was subjected to maxillary sinus opening and removal of the inner wall. The lesion was resected en bloc from the inferior and anterior wall. Part of the periosteum was also removed from the maxillary sinus. The sample was sent for histological study. The biopsy findings confirmed follicular ameloblastoma (solid/multicystic).

Postoperatively, no complications were reported, and the patient was discharged on [Redacted]. Ten days postoperatively, endoscopy revealed unobstructed airflow through the right nasal cavity. Three months of follow-up unveiled no complication, and symptoms were effectively alleviated.

Discharge Medications:
[None specified]

The patient is advised to follow-up for outpatient care as scheduled. The patient presents no restriction to normal activity.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [redacted]
Sex: Male            Date of Admission: [redacted]         Date of Discharge: [redacted]

HOSPITAL COURSE:

The patient was an 81-year-old man with a past medical history notable for postinfectious glomerulonephritis, two coronary bypass surgeries, aortic valve replacement, cholecystectomy, benign prostatic hyperplasia, and right hemicolectomy for colon cancer.

During routine follow-up after his colon cancer surgery, the patient reported experiencing new nonspecific abdominal pain. Imaging studies revealed bilateral perirenal masses that were later confirmed to be rind-like bilateral perirenal masses. After conducting core biopsies, a presumptive diagnosis of Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) was made.

Further imaging studies were conducted, with bone scans showing bilateral sclerotic lesions in all long bones of the arms and legs. However, the cerebral scan was reported to be negative.

Immunohistochemical analysis was conducted on the biopsy sample, with the biopsy confirming the diagnosis of ECD. A small lymphocytic lymphoma diagnosis was also made, based on the immunohistochemical analysis findings.

The patient developed mild bicytopenia, anemia, and thrombopenia of an unknown cause one year after the initial diagnosis, with subsequent bone marrow biopsies revealing minimal medullary infiltration by SLL, without ECD involvement.

The patient was kept under close observation without any treatment and had a favorable follow-up. He expired five years following his diagnosis of ECD.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES:

1. Rind-like bilateral perirenal masses
2. Erdheim-Chester Disease
3. Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:

The patient has been discharged and should follow up with his primary care physician and oncologist as per previous instructions.

Hospital Course:
The five-year-old male with a known case of Cockayne syndrome type B presented with jaundice, mild hepatomegaly, and pitting edema of the lower limbs. The patient had been treated with amoxicillin and metronidazole for a dental infection one week prior to admission. Three days after the onset of medication, the patient developed jaundice, drowsiness, lethargy, and anorexia. Initial evaluation for HBV, HCV, autoimmune hepatitis, and hypothyroidism were negative. The patient had previously experienced elevated liver enzymes at age 2 years and was treated with ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) and observed to have normalized levels without liver biopsy. The patient was hospitalized and treated with cefotaxime, vitamin K, pantoprazole, plasma, and albumin transfusion. The patient's general condition gradually improved, and the INR and liver enzymes normalized. The patient was discharged after 8 days with a prescription for UDCA.

Follow-Up:
Further evaluations performed one month after discharge depicted elevated liver enzymes, total bilirubin, and direct bilirubin. Treatment with UDCA was continued, and follow-up was continued.

Discharge Medications:
- Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA)

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: ______________

Admission Date: ____________

Discharge Date: ____________

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our institution with progressive neurological symptoms. He had a history of seropositive Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) that was managed with maintenance methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine and low-dose prednisone. The patient developed fluctuating confusion, word-finding difficulty, right-sided weakness and gait imbalance. An evaluation was done by the neurologist which confirmed the presence of neurological deficits. An MRI scan showed areas of scattered restricted diffusion and enhancement within the cortex and leptomeninges of the left hemisphere near the vertex, suspicious for meningoencephalitis. CSF analysis also demonstrated lymphocytic meningitis with negative, bacterial and fungal cultures. 

The patient was started on antiepileptic medication and a whole-body PET scan was done to rule out underlying malignancy. A bone marrow biopsy was also done to rule out lymphoid neoplasm. An open meningeal biopsy was performed and gross examination revealed thickening and opacification of the meninges. The histopathological findings were consistent with leptomeningeal involvement by nodular rheumatoid meningitis.

Immunosuppressive therapy with monthly cyclophosphamide and high-dose corticosteroids was initiated for 6 months and then the corticosteroids were tapered. The patient's neurological examination improved one month post treatment initiation, although confusion and bilateral postural tremor persisted. Most parkinsonian features also largely resolved following immunosuppressive therapy. 

Repeat MRI 3 months after treatment initiation showed complete resolution of previous findings, and CRP levels also normalized. The patient was eventually transitioned to a long-term care facility due to the persistent behavioral and cognitive deficits with intermittent periods of agitation.

Diagnosis:
Leptomeningeal involvement by nodular rheumatoid meningitis

Course:
The patient was admitted for investigation of progressive neurological symptoms and was treated with immunosuppressive therapy. The patient's neurological examination improved one month post treatment initiation, although confusion and bilateral postural tremor persisted, and most parkinsonian features largely resolved following immunosuppressive therapy. Repeat MRI 3 months after treatment initiation showed complete resolution of previous findings.

Discharge Condition:
The patient has been transitioned to a long-term care facility due to persistent behavioral and cognitive deficits with intermittent periods of agitation.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 19-year-old African-American female presented to the emergency department with subacute onset of left-sided hemianesthesia that started in the left hand and gradually progressed proximally to the entire left upper and lower extremities, and then the right side of the body over a course of two weeks. The patient also reported bifrontal throbbing headache and decreased bowel and bladder sensation, but no episodes of bowel or bladder incontinence. During physical examination, the patient had 4/5 strength in the left upper extremity and 5/5 strength in the right upper extremity. She had decreased sensation to light touch on the left side of her body and a mild decrease in rectal tone. MRI of brain and spine showed a sharply delineated ovoid mass within the spinal cord at the level of C3 that measured approximately 1.7 cm (SI) x 6.4 mm (AP). Based on the radiological findings, low-grade astrocytoma, ependymoma, and inflammatory or demyelinating lesion were in the differential diagnosis.

Following the radiological findings, the patient was treated with steroids and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was obtained. CSF analysis was positive for oligoclonal bands, which raised the suspicion for a demyelinating lesion. The patient was then treated with a combination of high-dose steroid and five plasma exchange sessions.

After treatment inpatient, the patient’s left-side weakness and numbness showed significant improvement. She was further assessed by physical and occupational therapy, and was cleared for discharge.

Patient’s discharge medication was prescribed, and discharge teaching was provided to the patient. The patient continues to do well, and the repeat MRI showed mild reduction in the size of the lesion. At the time of discharge, the patient was referred to a neurologist for further monitoring and management of her condition.

Summary:

A 19-year-old African-American female presented with left-sided hemianesthesia and associated weakness. MRI showed a sharply delineated ovoid mass within the spinal cord at the level of C3. After CSF analysis, a demyelinating lesion was suspected and treated with a combination of steroids and plasma exchange sessions. The patient showed significant improvement in her left-side weakness and numbness after treatment, and was cleared for discharge. Patient was prescribed post-discharge medication, and provided with discharge teaching. The patient was referred to a neurologist for appropriate follow-up and management.

Patient Name: [Redacted]
DOB: [Redacted]
Admission Date: [Redacted]
Discharge Date: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:

Admission: A 28-year-old female patient in her 26th week of gestation was admitted to the emergency department with complaints of dizziness and palpitation for the past 2 weeks. The patient had a complicated previous pregnancy due to severe preeclampsia requiring caesarian section. Lab test results revealed severe anemia and leukocytosis with blasts, confirming acute myeloid leukemia.

Management: The patient was initiated on induction chemotherapy with daunorubicin and cytarabine, which led to myopericarditis, managed with analgesia, beta blockers, steroids, and aspirin. Afebrile neutropenia during induction required admission to the critical care unit, managed with antibiotics as per local protocol. Patient achieved hematological remission post-chemotherapy and was administered 5-azacytidine to prevent disease relapse. Elective cesarean section was performed at 35 weeks of gestation, with dexamethasone administered for lung maturity. The patient delivered a baby girl weighing 1670g with apgars 9 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes and arterial cord PH 7.32, who was admitted to the NICU and stayed 2 weeks for observation.

Outcome: The patient had a favorable recovery and was given high dose cytarabine consolidation, planned for 3 cycles with midostaurin. The baby had a normal ECHO with tiny PDA left to right shunt and was scheduled for regular follow-up after 6 and 12 months for development.

Final Diagnosis: Acute Myeloid Leukemia

Discharge Plan: The patient was discharged in stable condition with recommendations for ongoing care from the hematological and obstetric teams. Recommendations included follow-up appointments to monitor chemotherapy effectiveness, regular laboratory testing to monitor for relapse, and follow-up visits for the infant's developmental progress.

Hospital Course Summary:

This hospital course summary pertains to a 35-year-old male who presented to the Emergency Department with a 10-day history of high-grade fever, shortness of breath, palpitations, and joint pain. The patient was found to have a history of intravenous drug abuse but denied any other medical conditions or allergies. A review of other organ systems was unremarkable. The patient had a known ostium secundum with left-to-right shunt, which was previously diagnosed by transoesophageal echocardiography. Further tests were conducted, including complete blood cell count, malarial and dengue tests, and serology for HIV and hepatitis. The CBC showed a slightly low hemoglobin level and an elevated total leukocyte count. All other tests were insignificant.

Given the persistent high-grade fever, Infective Endocarditis (IE) was suspected, and echocardiography and blood culture were performed. Echocardiography showed no vegetation. However, blood samples were found to be positive for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and treated accordingly with intravenous vancomycin and gentamicin for a period of six weeks. After the fever subsided, surgery for the closure of ASD was performed successfully. The patient was discharged from the hospital after good recovery and referred to a rehabilitation center for drug abuse. Continued monthly follow-up visits have since shown that the patient continues to do well.

Discharge Summary:

Mr. X, a 35-year-old male, was admitted to the Civil Hospital Karachi Emergency Department with a 10-day history of high-grade fever, joint pain, palpitations, and shortness of breath. The patient had a known ostium secundum with left-to-right shunt previously diagnosed by transoesophageal echocardiography. Upon physical examination, the patient was found to be dehydrated but responsive and alert. Blood pressure was slightly low, and respiratory rate was somewhat elevated with high-grade fever. Cardiovascular examination was negative for any murmur, and the lungs were clear on auscultation. Abdominal examination was also normal, except for an enlarged spleen.

The patient underwent a series of laboratory tests, including complete blood cell count, malarial and dengue tests, and serology for HIV and hepatitis. CBC showed a slightly low hemoglobin level and an elevated total leukocyte count. The other tests were negative.

Further, echocardiography and blood culture were performed due to a persistent high-grade fever, to which Infective Endocarditis (IE) was suspected. Echocardiography showed no vegetation. However, blood samples were found to be positive for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and treated accordingly with intravenous vancomycin and gentamicin for six weeks. After the fever subsided, surgery for the closure of ASD was performed successfully.

The patient responded well to treatment and showed good recovery. The patient was discharged and referred to a rehabilitation center for drug abuse. Follow-up visits have shown that the patient continues to do well.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with a single gunshot wound to the abdomen and underwent exploratory laparotomy. At the index operation, he received a right hemicolectomy with end ileostomy due to colon avulsion with ischemia to the hepatic flexure. In addition, PD with choledochojejunostomy, pancreaticojejunostomy, and gastrojejunostomy was performed to manage an entrance and exit wound involving the duodenum's ampulla of Vater and distal common bile duct. He developed a high-grade obstruction at the biliary anastomosis postoperatively and underwent serial attempts at percutaneous cholangioplasty and stenting without success. The subsequent long-term management included percutaneous transhepatic drainage (PTD) and operative revision of the anastomosis to hepaticojejunostomy.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was discharged after a prolonged hospital course, which involved surgical management of a gunshot wound to the abdomen. He received a right hemicolectomy and PD during the initial operation. Postoperatively, he developed a high-grade biliary obstruction that was managed with long-term PTD and operative revision to hepaticojejunostomy. The patient had an unremarkable recovery from the revision and was discharged in stable condition. The patient should follow up with his healthcare provider to ensure that there are no long-term complications from his injuries.

Hospital Course: 
The patient, a 33-year-old male, presented with lower abdominal pain. A contrast-enhanced CT abdomen and pelvis revealed a large pelvic mass, initially suspected to be a soft tissue sarcoma. A subsequent staging FDG-PET/CT scan demonstrated intense FDG-avidity in relation to the pelvic mass lesion, a mildly FDG-avid left para-aortic node deemed highly suspicious for metastasis, and an absent left testis. Further history revealed an absent left testis from birth that was never brought to medical attention. 

Diagnostic Assessment: 
CT-guided biopsy of the pelvic mass revealed a seminoma with normal tumor markers. Open resection of the pelvic mass confirmed it to be arising from an intra-abdominal testis, with focal residual seminiferous tubules evident and showing germ cell neoplasia in situ. Restaging FDG-PET/CT performed 3 months after surgical resection demonstrated interval progression of the pre-existing FDG-avid left para-aortic node, confirming metastatic involvement.

Management and Treatment: 
The patient was subsequently commenced on BEP chemotherapy. 

Follow-up and Discharge: 
The patient was discharged with appropriate follow-up care.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Patient Name]

Medical Record Number: [Medical Record Number]

Admission Date: [Admission Date]
Discharge Date: [Discharge Date]

Admitting Diagnosis:
Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)-positive female patient with history of pulmonary tuberculosis (TB), presenting with fever, cough, and hemoptysis for the past two months.

Hospital Course:
The patient received a thorough clinical examination upon admission, which revealed diffuse rhonchi on the right side of her chest. Chest x-ray (CXR) revealed a cavitary lesion in the right lung field with homogenous opacity in the middle zone of her right lung. CT scan showed a cavitary lesion in the right middle lung and a tree-in-bud appearance in the left lung (lingual). Sputum samples were collected and subjected to fluorescence microscopy after auramine staining and nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (TB). Microscopy showed acid-fast bacilli (AFB) but the NAAT was negative for M. tuberculosis. Culture on liquid media showed nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), which was identified as Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) at the National Reference Laboratory.

The patient received treatment with azithromycin, rifampicin, ethambutol, and amikacin (Mikacin) for two months. Sputum conversion was detected after four months and treatment continued for a further 12 months after sputum conversion.

Summary of Findings:
- HIV-positive female patient with history of pulmonary TB
- Fever, cough, and hemoptysis for two months
- CXR showed a cavitary lesion in the right lung field with homogenous opacity in the middle zone of her right lung
- CT scan showed a cavitary lesion in the right middle lung and a tree-in-bud appearance in the left lung (lingual)
- Sputum samples were positive for AFB on microscopy and NTM on culture
- NTM was identified as MAC at the National Reference Laboratory
- Treatment with azithromycin, rifampicin, ethambutol, and amikacin (Mikacin) for two months was successful in achieving sputum conversion after four months
- Treatment was continued for a further 12 months after sputum conversion

Discharge Medications:
None.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient should follow up with their infectious disease specialist and continue to take their antiretroviral medication as prescribed. The patient should also adhere to all recommended infection control measures.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital for acute abdominal pain. A comprehensive evaluation was done which revealed mild acute pancreatitis with no definitive cause aside from his use of the antibiotic amoxicillin/clavulanic acid. He was managed with aggressive IV hydration and pain management with bowel rest for 2 days. The patient showed significant improvement within 72 hours and was discharged home.

History and Physical Exam:
A 58-year-old man presented to the emergency department for acute abdominal pain, mainly in the epigastric area. He reported sharp pain with a severity of 8/10 that was non-radiating, worsened with movement and mildly improved with rest. The pain was associated with nausea and heaves. The physical exam was only notable for epigastric tenderness.

Diagnostic Assessment:
Laboratory values showed mild leukocytosis, increased levels of serum lipase, amylase, and CRP. Abdominal CT revealed acute pancreatitis without pseudocyst formation. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) and abdominal ultrasound were done to eliminate the possibility of gallstones, biliary sludge, biliary ductal dilatation, or choledocholithiasis. Endoscopic ultrasonography was done as an outpatient and ruled out biliary microlithiasis.

Discussion:
The most plausible cause of the patient’s acute pancreatitis was his use of amoxicillin/clavulanic acid prior to presentation. Similar symptoms were experienced by the patient several years ago after taking the same antibiotic, albeit without medical attention at that time. The patient was then diagnosed with mild acute pancreatitis with a score of 0 on the Bedside Index of Severity in Acute Pancreatitis.

Summary:
A 58-year-old man presented with acute abdominal pain which was diagnosed as mild acute pancreatitis. There was no definitive cause other than use of amoxicillin/clavulanic acid that the patient had taken. Diagnostic assessments showed no other abnormal findings and the patient was managed with IV hydration and pain management while fasting for 2 days. He showed significant improvement and was discharged home. Follow-up care was recommended with a gastroenterologist for further evaluation and discussion of possible cause and prevention of future occurrences.

Hospital Course: The patient, a 43-year-old Caucasian male with a history of hypertension and intractable seizures, was admitted for craniotomy and intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) monitoring. Previous EEG recordings revealed right frontal and right parietal onset seizures, but depth insular or hippocampal electrodes were not placed during the recording.

Diagnostic and Therapeutic Procedures: The patient underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), functional MRI (fMRI), and positron emission tomography (PET) scans. The PET scan showed reduced uptake in the right hemisphere and right basal ganglia. fMRI showed a language predominance in the left hemisphere. Brain MRI showed post-craniotomy changes over the right parietal region, without evident parenchymal lesions. The patient was status-post vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) implantation, video-EEG (vEEG), and a prior right-sided craniotomy and grid placement for an intracranial electrodes study. vEEG monitoring revealed tonic-clonic seizures with loss of consciousness. Given the prior non-confirmatory iEEG, depth electrodes were placed in the right hippocampus and insula (anterior and posterior), in addition to an 8x8 grid over the neocortex to confirm the localization of seizure foci.

Summary of Hospitalization: ECoG done during the operation confirmed that seizures were originating from the right anterior insular cortex and rapidly spreading to the right frontal and temporal operculum. Subsequently, the patient underwent a right frontotemporal insula lobectomy without serious complications, except minimal left-sided weakness. The patient was monitored in the intensive care unit (ICU) following surgery, which demonstrated improvement in participation and alertness. He has remained on his medication regimen and seen occupational therapy/physical therapy (OT/PT) to improve weakness. At six months post-surgery, the patient reported no seizures and noted an improvement in his left-sided weakness.

Age: 74
Gender: Male

Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the Emergency Department with abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and distension for five days. On examination, a tender irreducible swelling was identified in the right inguinal region. The patient's vital signs were normal, while bowel sounds were sluggish. The lab results showed high blood sugar, white blood cell count, and serum potassium. An abdominal ultrasound revealed the presence of a cystic-like lesion in the right inguinal region, resembling a bowel loop.

The patient underwent a surgical procedure to explore the region of the inguinal hernia, during which a Foley's catheter balloon was discovered in the sliding part of the bladder within the hernia. The hernia was identified as a direct sliding Ogilvie inguinal hernia, which was repaired. During a subsequent exploratory laparotomy, the patient was found to have a superior mesenteric artery occlusion causing strangulation of most of the transverse colon, all right colon, and all small bowel, except the first 100 cm of jejunum. The gangrenous bowel was resected surgically, and an end-to-end jejuno-colonic anastomosis was performed.

Despite the surgery, the patient's condition deteriorated until he died on the 5th day post-operation due to cardiac issues.

Diagnosis at Discharge:

The patient was diagnosed with strangulated right inguinal hernia causing intestinal obstruction and superior mesenteric artery occlusion.

Instructions at Discharge:

The patient, unfortunately, passed away, so no instructions at discharge are relevant.

Follow-Up:

There is no follow-up required as the patient passed away.

Patient Name: [Insert Name]
Medical Record Number: [Insert MRN]
Admission Date: [Insert Date]
Discharge Date: [Insert Date]

Reason for Admission:
The patient was admitted to the hospital due to severely impairing dizziness and anemia.

Hospital Course:
Upon initial examination, the patient was diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and had been treated with oral corticosteroids, methotrexate (MTX) 10 mg weekly, and/or a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug. Her condition had been steady for 16 months, but she experienced multiple symptoms in the following 8 months, leading to hospital admission.

Laboratory results showed normocytic anemia, with hemoglobin (Hb) count of 34 g/L and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 138 mm/h. Additional tests showed rheumatoid factor of 223 IU/mL, anti-cyclic peptide containing citrulline of 885.6 RU/mL, and vitamin B12 of 368 pmol/L. MTX was discontinued and glucocorticoids were administered for 12 weeks. However, the patient's hemoglobin level declined to 32 g/L, and additional red blood cell transfusions were required.

Re-examination revealed dysplastic features on hematopoietic lineages on bone marrow aspiration, leading to a diagnosis of treatment-related myelodysplastic syndrome (t-MDS). The patient's medical history and laboratory parameters suggested MTX was responsible for bone marrow toxicity. Tocilizumab was added to the treatment regimen, which resulted in clinical benefit and improvement in the patient's symptoms. The patient was discharged from the hospital after one month of treatment.

Follow-up visits showed no obvious abnormalities in the patient's laboratory results and bone marrow aspiration results. The prompt resolution of the patient's serological, physical, and pathological abnormalities was achieved with tocilizumab treatment. After six months of treatment, the patient refused further injections, leading to symptoms returning. Despite relapse, the patient's laboratory examination was stable, and symptoms significantly improved after treatment was resumed.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Treatment-related myelodysplastic syndrome (t-MDS)

[Insert medications]

The patient requires follow-up visits with their rheumatologist and hematologist to monitor their condition.

2. The patient should avoid alcohol consumption and smoking.
3. The patient should follow up regularly with their healthcare providers.
4. The patient should contact their healthcare provider if they experience any unusual symptoms or side effects.

Admitting Diagnosis: Acute drug-induced liver injury

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with complaints of chest pain, fatigue, palpitations, and shortness of breath. She had been taking a herbal supplement for weight loss named Hydroxycut for three months. On admission, her vitals were significant for tachycardia and low oxygen saturation. Physical examination was positive for obesity and mild asterixis bilaterally, and there was no encephalopathy, scleral icterus, or hepatosplenomegaly.

Laboratory analysis showed leukocytosis and severe transaminitis, with ALT and AST levels significantly elevated. Further investigations for other etiologies of acute liver injury were inconclusive. Abdomen Ultrasound showed hepatomegaly, and CT scan of the chest showed developmental abnormalities like scoliosis and lung hypoplasia.

The patient was diagnosed with acute drug-induced liver injury, likely due to Hydroxycut, and was treated with N-acetylcysteine. Transaminases trended down during the course of hospitalization after the medication was discontinued.

The patient was discharged in stable condition with follow-up instructions for outpatient hepatology. She was advised to avoid any herbal supplements without consulting a medical professional, and to report any adverse reactions or symptoms as soon as possible.

The patient was advised to follow-up with a hepatologist as an outpatient for further monitoring of liver function tests, and to avoid any medication or supplements that may harm liver function. The patient was also advised to make lifestyle changes to lose weight and reduce obesity.

Medications:
No medications were prescribed at the time of discharge.

Patient Condition at Discharge:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with improved liver function tests.

Discharge Summary:

Patient was a term female delivered via repeat caesarean section with vacuum extraction and had mild respiratory distress and physiologic jaundice in the postnatal period. On DOL 3, the patient presented to the hospital with poor feeding and lethargy and was found to have severe metabolic acidosis. Upon admission, the differential diagnosis included inborn error of metabolism, shock due to sepsis and hypovolemia, or cardiogenic etiology. Empiric antibiotics were initiated for suspected sepsis, though later found to be negative. An echocardiogram demonstrated mitral and tricuspid regurgitation with severely depressed left ventricular function, indicating acute heart failure. The patient responded well to treatment with milrinone, and her ejection fraction improved. She was transferred to another hospital with a metabolic specialist where complete workup demonstrated no inborn errors of metabolism, but did show right kidney hypoplasia with reduced perfusion, suggesting a renovascular etiology of hypertension. Medication management was adjusted and patient was discharged with home blood pressure monitoring system. At 5 months of life, patient was still on enalapril and amlodipine, and her blood pressures were moderately controlled. Follow-up renal ultrasound demonstrated small right kidney and a normal left kidney. The patient's growth and development were appropriate for post-conceptual age.

The patient, a 25-year-old male with no significant medical history, presented to the hospital as a living liver donor. The donor right hepatectomy procedure was successful and uneventful. The patient was discharged on postoperative day six after experiencing successful postoperative management and improvement in pain scores. DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient: [Name], [Age], Female

Healthcare worker who had immigrated from India with a recent onset of acute severe back pain, radiating down both legs, was worse at night and with activity, and relieved with naproxen and oral methylprednisone. Past medical, surgical, and social history were otherwise unremarkable. A mechanical etiology was suspected and managed conservatively with physical therapy.

Over weeks, the patient developed urinary frequency, constipation, and dysmenorrhea. She was initially diagnosed with pelvic floor dysfunction. Her back pain continued to progressively worsen over the following months and was started on prednisone. She did report unintentional weight loss but denied other constitutional symptoms. Her physical exam remained normal, except for right sacroiliac joint and lumbar spinal tenderness. The straight leg raising test was also positive bilaterally.

An MRI of the pelvis and lumbar spine demonstrated bone marrow edema in the inferior aspect of the right sacroiliac joint, thought to be consistent with an early stage of sacroiliitis. Schmorl's node at L4 was also reported. The patient was then diagnosed with early-stage ankylosing spondylitis. The rheumatology service was consulted, and she was treated with hydroxychloroquine and prednisone.

Hydroxychloroquine was stopped after two weeks due to the development of myalgia and visual floaters. Immunosuppressive therapy was proposed as an alternative, so a QuantiFERON-TB Gold test© was ordered. This resulted as positive. A needle biopsy was then performed, revealing necrotizing granulomas with rare acid-fast bacilli. The sputum analysis was then found to be positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. She was started on a four-drug regimen of isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide.

Despite medical management, she was admitted to the hospital a year after the onset of her symptoms with fever, severe nausea, and emesis. Repeat CT of the lumbar spine without contrast showed a lytic lesion in the L4 vertebral body with a partial compression fracture and mild retropulsion of bone into the ventral spinal canal. A repeat lumbar MRI showed edema and enhancement of the L4 vertebral body with erosive changes and subligamentous spread consistent with tuberculous discitis and osteomyelitis. There was an epidural collection at the L3-4 level, with sub-articular zone involvement. The left neural foramen and exiting nerve root were also involved.

At this point in time, the neurosurgery service was consulted. Due to the small size of the epidural component, a stable neurologic exam without any focal deficits, patient preference, and aggressive medical management was recommended. However, the patient continued to have a persistent fever above 38°C, worsening radicular pain, and declining functional status. The follow-up MRI revealed an expanding epidural abscess and eroded lumbar vertebrae with progressive kyphosis as compared with two months prior. Her spine was stabilized with a thoracolumbosacral orthosis (TLSO) brace to minimize the risk of neurological decline.

A second opinion was then sought from an outside hospital. A two-month course of intravenous amikacin was added to her antimicrobial regimen. Despite the physical deformity and our continued recommendation for surgery, the patient has continued to prefer non-surgical management. Her most recent MRI performed 18 months after the diagnosis of spinal tuberculosis and initiation of anti-tuberculosis therapy showed decreased evidence of osteomyelitis and resolution of the psoas collection. A plain radiograph was also performed, which showed stable loss of vertebral body height and stable grade 1 spondylolisthesis at L3-4, without any increase in angular deformity or motion seen in the flexion-extension views.

The patient has continued to request non-surgical management and has since requested not to undergo any additional follow-up imaging. At the most recent clinical follow-up at 22 months after initial diagnosis, she is neurologically intact and ambulatory with minimal back pain.

Admission Date: [Date]

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 24-year-old male active military personnel, was admitted with complaints of profound diminution of vision in his right eye of 5 days duration. He had been diagnosed with dengue hemorrhagic fever about 20 days earlier, treated with supportive therapy only without any blood/blood component infusion, and discharged from hospital 10 days earlier. During hospitalization, his lowest platelet count was 40,000 per microliter of blood without any ocular symptoms. 

Upon initial examination, the patient’s best corrected visual acuity was 20/400 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye. Anterior segment examination in both eyes was normal. Fundus examination in the right eye revealed premacular hemorrhage about 2 disc diameters in size occupying the central macula due to a splinter hemorrhage at the superonasal aspect of the disc. 

The patient was informed and counseled about different treatment approaches including “wait-and-watch” for spontaneous recovery, pars plana vitrectomy, and a novel technique of pneumatic displacement with intraocular gas tamponade. Due to being in active military service with dominant eye involvement, the patient was treated with 0.3 ml of C3F8 (100%) injected intravitreally. 

He responded well to treatment with partial displacement and absorption of sub-ILM blood by day 3 post-C3F8 injection and complete clearing of sub-ILM blood by the end of the first week. His present systemic work-up was normal and platelet counts revealed mild thrombocytopenia (120,000 per microliter of blood).

The patient was discharged with normal foveal contour, remnants of ILM seen over the macula, and recovery of vision to 20/20 without any metamorphopsia or scotoma.

Diagnoses:

1. Premacular hemorrhage due to dengue hemorrhagic fever

Procedures:

1. 0.3 ml of C3F8 (100%) injected intravitreally
2. Paracentesis in the operating theatre
3. Pneumatic displacement with intraocular gas tamponade

Condition on Discharge:

The patient was discharged with a stable condition with normal foveal contour, remnants of ILM seen over the macula, and recovery of vision to 20/20 without any metamorphopsia or scotoma.

The patient was admitted with complaints of abdominal pain in the epigastric region, weight loss, and fever. He had a past medical history of low back pain. Physical examination was normal. Follow-up F-18 FDG PET/ CT revealed a complete response to ATT with no residual disease.

1. Abdominal pain in epigastric region, weight loss, low back pain
2. Sacroiliitis
3. Gastric ulcer at the incisura angularis, granulomatous gastritis
4. Granulamatous lymphadenitis with granulomas including giant cells, suspecting TB
5. Ankylosing spondylitis

The patient was put on ATT consisting of (2HREZ/7HR) regimen. At the 6th week of treatment, he gained weight about 6 kg, and he was feeling healthy. Hemoglobin was 12.6 gm/dL. Follow-up F-18 FDG PET/ CT revealed a complete response to ATT with no residual disease.

Discharge Date: [insert date]

Admission Diagnosis: Unconsciousness and melena.

Hospital Course:
The patient [Insert name], [Insert patient age], [Insert gender] was admitted to the hospital due to unconsciousness followed by melena. The upper endoscopy revealed a stomach full of fresh blood. Hemodynamic instability was observed, and the patient underwent intubation and polytransfusion. The angiography suite further showed the existence of a saccular aneurysm of 2.5 cm in diameter on the distal third of a splenic artery, which was embolized with microcoils, enabling hemodynamic stabilization. The CT scan demonstrated a distal pancreatic tumor abutting the posterior gastric wall, which was found to be responsible for the splenic artery erosion, developing and secondary rupture of a false aneurysm in the gastric cavity. Further biopsies were performed on the margins, revealing invasive pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Later, the patient presented a slow decrease in blood hemoglobin levels. A new contrast-enhanced CT scan revealed a new retrogastric blood extravasation originating from the distal third of the splenic artery. A super-selective catheterization of the gastroepiploic arteries allowed coil embolization of the distal splenic artery, stopping the bleeding. After three months of chemotherapy, the pancreatic adenocarcinoma's size was reduced, but liver and bone metastases occurred. The patient eventually died eight months later.

Discharge Diagnosis: Invasive pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient was discharged after receiving appropriate treatment and care. The patient should follow up with their primary care physician and oncologist for further management and evaluation of the invasive pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. The primary care physician should ensure that the patient receives an appropriate follow-up plan, including regular check-ups, diagnostic imaging, and laboratory testing. The patient should be advised to take care of his health and manage their diet and exercise regularly. In case of any emergency, the patient should immediately contact a healthcare provider.

Patient Name: [Name]
MRN: [Medical Record Number]

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient, a 29-year-old male of Asian Indian origin, presented with a viral upper respiratory infection (URI) characterized by nasal discharge, mild nasal and sinus congestion, general myalgia, and low-grade fever. A clinical diagnosis of viral URI was made and was treated with over-the-counter (OTC) acetaminophen-nasal decongestant formulations. The patient had a similar episode of viral URI approximately two months ago, which was treated with similar medications at a different outpatient clinic.

Subsequent follow-up visits revealed transient non-mucoid rhinorrhea and the observed compulsive habit of removing nasal hair follicles using metal instruments. The patient had nasal tenderness, inflammation, and an enlarged and stenotic nare on the left side. The patient had an intact sensorium with no significant issues regarding his decision-making capacity, understanding, mood, or memory. A psychiatric evaluation identified this patient to have a generalized body-focused repetitive behavior (BFRB) disorder.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:
The patient was discharged with a diagnosis of rhinotillexomania, a condition characterized by a compulsive habit of removing nasal hair follicles. The patient received a trial of behavioral therapy, which included regular nail trimming, continuous hand hygiene, and aversion conditioning. The patient voluntarily accepted aversion therapy and regularly dipped his second and third digits in malodorous oil to produce a strong aversion response to his nasal habit. Regular digital nail trimming with sufficient hand hygiene also reduced the risk of any intranasal lacerations and its resulting infection. 

The patient declined any need for surgical correction of the stenosis. The prognosis was improved based on the ego-dystonic nature of this case, where the patient recognized the abnormal pattern as unhealthy. The patient reported a nearly complete cessation of both morning rhinorrhea episodes as well as nasal digital exploration episodes after three months of behavioral modification therapy.  

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:
- Rhinotillexomania

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:
- None

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient was advised to follow up with the primary care provider as needed. 

DISCHARGE CONDITION:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with improved symptoms. 

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
- Continue behavioral therapy regimen and aversion conditioning
- Maintain regular nail trimming and hand hygiene
- Avoid repetitive episodes of nasal hair removal
- Follow up with the primary care provider as needed

Discharge Diagnosis: End-stage Congestive Heart Failure, Right-Sided IE, Sepsis

Hospital Course:
A 68-year-old Taiwanese man was admitted for a second time to our hospital for worsening symptoms of dyspnea and low back pain. During his first admission, the patient was diagnosed with OSSA bacteremia, and a sternal fracture with a closed perifocal hematoma was found. On the second admission, a physical examination revealed the presence of bilateral crackles, a right-side wheeze on chest auscultation, and a palpable fluctuant, non-tender mass over the anterior chest wall. Laboratory data showed severe metabolic acidosis, and computed tomography revealed a hypodense lesion with a peripherally enhanced wall and bone involvement in the sternal region and multiple septic emboli lesions in the bilateral lung fields. Additionally, there was a paraspinal hypodense lesion with a peripherally enhanced wall and air-trapping over the T11 level. Percutaneous drainage from the T11-T12 paraspinal space was done on day 2, and only minimal pus-like fluid was obtained for culture. Because of the septic pulmonary emboli, TEE was arranged, and it showed an oscillating mass over the anterior and septal leaflets of the tricuspid valve and moderate tricuspid regurgitation.

The patient was promptly treated with intravenous antibiotic agents (piperacillin and levofloxacin), but his hemodynamic status and oxygen saturation rapidly deteriorated during observation. Cardiovascular and chest surgeons were consulted immediately for emergency surgical intervention, but the family did not wish to pursue aggressive interventions.

The patient was transitioned to comfort care, and he eventually expired on day 4. The diagnosis was right-sided IE complicated with sternal abscesses, septic pulmonary emboli, and lumbar spondylodiscitis.

Discharge Instructions:
The patient has passed away, and no further follow-up is required. Please contact the family to provide support during their time of grief.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]                 Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient was a 61-year-old woman who presented with bilateral breast masses detected on routine mammography screening. A core biopsy demonstrated that the masses were invasive ductal carcinoma. The right-side mass was ER+, PR low and HER2/neu+, while the left mass was triple-negative. CT scan revealed bilateral breast malignancies, a suspected left internal mammary lymph node metastasis, and borderline left axillary lymph nodes. Bone scan showed lytic bone metastases in the pelvis, right acetabular roof, sacrum and right supra-acetabular areas. The patient received weekly paclitaxel, Herceptin and Pamidronate as initial therapy, but after 6 months, the disease progressed in the breast, liver and bone. Subsequently, several regimens were tried without success, including Vinorelbine plus Herceptin, Lapatinib plus Capecitabine, and weekly doxorubicin plus paclitaxel. To manage the progression, radiation therapy (RT) was initiated on the left breast, supraclavicular area and internal mammary chain (IMC) using a standard 4-field technique and an electron patch for the IMC. However, the patient developed disease progression in the right lung and liver, resulting in stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) being administered to the lung. Three months later, the patient demonstrated signs of progression in the left supraclavicular area with axillary and subpectoral lymph nodes. After radiotherapy to these areas, the patient received two cycles of Eribulin. She developed a skin rash consistent with RR reaction, prompting the discontinuation of the medication. After a re-challenge with Eribulin, the patient experienced a severe skin recall reaction in the left chest wall and supraclavicular area. The patient was given steroids, cetrazine hydrochloride and ranitidine, but unfortunately, she progressed with multiple brain and right neck metastases. Palliative RT was administered to the brain and right neck metastases before the patient was discharged.

Hospital Course Summary:
The 61-year-old female patient with bilateral breast masses was treated with weekly paclitaxel, Herceptin and Pamidronate during her stay in the hospital. Various therapy regimens were tried, including Vinorelbine plus Herceptin, Lapatinib plus Capecitabine, and weekly doxorubicin plus paclitaxel but were unsuccessful. The patient subsequently underwent multiple radiation therapies along with stereotactic body radiotherapy. She was given two cycles of Eribulin, which caused a RR reaction that worsened when she was re-challenged with Eribulin. The patient eventually developed multiple brain and right neck metastases, prompting the administration of palliative RT. The patient was discharged from the hospital following these procedures.

Hospital Course:

A 10-year-old male was admitted for conventional root canal treatment to treat the right maxillary lateral incisor due to positive responses to percussion and palpation in the apical region. Radiographic examination revealed dens invaginatus type III associated with periradicular lesion. The procedure was performed under local anesthesia and absolute isolation. Both primary and secondary canals were necrotic pulp. Root canal treatment was performed using step-back technique and Gates-Glidden drills. The final irrigation of both canals was carried out with 17% ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, followed by obturation with gutta-percha cones and Sealapex sealer cement. Calcium hydroxide was used as an intra-canal medication. The access cavity was restored with a light-cured composite resin. The patient returned for a second visit for the removal of the calcium hydroxide and the tooth was asymptomatic. Clinical and radiographic control sessions were carried out at 6, 12, and 18 months after treatment. During the follow-up period, no signs and symptoms related to the respected tooth were reported by the patient. Bone neoformation was noticed in the periapical area. A cone beam computed tomography 6-years after root canal treatment showed no further complications.

Hospital Course: The 11-month-old previously healthy female patient was admitted to the pediatric emergency room due to fever and vomiting 6-8 hours after receiving the second dose of the 4CMenB vaccine on the left lateral thigh. She had received prophylactic paracetamol before the vaccination. Physical examination showed irritability and tachycardia with good perfusion. The patient's heart rate was over 200 per minute at rest without any cardiac murmur or additional heart sounds. Laboratory workup revealed normal results for hemoglobin, white blood cell count, platelet count, CRP, and procalcitonin, respectively. Influenza A and B, respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus nasopharyngeal swab antigen assays, and streptococcal pharyngeal swab antigen test were all negative. Plasma glucose and other biochemistry values were normal but the creatinine kinase-MB was elevated.

Medical Management: After verifying SVT with narrow QRS complex without p waves, vagal stimulatory maneuvers were applied but the heart rate did not normalize. Rapid adenosine infusion protocol with 100 μg/kg was injected via a large antecubital venous catheter. The SVT did not reverse after the first adenosine injection. Then, second, third, and fourth adenosine injections were given with dosage increment to a maximum dose of adenosine (350 μg/kg, total 3000 μg). The patient's heart rate was converted to normal sinus rhythm after infusion of the fourth dose of adenosine, total of 2 hours of arrival. Maintenance treatment was then started using oral propranolol (3 mg/kg/day, every 8 hours).

Echocardiography: Echocardiography revealed normal cardiac anatomy with slightly decreased left ventricle function (EF: 48%) during SVT, which normalized after two days.

Follow-up: The patient was followed for 3 months and no recurrence of SVT was detected.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Chief Complaint:
Substernal chest pain radiating to the right shoulder

History of Present Illness:
The patient, a 52-year-old male with a medical history of Evan’s syndrome, hypertension, beta-thalassemia, and situs inversus, presented to the emergency department with substernal chest pain radiating to the right shoulder that woke him up from sleep. The chest pain was intermittent and crushing and lasted for two days.

Physical Examination:
On physical examination, the patient had a heart rate of 138 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 141/96 mmHg.

Diagnostic Results:
Initial 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) showed poor R-wave progression and flat T-waves in precordial leads and ST-elevation in inferior leads. A right-sided 12-lead ECG was obtained subsequently, which showed ST elevations in V4R, V5R, V6R, III, and aVF suggestive of inferior-lateral ischemia.

Hospital Course:
The patient was treated with aspirin, heparin, and ticagrelor, and was taken to the cardiac catheterization lab. The patient was found to have an occluded right coronary artery and underwent right coronary artery stenting for obstructive disease. The right-sided 12-lead ECG was essential in detecting lateral ischemia in this patient with dextrocardia.

Summary:
The patient, with a history of hypertension, Evan’s syndrome, beta-thalassemia, and situs inversus, presented to the emergency department with two days of substernal chest pain radiating to the right shoulder. He was diagnosed with inferior-lateral ischemia based on a right-sided 12-lead ECG, showing ST elevations in V4R, V5R, V6R, III, and aVF. The patient underwent right coronary artery stenting in the cardiac catheterization lab. He was treated with aspirin, heparin, and ticagrelor.

Admitting Diagnosis: Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) 

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our institution with epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and pain located around the lumbar area lasting for one week. Clinical examination did not reveal any palpable abdominal masses or abdominal tenderness. Blood tests displayed hypercalcemia and parathyroid hormone level. An ultrasound was performed afterward, which did not reveal any thyroid or parathyroid abnormalities. Additional scans detected an ectopic adenoma located in the lower anterior mediastinum after which a mid-sternal thoracotomy was scheduled. A drainage was placed into the left side of the thoracic cavity, and the patient was discharged post 5th day when the drainage was finally removed. 

Diagnosis and Treatment:
The mass was identified as an ectopic parathyroid adenoma which was composed predominantly of oxyphil cells arranged in an acinar pattern. Serum calcium levels and iPTH remained normal after the 6 months follow-up.

The patient was advised to follow a proper diet and exercise regularly for general health and well-being. No further appointments were scheduled.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: Mar 2013
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the nephrology department in Mar 2013 due to four years of recurrent acute pyelonephritis. She had impaired renal function, hypocalcemia, and renal parenchymal stones with bilateral nephrocalcinosis. During the subsequent three years of follow-up, she had six attacks of acute urinary tract infection (UTI). A genetic test was performed to exclude the possibilities of comorbid diseases or potential mutations of other genes that could affect the renal reabsorption of calcium and magnesium. The test revealed a homozygous mutation in CLDN16 gene, which leads to Familial Hypomagnesemia with Hypercalciuria and Nephrocalcinosis (FHHNC). The patient had a family history of this genetic disease, and four of her unaffected family members also carried a heterozygous mutation in the same gene. Unfortunately, the patient developed end-stage renal disease (ESRD) at the age of 36, and the gradient of GFR decline was calculated to be 4.3 ml/min per 1.73 m2/yr during the follow-up.

Diagnosis:
The patient had Familial Hypomagnesemia with Hypercalciuria and Nephrocalcinosis (FHHNC).

Treatment:
Calcitriol and calcium were used in the treatment, but the effect on serum calcium was limited. Treatment with magnesium was not feasible. During the follow-up, the patient had undergone six attacks of acute UTI.

Conditions on Discharge:
The patient was discharged with end-stage renal disease due to FHHNC at the age of 36. During the follow-up, the gradient of GFR decline was calculated to be 4.3 ml/min per 1.73 m2/yr.

Follow-up Instructions:
The patient should be monitored for the progression of the FHHNC. A regular renal function evaluation should be performed to ensure the condition's stability. The patient should seek medical attention if any symptoms related to urinary tract infections appear. The patient should also consult a genetic counselor to discuss the possibility of passing the gene mutation to offspring.

Patient Name: N/A

Date of Admission: N/A

Hospital Course:

The patient is a 55-year-old female with no significant medical history, who was admitted due to a dry cough for one month, decreased exercise tolerance, and dyspnea on exertion, associated with bilateral pleuritic chest pain. She was admitted with vital signs that were within normal limits, and a pulmonary exam revealed bibasilar “Velcro-like” dry inspiratory crackles. A chest radiograph showed bibasilar airspace infiltrates more pronounced on the left.

Initial laboratory tests revealed microcytic anemia, elevated C-reactive protein level, and an elevated creatine kinase level. The patient received treatment for community acquired pneumonia with no significant improvement.

A rheumatology workup was ordered due to the patient's age, gender, and radiological findings suspicious for ILD. This revealed positive results for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, cyclic citrullinated peptide, and anti-Jo-1 antibody. A subsequent right quadriceps muscle biopsy revealed active, mild myopathy with focal subtle endomysial fibrosis suggestive of an immune-mediated etiology.

The patient was ultimately diagnosed with antisynthetase syndrome presenting primarily with ILD, and started on intravenous pulse dose steroids along with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), which resulted in significant improvement in her clinical symptoms. The patient was discharged home on tapering steroids, MMF, and oxygen supplementation with close follow up. 

The patient was treated outpatient with rituximab, which allowed her to be weaned off oxygen supplementation and eventually regain her baseline level of activity. A follow-up computed tomography of the chest showed interval decrease in her bibasilar infiltrates.

After 5 months of treatment, there was an improvement in pulmonary function tests. Her diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide and forced vital capacity significantly improved.

Discharge Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with antisynthetase syndrome presenting primarily with ILD.

Treatment:

The patient was treated with intravenous pulse dose steroids, mycophenolate mofetil, and rituximab.

Follow-Up:

The patient was discharged home with oxygen supplementation and scheduled for close follow-up.

Impression:

The patient was successfully treated for antisynthetase syndrome presenting primarily with ILD, and her clinical symptoms significantly improved after receiving intravenous pulse dose steroids, mycophenolate mofetil, and rituximab.

The patient was admitted to the pediatric urology department of Saint-Petersburg State Pediatric Medical University in August 2017 with complaints of continuous wetting and recurrent urinary tract infection (UTI). Prenatal ultrasound revealed left pelvi-ureteric dilation, and subsequent examination at 1 year 5 months revealed a ureterocele and complete left kidney duplication.

Further investigation revealed that the left kidney consisted of three moieties with megaureter of the upper moiety and rounded contrast defect in the bladder - ectopic ureterocele. In September 2017, cystoscopy and laser dissection of ureterocele were performed, and a new formed upper moiety ureteral orifice was able to discharge urine without stenosis or inflammation.

Subsequent investigations over the course of 7 months indicated that urinary incontinence decreased significantly, and ultrasounds revealed much smaller dilation of the upper moiety pelvi-ureteric system and 5 mm in diameter residual cavity of ureterocele in the bladder. Grade of VUR decreased from IV to I. The investigations 1 year 6 months after surgery demonstrated good results, with no complaints for UTI symptoms, uncomplicated voiding, and decreased parenchymal mass of the upper moiety but improvement of absorption and transport function.

PLAN:

The patient's treatment was successful, and examination is planned in 3 years to confirm the persistence of successful outcome of treatment.

Hospital Course:
A 40-year-old African American multiparous woman with known chronic hypertension was admitted to the hospital at 21 weeks' 4-day gestation due to hypertensive emergency. She had a marked increase in blood pressure and laboratory evaluation notable for hemoglobin, platelet count, alanine transaminase (ALT), aspartate transaminase (AST), and creatinine. The patient was transferred from another medical center to our medical center for management of hypertensive emergency. Protein, blood, and nitrites were detected in the urine dipstick and urine drug screen was positive for methamphetamines and marijuana. On arrival, blood pressure peaked at 205/114 mmHg, and laboratory findings were similar to those noted above. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level was elevated and haptoglobin was low with schistocytes detected in the peripheral smear. Urine protein/creatinine ratio was high, and the estimated fetal weight by ultrasound was appropriate for gestational age. Following severe preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome, termination of pregnancy was recommended and agreed upon by the patient. Magnesium sulfate was initiated for seizure prophylaxis, and the patient was managed in the intensive care unit with an intravenous nicardipine drip. Within 12 hours of misoprostol induction of labor, she had a vaginal delivery of a nonviable female neonate. Post-delivery, severe hypertension persisted despite triple-agent antihypertensive therapy. The patient was discharged home on an oral regimen of chlorthalidone, amlodipine, and telmisartan.

Diagnosis:
Following delivery, thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) persisted. Laboratory findings showed clinical features of hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia. Due to the persisting hypertension, the diagnosis of HELLP syndrome was questioned. The patient was screened for alternative TMA etiologies including aHUS, TTP, and vitamin B12 deficiency. TTP was less likely as ADAMTS13 activity was 75% (normal >67%). Meanwhile, vitamin B12 level was undetectable <146 ρg/ml (normal 213-816 ρg/ml), with intrinsic factor blocking antibodies being positive, consistent with pernicious anemia. Other causes of anemia were ruled out with normal iron panel, hemoglobin electrophoresis, and folate level.

Treatment Plan:
Following the diagnosis of pernicious anemia, the patient was started on subcutaneous B12 injections at a dose of 1000 mcg daily. During postpartum hospitalization, the patient received 5 injections of vitamin B12. The patient was discharged home with a plan for continued B12 supplementation and close outpatient follow-up.

Follow-up:
At 2 weeks postpartum, the patient had normal blood pressure and was clinically well, but declined additional laboratory testing. The patient was advised to follow up with her primary care physician and obstetrician for continued management of chronic hypertension and pernicious anemia with necessary monitoring. The patient was also advised on appropriate lifestyle modification measures to prevent hypertension exacerbation and to maintain the nutritional requirements for improving pernicious anemia.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient, a 72-year-old male with a past medical history significant for CLL, was admitted to the hospital after presenting to the emergency department with headache and seizure-like activity. The patient's initial workup including CT of the head, EEG evaluation, CHEST, ABDOMEN, AND PELVIS CT, and infectious workup with blood culture, urine culture, quantiferon-TB, histoplasma, blastomyces, influenza, RPR screen, and HIV were all negative. However, a lumbar puncture revealed cerebrospinal fluid with elevated WBC and protein levels, indicative of a neurological issue. The patient was started on anticonvulsants and transferred to our institution for further workup and management.

Over the course of his hospitalization, the patient's neurological status continued to decline despite treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics and antivirals. A repeat CT of the head showed hydrocephalus, and an external ventricular drain was placed, but there was no improvement in the patient's status. Ultimately, the patient expired within two weeks after he presented with the neurologic symptoms after support was withdrawn per family request.

Autopsy of the brain showed diffuse cerebral edema with right-sided predominance on gross findings. There were multiple areas of hemorrhagic necrosis including the bilateral frontal lobe, right parasagittal posterior frontal lobe, left temporal lobe, bilateral medial occipital lobe, and paraventricular areas. Microscopic findings revealed parenchymal necrosis with mixed inflammation, amebic trophozoites, and occasional cysts. This mixed infiltrate was seen involving the meninges. The amebas were prominent around vessels, and occasional multinucleated giant cells were seen. The autopsy brain was sent to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and immunohistochemical stains were performed, which identified Acanthamoeba species with no evidence of Naegleria fowleri. His final diagnosis based on autopsy was necrotizing meningoencephalitis with morphologic and immunohistochemical evidence of Acanthamoeba species.

Recommendations:
The patient's family was advised of the autopsy findings and advised to seek appropriate medical follow-up, considering their risk factors for the same. This discharge summary was dictated and reviewed with the patient's family. They were advised to follow up with their primary care physician and neurologist for any further care, and not to hesitate to seek urgent medical attention if the patient experienced any unusual symptoms. The family was given the contact information for emergency and urgent care facilities in the patient's vicinity. The patient's condition at the time of discharge was deceased.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 69-year-old male, presented to the clinic with pain, swelling in the bilateral groin, and frequent voiding, which were resolved postoperatively. CT scan findings confirm the recurrent bilateral bladder hernia after undergoing bilateral transabdominal preperitoneal repair (B-TAPP) three years earlier at another hospital. Hence, the patient underwent median transabdominal preperitoneal patch (TAPP) repair with bladder takedown.

Procedure:

Under general anesthesia, the patient underwent median TAPP repair with bladder takedown approach. A laparoscopic self-fixating mesh was successfully introduced to the peritoneal cavity and fixed with Cooper's ligament and the rectus sheath by a mesh fixation device. The urinary bladder was sutured with the ventral peritoneum to close the preperitoneal space and to screen the mesh using a barbed suture device.

Outcome:

The patient was discharged three days after the procedure with no complications, and his preoperative symptoms disappeared. The postoperative CT scan showed no recurrence of the bilateral supravesical bladder hernias.

Plan:

The patient will have a follow-up appointment in a month to monitor their healing progress.

Hospital Course Summary:

Patient Information: A 12-year-old female was evaluated for possible meningitis after travel to the Philippines in September 2017. The patient was also noted to have infected insect bites on her lower extremities, and wound cultures grew a coryneform isolate. The onset of cutaneous diphtheria was later diagnosed.

Assessment and Plan:
The patient received medical care and was given a prophylactic course of erythromycin. Swabs from 11 asymptomatic contacts were obtained before the prophylactic course; all cultures were negative. Nose and throat swabs were not collected from five contacts who had already started antibiotics prophylaxis. Four unvaccinated close contacts received diphtheria toxoid-contain vaccines. The patient and 12 contacts were up-to-date for diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccine and did not require additional doses. No further treatment was deemed necessary.

Impression:
The patient was diagnosed with cutaneous diphtheria, which was likely acquired during the travel to the Philippines. The patient and her contacts received appropriate prophylactic treatment and vaccination, thus preventing further spread of the disease. The patient was discharged with no further follow-up needed.
