Hospital Course:
The patient, an 81-year-old male with an unremarkable medical history, was admitted to our department on [Redacted] with complaints of increasing dysphagia and dysphonia. Physical examination revealed a solid, painless, mobile mass extending to the right and central areas of the neck. Ultrasound and CT scan confirmed a giant, heterogeneous, and hypodense mass (95×72×145mm) extending from the hyoid bone to the retrosternal area with compression, narrowing, and left displacement of larynx and trachea.

The patient underwent fine needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) that was inconclusive, and a core needle biopsy was performed with a suspicion of a solitary fibrous tumor. Consequently, a surgical excision of the tumor was performed. The patient underwent the procedure without any complications, and the tumor was macroscopically removed while preserving the thyroid gland.

Postoperative histopathological and immunohistochemical analysis revealed a final diagnosis of fibrosarcoma (G2: moderately differentiated). The spindle cell areas were focally immunoreactive to CD34, BCL2, and CD99. However, they had no reactivity to CK, desmin, S-100, STAT6, CD31, TTF-1, AE1/AE3, EMA, and HMB-45. In the head and neck, oncological multidisciplinary team complementary treatment with radiotherapy was decided although the patient refused it.

Follow-up: 
After one year follow-up, there were no clinical or radiological signs of recurrence.

Discharge Diagnosis: Fibrosarcoma (G2) of cervical region

The patient is advised to continue follow-up with their primary care physician.

Brief Hospital Course: A nine-day-old male newborn was admitted to the hospital due to fever and poor general condition. He was diagnosed with SARS-CoV-2 at admission and developed respiratory failure and diarrhea with enterorrhagia, which led to PICU admission. He was supported with noninvasive ventilation and treated with antibiotic wide coverage. In the subsequent three days, his neurological condition deteriorated with impaired consciousness and pathological spontaneous motricity, leading to intubation and mechanical ventilation. The chest radiograph and CT scan showed a picture of bilateral interstitial pneumonia with an extensive area of atelectasis in the basal site. 

Diagnostic and Therapeutic Procedures: Nasopharyngeal swabs and bronchoalveolar lavage were performed to assess the SARS-CoV-2 viral load. SARS-CoV-2 variant determination was performed by SNP detection approach, suggesting VOC 202012/01 Lineage B.1.1.7 variant. Anti-SARS-CoV-2 hyperimmune plasma and medications like dexamethasone and remdesivir were administered. A lumbar puncture was performed, and the metabolic test on blood and liquor were normal. Immunological screening showed no abnormalities. The EEG showed hypovolted brain electrical activity with a discontinuous pattern. The cerebral CT scan was normal, but the brain MRI showed deep medullary vein thrombosis associated with cytotoxic edema in the deep periventricular white matter, which was treated with enoxaparin. Extended thrombophilic screening including homocysteine, anticardiolipin antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, anti-beta-2-glycoprotein antibodies, protein S, protein C, activated protein C resistance, lupus anticoagulant, factor XIII, von Willebrand factor antigen, Factor V Leyden mutation, factor II prothrombin mutation, and MTHFR mutation were normal. 

Condition at Discharge: The patient's condition progressively improved, and after 13 days, he was extubated and in four more days became oxygen independent. At the five-month follow-up visit, the baby was doing well, without any clinical problems. The T1-weighted MRI showed significant reduction in linear hyperintense lesions, normal intensity of periventricular white matter, and enlargement of lateral ventricles. 

Discharge Medications: Not Applicable

Follow-Up Plan: The patient was discharged from the hospital after 42 days with detailed instructions for close follow-up with his healthcare provider.

Small bowel strangulated hernia through vaginal cuff.

The patient's condition on discharge improved, and she was advised to follow up with her surgeon for further evaluation and management.

The patient was advised to avoid any physical activity or lifting heavy objects for several weeks and follow up with her surgeon as scheduled.

None.

Not applicable.

The 25-year-old female patient presented to the outpatient medicine department with a one-month history of dry cough that was provisionally diagnosed as upper respiratory tract infection. She had shortness of breath during cold seasons suggestive of bronchial asthma. No significant past medical or surgical history was identified. On examination, she was noted to be ill-looking with mild tachypnea and had cardiomegaly with RV type apex and dilated main pulmonary artery segment on chest X-ray. The echocardiogram demonstrated severe mitral stenosis with ASD secundum. The patient was treated with rheumatic heart disease prophylaxis and a low dose of diuretics along with treatment for her presenting ailment.

Discharge Summary:

The patient has been discharged from our care with a diagnosis of severe mitral stenosis with ASD secundum. Our medical team has provided her with appropriate treatment, counseling, and referred her to a tertiary level hospital with all the required facilities for further evaluation and treatment. She underwent mitral valve replacement with metallic prosthetic valve and patch closure of ASD at a higher center. The patient had occasional shortness of breath, which she thought might be due to bronchial asthma. However, our examination revealed it to be due to her severe mitral stenosis and ASD secundum.

Our findings indicated a hugely dilated right atrium and right ventricle with restricted opening of the mitral valve. The patient had a mean pressure gradient across the MV of 5mmHg with an MVA of 3.77cm2. Furthermore, the left atrial diameter in the M-mode echo was 32.73mm. The ECG showed right bundle branch block with right-axis deviation.

Continuous waveform Doppler across the tricuspid valve revealed a maximum velocity of 3.65m/s. Measured PASP according to the Bernoulli equation was 53.31 + 5 mm Hg = 58.31 mmHg. Our findings also revealed the presence of an atrial septal defect measuring 17.38mm in the apical 4 chamber view and 13.43mm in the subcostal view. The right ventricle was dilated with a diameter of 55–60mm at the base in the A4CV. However, all rims of ASD were adequate (more than 5mm).

As the patient presented with severe mitral stenosis and ASD secundum, it warranted immediate intervention to prevent the rising pulmonary artery pressure by increased flow through the right-sided heart. The patient had undergone surgical repair as experience regarding percutaneous treatment is inadequate in our centers. 

In conclusion, our medical team provided appropriate care and counseling to the patient, and the patient underwent mitral valve replacement with metallic prosthetic valve and patch closure of ASD at a higher center. She will require follow-up appointments and appropriate cardiological interventions in the future, as deemed necessary by her care team.

Hospital Course:
The patient is a 12-year-old boy who presented with a metaphyseal mass of the right humerus. A core biopsy was performed which revealed a bland spindle-cell proliferation with few osteoclast-type giant cells and focal siderin depositions. It was inconclusive whether this mass was an aneurysmal bone cyst. Further testing with USP6 FISH was performed. Additionally, NGS revealed that both the core biopsy and subsequent curettage showed FUS-NFATC2 fusion. Also, FUS FISH was performed for verification which showed the classical break-apart pattern without amplification. The MIB1 staining for the lesional tissue indicated levels below 5%. The immunohistochemistry studies showed diffuse expression of EMA and CD99, but negativity for SMA, desmin, S100, CD34, and synaptophysin. The patient underwent a curettage which did not show that there was a high-grade tumor. Upon follow-up MRI at 8 months, there was no evidence of recurrent tumor.

Admitting Diagnosis: Secondary hyperparathyroidism (SHPT)

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with a 2-year history of progressively aggravating bone pain, and the diagnosis of SHPT was established. Preoperatively, her i-PTH level was >2500 pg/mL, ionized calcium level was 3.05 mmol/L and serum phosphate level was 1.75 mmol/L. The 99mTc-MIBI three-phase imaging confirmed the presence of bilateral, irregular masses under the thyroid lobes on the 15- and 120-minute images.

The patient underwent parathyroidectomy (removal of all three enlarged parathyroid glands) and parathyroid serum transplantation. Postoperatively, the patient's symptoms of bone pain had significantly alleviated, and her i-PTH levels decreased to 116 pg/mL, 51 pg/mL and 27.4 pg/mL at 30 and 60 minutes and 24 hours after surgery, respectively. Her serum phosphate level gradually dropped to the normal range, but symptomatic hypocalcaemia increased postoperatively. The patient was discharged from the hospital 7 days after the operation.

The patient developed bone pain on the 10th day after surgery and was closely monitored for her hormone levels and clinical symptoms. Analgesic treatment was initiated, and the patient appeared well. On the 17th day after surgery, her i-PTH level dropped below 300 pg/mL, and the symptoms of bone pain markedly reduced. At the 3-month follow-up, there were no significant complications.

The patient is recommended to schedule regular follow-up appointments with her healthcare provider.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 71-year-old female with reported history of dementia and depression

Hospital Course:

The patient was brought in for refusal to eat, walk, or talk by her family who stated her history of hospital visits and diagnosis of dementia. She was on carbidopa-levodopa, memantine, quetiapine, selegiline, and sertraline, but her primary care physician was not provided. Upon arrival, she had hypothermia and bradycardia with low oxygen saturation, and her physical examination revealed cachexia and hair loss. She was treated with vasopressors, intubated for airway protection, and transferred to the Medical Intensive Care Unit for further evaluation. Her laboratory workup was significant for low blood cell counts and elevated CK levels, but there was no evidence of hemorrhage or infectious process. A CT scan and MRI revealed ischemic infarctions involving various cerebral arteries. 

The patient's family opted not to have her undergo bone marrow biopsy, but a peripheral blood smear and flow cytometry showed no abnormalities. The patient was treated with normal saline, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, hydrocortisone, and intravenous levothyroxine. Her white blood cell count and platelets improved with levothyroxine, and she received 2 units of packed red blood cells for a sudden decline in hemoglobin. Although her Hb improved after transfusion, the patient did not recover consciousness and expired after 32 days as an inpatient.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Ischemic infarctions involving various cerebral arteries, hypothyroidism

Hospital Course:

The patient was treated with normal saline, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, hydrocortisone, and intravenous levothyroxine for ischemic infarctions involving various cerebral arteries and hypothyroidism. Her white blood cell count and platelets improved with levothyroxine, and she received 2 units of packed red blood cells for a sudden decline in hemoglobin. Although her Hb improved after transfusion, the patient did not recover consciousness and expired after 32 days as an inpatient. 

Discharge Condition:

The patient expired.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:

The patient is a 55-year-old male who presented with anemia and was diagnosed with right colon cancer in February 2018. He underwent laparoscopic right colon resection and was diagnosed with PT3N0M0 with 0/16 positive nodes and perineural invasion. In June 2018, he presented with problems with digestion and pain after eating, and his CEA had increased to 940 ng/ml. Repeat CT scan showed multiple nodules within the greater omentum compatible with peritoneal metastases. In July 2018, the patient underwent exploratory laparotomy and HIPEC-melphalan treatment. The resection was judged to be a palliative effort.

Hospital Course:

The patient underwent laparoscopic right colon resection in February 2018, with a successful removal of the tumor. However, peritoneal metastases were discovered in June 2018, which required exploratory laparotomy and HIPEC-melphalan treatment in July 2018. During the exploration, the posterior surface of the liver was layered by cancer, and the undersurface of the right hemidiaphragm was covered by tumor nodules. The old ileocolic anastomosis was involved and needed to be resected, and the umbilical port site was infiltrated by cancer. Near complete resection was possible by cytoreductive surgery.

Clinical Findings:

On histopathologic examination, the tumor was moderately to poorly differentiated, and the cancer was moderately to poorly differentiated compatible with the primary tumor in all tissues submitted. The peritoneal cancer index was 28, and the CC score was 2.

Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with right colon cancer and peritoneal metastases.

Treatment/Care Plan:

The patient underwent laparoscopic right colon resection and was diagnosed with PT3N0M0 with 0/16 positive nodes and perineural invasion. Systemic chemotherapy was not recommended. In June 2018, the patient presented with peritoneal metastases, which required exploratory laparotomy and HIPEC-melphalan treatment in July 2018. Near complete resection was possible by cytoreductive surgery. The resection was judged to be a palliative effort, and the major goal was to relieve intestinal obstruction and to prepare the patient for rapid initiation of palliative systemic chemotherapy. Follow-up care will be provided by the medical team.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient presented with cardiogenic shock following an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and was successfully resuscitated. Emergency coronary angioplasty was performed, and the patient was admitted to the intensive care unit. Antiplatelet therapy was started while the patient was placed on veno-arterial extracorporeal life support (VA-ECLS) due to tachyarrhythmia-related cardiovascular compromise. In response to acute onset pulmonary edema, a LAVD (Impella 5.0) was placed. Subsequently, the patient developed a right cerebellar infarct, diagnosed through a CT scan. Impella 5.0 was then replaced by a centrifugal continuous-flow ventricular assist device (HVAD). However, the patient developed neurological deficits suggestive of IS (left hemiparesis) seven hours after waking up from anesthesia. Emergency DHC was performed after a complete right sylvian IS with significant mass effect was revealed by a CT scan. Post-surgery, the patient's condition gradually improved, and he was ultimately transferred to a rehabilitation center. The patient underwent HT and cranioplasty five months and one month post-DHC, respectively, without any complications.

Cardiogenic shock, tachyarrhythmia-related cardiovascular compromise, pulmonary edema, right cerebellar infarct, IS, left hemiparesis.

None

PROCEDURES:
Emergency coronary angioplasty, LAVD placement, HVAD placement, emergency DHC, HT, cranioplasty.

None specified.

DISCHARGE DISPOSITION:
Transfer to a multidisciplinary rehabilitation center.

Diagnosis: Gunshot wound to the right lower extremity.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 16-year-old male, was admitted to our institution with a gunshot wound to the right lower extremity. On physical examination, two bullet entry points were seen at the right popliteal fossa and dorsal soft tissues of the distal right leg. Initial radiographs were normal, but a Computed Tomography Angiography (CTA) showed a retained bullet fragment, an 8 mm soft tissue density, and a 10 cm occlusion of the peroneal artery. An angiogram was done, which showed an abrupt cutoff of the popliteal artery adjacent to the bullet fragment. Repeating the angiogram with the patient's right leg in a different position demonstrated mild short segment narrowing of the popliteal artery.

Treatment:
The patient was subsequently taken to the operating room for exploration and removal of the bullet fragment. An intraoperative angiogram was normal, and the anterior and posterior tibial arteries were patent without any evidence of injury or flow-limiting stenosis.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with instructions to take rest and follow-up with outpatient physical therapy for wound care.

Follow-up Plans:
The patient will follow up with an orthopedic surgeon and an interventional radiologist for evaluation and ongoing management of the injury.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with decreased visual acuity, redness, and discharge in his right eye. After taking an epithelial scraping and sending it to the laboratory for culture, empirical antibiotherapy was initiated along with topical colistin. The patient was closely monitored for ocular tolerance and toxicity, as well as for any signs of nephrotoxicity. After one month of treatment, complete resolution of the keratitis with residual scarring was noticed. Penetrating keratoplasty was performed after five months of presentation. The patient's best-corrected visual acuity remained stable during follow-up with no recurrence of infection.

The patient presented with severe hypopyon and an extensive corneal ulcer with surrounding infiltrate, which was identified as MDR P. aeruginosa keratitis.

Empirical antibiotherapy with fortified topical antibiotics (vancomycin 50 mg/mL, ceftazidime 50 mg/mL hourly) was initiated, and topical colistin was started after microbiological evaluation identified the causative agent to be MDR P. aeruginosa. Dosing of the topical colistin was tapered over time.

Follow-Up:
The patient was discharged with instructions to follow-up with the treating physician to continue monitoring his visual acuity and ocular tolerance.

Patient Information:

Discharge Date: [Discharge Date]
Admission Diagnosis: Granulomatous thyroiditis
Discharge Diagnosis: Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH)

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our establishment with complaints of polyuropolydipsic syndrome and a one-year history of amenorrhea-galactorrhea. The physical examination was normal except for bilateral galactorrhea. The water deprivation test results were in favor of central diabetes insipidus (DI). The hormonal tests revealed pan-hypopituitarism, with a very low Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) level and Luteinizing hormone (LH) level below the reference range. An inappropriate Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) level suggested secondary adrenal insufficiency. The patient was given hormone replacement therapy including desmopressin acetate, oral hydrocortisone, and levothyroxine for this condition.

Eight months later, the patient presented with a left retroauricular bone pain and preauricular and submandibular lymphadenopathies, along with dental pain and tooth mobility. The facial and temporal bones CT-scan revealed a lytic lesion of the horizontal branch of the right mandible and a significant lytic lesion of the left petrous bone, which strongly indicated LCH. Immunohistochemistry study revealed a strong positivity of histiocytes for the CD1 antigen and the S100 protein.

The extension assessment of the disease included a thoracic CT-scan that revealed peripheral pulmonary micronodules, some of which were excavated. The treatment consisted of a chemotherapy combining vinblastine and prednisone. After four months of treatment, favorable evolution was noted, with a clear relief of headache, disappearance of the left retroauricular pain and complete regression of the lytic lesion.

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with a diagnosis of LCH after successful chemotherapy treatment. The patient still required the same doses of pituitary hormones replacement therapy.

Follow-up Instructions:
The patient should follow up with an endocrinologist and oncologist for regular evaluations of pituitary hormone replacement therapy and to monitor for any relapse. The patient should continue taking hormone replacement therapy as prescribed.

Hospital Course:
This is a summary of the hospital course of a 31-year-old female patient who was admitted to our hospital with a mass on the right neck. The patient underwent several diagnostic tests, which revealed an enlarged right lobe of the thyroid with nodules of uncertain nature. The patient agreed for an operation to eliminate the possibility of a tumor. Pathological examination of a thyroid nodule led to the diagnosis of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.

Findings:
Examination revealed a 3-cm mass on the right neck with no pain and with movement during swallowing. Color Doppler Ultrasound revealed enlargement of the right lobe of the thyroid, tallish echo nodules, 19 × 11 mm, of uncertain nature, and the absence of images manifesting the left lobe. CT showed an enlarged right lobe and the absence of images manifesting the left lobe and showed no sign of tracheal compression. Laboratory tests showed normal thyroid and parathyroid gland function.

Treatment Given:
The patient underwent an operation to eliminate the possibility of a tumor. During surgery, the left lobe of the thyroid and the left side of the parathyroid gland were found to be absent, and a hard nodule was detected on the right lobe of the thyroid simultaneously. The operation was immediately terminated after the pathological examination of the thyroid nodule led to the diagnosis of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. The patient has since recovered well and accepted thyroxin tablets.

Follow-up:
The patient has been discharged from the hospital. Follow-up appointments have been made to monitor the patient's condition. The patient has been advised to continue taking medication as prescribed and to maintain a healthy lifestyle.

Summary:
This patient was admitted to our hospital with a mass on the neck, which was later identified as an enlarged right lobe of the thyroid with nodules of uncertain nature. The patient underwent an operation to eliminate the possibility of a tumor, which revealed the absence of the left lobe of the thyroid and left side of the parathyroid gland, as well as a hard nodule on the right lobe. Pathological examination of the thyroid nodule led to the diagnosis of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. The patient has since recovered well and accepted thyroxin tablets. Follow-up appointments have been made to monitor the patient's condition.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our hospital with exacerbated hemoptysis and exertional dyspnea due to a 20-year history of bronchiectasis. Physical examination revealed dullness to percussion and breath sounds were not audible on the left side of the chest. Chest computed tomography revealed a destroyed left lung, with visible dilated right middle and lower bronchi. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) revealed normal cardiac structure and function. The patient underwent left pneumonectomy surgery 10 days after admission.

After surgery, the patient complained of slight breathlessness and reported high blood pressure, heart rate, and respiration rate. Laboratory investigations revealed hemoglobin level, troponin-T, and aspartate transaminase within abnormal ranges. Chest radiography revealed large left pleural effusions four days after surgery, which was drained via thoracentesis.

The patient lost consciousness during thoracentesis, and the procedure was stopped immediately. She was diagnosed with shock, with suspected acute cardiac tamponade. Pericardiocentesis was performed, which succeeded via an apex approach under TTE guidance. A tube was placed and retained for the next 36 hours, draining a total of 330 mL of bloody fluid. The patient's BP gradually increased and HR decreased a few hours after discharge of the blood. Laboratory tests revealed that hemoglobin decreased and troponin-T and aspartate transaminase levels increased, indicating myocardial damage.

The patient was discharged from the hospital in good condition few days later.

Discharge Diagnosis:
- Bronchiectasis
- Left lung destruction

Discharge Medications:
[No medication information is provided in the case report.]

Follow-Up Instructions:
The patient should follow up with their primary care physician for further evaluation and management of their bronchiectasis. They should also follow up with a cardiologist for evaluation and further management of their acute cardiac tamponade.

Clinical Course:
The patient presented with intermittent vaginal leakage of urine. The patient underwent an elective cesarean section in 2014, followed by a second emergency cesarean section in 2017 due to bladder and uterine rupture. A Vaginal-Urethral Fistula (VUF) was discovered and managed through conservative approaches, including a Foley catheter draining the bladder for 2 months and oral antibiotics to treat recurrent urinary tract infections. The VUF was surgically repaired seven months after the second delivery. A Pfannenstiel incision was used to access vesicouterine space for a transvesical approach to the fistula tract. The margins of the fistula were elevated and excised before bladder and uterus were drawn together with fine sutures. The uterus was closed with a 2-0 polyglycolic acid suture, and the bladder with 3-0 suture. A 3-way Foley catheter (20 Fr) was inserted into the bladder while fibrin sealant patch and omental flap interposed between the uterus and bladder. Postoperative care was provided to the patient for 10 days. The patient's operation was uneventful, with no intraoperative and postoperative complications. The total operative time was 150 min, with blood loss less than 100 ml during the first postoperative day.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted for surgical repair of the VUF. The surgery had no complications, and the patient's pain was managed with analgesic regimens. The patient's urine output was well-maintained with a 3-way Foley catheter (20 Fr) inserted into the bladder, which was removed 30 days after the surgery. The patient was discharged in stable condition with a recommendation for follow-up at 3, 6, and 12 months.

Diagnosis/Procedure:
Vaginal-Urethral Fistula (VUF)
VUF surgical repair
Cesarean section

Follow-up:
The patient was discharged with a recommendation for follow-up at 3, 6, and 12 months after surgery. Retrograde cystography was given at 1 month, revealing bladder integrity without leakage. The patient is currently being followed up, with no signs or symptoms of recurrence six months after surgery.

Hospital Course:

Admission: The patient presented with fever, cough, and hemoptysis, and was diagnosed with squamous lung carcinoma and recurrent cancer in the residual lung. CT scans indicated radiation pneumonia and the patient was administered intravenous methylprednisolone for 10 days. The patient's condition improved, and his steroid doses were gradually tapered.

Progression: However, three weeks after the last dose of pembrolizumab (a medication used to treat cancer), bilateral ground-glass opacities (GGOs) were detected, suggesting an infection. Despite receiving antibiotics and methylprednisolone, the patient's condition did not improve. Further CT scans indicated deterioration in the lungs.

Outcome: Despite receiving appropriate treatment, the patient's condition worsened, and the patient died two weeks after admission due to respiratory failure.

Follow-up: The patient's family was informed of his condition and the measures taken to treat him. They were advised to follow-up with their primary care provider. 

Summary: The patient was admitted to the hospital with a diagnosis of squamous lung carcinoma and radiotherapy for recurrent cancer. The patient's condition initially improved with intravenous methylprednisolone, but the patient later developed an infection with Pneumocystis jirovecii and CMV DNA, which was treated with various medications. Unfortunately, despite the best efforts of his medical team, the patient did not respond to treatment and passed away due to respiratory failure.

Diagnosis: Homozygote P85Rfs*6 mutation in exon 1 of the GALNT3 gene 

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 10-year-old female, was admitted with complaints of pain, swelling, and limited movement in her left elbow. She had previously undergone surgery for similar symptoms at the age of 8 years. After examination and testing, she was diagnosed with bilateral calcinosis in her elbows and right upper thigh, along with hyperphosphatemia.

The patient's laboratory results showed marked hyperphosphatemia, normal serum creatinine, 25-hydroxyvitamin D and parathormone levels, and an elevated TmP/GFR ratio, consistent with HFTC. Direct radiographs demonstrated radio-opaque soft tissue masses around the elbows bilaterally and right upper femur diaphysis. Bone mineral density Z-score was 0.7.

Dental and ophthalmological examination showed no involvement, but milimetric calcified plaques were present inside the right lower eyelid. A next-generation sequencing (NGS) test revealed a novel homozygote P85Rfs*6 (c.254_255delCT) mutation in exon 1 of the GALNT3 gene. In silico analyses confirmed that the mutation led to frameshift and a premature stop codon. Both parents were found to be heterozygous carriers for the same mutation.

During her stay at the hospital, the patient was treated with medical management and supportive care, which eventually led to significant improvement in her condition. The patient was discharged with instructions to follow up with her primary care provider and specialists as needed.

Summary:

This 10-year-old female patient was admitted with complaints of pain and swelling in her left elbow. She was diagnosed with bilateral calcinosis in her elbows and right upper thigh, along with hyperphosphatemia. The patient was treated with medical management and supportive care, which led to significant improvement in her condition. She was discharged with instructions for follow-up care.

Patient Name: [redacted]

Age: 67

Gender: Female

Diagnosis: Renal amyloidosis

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the nephrology department due to the development of nephrotic syndrome. She had been taking oral cyclophosphamide for lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma for four years. The patient exhibited bilateral leg edema and weight gain, along with hypoalbuminemia and preserved kidney function. Urine tests indicated a high level of urinary total protein-to-creatinine ratio. Serum immunoglobulin levels showed IgM-kappa monoclonal gammopathy.

Renal biopsy performed on the patient suggested the presence of amyloidosis. Electron microscopic analysis showed non-branched fibrils. The patient's bone marrow aspirate also confirmed the previous diagnosis of lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. After the diagnosis, the patient was prescribed oral fludarabine and experienced gradual improvement in their proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia over one-and-a-half years. 

LMD-LC-MS/MS was conducted, which identified mu heavy-chain and kappa light-chain with mu heavy-chain predominance. LC-MS/MS confirmed that both the identified immunoglobulins compose amyloid fibrils. The patient was eventually diagnosed with "kappa type renal AL amyloidosis with non-amyloid forming monoclonal IgM-kappa deposition".

The patient was discharged in a stable condition and advised to follow up regularly with the nephrology department.

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 48-year-old man with a history of alcohol abuse, presented to the gastroenterology department in November 2006 complaining of severe epigastric pain and nausea for two days. The laboratory findings were suspicious for pancreatitis and the patient underwent computed tomography (CT), which showed an edematous pancreas tail and fluid in the anterior prerenal space and fascia. He had two similar episodes of acute tail pancreatitis in the following months. 

In September 2009, the patient presented with vague epigastric pain of several weeks duration. Serum amylase and lipase levels were normal, but the cholestatic parameters were mildly elevated. A magnetic resonance (MR) study was performed, which demonstrated moderate chronic pancreatitis of the tail with atrophy and irregular bordering of the Wirsung’s duct. Helicobacter pylori gastritis was also diagnosed. 

In February 2012, the patient presented again to the gastroenterologist with epigastric and left upper quadrant pain. Contrast-enhanced CT scan was performed to evaluate the known chronic pancreatitis and other causes of pain. The study surprisingly revealed a hypervascular lesion in the pancreatic tail consisting of a conglomeration of small hypervascular spots and blood vessels. Further examinations were performed in order to differentiate a vascular malformation from a hypervascular pancreatic tumor, especially an islet cell tumor or a hypervascular metastasis. Contrast-enhanced MR study showed a focal area of heterogeneous contrast enhancement without an apparent nodular component. The subsequent angiography showed two large feeding arteries in the early arterial phase, followed by a racemose vascular network, an early transient dense parenchyma stain in the early portal phase and early wash-out of the lesion in the portal phase. Based on these findings, a pancreatic arteriovenous malformation was suggested. 

The patient underwent resection of the pancreas tail and postoperative recovery was uneventful. Histopathologic examination revealed sequelae of chronic pancreatitis and numerous dilated blood vessels accompanied by blood clot formation and intimal hyperplasia. The histopathological findings were consistent with a pancreatic AVM. 

Discharge Summary:

The 48-year-old male patient who was diagnosed with a pancreatic arteriovenous malformation (AVM) and chronic pancreatitis has been discharged. He presented with severe epigastric pain and nausea in November 2006, and underwent computed tomography (CT) which showed an edematous pancreas tail and fluid in the anterior prerenal space and fascia. In September 2009, a magnetic resonance (MR) study was performed due to vague epigastric pain, which indicated moderate chronic pancreatitis of the tail with atrophy and irregular bordering of the Wirsung’s duct. A Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (HPS) gastritis diagnosis was also made. In February 2012, a contrast-enhanced CT scan was performed which revealed a hypervascular lesion in the pancreatic tail, implying the presence of a pancreatic arteriovenous malformation. The patient underwent resection of the pancreas tail and postoperative recovery was uneventful. Histopathologic examination revealed sequelae of chronic pancreatitis and numerous dilated blood vessels accompanied by blood clot formation and intimal hyperplasia that was consistent with a pancreatic AVM. The patient's condition was managed appropriately and he was discharged in a stable condition.

Discharge Summary:
Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Abdominal wall tumor
Principal Diagnosis: Foreign-body granuloma
Secondary Diagnosis: Elevated inflammatory markers

Hospital Course:
A 57-year-old Japanese man was admitted to the hospital with increasing right lower abdominal pain. On initial examination, an abdominal wall tumor was detected using transabdominal ultrasound. Laboratory results revealed elevated inflammatory markers. Helical computed tomography (CT) revealed a solid mass and magnetic resonance imaging showed a mass that exhibited low intensity. Positron emission tomography–CT revealed fluorodeoxyglucose accumulation.

The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy and a malignant tumor was suspected. Intraoperative findings at laparotomy revealed an elastic, hard, milky-whitish mass with a rough surface and capillary growth in the right lower quadrant. The mass was completely removed, and the surgical margin secured. Pathologic examination revealed that these masses were foreign-body granulomas consisting of string-like crystals and a foreign-body giant cell. Immunohistological staining was positive in cells surrounding phosphoglyceride crystals. The patient underwent regular follow-up abdominal ultrasound examination and CT postoperatively. As of 3 years after the procedure, no signs of recurrence have been detected.

Discussion:
PGDD is a rare disease characterized by deposition of phosphoglyceride crystals. It can sometimes form a large mass and be misdiagnosed as a malignant tumor. Little is known about its etiology and pathogenesis. This deposition disease is apparently triggered by injury and subsequent macrophage aggregation, with a histological picture of deposited crystal radiating from the cell membranes of epithelioid cells. No specific markers exist for PGDD, and differentiating this disease from malignant tumors without pathological examination is difficult.

Conclusion:
In conclusion, a foreign-body granuloma was discovered during the patient's exploratory laparotomy. The mass was completely removed, and the surgical margin secured. Regular follow-up has not revealed any findings suspicious of recurrence.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: XXXX
Dates of Admission: XX/XX/XXXX to XX/XX/XXXX

Summary:
The patient is a 46-year-old female who was admitted to the hospital with a history of a painless left supraclavicular mass and subsequent diagnosis of liquid silicone migration. The patient underwent multiple imaging studies, including ultrasound, CT, and MRI, which revealed a complex, heterogenous collection that extended from the left supraclavicular fossa into the left chest wall and the proximal, medial part of the left arm. The imaging studies also showed a slightly enhancing rim around arm collections that suggested superimposed inflammation or infection. After consented intravenous contrast administration, the patient again had a CT neck and left upper limb, which showed extensive hypodense material within the distribution of the previously identified silicone migration site with a new distribution of hypodense material in the left arm, correlating well with the ultrasonographical findings. A slightly enhancing rim surrounding the arm collection suggested superimposed inflammation or infection. Following a large volume of pus (within a fluid pocket extending from the medial aspect of the left arm to the left axilla and supraclavicular fossa) drainage, the patient was placed on intravenous cephalexin followed by a long course of oral flucloxacillin. The patient subsequently agreed to bilateral mastectomy with reconstruction after completing the treatment course.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to her general practitioner with a painless left supraclavicular mass and was referred to interventional radiology for further investigation and possible treatment of the presumed lymphangioma, which was later diagnosed as liquid silicone migration. The patient underwent ultrasound and non-contrast CT initially, which was of little help forming a differential diagnosis for the mass. Upon further investigation, the patient reported having had an elective mastopexy in Russia three years prior, which followed with free liquid silicone injection for fuller appearance. The patient’s history included recent domestic violence but denied any breast trauma. An MRI was performed to further define the mass and its vascularity before treatment, revealing a well-defined, T2 and STIR high signal complex cystic lesion extending from the lower anterior left neck posteriorly into the supraclavicular fossa, as well as an asymmetry of the injected material into both breasts, with silicone migrating around the lateral border of the left pectoralis major muscle. 

The patient was then diagnosed with liquid silicone migration and advised to undergo bilateral mastectomy with reconstruction. Later, the patient represented acutely unwell, septic, with a swollen, tense left biceps region and left upper limb cellulitis. Upon the suspected abscess collections being relayed to the treating surgical team, a large volume of pus (totalling approximately 600 ml) was drained. The patient received intravenous cephalexin followed by a long course of oral flucloxacillin.

Conclusions:
In conclusion, the patient was admitted with a painless left supraclavicular mass and later diagnosed with liquid silicone migration. The patient underwent ultrasound, non-contrast CT, and MRI studies to further investigate the mass. After contracting acute left upper limb cellulitis triggered by suspected abscess collections, the patient received intravenous cephalexin followed by a long course of oral flucloxacillin. The patient agreed to bilateral mastectomy with reconstruction after completing the treatment course.

He was also started on continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) due to acute kidney injury after becoming oliguric. The patient was on maximal life support with multiple vasopressors, CRRT, inhaled nitrous oxide, paralysis, phenobarbital coma, and stress dose steroids.

Unfortunately, despite all efforts, the patient continued to deteriorate and ultimately expired secondary to ARDS on [DATE].

Unfortunately, the patient expired in the hospital.

Admission Diagnosis: Vascular dementia

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the medicine service after being found wandering and displaying an altered mental status. Neurology and psychiatry services were consulted, and the patient was diagnosed with vascular dementia based on neurocognitive deficits and the neuroimaging finding of encephalomalacia. No acute psychiatric interventions were recommended at the time. However, the patient was later re-consulted to psychiatry services due to a bizarre delusion, and medications were prescribed. The patient later developed muscle rigidity and an elevated WBC count, leading to a diagnosis of NMS. The patient's primary treatment team discontinued the medication and consulted psychiatry. The patient no longer displayed agitation or psychosis and was deemed stable to be discharged to a nursing home.

Medications were not specified in the case report.

The patient was referred to a nursing home for further care and management of the underlying vascular dementia. Follow-up appointments were not specified in the case report.

The patient, a 59-year old male with an unknown medical and psychiatric history, was admitted to the hospital with an altered mental status and diagnosed with vascular dementia. The patient later developed NMS and was treated with intravenous hydration and parenteral lorazepam. CSF analyses pointed towards an infectious etiology, with HSV as a possible primary pathogen. The patient was discharged and referred to a nursing home for further care and management.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information: The patient is a 50-year-old male with a history of solid organ transplantation and metastatic squamous cell carcinoma.

Hospital Course:

Admission: The patient was admitted to our hospital with low-grade fevers, oliguria, fluid retention, and an enlarged and tender renal allograft 13 days after receiving the first dose of nivolumab. Laboratory testing revealed marked acute kidney injury with a creatinine of 4.4 mg/dL. He was treated empirically for acute rejection with a 3 day methylprednisone pulse but without improvement. A renal biopsy was deferred, and hemodialysis was initiated for volume overload and electrolyte disturbances.

Treatment: Nivolumab, a cancer immunotherapy drug, was continued every two weeks while the patient remained on hemodialysis. Imaging after 4 weeks demonstrated a partial regression in tumor burden and lymphadenopathy. The patient was maintained on hemodialysis, but has been able to travel and return to an active lifestyle.

Discharge Condition: The patient was discharged after an allograft nephrectomy was performed 2 months after stopping his immunosuppression. Histologic evaluation revealed hemorrhagic infarction with features of acute and chronic vascular rejection. Most recent imaging 18 months after treatment initiation shows stable tumor regression.

Follow-up plan: The patient will continue treatment with nivolumab and hemodialysis as needed. Further follow-up will be required to evaluate the patient's progress and condition.

CLINICAL COURSE:
The patient, a 48-year-old male, was admitted to the psychiatric emergency room with dysmorphic mood. Subsequently, he was referred to medical service to manage hyponatremia. The patient had a past medical history of lumbar spondylosis managed with intermittent nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use. He occasionally consumed alcohol but denied having any history of diabetes, prediabetes, obesity, binge drinking, abdominal trauma, any offending drugs, and any procedures including endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography. The family history was unremarkable.
During admission, the patient experienced abdominal discomfort that worsened alongside a fever. The patient developed tachycardia and hypotension, and the physical examination was notable for mild tenderness in the epigastrium. Laboratory investigations showed increased levels of hematocrit, leukocytes with neutrophil predominance, platelets, creatinine, C-reactive protein, amylase, and lipase. An alarming laboratory finding was a severe elevation of TGs with mild AP. The diagnosis of HTG-induced AP was established.
The patient received aggressive intravenous rehydration therapy, antiemetics, opioids for pain control, and insulin to decrease TG levels. The patient's condition improved significantly, and apheresis was not performed due to the response to insulin therapy alone. The patient was discharged after his condition had improved, and he began tolerating oral feeds. Fenofibrate was initiated, and empiric antibiotic therapy was stopped due to negative blood cultures.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS:
HTG-induced AP.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient is advised to continue fenofibrate therapy indefinitely to prevent further attacks of AP. The patient is asked to follow a healthy diet and avoid alcohol intake. If the patient experiences any recurring symptoms, he should seek medical attention immediately.

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient is recommended to follow up with the primary care provider for further monitoring of the TG levels. The TG levels were recorded at 230 mg/dL after three months from the time of discharge.

Patient Name: [REDACTED]  Sex: Male  Age: 3-year-old

Admission date: [REDACTED]  Discharge date: [REDACTED]

Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Reason for Admission:

The patient, a 3-year-old Middle Eastern boy, was admitted for a defect in the midline of his neck that was causing a mucosal-like raw surface and greenish, thick residue occluding the opening. Adenoidal hypertrophy was also noted in the patient.

Hospital Course:

An MRI was performed, indicating a soft tissue mass with no fistula tract. Despite contrast material being injected through the opening, the diagnosis of MCC was established, and surgical removal with immediate closure with multiple Z-plasties was performed.

During the surgery, the sinus at the caudal end of the lesion was probed and followed caudally until it ended, which was found to be approximately 2 cm long. The cranial end of the defect had a fibrous band extending up to the mandible, which was resected together with the cervical lesion. The midline lesion was found to be superficial, and hence the excision was done at the subdermal level. A double Z-plasty was found to be sufficient for the closure.

Pathological examination confirmed the clinical diagnosis of stratified squamous epithelial cells covering the cleft with few adnexial structures at the dermal level. A one-month follow-up examination revealed an uneventful healing period, and the patient was able to move his head in all directions without any restriction or pain. A 14-month follow-up examination showed an acceptable level of scarring not causing any restriction of neck movements.

Impression:

The patient's neck defect was successfully corrected through surgical removal and immediate closure with multiple Z-plasties. The patient had an uneventful post-operative course, with no complications or adverse events noted.

Recommendations:

The patient should be monitored for any signs of recurrence and should be scheduled for regular follow-up appointments with his healthcare provider. The patient and his family should also be educated on proper wound care and should be encouraged to seek medical attention if any concerning symptoms arise.

Reason for Hospitalization:
The patient was admitted to the hospital for the treatment of intractable gastroesophageal varices (GV) due to liver cirrhosis prior to surgery for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

Hospital Course:
Endoscopic sclerotherapy was performed 4 years previously, but GV were worsening. The Child-Pugh score was 6 (class A). Angio-computed tomography (CT) was performed prior to treatment to evaluate the hemodynamics of GV and work up for HCC. CT during arterial portography (CTAP) was performed via the superior mesenteric artery, and the scanning revealed GV to drain mainly into the left inferior phrenic vein, and the gastrorenal shunt was absent. The main feeding vessels of GV were the posterior and short gastric vein. The left internal thoracic vein, pericardial phrenic vein, and left inferior pulmonary vein were observed to be collateral veins.

The patient received balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration (BRTO) from the left inferior phrenic vein initially, but mild stenosis between the inferior vena cava (IVC) and inferior phrenic vein, and the shunt angle, prevented the introduction of the 6 Fr balloon catheter. Therefore, coil-assisted retrograde transvenous obliteration (CARTO) was planned and attempted from the same single route. Appropriately sized detachable coils were deployed, and ethanolamine oleate with iopamidol (EOI) was gradually injected to embolize up to the coil in the outflow shunt, varices, and other minor collaterals.

The patient was recovered and discharged from the hospital one week after the procedure. A contrast-enhanced CT was performed, which confirmed complete occlusion of GV. No complications were encountered.

Summary:
The patient was admitted to the hospital for the treatment of intractable gastroesophageal varices (GV) due to liver cirrhosis prior to surgery for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). After balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration (BRTO) was unsuccessful due to mild stenosis and shunt angle, the patient underwent coil-assisted retrograde transvenous obliteration (CARTO) using appropriately sized detachable coils, followed by injection of ethanolamine oleate with iopamidol (EOI). The procedure was successful, and the patient was discharged one week after recovery with complete occlusion of GV confirmed by a contrast-enhanced CT.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [Redacted]
Age: 68
Date of Admission: [Redacted]
Date of Discharge: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:

The patient presented with poor appetite, fatigue, occasional mild lower abdominal discomfort, and body weight loss of 10 kg over 6 months. He had no nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or tarry or bloody stool symptoms, but he did experience frequent urination with mild dysuria. He was examined in the outpatient department and had a cystoscopy performed, which showed that everything was normal apart from external compression of the dome and posterior wall of the bladder.

An abdominal sonography and a CT scan of the abdomen revealed a large, presacral, solid mass lesion (13 × 11 × 9 cm) surrounded by the bowel with gas content, which was compressing anteriorly against the bladder.

The patient then underwent an exploratory laparotomy with removal of the pelvic tumor and segmental resection of the ileum. A fistula tract from the ileum lumen into tumor was seen in the specimen. No severe adhesion was seen with easy division between the tumor mass and bladder. The pathological examination revealed that the tumor had invaded the submucosa and muscle layer of the ileum and mesentery. Dog-1 and CD117 staining were positive according to the immunohistochemistry report. 

Diagnosis:

The patient was diagnosed with an exophytic gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of the ileum with fistula formation and mesenteric invasion, pT4N0M0, stage III-B.

Treatment:

The patient was referred to the oncology department and was administered 1-year adjuvant imatinib targeted therapy. No tumor recurrence has been noted to date.

Condition on Discharge:

The patient's condition improved significantly during his hospital stay and he has been discharged in a stable condition. The patient was advised to follow up with the oncology department for further management.

Follow-up:

The patient was advised to return for follow-up appointments with the oncology department for further management.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted], Age: 52 years, Sex: Female
Admission Date: [redacted] | Discharge Date: [redacted]
Admitting Diagnosis: Recurrent plasmacytoma arising from the anterior elements of C1 and C2 vertebrae

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with complaints of dysarthria and was diagnosed with a recurrent plasmacytoma arising from the anterior elements of the C1 and C2 vertebrae. The patient had a history of a similar tumor 16 years ago, which was diagnosed as plasmacytoma at that time. The patient underwent cervical spine fusion and mass reduction surgery, followed by additional radiotherapy. However, the patient dropped out from the treatment course.

During the current admission, the patient underwent excisional biopsy of the tumor, which revealed diffuse proliferation of plasmacytoid tumor cells with pale paranuclear area and dense chromatin. The tumor cells showed dual expression of kappa and lambda light chains. Bone marrow biopsy showed no evidence of plasmacytes showing dual expression or deviation of kappa and lambda light chain. CT and MRI revealed no skeletal abnormality except for the primary lesion, and absence of end-organ damage attributable to proliferative plasma cell disorder.

After diagnosis, the patient underwent nine courses of VRD therapy, which reduced the size of the lesion. The patient's condition improved, and two years after diagnosis, the lesions have not increased in size. Bone marrow examinations have shown no progression to plasma cell myeloma.

Hospital Discharge:
The patient was discharged in stable condition and was advised to follow-up with the oncology clinic regularly. The oncology team provided medication management and other treatment advancements for the patient's diagnosed condition. Further monitoring of the patient's condition, including a follow-up MRI was recommended for future health management.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 52-year-old African American male, was admitted to the hospital with persistent fever after being discharged one week earlier for diarrhea caused by Clostridium difficile colitis. During the prior hospitalization, the patient was started on allopurinol for an acute gout flare, after which he developed a generalized rash that was treated with a prednisone taper for a suspected drug rash.

Past Medical/Surgical History:
The patient's past medical history included hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 5, osteoarthritis, GERD, and gout.

Assessment:
On initial examination, the patient was febrile with skin excoriations noted but no rash or lymphadenopathy. Laboratory data demonstrated anemia of chronic disease, low hemoglobin, thrombocytopenia, elevated creatinine and BUN, and elevated liver enzymes.

Treatment:
The gastroenterology service was consulted due to worsening LFTs, which were not responding to treatment. The patient's LFTs improved after receiving N-acetylcysteine (NAC).

Diagnosis:
Due to the patient's elevated liver enzymes, peripheral eosinophilia, and negative workup for alternative processes, DRESS syndrome was suspected.

Discharge Plan:
The patient was discharged on day seven after receiving appropriate treatment and showing significant improvement. A follow-up appointment was scheduled with his primary care physician.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY:

Admission Date: February 2017
Discharge Date: May 2019

Admitting Diagnosis: Abnormal chest x-ray, dry cough, and worsening shortness of breath

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 69-year-old male with a history of myocardial infarction, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, hypertension, coronary artery disease, mitral valve regurgitation, subdural hematoma, and diabetes mellitus, was admitted due to an abnormal chest x-ray and worsening respiratory symptoms. The chest x-ray showed interstitial changes attributed to probable drug toxicity. The patient underwent chest computed tomography without contrast, which showed a diffuse mosaic pattern with evolving interstitial lung changes. Two weeks later, a repeat chest x-ray showed worsening bilateral interstitial markings predominantly at the bases. 

During the hospital course, the patient was seen by various specialists for persistent hemoptysis and worsening dyspnea. Various medications were tried, including apixaban and several asthma medications, without a proven history of obstructive lung or airway disease. The patient underwent a chest CT, which showed asymmetrically patchy, bilateral ground-glass opacities raising the suspicion of possible pulmonary fibrosis, pneumonia, pneumonitis, or asymmetric pulmonary edema. Despite being managed medically, the patient continued to report shortness of breath and cough, which became productive over time. 

In April 2019, the patient underwent bronchoscopy, and bronchial washings from the right lung were sent for analysis. The sample was positive for pigmented macrophages, mixed inflammatory cells, and squamous cells. The patient underwent a second bronchoscopy on May 8th, 2019, which did not show any malignancy. However, transbronchial biopsies were consistent with UIP, and the Envisia Genomic Classifier was utilized to support these findings.

Disposition and Condition at Discharge:
The patient was discharged in stable condition and will continue to be followed up by his healthcare provider for ongoing management of his condition.

Follow-up Plan:
The patient will follow up with his healthcare provider for ongoing management of his condition and further treatment options.

Stable

Follow-up with cardiology to monitor her condition.

Discharge Summary
Patient Name: [redacted]
Gender: Female
Age: 51 years
Admission Date: [redacted]
Discharge Date: [redacted]
Length of Stay: 34 days

Admission Diagnosis and Reason for Hospitalization:
The patient was admitted with cauda equina syndrome secondary to epidural lipomatosis, which required an emergency laminectomy.

Hospital Course:
On the first day post-laminectomy, the patient experienced symptoms of sore throat, dysphagia, and chest pain. A CT scan revealed fluid along a distended thick-walled oesophagus suggestive of oesophagitis. Despite antibiotic therapy, the patient’s symptoms persisted, and repeat CT scan performed 6 days later showed extramural gas locules with associated fat stranding adjacent to the gastro-oesophageal junction (GOJ), which was consistent with perforation. The patient underwent an emergency laparoscopic trans-hiatal repair. Intra-operative findings showed a 2 cm mucosal tear at the superior lesser curve extending to the GOJ. A nasojejunal tube was placed for enteral feeding post-operatively. The duration of surgery was 180 minutes. The patient’s post-operative course was complicated by a pericardial effusion, which was treated with a pericardial window.

Condition at Discharge:
At the time of discharge, the patient was stable, and her follow-up at 4 months was unremarkable. Gastroscopy revealed a well-healed gastric ulcer at the cardia.

Instructions upon Discharge:
The patient was discharged with instructions to follow-up with her primary care physician and gastroenterologist. She was given a prescription for pain management as needed. It was also recommended that the patient follow a low-fat and low-acid diet.

Follow-up Care:
The patient was advised to follow-up with her primary care physician and gastroenterologist for monitoring of symptoms and management of her gastric ulcer.

Discharge Medications:
Pain management medication was prescribed for the patient upon discharge.

Discharge Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with gastro-oesophageal perforation following laparoscopic repair.

Discharge Summary

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with a complaint of a pelvic mass that had been found nine years before, and rapidly grew larger recently. The physical examination revealed a 10 cm pelvic mass. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan identified a 10.5 × 8.5 × 11.8 cm cyst with a 4.5 × 5 × 5.5 cm bright area in the cystic wall of the left ovary. The serum CA125 was 58.3 U/mL (normal range ≤ 35 U/mL), and AFP was 11.5 ng/mL (normal range ≤ 7.0 ng/mL). The patient underwent a staging surgery including total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TAHBSO), omentectomy, pelvic and para-aortic lymphadenectomy. 

The intraoperative findings showed a large cystic mass in the left ovary that was adhered to the fallopian tube and the left pelvic wall. No other abnormalities were found in the abdominal and pelvic organs. The tumor was staged as FIGO IIa. The patient received six courses of TP (paclitaxe and carboplatin) chemotherapy post-operatively. 

The patient was diagnosed with a recurrent solitary tumor in the left lower lobe of the lung 18 months after her surgery and underwent left inferior lobectomy of the lung and bronchial lymphadenectomy in another hospital. She has been alive with no evidence of disease for 40 months after her first surgery.

Diagnosis:
- Pelvic mass, left ovary
- Recurrent solitary tumor in the left lower lobe of the lung

Treatment:
- Total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TAHBSO)
- Omentectomy
- Pelvic and para-aortic lymphadenectomy
- Six courses of TP (paclitaxe and carboplatin) chemotherapy
- Left inferior lobectomy of the lung
- Bronchial lymphadenectomy

Condition on Discharge:
The patient's condition is stable, and she is considered improved compared to her initial condition. She is currently asymptomatic and has been cleared for discharge.

Follow-up:
The patient is advised to follow up for further evaluation as per her oncologist's recommendations.

Date of Discharge: N/A

Reason for Admission:
The patient was admitted due to vaginal bleeding, lower abdominal pain, and difficulty with urination at sixteen weeks and one day of gestation.

Hospital Course:
The patient was diagnosed with a low position of the placenta and was receiving daily progesterone therapy during her admission. During her stay, she experienced worsening lower abdominal pain and difficulty with urination but was transferred to a tertiary hospital for further evaluation.

Diagnostic Findings:
Ultrasound examinations revealed a uterine retroversion with the fundus bending to the posterior fornix and an anteriorly transfixed cervix behind the pubic symphysis, resulting in fundal implantation of the placenta. However, a healthy female infant was vaginally delivered at 38 weeks of gestation with adequate biometric measurements for gestational age.

Clinical Course:
Attempts to reduce incarceration by intravaginal pressure and knee-chest position were unsuccessful. However, substantial incarceration was relieved by applying transvaginal fundal pressure during a second attempt.

Diagnoses:
The patient had a history of lymphatic tuberculosis and bilateral obstruction of the fallopian tubes with uterine retroversion. She was diagnosed with a low position of the placenta and uterine retroversion during admission.

Procedures:
The patient was indwelt with a Foley catheter, and transvaginal fundal pressure was applied to relieve incarceration.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient was discharged in good condition with no further complications.

Follow-Up Care:
The patient may require follow-up appointments with a healthcare provider for further monitoring.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with complaints of paresthesias in the left foot for nine months. A thorough neurological examination showed intact sensations to gross touch and pinprick and no foot drop. The laboratory workup revealed no significant abnormalities except for an elevated mean corpuscular volume. Electrodiagnostic studies were done and reported to be normal. Nerve conduction study showed no significant side-to-side difference in antidromic sensory responses and therefore ruled out any possibility of neuropathy, radiculopathy, or tarsal tunnel syndrome. Subsequently, a neuromuscular ultrasound evaluation of bilateral Dorsal Cutaneous Peroneal Nerves (DCPNs) at the level of the ankle revealed a significantly enlarged left DCPN with a cross-sectional area of 27.88 mm2 at the level of the ankle. The patient was diagnosed with focal neuropathy of the left DCPN.
 
Condition on Discharge:
The patient's symptoms have improved, and the patient can perform daily activities without difficulty. The patient was discharged with a pain management plan and advised to follow up with the neurology clinic for further evaluation. 

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient will follow up with the neurology clinic for further evaluation and management.

Discharge Date: [insert date]

Patient Name: [insert name]               Medical Record Number: [insert number]

Reason for Admission:
The patient was admitted due to suspicion of a mycotic aortic aneurysm and severe infection.

Hospital Course:
The patient underwent intravenous antibiotic therapy for four weeks and was started on tazobactam/piperacillin hydrate. Computed tomography angiography showed a descending aortic aneurysm measuring 70 × 70 mm, which extended 20 mm in only 2 weeks. Transcatheter endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) was performed under local anesthesia using two 37 × 200 mm Conformable stent grafts (W. L. Gore & Associates, Inc., Newark, DE, USA) to prevent aortic rupture.

Upon discharge, the patient was afebrile with a normal white blood cell count and C-reactive protein level. Oral antibiotics were continued for 18 months. The patient underwent monitoring by computed tomography 15 months after the TEVAR, and the aneurysm had regressed significantly, measuring 53 × 53 mm. The patient had no further signs of infection at the time of writing.

Diagnosis:
Descending aortic aneurysm

Procedures:
Transcatheter endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR)

Condition at Discharge:
The patient was discharged without serious complications.

Follow-Up:
The patient was monitored via computed tomography 15 months after TEVAR repair, at which point there was significant regression of the aneurysm. The patient was free from antibiotics at the time of writing.

Hospital Course:
This 86-year-old postmenopausal woman (gravida 2 para 2) was admitted to the Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Department at the university hospital for perineal pain and dysuria related to labial fusion. Physical examination revealed extensive labial fusion with atrophic mucosa and two 3 mm pinholes for urination. Manual separation of the adhesion under general anesthesia was followed by mucosa removal using VERSAJET and dissection through a small hole just anterior to the vagina. Bilateral 3 × 7 cm vulvoperineal flaps with perforators from the superficial external pudendal artery were designed and transferred under the skin incision. The patient was instructed to undertake bed rest with the hips in abduction to prevent readhesion and optimize flap perfusion. The patient underwent rehabilitation during her admission until discharged.

Physical Examination:
- Both labia majora had extensively fused together and the mucosa was atrophic
- Two pinholes each with a 3 mm diameter were observed, one at the fused midline and the other directly above the vaginal orifice
- Erythema and local warmth were observed in the bilateral labia majora, although mass or white lesions and hardening of the skin were not observed
- The clitoris, vestibule, labia minora, and external urethral meatus could only be observed by recognizing the two pinholes along the fused midline

Diagnostic Tests:
- Virology tests were positive for human herpes virus type 1 and type 2 antibodies
- Endocrine tests showed a marked decrease in estradiol levels (5.0 pg/mL)
- MRI revealed no abnormality except for the absence of a uterus due to prior hysterectomy
- Infiltration of neutrophils was observed in the epithelium. Inflammatory cell infiltration mainly included lymphocytes, and plasma cells were observed in the dermis

Treatment and Procedure:
- Manual separation of the adhesion under general anesthesia
- Mucosa removal using VERSAJET and dissection through a small hole just anterior to the vagina
- Design and transfer of bilateral 3 × 7 cm vulvoperineal flaps with perforators from the superficial external pudendal artery under the skin incision
- Insertion of drainage tubes (15 Fr) subcutaneously on both sides
- Insertion of a Foley catheter into the bladder
- Instruction for the patient to undertake bed rest with the hips in abduction to prevent readhesion and optimize flap perfusion

Follow-up:
- Temporary edema of the flap was observed on postoperative day 2, but it gradually resolved by postoperative day 6 due to continuous hip abduction
- Bilateral flap drains and the Foley catheter were removed on postoperative day 7 when ambulation started
- Sutures were removed on postoperative day 14 with no findings of tightness or pain
- No recurrence was observed after postoperative 18 months

Hospital course summary: The patient was admitted with worsening dyspnea, cough, chills, and body aches. He was initially treated for bronchitis and diastolic congestive heart failure exacerbation with diuretics, bronchodilators, and antibiotics. Despite treatment, the patient's condition did not improve, prompting further evaluation with a transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) and subsequent transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE). These tests revealed a small-to-moderate sized supracristal ventricular septal defect (VSD) with a left-to-right shunt and a ruptured right sinus of Valsalva. The patient was transferred to a tertiary care facility for urgent surgical repair of the acute left-to-right sinus of Valsalva - RVOT (right ventricular outflow tract) shunt and the supracristal VSD. The aortic root was accessed via a transaortic route and the aneurysmal dilation in the right coronary sinus was resected with a bovine pericardial patch. The SVSD was repaired with a bovine pericardial patch, while the aortic valve remained uninvolved. Postoperatively, the patient recovered well and was discharged.

The procedures performed included a transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE), a subsequent transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE), and an urgent surgical repair of the acute left-to-right sinus of Valsalva - RVOT shunt, and the supracristal VSD.

Later, the patient underwent urgent surgical repair of the acute left-to-right sinus of Valsalva - RVOT shunt and the supracristal VSD.

Admitting Diagnosis: Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA), Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA), Type B Interrupted Aortic Arch (IAA), Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD), Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PHT).

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 1-month old male infant, was admitted to our facility with symptoms of tachypnea and cyanosis. Further diagnostic testing revealed that the patient had TGA, PDA, Type B IAA, VSD, and PHT. In October 2019, the patient underwent a single-stage primary surgical repair, which included aortic arch reconstruction, VSD closure, and an arterial switch operation of the transposed great arteries. The patient remained in the intensive care unit for 12 days, during which he was closely monitored for any postoperative complications. The patient's vasoactive-inotropic score (VIS) was 17.5 at the first hour after the operation and 16 after 24 hours. Nitroprusside was used to reduce afterload. N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) was 22,914.00 pg/ml the first day after the operation and decreased to 7101.00 pg/ml after 2 days. The ventilation time was 91 hours. Postoperative echocardiography and computed tomography angiography showed that the patient's condition had significantly improved and there were no aortic or pulmonary regurgitations.

Discharge Diagnosis:
The patient was discharged without any significant complications. Follow-up appointments were scheduled with the cardiologist to monitor the patient's condition and ensure that he remains symptom-free.

Disposition:
The patient was discharged to home with his mother for continued recovery.

The patient, a 1-month old male infant, was admitted to our facility with symptoms of tachypnea and cyanosis and diagnosed with TGA, PDA, Type B IAA, VSD, and PHT. The patient underwent a single-stage primary surgical repair in October 2019, and his postoperative course was largely uneventful. He was discharged to home with his mother and was instructed to follow-up with the cardiologist for continued monitoring and care.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 50
Gender: Female
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital for evaluation of an adrenal lesion seen on abdominal ultrasound, which was later confirmed to be a benign schwannoma. An Adrenal MRI revealed a soft tissue necrotic encapsulated mass of right adrenal gland origin, which was 10 × 9 cm in size, with areas of necrosis and calcifications without local invasion. The patient was completely asymptomatic and the physical exam was normal.

Endocrinological evaluation was done with normal hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis function and no hyper secretion of catecholamines. An adrenal scan was performed, which showed a well-encapsulated heterogeneous mass without any signs of invasion.

A laparoscopic transperitoneal adrenalectomy was planned, but during the surgery, due to the adherent nature of the tumor to the vena cava, the surgery was converted to open surgery by a sub-costal incision. The tumor was successfully removed during the surgery, and a drain was placed in the retroperitoneum. The patient's operative time was 200 minutes. Blood loss was 850 cc, and no transfusion was required. The drain was removed on the second post-operative day, and the patient was discharged on the sixth day after surgery.

Diagnostic Findings:

Histopathological examination of the tumor showed a benign schwannoma. The tumor consisted of spindle cells with alternating areas of compact hypercellularity with irregular streams and without atypia or mitosis. Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated negative CKAE1-AE3, synaptophysine, and chromogranine. In contrast to these results, S-100 and CD68 (PGM1) staining were diffuse and positive across the tumor.

Recommendations:

The patient should follow up with their primary care physician for routine checkups and monitoring of their health. Further follow-up visits may be needed to ensure complete recovery.

Summary:

The 50-year-old female patient underwent surgery for the removal of a benign schwannoma in her right adrenal gland. The surgery was initially planned as a laparoscopic transperitoneal adrenalectomy but was converted to open surgery due to the adherent nature of the tumor to the vena cava. The tumor was successfully removed during the surgery, and the patient was discharged on the sixth day after surgery. The patient's histopathological examination showed a benign schwannoma. The patient should follow up with their primary care physician for routine checkups and monitoring of their health.

Discharge Summary

Patient: 56-year-old male with rectal mucosa highly differentiated adenocarcinoma at T3N2M1a stage and multiple metastatic tumors in the liver.

Hospital Course: The patient presented with intermittent hematochezia and perianal distension pain for 1 year and was diagnosed with glandular dysplasia in the rectal mucosa. The patient received one cycle of FOLFOX chemotherapy, which was terminated due to severe gastrointestinal reactions and subsequently underwent gamma knife radiotherapy for rectal lesions. Following radiation treatment, the frequency of defecations was reduced to >10 times, but <20 times a day with mucous bloody defecation.

Treatment: The patient received allogeneic CIK cells once a week for 3 weeks with smooth treatment process, and after half a year, reexamination revealed a small cyst in the right anterior lobe of the liver with no liver metastatic tumor found. The patient's acute and late toxicities of gastrointestinal and hematological adverse events have been decreased to be Grade 1 according to Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events v3.0 (CTCAE).

Follow-up: The patient's tumor markers CA-125 and CA-199 returned to normal levels, and the dosage performance of gamma knife radiotherapy for rectal lesions was successful as shown in Fig. 

Conclusion: The clinical study was approved by the Ethical Committee, and the participant signed an informed consent about the benefits and risks of the procedure. The patient has provided informed consent for publication of the case.
