Patient Name: [REDACTED]
 
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]

Admitting Diagnosis: Abnormal placentation at 29 weeks of gestation

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 32-year-old G5P4 woman, was admitted to our Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology due to a diagnosis of abnormal placentation during a routine ultrasound at 29 weeks of gestation. She had a history of previous cesarean delivery due to placenta previa. High precision clinical diagnosis of invasive placentation was conducted. An elective cesarean section was scheduled for 36 weeks of gestation. After exploratory laparotomy, the intra-abdominal findings showed an array of invasive placentation within the lower uterine segment. After initial bladder displacement, a transverse uterine incision was proceeded above the lower section of the uterus by avoiding the placental bed. A healthy baby girl of 5 pounds, 8 ounces was delivered. However, the patient had severe hemorrhage, and an immediate cesarean hysterectomy was performed. The placenta penetrated only up to the myometrium and reached the serosa to some extent, along with the formation of several hematomas on the bladder mucosa. The estimated blood loss was 6 L, and six units of whole blood and 1500 mL of free-frozen plasma (FFPs) were transfused. The patient's Foley's catheter was retained for 5 days. Her postoperative course was uneventful, and she was discharged on the sixth postoperative day in favorable recovery conditions.

Discharge Condition:
The patient's condition at the time of discharge was stable and favorable.

Discharge Medications:
No new medications were prescribed at the time of discharge.

Follow-up:
The patient is recommended to follow up with her Obstetrician-Gynecologist (OB-GYN) and undergo regular check-ups as advised.

Discharge Disposition:
The patient was discharged to her home in favorable recovery conditions.

Dates of Discharge: February 5, 2019

The patient presented to the clinic with moderate pain, erythema, and light edema at the sting site. The patient was discharged after clinical improvement.

Follow-up Care:

The patient was instructed to monitor the site of injury for any signs of infection and to return if he experiences any worsening of symptoms. No further treatment was required for this injury.

Final Diagnosis: Scorpion Sting 

Summary:

A 27-year-old male sales person presented with a scorpion sting on the left gluteal region after an incident at the Supply Centre of Belém, Pará. He was managed with anti-arachnid serum, symptomatic treatment, life support, and active observation for six hours. The incident was classified as low-risk and the patient was discharged after clinical improvement. No further treatment was required.

The patient was counselled and reassured regarding her symptoms.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [Redacted]
Gender: Female
Age: 45 years
Medical History: Diabetes mellitus, Hypertension, Iron deficiency anemia

Hospital course:
The patient was referred to our surgical outpatient department with complaints of mild intermittent pain in the left hypochondrium area for 10 months. On general physical examination, the patient was well-nourished, in mild pain, and had no pallor or jaundice. Abdominal examination revealed mild tenderness in the left hypochondrium area with no palpable masses. Laboratory examination revealed normal ranges for liver function test, renal function test, and the coagulation profile. Hormonal profiles were also found to be normal. CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large fatty mass measuring 16x11x10 cm on the left upper abdomen, displacing the left kidney inferiorly, laterally and partially encasing the medial aspect and the upper pole of left kidney reaching to the level of the left renal vessels inferiorly and abutting the diaphragm superiorly. It was also displacing the limbs of the left adrenal gland and abutting the posterior surface of the spleen and the inferior surface of the pancreatic tail. Small interspersed vascular branches from the left renal vessels noted along the margin and within the mass. The radiological impression was AML versus liposarcoma. The patient underwent CT guided biopsy for the adrenal mass which was negative for liposarcoma, and then was prepared for the surgery with preoperative percutaneous trans-arterial angiographic embolization of the feeding vessels followed by exploratory laparotomy and en-bloc resection of the left adrenal gland. Gross examination revealed a mass containing predominantly lobulated homogenous yellow fatty cut surfaces displacing the adrenal gland. There were no areas of hemorrhage or necrosis. Microscopically, the tumor composed of a mixture of mature adipose tissue, smooth muscle fibers, and aberrant dilated vasculatures. Immunohistochemical stains showed that the neoplastic cells are positive for Human Melanoma Black-45 (HMB-45) and Melan-A. The histological and immunohistochemical findings supported the diagnosis of adrenal AML. The postoperative recovery was uneventful, and the patient was discharged home at post-operative day 5 with regular follow-up in our outpatient department clinic. 

Discharge Diagnosis:
Adrenal Angiomyolipoma

Stable

Treatment/Interventions:
Percutaneous trans-arterial angiographic embolization, exploratory laparotomy, En-bloc resection of the left adrenal gland

Discharge Summary:

Patient was a 68-year-old male who was admitted to our neurological department with a history of visual impairments, psychomotoric deficits, sensory aphasia, and disorientation. The patient had been previously admitted twice to another hospital, displaying symptoms of hemianopsia to the right, and an enlargement of lesions in both hemispheres predominantly affecting the left white matter. The patient was later diagnosed with Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML).

Upon admission to our facility, the patient underwent extensive diagnostic procedures, including whole-body PET/CT, CSF analysis, blood tests, and biopsy, which revealed pleocytosis, raised protein concentration, normal HLA-DR-expression, and phenotyping of lymphocytes. The patient was also tested negative for various autoimmune encephalitis antibodies and immunodeficiency. The CSF PCR revealed a positive JCV, which was confirmed by a positive JCV-antibody-index in the serum.

During inpatient treatment, the patient was started on intravenous aciclovir to combat a positive tracheal exudate for HSV. The patient also developed seizures, which were managed with a combination of antiepileptic drugs. After the incidence of PML-IRIS, the patient was treated with high dose corticosteroids, which significantly reduced the seizures and allowed the anticonvulsive treatment to be scaled back.

Following the completion of treatment, the patient was transferred to a rehabilitation facility where the symptoms persisted. Unfortunately, the patient's condition worsened, and he eventually developed severe dysphagia, making oral intake of food and fluids impossible. The patient was transferred to a nursery home, but succumbed to a respiratory infection and pulmonary insufficiency.

Overall, the patient's treatment course was complex and involved multiple interventions in multiple systems.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:

Name: [REDACTED]
DOB: [REDACTED]
Gender: Female
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Admitting Diagnosis: Ectopic Adrenocorticotropic Hormone Syndrome (EAS) with lung masses
Discharge Diagnosis: EAS with lung masses, history of misdiagnosed microprolactinoma

Hospital Course:

The patient, a 30-year-old Vietnamese female, presented to the clinic with symptoms of fatigue, muscle weakness, memory loss, unintentional weight gain, hair loss, and amenorrhea. She had a history of microprolactinoma treated with cabergoline and a follow-up pituitary MRI showed normal results, but was unexpectedly discontinued due to misdiagnosis. Physical examination revealed facial acne, hirsutism, round face, lipodystrophy, central obesity, and muscle wasting in her lower extremities. Her morning cortisol level was elevated at 53.6 (normal range: 4.3-22.4mcg/dl), and ACTH level was significantly elevated at 147 (normal range: 0-46pg/ml). She underwent a low-dose 1mg and a high-dose 8mg dexamethasone suppression test, which failed to suppress cortisol. 

During her hospitalization, a chest x-ray was performed and showed two left upper lobe lung masses, which were confirmed to be well-differentiated NET on a biopsy. The Ki-67 proliferation index was low <2%, and the lung biopsy stained positive for synaptophysin, chromogranin, and pancytokeratin. A DEXA scan showed normal results, but a spontaneous rib fracture was diagnosed, confirming a diagnosis of osteoporosis as a result of excess endogenous glucocorticoid production.

Positron emission tomography showed hypermetabolic activity within the lung masses, left hilum, and mediastinal lymph nodes. Mild metabolic activity in the medial limb of the left adrenal gland was present, which could indicate a small adenoma.

The patient underwent a wedge resection of her left upper lobe and was treated with a steroid taper perioperatively. The patient's surgical margins were clear. She required intermittent insulin therapy for hyperglycemia.

The patient was given a diagnosis of EAS with lung masses, with a history of misdiagnosed microprolactinoma. She was discharged with recommendations for follow-up care and management. 

Final Diagnoses:

1. Ectopic Adrenocorticotropic Hormone Syndrome (EAS) with lung masses, confirmed on biopsy as well-differentiated NET.
2. Misdiagnosed microprolactinoma.

Procedures:

1. Wedge resection of left upper lobe to remove lung masses.

Medications on Discharge:

1. None.

Follow-up Care:

1. Patient recommended to follow up with an endocrinologist to manage EAS and osteoporosis.
2. Patient recommended to follow up with a pulmonologist for monitoring of lung masses.
3. Patient recommended for regular lab monitoring including cortisol and ACTH levels, electrolytes, and blood glucose levels.

Hospital Course:

This 32-year-old previously healthy male patient presented to our outpatient department with complaints of high fever, sore throat, mild diarrhea, and severe myalgia in various muscles of the body. On physical examination, the patient showed no signs of paresis, muscle tenderness, or skin eruptions. A differential diagnosis was established, which included periodic paralysis, myasthenia gravis, adult-onset Still’s disease, fibromyalgia, and chronic fatigue syndrome. To rule out the possibility of these diseases, a series of tests were conducted, including an antigen-based rapid diagnostic test for influenza virus and testing for circulating anti-nuclear, anti-acetylcholine receptor, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies. The patient was also tested for coxsackievirus and echovirus.

The patient was finally diagnosed with severe epidemic myalgia caused by HPeV-3 infection. The virus was detected in the patient's stool and blood samples, as well as his son's stool sample. It was confirmed that his son transmitted the HPeV-3 virus to him. The patient's parents, wife, and newborn daughter were tested for the virus, but all their results were negative.

The patient's severe myalgia, fever, and orchiodynia gradually improved without any specific treatment. The patient's cytokine levels were also measured at the initial visit and 2 weeks later, and while his TNF-α, IL-10, and IL-12 levels were below their respective cutoff values, his IL-6 level was elevated at both visits.

The patient had no difficulty moving his whole body after a week, and there were no residual symptoms or sequelae.

Final Diagnosis:

Severe epidemic myalgia caused by HPeV-3 infection.

Condition on Discharge:

The patient's condition had significantly improved and all symptoms had resolved.

Medications on Discharge:

N/A

Follow-Up Instructions:

The patient was advised to follow a healthy lifestyle and seek immediate medical attention if he experienced any new symptoms. No specific follow-up instructions were advised.

Hospital Course Summary:

Patient is a 67-year-old female with a history of scoliosis and early osteoporosis who presented with a non-productive cough, unintentional weight loss, and daytime fatigue. Chest radiograph showed possible right middle lobe pneumonia. Treatment with levofloxacin was initiated, but patient developed severe diarrhea due to Clostridium difficile colitis. A CT scan of the chest was performed, revealing right middle lobe and lingula bronchiectasis, nodularity, and mucus impaction. Patient was put on airborne isolation for pulmonary tuberculosis and an induced sputum sample was negative for MTB PCR probe. However, bronchoscopy with lavage showed smear positive for AFB, and eventually grew M. avium.

The patient was discharged from the hospital on a combination of ethambutol, rifampin, and azithromycin three times weekly to be continued for three months. Repeat CT imaging at 6 months showed an improvement with fewer lung nodules and less mucus impaction. 

Overall, the patient has responded well to treatment for M. avium infection with significant improvement in her respiratory symptoms and ability to gain weight. Follow-up care will be important to monitor her progress.

Hospital Course:
The 79-year-old female was admitted for evaluation of palpable tumors in the breasts. Bilateral high grade invasive breast cancer was diagnosed based on mammography and confirmed by biopsy. Staging examination revealed a 6 cm mass in the right kidney, which was found to be a RCC. The patient underwent bilateral mastectomy and right nephrectomy. Immunohistochemistry analysis revealed metastasis of breast cancer to the RCC.
Treatment:
The patient was treated with trastuzumab, anastrozole, and irradiation of the right chest wall and supraclavicular region as palliative therapy. Palliative radiotherapy of the humerus was also performed, followed by therapy with fulvestrant and denosumab after the development of a new metastasis.
Outcome:
Despite treatment, the patient reported worsening of chronic heart failure and rapid deterioration of general health status. The patient passed away 3 years after diagnosis of breast cancer while in mostly stable conditions of cancer disease.

History:
The patient, an 88-year-old female with gastric cancer, was admitted to the emergency department (ED) after experiencing cardiac arrest in an outpatient clinic. She had a downtime of several minutes without chest compressions. The patient received cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) by emergency medical services at the site of the incident, which was continued by the ED staff upon arrival.

Upon arrival in the ED, routine procedures were performed, including rhythm and pulse check, along with other tests. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed that the patient had a collection of echogenic material in the ventricles associated with cardiac standstill. Given the cardiac standstill and echodensities, it was decided to stop resuscitation. Unfortunately, despite the best efforts of the medical team, the patient could not be resuscitated, and she passed away in the ED.

The patient died in the ED. No further clinical report was deemed necessary.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 32-year-old female
Date of Admission: [date]
Date of Discharge: [date]

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted after experiencing an accident 3-months postpartum with symptoms including global aphasia, dizziness, and paralysis of right limbs. A brain scan confirmed moderate-sized infarcts involving the left frontal-parietal cortex, and magnetic resonance angiography showed dissection forming in the proximal initial segment of left internal carotid artery with severe local stenosis. Medication was given without interventional therapy, and, 10 days from onset, clinical symptoms improved significantly.

Lab Results:
Complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, glucose, total protein, albumin, thyroid function tests, antinuclear antibody (ANA), antiextractable nuclear antigen (ENA) antibodies, anti-double stranded DNA (dsDNA) antibodies, complement, immunoglobulins, and rheumatoid factor (RF) were normal.

Imaging:
Computed tomography (CT) showed no cerebral hemorrage, and Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed the infarcts. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) later confirmed the dissection in the proximal initial segment of left internal carotid artery with severe local stenosis, as well as collateral pathways through various arteries and branches.

Treatment:
Aspirin (100 mg/day) and clopidogrel (75 mg/day) were given, and no emergency endovascular treatment was performed. Medication was continued without interventional therapy, and clinical symptoms improved.

Follow-up:
Repeat DSA was performed at 3-month follow-up. Left CCA angiography showed residual aneurysm in the area where carotid dissection occurred originally, with no significant stenosis. Furthermore, a small artery originated from the posterior vertical segment of cavernous ICA, and the distal segment was not clearly visible.

Outcome:
The patient remained clinically stable and was very satisfied with the treatment.

Follow-up Plan:
No further treatment is required for the patient at present, but consistent monitoring and follow-up is recommended.

The patient presented with advanced primary open-angle glaucoma in both eyes and underwent phacoemulsification combined with KDB goniotomy in the right eye and phaco alone in the left eye. Advanced primary open-angle glaucoma

Toric lenses were placed to correct his astigmatism, but postoperatively, the lenses had rotated, and the right eye's astigmatism had shifted significantly. The patient was admitted to the hospital for assessment of ongoing minor choreiform movements and left sided paraesthesia. Evaluation revealed fixed-dilated pupils and a cerebral MRI scan showed extensive periventricular deep white matter hyperintensity and a lesion in the right basal ganglia. Iris OCT showed absence of thickening in the central portion and a distinct hyporeflective layer just anterior to the iris pigment epithelium (IPE) near the pupillary border. OCTA showed flow signal within the radial filiform projections. The patient was diagnosed with MMD-like cerebral arteriopathy in association with PDA and congenital mydriasis, related to ACTA2 mutations.

Treatment and Management:
Therapy with aspirin was continued.

Follow-up and Recommendations:
The patient should continue therapy with aspirin as recommended by the physician.

The patient's prostate cancer is metastatic and his treatment with pembrolizumab is ongoing.

Hospital Course Summary:

Patient, a 90-year-old female, was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus over a decade ago. Upon presentation, her HbA1c levels were well-controlled with glimepiride and metformin. However, due to drug overdose concerns, the medication was discontinued, and the patient was prescribed a low hypoglycemia risk, dipeptidyl peptidase 4 inhibitor, teneligliptin. Within six months, the patient's HbA1c levels increased to 10.2%. To minimize hypoglycemia risk, 2mg of exenatide-LAR injections were administered once weekly. These injections led to a rapid decrease in HbA1c levels. Subsequently, the dosage frequency was reduced to once-a-month administration, allowing the patient to receive treatment easily, despite cognitive loss. No changes were observed in liver and renal functions, and the patient's body weight remained stable throughout. Home care providers administered drugs without complication after the patient sustained a spinal compression fracture. The patient did not exhibit any adverse events with exenatide-LAR treatment. 

Findings:

- Type 2 diabetes mellitus
- Stable renal and liver function 
- No adverse events with exenatide-LAR treatment
- No changes in body weight 
- Stable HbA1c levels with once-a-month exenatide-LAR administration

Impressions:

- Well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus with low hypoglycemia risk drug administration 
- Successful reduction in HbA1c levels with exenatide-LAR treatment without adverse effects, allowing for easy administration despite cognitive decline

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 37-year-old Japanese man, was admitted to our hospital due to multiple brain metastases. On physical examination, there were no abnormalities except for elevated levels of tumor markers. Bronchoscopy was performed on the fourth day of admission, revealing adenocarcinoma cells exhibiting a papillary pattern. The patient was diagnosed with ALK-positive lung cancer with cerebral metastases and started on alectinib. Pulmonary and hilar lymph node lesion reduction were found on chest CT and whole brain irradiation was performed for brain metastatic lesions.

Approximately 96 days after start of treatment, the patient experienced headaches and nausea and was re-hospitalized for systemic management, including pain care. The patient's Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status was lower than that at the onset of alectinib administration, and oral medications were given for pain relief. A few days after start of oral medication, palliative treatment was started using morphine hydrochloride infusion due to difficulty in taking orally administered medications. Administration of alectinib was discontinued, and the patient subsequently experienced a worsening of his general condition and state of consciousness.

After his death, pathologic dissection was performed, revealing severe cerebral edema and compression of the brain stem. The primary lesion in the left lung was re-evaluated histopathologically, and the proportion of the squamous cell carcinoma component was higher than that of the left lung.

Summary:
The patient was admitted to our hospital with multiple brain metastases and was diagnosed with ALK-positive lung cancer. Treatment with alectinib was started, resulting in lesion reduction. However, the patient experienced a worsening of his general condition and was re-hospitalized for systemic management and pain care. Administration of alectinib was discontinued, and the patient subsequently died due to respiratory arrest caused by brain stem compression. Pathologic dissection revealed a higher proportion of the squamous cell carcinoma component than the left lung.

Hospital Course:

The 76-year-old Korean female was admitted with symptoms of jaw opening restriction and dysphagia. She had been diagnosed with TMD with disc dislocation previously and had symptoms that worsened over the course of 10 days, prompting a visit to the hospital's department of neurology. Tests, including brain MRI, neck/head CT, and VFSS, were performed but did not provide a conclusive diagnosis, with only cricopharyngeal dysfunction identified via VFSS. She was diagnosed with disc displacement without reduction with limited opening according to the Diagnostic Criteria for Temporomandibular Disorders.

The patient received integrative KM treatment, including acupuncture, herbal acupuncture, cupping therapy, CMT and herbal medicine. She also received dry cupping therapy on the posterior neck region and upper trapezius muscle at eight tender points once a day for 5 min. Upon completion of treatment, the patient's left lateral excursion increased from 10 to 15 mm, right lateral excursion increased from 3 to 11 mm, and protrusion movement increased from 5 to 7 mm. Pain VAS of the left TMJ and temporalis muscle decreased from 16.5 to 3 mm and 31 to 10 mm, respectively. JFLS-8 score decreased from 52 to 20.

The patient's maxillary condyle remained in the mandibular fossa even when she attempted to open her mouth widely at the time of admission; however, the left mandibular condyle was slightly translated to the mandibular fossa and moved forward to the articular tubercle 22 days after admission. The patient could breathe voluntarily and could eat soft and liquid diet without aspiration after she was able to open her mouth to 15 mm, and the Leven tube was removed 9 days after admission. No severe adverse effects were observed during the treatment period. Minor bleeding at the acupuncture site or BV injection site was observed. One of her front teeth, which had been shaking in the past, was missing regardless of the treatment.

The patient was discharged from the hospital and followed up by telephone on February 14, 2019. The absence of TMD symptoms and dysphagia after discharge was confirmed. The patient reported that she had been doing well without recurrence for two years after she was discharged from the KM hospital.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient, a healthy 7-year-old boy, was referred from the dental emergency department to the pediatric dentistry department at the Dental School of Casablanca due to dental trauma. Clinical examination revealed a flexible splint on the maxillary teeth and a coronal restoration on tooth 11 with a glass ionomer. Radiographic examination showed incomplete root formation of both central incisors.

Emergency treatment was carried out on the same day, and repositioning of tooth 11 was done with gentle digital pressure. One week after the trauma, the patient presented with intraoral swelling on tooth 11 revealing necrosis. An endodontic treatment was performed, and calcium hydroxide was placed as intracanal medication.

After six months, a radiolucent lesion in the periapical region was observed in tooth 21. A negative response to the cold test confirmed pulp necrosis, and revascularization was performed due to the immaturity of the tooth and thinness of the root. MTA was placed in the cervical third of the root canal, and the access cavity was sealed with a glass ionomer.

Follow-up appointments were scheduled, with the patient being recalled four weeks after the first appointment. In the second session, the root canal was irrigated gently with 2% sodium hypochlorite and saline solution, followed by MTA placement in the cervical third of the root canal.

Three months after revascularization treatment, visible root edification was observed, and after 24 months of apexification treatment on tooth 11, an apical barrier was formed. The apical third was sealed using MTA, and the coronal two-third with warm gutta-percha.

The patient was clinically and radiologically asymptomatic at the time of discharge. Follow-up appointments were scheduled to monitor the patient's progress.

Discharge Diagnosis: Dental Trauma 

Condition at Discharge: Asymptomatic 

Discharge Instructions:

The patient is advised to maintain good oral hygiene, including brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and flossing once a day. The patient should avoid hard foods until the root has completely formed. Follow-up appointments have been scheduled to monitor the patient's progress.

Primary Care Provider: Not specified

Discharge Summary:

Patient 1, a seven-year-old boy, was admitted to the hospital with symptoms of muscle weakness, inactivity, and hypotonia. Initial laboratory tests showed elevated levels of lactate dehydrogenase, CK, and aldolase. Electromyography (EMG) results indicated low amplitude and duration of the motor unit action potential (MUAP).

Further investigations at age two years and six months revealed weak and patchy sarcolemmal labeling with merosin antibody on immunohistochemical (IHC) analysis. Muscle biopsy showed severe myopathic atrophy with endomysial fibrosis, consistent with a diagnosis of muscular dystrophy.

During the course of his hospitalization, the patient developed kyphosis, short elbow, and contractures of the elbow and wrist. However, his cognitive abilities remained unimpaired, with an IQ score estimated to be 160. The patient was discharged with a working diagnosis of MDC1A based on his clinical and biochemical findings.

Follow-up laboratory investigations at age seven showed a decline in CK and aldolase levels. The patient was able to attend a regular school without any significant restrictions.

The hospital course was marked by a comprehensive evaluation that led to the identification of a rare muscular dystrophy disorder. Appropriate supportive and rehabilitative measures were instituted during the hospitalization and will continue to be managed on an outpatient basis.

Overall, the patient received timely and thorough medical care throughout his hospitalization, with satisfactory resolution of some of his presenting symptoms. Further follow-up is required to monitor the patient's long-term prognosis and outcomes.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 76-year-old male linguistics professor

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the emergency room with a two-week history of worsening confusion, memory issues, word-finding difficulty, and unsteady gait. He also experienced agitation, hallucinations, and weakness. His symptoms progressed with the patient too weak to ambulate and experiencing incontinence of urine and stool. 

Medical History:
The patient had a history of coronary artery disease, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, asthma, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. There was no personal or family history of malignancy or dementia. He had never been screened for malignancy. There was no history of hunting or consuming game meat. 

Physical Examination:
On exam, the patient had stable vitals. His mucous membranes were dry, and his jugular venous pressure (JVP) was flat. Cardiac, respiratory, and abdominal exams were unremarkable. Neurological exam revealed a slight upward gaze palsy, and velocity-dependent hypertonia in the upper extremities. Reflexes and sensation were intact.

Lab and Imaging Studies:
White blood cell count was 2.7 × 109, hemoglobin was 134 g/L, and platelets were 196 × 109. The electrolytes and extended electrolytes were within normal limits except for a low sodium level. MRI showed diffuse parenchymal volume loss and mild microangiopathic changes. EEG was abnormal but nonspecific. CSF showed a nucleated cell count within normal limits, normal glucose, and slightly elevated protein. Oligoclonal bands were not detected in the CSF. 

Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with sCJD based on the postmortem autopsy that demonstrated microspongiosis, neuronal loss, and gliosis in the cortex, hippocampus, basal ganglia, and cerebellum.

Disposition:
The patient was discharged to a palliative care facility where he passed away eight weeks after presentation. 

Follow-up:
None specified.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:

Patient Name: Not provided
Gender: Male
Age: 48 years
Admission Date: Not provided
Discharge Date: Not provided

Medical History:

- Diagnosis of Desquamative Interstitial Pneumonia (DIP) attributed to smoking cigarettes and cannabis
- HIV Positive
- Excellent control of HIV infection
- Underwent bilateral lung transplant
- Developed an episode of Grade A1 minimal acute cellular rejection
- Had an enterovirus/rhinovirus graft infection with significant allograft dysfunction

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the hospital for bilateral lung transplant due to his worsening interstitial lung disease. The patient had undergone a surgical lung biopsy in the past, which had confirmed his diagnosis of DIP. His HIV infection was under good control with no history of AIDS-defining illnesses. Prior to transplantation, he had been taking cobicistat, elvitegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir for HIV management. However, this regimen was changed to abacavir, dolutegravir, and lamivudine due to pharmacokinetic interactions that could affect the transplant.

The patient was induced with basiliximab, methylprednisolone, and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) at the time of transplantation. The induction immunosuppression was followed by maintenance immunosuppression that included MMF, prednisone, and tacrolimus. The patient had a smooth hospital course with no complications, and he was discharged 18 days post-transplant.

During his stay, the patient had an episode of Grade A1 minimal acute cellular rejection, which was not treated initially. The patient also had an enterovirus/rhinovirus graft infection with significant allograft dysfunction detected 11 months after the transplant. At that time, he received a short course of methylprednisolone, and his prednisone dose was subsequently tapered down to a baseline of 10 mg daily.

The patient's markers for HIV infection remained under good control throughout his stay. Upon discharge, the patient had normal functional status, no dyspnea, and normal ambulatory oxygenation.

Follow-up Recommendations:

The patient is advised to continue taking his medications as prescribed. Follow-up with his primary care physician and lung transplant team is recommended at regular intervals to monitor his lung function and manage any potential complications. The patient should return to the hospital immediately if he experiences any shortness of breath, fever, or any other symptoms that concern him. Additionally, the patient is encouraged to maintain a healthy lifestyle and quit smoking to prevent any possible complications from the lung transplant.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [To be determined]
Age: 72 years
Sex: Female

Hospital Course:

Presentation:

The patient was admitted to our department on February 8, 2017, complaining of severe cough and white sputum with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status (PS) of 2.

Medical History:

The patient underwent radical resection of the left lung cancer in July 2011 because of a mass revealed by computed tomography (CT) of chest. Pathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, with a stage of IIIA (pT1N2M0) based on the NCCN tumor-node-metastasis classification system. The patient received gemcitabine and carboplatin regimen as adjuvant chemotherapy for 4 cycles, followed by paclitaxel and carboplatin as first-line chemotherapy for 4 cycles as tumor recurrence and intrapulmonary metastases were detected during routine review on July 19, 2013. The active EGFR mutation (L858R in exon 21) was found in November 2013, and thus she was prescribed icotinib orally at a dose of 125 mg 3× a day as maintenance therapy. In October 2014, the tumor was evaluated as PD again, which led to second-line chemotherapy involving docetaxel monotherapy for 4 cycles. The patient received paclitaxel monotherapy for 4 cycles as the regimen was discontinued due to her severe nausea, vomiting, anorexia, and fatigue while being prescribed with gemcitabine and cisplatinum as third-line chemotherapy. The genetic analysis using her peripheral blood sample displayed that T790 M was negative, and thus icotinib was continued as maintenance therapy. 

On August 27, 2015, the chest CT showed progressive tumor in the left lung, and gemcitabine and cisplatinum were prescribed as third-line chemotherapy, which was discontinued due to her severe side effects, and paclitaxel monotherapy was continued. The patient was prescribed apatinib alone orally at a dose of 250 mg/d after being admitted with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status (PS) of 2 on February 8, 2017, which led to remarkable tumor regression. The chemotherapy regimen was continued, and the chest CT was performed every 2 months to assess the tumor. On October 23, 2017, the chest CT indicated stable disease in the left lung, but the woman attended our hospital for chest pain with a bad ECOG PS of 3 two months later on December 15, 2017. The chest CT verified PD of left lung cancer and serious infection of both lungs, and although she received anti-infective and supportive treatments, she died of respiratory failure 2 weeks later.

Conclusion:

The patient had been taking icotinib as maintenance therapy between line-to-line chemotherapy until the administration of apatinib in her whole course of anti-tumor treatment. Hypertension of grade 1 occurred in her whole course of apatinib treatment, which was tolerated and manageable with no dose adjustment or drug withdrawal.

Hospital Course:
This 65-year old male patient presented with complaints of severe pain in his right hand which gradually worsened. The clinical examination revealed swollen, warm, and erythematous nodules on his hand, exhibiting spontaneous outflow of serous fluid. The patient had a history of anti-CCP and RF positive RA. The diagnosis of Orf disease was made in an immunocompromised patient with a history of occupational exposure to sheep. Surgical debridement of the inflamed cutaneous area was performed. Treatment was started with amoxicillin with clavulanic acid, which proved ineffective. Immunosuppressive drugs were discontinued, except for methylprednisolone, which was increased to maintain RA in remission. Ten days after the aforementioned interventions, the patient's hand improved, and two months later, the nodules improved, leaving a scar at the initial sites of inflammation. RA remained in remission, and the patient was discharged with a regular follow-up. 
 
Diagnosis:
Orf disease in an immunocompromised patient with a history of occupational exposure to sheep. 

Hospital Course summary:
This is a 65-year-old male patient, who presented to the outpatient clinic with severe pain in his right hand and was subsequently diagnosed with Orf disease. The patient had a three-year history of anti-CCP positive and RF positive RA. The diagnosis was made in an immunocompromised patient with a history of occupational exposure to sheep. The patient underwent surgical debridement of the inflamed cutaneous area and was initiated on amoxicillin with clavulanic acid. However, the lesion did not improve. Immunosuppressive drugs were discontinued, except for methylprednisolone, which was increased to maintain RA in remission. Ten days after the interventions, the patient’s hand showed improvement. Concurrently inflammatory markers improved. Two months later, the nodules improved, leaving a scar at the initial sites of inflammation. RA remained in remission, and the patient was discharged with a regular follow-up.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
- Name: [Redacted]
- Age: 28
- Sex: Female
- Admission Date: [Redacted]
- Discharge Date: [Redacted]
- Reason for Hospitalization: Bronchoalveolar lavage

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital for bronchoalveolar lavage to evaluate newly discovered cavitary lesions. Prior to the procedure, the patient's medical history was reviewed and revealed that she had severe pulmonary hypertension secondary to Gerbode defect, a left to right shunt between the left ventricle and the right atrium. The patient was currently on several medications, including sildenafil, treprostinil, and ambrisentan, for her pulmonary hypertension.

The anaesthetic approach for the bronchoscopy was carefully planned due to the severity of the patient's pulmonary hypertension. Topicalization of the airway was done using 4% lidocaine, and a low-dose bolus of dexmedetomidine was given to avoid suppression of spontaneous respiration. The patient was placed on OptiFlow intranasal delivery of oxygen at 70 L/min while in the sitting position. Dexmedetomidine continuous infusion was given throughout the procedure. Fentanyl was given in divided doses to manage coughing, and ondansetron was given prior to the conclusion of the procedure to prevent nausea.

The total time from induction to emergence was 23 minutes. The patient's oxygen saturation was maintained above 96% for the entire procedure, and mean arterial pressure was maintained at 80-90 mmHg. The patient was alert and responsive to verbal stimuli throughout the procedure.

The patient was transported from the bronchoscopy suite to the post-anaesthesia recovery unit, where she met all criteria for discharge to regular nursing floor. No complications were noted post-operatively. The patient was very satisfied with the procedure and had minimal recall.

Discharge Instructions:
At the time of discharge, the patient was advised to continue with her current medications as prescribed by her primary care physician. The patient was also instructed to follow up with her pulmonologist for further evaluation of her pulmonary hypertension.

Follow-Up:
The patient will follow up with her pulmonologist for further evaluation of her pulmonary hypertension.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 10-week-old female Golden Retriever puppy, was admitted to the University of Florida Small Animal Hospital for further evaluation and exploration of surgical treatment options for her congenital anomalies. The patient was bright, alert, and in good condition on presentation and underwent advanced imaging, including contrast computed tomography, vaginocystourethrogram, and retrograde colonogram, to further define the abnormalities. Orthopedic and vertebral anomalies were ruled out on abdominal radiography, and the visible portion of the thorax was within normal limits. Lidocaine was administered during the procedure, and the patient remained under general anesthesia with isoflurane inhalant. On examination, the left anal orifice was situated 3-4 mm off midline, was smaller in diameter, and had a slit-like appearance compared to the right anal opening. The patient had mild discomfort on rectal digital palpation and a pain response when palpated more cranially. Further physical examination revealed a complete ventral to dorsal soft tissue septum bisecting the vulva. Abdominal radiography revealed a normal-sized stomach and normal intestinal and colon distribution. An aberrant cranial mesenteric artery and a completely absent caudal mesenteric artery were observed. Due to the urogenital findings and urinary incontinence, the owner elected humane euthanasia.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was a 10-week-old female Golden Retriever puppy with congenital anomalies of the anal and urogenital regions. The patient was referred to the University of Florida Small Animal Hospital for further evaluation and exploration of surgical treatment options. Advanced imaging, including contrast computed tomography, vaginocystourethrogram, and retrograde colonogram, was performed to further define the abnormalities. The patient had mild discomfort on rectal digital palpation and a pain response when palpated more cranially. An aberrant cranial mesenteric artery and a completely absent caudal mesenteric artery were observed on abdominal radiography. Due to the urogenital findings and urinary incontinence, the owner decided on humane euthanasia. A necropsy was performed, and the final diagnosis was urinary bladder bifurcation with vaginal and colonic duplication. The patient remained bright, alert, and in good condition throughout her hospitalization.

Hospital Course:
The patient presented with a 1-year history of progressive pharyngeal discomfort and was diagnosed with a Killian-Jamieson diverticulum (KJD) via an esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) and cervical computed tomography (CT). The patient underwent a diverticulectomy with cricopharyngeus myotomy and proximal esophageal myotomy. Postoperatively, the patient experienced staple line leakage and cervical redness and pain but responded well to fasting and percutaneous abscess drainage. The patient had no further complications and was asymptomatic at 5 months post-surgery.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was discharged from our institution post-diverticulectomy. The patient was placed in the supine position with a pad underneath her shoulders to hyperextend her neck. A collar incision was performed, and the diverticulum was mobilized after identifying and preserving the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve was found immediately anterior to the base of the diverticulum. The diverticulum was resected at its base using a linear stapler (ETS-Flex45). The patient experienced staple line leakage and cervical redness and pain but responded well to fasting and percutaneous abscess drainage. A gastrograffin swallow examination was performed, revealing no evidence of leakage, and the patient began oral intake. At 5 months post-surgery, the patient was asymptomatic.

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Age: 60 years old
Gender: Female
Admission Date: [redacted]
Discharge Date: [redacted]
Admitting Diagnosis: Low back pain with lateral aspect of left leg pain and severe neurogenic claudication

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with a chief complaint of low back pain with lateral aspect of left leg pain and severe neurogenic claudication. Imaging studies revealed narrowing of L4-L5 disc space and degenerative spondylolisthesis of L4-L5 with severe bilateral foraminal stenosis and moderate central stenosis. She underwent MIS-OLIF with decompressive laminectomy and fixation with cortical bone trajectory screws at L4-L5. During the surgery, the left common iliac artery was identified in the operating field. As a result, the retractor blades and stability pin were removed and the guide wire was replaced more posteriorly. A 6° lordotic-angled MIS-OLIF PEEK cage was inserted into the intervertebral disc space. However, the final position of the cage revealed the tantalum marker had been pushed more to the right side of the vertebral body. Posterior decompressive laminectomy at L4-L5 and cortical bone trajectory screw fixation was then performed in the prone position. Postoperatively, the patient developed pain and numbness on her right leg corresponding to L4 dermatome due to the position of MIS-OLIF PEEK cage being placed too deep over the edge of the right lateral vertebral body.

A second operation was performed to reposition the MIS-OLIF PEEK cage. Unfortunately, removal of the cage was unsuccessful as it became stuck and attached to the vertebral bodies. The patient was then placed in reverse jack-knife position for opening of the right lateral intervertebral disc space, and the MIS-OLIF PEEK cage was gently pulled back and adjusted to an acceptable position.  

At 3 months follow-up, her back and leg pain had significantly improved, and her right leg numbness disappeared. The Oswestry Disability Index was 64.4 at preoperative time and was 26 and 20 at 2 weeks and 3 months postoperative, respectively.

Discharge Diagnosis:

Low back pain with lateral aspect of left leg pain and severe neurogenic claudication with degenerative spondylolisthesis of L4-L5

Hospital Course:

The patient underwent MIS-OLIF with decompressive laminectomy and fixation with cortical bone trajectory screws at L4-L5, followed by a subsequent surgery to reposition the MIS-OLIF PEEK cage which had been malpositioned. Postoperatively, the patient experienced improvement in her back and leg pain, as well as disappearance of her right leg numbness. The patient was discharged in good condition with recommendations for physical therapy, follow-up appointments, and close monitoring of any new symptoms.

Reason for Admission:
The patient was admitted due to a history of 2-hour chest pain and numbness of left upper arm before 5 days. The electrocardiogram (ECG) indicated acute inferior wall myocardial infarction (MI).

The patient presented at 8-month follow-up with an anticardiolipin antibody level less than 2.0 RU/ml and a lipid profile showing a TG of 0.64 mmol/L, TC of 4.15 mmol/L, LDL-C of 3.47 mmol/L, and HDL-C of 1.01 mmol/L.

The patient was diagnosed with acute inferior wall myocardial infarction (MI) which was treated with anticoagulation, double antiplatelets, and lipid-modulating therapy. CAG showed RCA stenosis with 70% in-stent restenosis. At 6-month follow-up, the patient showed a good recovery with a level of anticardiolipin antibody (ELISA method) less than 2.0 RU/ml and a lipid profile within a normal range. At 8-month follow-up, the patient continued to show a good recovery with a steady decline of lipid levels.

Recommendations:
The patient is advised to maintain a healthy lifestyle, including regular exercise and a diet low in saturated fats, to manage his cholesterol levels. The patient should visit the hospital for follow-up tests and treatment as prescribed. Date of Admission: [Date]
Date of Discharge: [Date]

Hospital Course: The patient was admitted to the pediatric unit at Civil Hospital Karachi (CHK) with complaints of fever, left-sided abdominal pain, and burning micturition. A thorough examination and diagnostic workup led to the diagnosis of hydatid cyst in the spleen. The patient was managed with multiple IV antibiotics and was started on oral albendazole. Follow-up ultrasounds showed reduction in size of lesions in the spleen and eventual disappearance of the lesions. The patient was discharged in a stable condition.

Clinical Findings: The patient presented with high-grade fever, left-sided abdominal pain, and burning micturition. Physical examination revealed pallor, tenderness in the left hypochondrium, and multiple enlarged lymph nodes at para-aortic, peripancreatic, perisplenic, and mesenteric regions.

Diagnostic Assessment: Laboratory tests including CBC, urinalysis, and blood cultures were performed. Elevated ESR and CRP were noted. An ultrasound of the abdomen revealed hypoechoic lesions over splenic parenchyma. Contrast-enhanced CT scan showed multiple ill-defined hypo-dense areas in the spleen suggestive of a splenic abscess. ELISA-based detection of IgG antibodies for echinococcus was positive.

Treatment: The patient was managed with triple antibiotic regimen of ceftriaxone, metronidazole, and cloxacillin in addition to oral 200mg albendazole twice a day. Repeat ultrasounds were performed every four weeks to monitor the size of lesions in the spleen. No surgical intervention was required.

Outcome: The patient's clinical condition improved with treatment and was ultimately discharged in a stable condition.

Follow-up: The patient was advised to continue oral albendazole and scheduled for regular follow-up.

Impression/Diagnosis: Hydatid cyst in the spleen. 

Discharge Medications: Oral albendazole 200mg twice a day.

Instructions: The patient should continue with oral albendazole and follow-up as scheduled. Any new or worsening symptoms should be reported immediately.

Signed,
[Name], MD
Pediatrician

Hospital Course:

The patient presented to the emergency department with worsening left flank pain, nausea, and subjective fevers. Physical examination findings were significant for left lower quadrant tenderness. The initial vital signs were significant for hypertension, tachycardia, and tachypnea. Lab work showed leukocytosis and an elevated creatinine value. The urinalysis revealed significant WBCs and RBCs per HPF with positive leukocyte esterase but no bacteria, and initial urine culture was contaminated. Diagnosis:

Plan:

- Continue levofloxacin
- Expectant management for ureteral stent
- Follow-up with urologist as an outpatient

Summary:

The stones were treated with a left ureteral stent placement and subsequent URS-LL procedure, and the patient clinically improved. The patient was discharged home with instruction to follow-up with a urologist as an outpatient.

[Discharge Summary]

Patient Name: [Name]
Medical Record Number: [MRN]

Admission Date: [Date]
Discharge Date: [Date]
Length of Stay: [Number of days]

Admitting Diagnosis: Abdominal Pain
Final Diagnosis: Biliary Cystadenocarcinoma

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with complaints of one-month-old abdominal pain. The initial evaluation revealed a large mass in the liver, which was suspected to be biliary cystadenocarcinoma. The patient underwent nonanatomic liver, cholecystectomy, and extrahepatic biliary tract resection surgery with anastomoses. Postoperative complications such as bile leakage were managed with drainage and stent placement. The patient received chemotherapy after surgery and remained disease-free after six years of follow-up.

Clinical Findings:

The patient's physical examination was unremarkable except for a palpable mass in the epigastric region. Laboratory findings, liver function tests, and tumor markers were all normal.

Imaging:

Abdominal computed tomography (CT) in our center revealed a 17x12x17 cm mass with solid and cystic components in the left lobe of the liver. Postoperative magnetic resonance imaging and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography revealed a leakage from the hepaticojejunostomy. Furthermore, intrahepatic bile duct dilatation was observed secondary to stenosis in both anastomoses.

Histopathology:

The excision specimen consisted of a 25x19x10 cm well-circumscribed mass with multiple areas of cystic degeneration, hemorrhage, and myxoid change. The microscopic examination revealed widespread cystic degeneration, hemorrhage, and necrosis along with small hypercellular nodules and myxoid areas harboring neoplastic cells. Neoplastic cells displayed moderate pleomorphism and nuclear hyperchromasia. Immunohistochemically, neoplastic cells were strongly and diffusely positive for CD56 and focally positive for vimentin, CD10, WT1 (cytoplasmic), Factor VIII, and desmin. Negativity was observed for Pancytokeratin (CK), ER, PR, CD31, lysozyme, smooth muscle actin, CD68, myoD1, HepPar1, and CD34.

Discharge Plan:

The patient was discharged in a stable condition with follow-up appointments and monitoring scheduled as appropriate. A detailed medical report will be provided to the patient's primary healthcare provider for further management.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 29-year-old male, presented at our hospital with a history of chronic anemia since childhood. The patient underwent gastroscopy and colonoscopy with normal results. Due to the persistence of the anemia, despite symptomatic treatment with oral iron, it was decided to extend the study with imaging techniques. A simple abdominal X-ray was performed revealing phleboliths in the right side of the pelvis. 

Diagnostic Results:
A small bowel study (SBS) with barium was performed, which showed poor distensibility and irregular contour in the distal ileum. Computed tomography enterography (CTE) was performed, which showed phleboliths and transmural wall thickening in a 10cm segment of the distal ileum with homogeneous contrast enhancement. No inflammatory changes were seen in mesenteric fat. No abdominal lymph nodes suggestive of malignancy were seen, and there was no involvement of adjacent organs. Based on these findings, the most likely preoperative diagnosis was haemangioma of the distal ileum. 

Treatment:
A laparotomy and segmental small bowel resection revealed a 10-cm ileum lesion that on pathology examination suggested a vascular nature due to its bluish purple coloration, compressibility, and presence of varices on its surface. The histopathological assessment revealed a vascular lesion compatible with haemangioma. After the patient recovered from surgery, he remained asymptomatic. 

Summary:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with chronic anemia and underwent several diagnostic tests, concluding the diagnosis of haemangioma of the distal ileum. A laparotomy and segmental small bowel resection was performed, followed by the successful removal of the lesion. The patient recovered well and was discharged without any major complications.

Hospital Course and Diagnosis:

The patient, a 57-year-old man with a significant medical history of hypertension and type II diabetes, presented to the emergency department with one day history of acute dizziness, retrosternal burning pain, and low serum sodium. The patient was initially investigated for coronary artery disease, with normal ECG and negative serial troponins, and was discharged on betahistine. Three days later, the patient presented again with increasing severity of dizziness, nausea, fatigue, and generalized headache, which revealed serum sodium levels of 112 mEq/L. The patient's laboratory results and further workup revealed SIADH due to underlying COVID-19 infection. The patient received treatment with slow hypertonic saline 3% infusion, oral fluid restriction, and was monitored for 72 hours with serum sodium levels that fluctuated between 124-130 mEq/L.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient was admitted to the Emergency Department with low serum sodium and acute dizziness, which was investigated for coronary artery disease. The patient was discharged on betahistine, but three days later, the patient presented again with increasing severity of dizziness, nausea, fatigue, and generalized headache, which revealed low serum sodium levels and further workup that revealed SIADH due to underlying COVID-19 infection. The patient received treatment with slow hypertonic saline 3% infusion, oral fluid restriction, and was monitored for 72 hours, with serum sodium levels fluctuating between 124-130 mEq/L. The patient was transferred to a quarantine facility, and did not develop any respiratory symptoms or fever.

Discharge Summary:

Admitted: [Date of admission]
Discharged: [Date of discharge]

Patient Information:
Name: [Patient's Name]
Date of Birth: [Patient's DOB]
Sex: Female
Admission Diagnosis: Suspected dental infection

Brief Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with suspected dental infection. She had a medical history of tuberculosis, hypertension, high cholesterol, and neurogenic bladder. Her surgical history included hip joint surgery at the ages of 11, 27, and 68 years.

The patient had visited an otolaryngologist for otorrhea of the right ear four weeks earlier. She was diagnosed with otitis media and treated with antibiotics. On the same day, the patient underwent extraction of the right mandibular canine and lateral incisor by the patient's family dentist. Two weeks earlier, the patient had visited the primary care doctor for regular follow-up and complained of fatigue, fever, dysgeusia, swelling and numbness of the neck, and backache, which continued after the extraction. On laboratory examination, C-reactive protein (CRP) was 11.46 mg/dL, and the white blood cell count was 11,000/μL. Subsequently, chest X-ray and computed tomography (CT) showed no abnormal findings, and she tested negative for influenza virus.

On examination, the patient complained of fever and discomfort of the tongue with dysgeusia. Although usually both the maxilla and mandible cause dentures to wear, this does not occur when the teeth have been extracted. Salivary function was relatively good, and there was no xerostomia observed. No trismus was found; the teeth extraction sockets had healed well. None of the other residual teeth exhibited any prominent caries or periodontal disease. There were no abnormal findings in the orofacial region except for the dysgeusia and redness and numbness at the apex of the tongue. Orthopantomography revealed no abnormal findings, including maxillary sinuses and temporomandibular joints. On physical examination, the patient's temperature was 38.5°C, and blood pressure was 125/75 mmHg. The serum CRP concentration was 19.4 mg/dL, and the WBC count was 14,700/μL. Given the history of tooth extraction, the patient was immediately referred to the division of cardiology for suspected IE.

The cardiologist took blood cultures, which were negative for bacteria, and an ultrasound cardiogram and transesophageal echocardiography showed neither clear vegetations nor regurgitation. For the remittent fever of more than 38.0°C, the patient was admitted to the cardiology clinic three days after the first visit and underwent a complete examination. Serum examination showed the following: PR3-ANCA < 1 IU/mL, MPO-ANCA 124.0 IU/mL, cytomegalovirus complement fixation test 8, ferritin 471 ng/mL, and CH50 60.0 U/mL. Sputum cultures, acid-fast bacterial cultures, and fecal cultures were negative. CT imaging showed no abnormal findings causing fever, and deep vein thrombosis was not found on ultrasonography of the veins of the lower extremities. There were no active symptoms related to the right otitis media other than depression of the eardrum on otolaryngological examination.

Fourteen days after the first visit, the patient was transferred to the Department of Rheumatology and Clinical Immunology because of the high suspicion of AAV, although renal dysfunction and findings of interstitial pneumonia were not evident. Twenty-seven days after the first visit, a renal biopsy was planned, but it was postponed due to influenza A infection. After the renal biopsy, which showed the findings of necrotizing glomerulonephritis, the patient was finally diagnosed with MPA (fever, MPO-ANCA-positive, CRP elevation, proteinuria, and histopathological findings of renal biopsy) 40 days after the first visit. Steroid therapy was then started with 30 mg prednisolone/day without immunosuppressive agents, and four days later, the patient was discharged. The inflammatory symptoms improved well, and the dysgeusia and numbness at the apex of the tongue disappeared four weeks later. At 20-week follow-up, prednisolone was tapered to 10 mg/day, and she was MPO-ANCA-negative.

Discharge Diagnosis:
The patient was diagnosed with MPA (microscopic polyangiitis).

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with suspected dental infection. She was transferred to the Department of Rheumatology and Clinical Immunology due to the high suspicion of MPA based on clinical symptoms and laboratory tests. The patient's renal biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of necrotizing glomerulonephritis. She was treated with steroid therapy, and her inflammatory symptoms improved well.

Discharge Medications:
None

Follow-up Care:
The patient is scheduled for follow-up appointments with the rheumatology department to monitor her condition. She will continue to receive steroid therapy to manage her MPA.
